questions.q: According to the Preface, what did How to Read a Book do immediately after its first publication in 1940?
options: It became a best seller and stayed at the top of the national list for more than a year
It was widely criticized by educators as too difficult for ordinary readers
It was adopted as a required textbook in most American high schools
It sold slowly at first and became popular only after its translations
questions.explain: Adler says that, to his surprise and delight, the book at once became a best seller and stayed at the top of the nationwide list for over a year. Nothing in the Preface mentions criticism, school adoption, or slow early sales.

questions.q: In the Preface, what solution does the new edition propose to the fad of speed-reading?
options: Abandoning speed altogether in favour of slow, careful reading
Variable-speed reading, reading different things at appropriate speeds
Speed-reading training that begins in the first six grades
Reading only nonfiction quickly and fiction slowly
questions.explain: The Preface proposes variable-speed reading, with the aim of reading better, sometimes slower and sometimes faster. It does not reject speed altogether; it rejects reading everything at the greatest possible speed.

questions.q: According to the Preface, where is most educational money and effort on reading instruction spent?
options: In college composition and rhetoric courses
In remedial programs for adults who cannot read
In the first six grades of school
In high-school literature classes
questions.explain: Adler says most educational ingenuity, money and effort goes into reading instruction in the first six grades, with little formal training beyond that. This is the failure he says has not changed in thirty years.

questions.q: In the Preface, what does Adler call the basic and controlling change in the book's organization and content?
options: The new rules for reading imaginative literature
The pyramid of books to read
The expanded treatment of speed-reading
The distinction of four levels of reading in Part One
questions.explain: Adler names the introduction in Part One of four levels of reading (elementary, inspectional, analytical and syntopical) as the basic and controlling change. The other items are additions, but not the organizing change.

questions.q: According to the Preface, which part of the new edition most closely parallels the original 1940 book?
options: Part Two, on the rules of Analytical Reading
Part One, on the levels of reading
Part Three, on different kinds of reading matter
Part Four, on Syntopical Reading
questions.explain: Only Part Two, setting out the rules of Analytical Reading, closely parallels the original, and even it was largely recast. Part Three is the most extensive addition and Part Four is wholly new.

questions.q: According to the Preface, where did Adler and Van Doren gain many of the new insights that went into the rewriting?
options: In a survey of high-school reading scores
In discussion groups on great books and executive seminars they led together
In editing the Atlantic Monthly's education articles
In teaching speed-reading courses to adults
questions.explain: Adler says that over eight years he and Van Doren ran great-books discussion groups and moderated executive seminars in Chicago, San Francisco and Aspen, and gained many new insights there. Speed-reading courses are something the book criticizes, not a source of insight.

questions.q: True or false: According to the Preface, Pascal observed that when we read too fast or too slowly, we understand nothing.
questions.explain: Adler quotes Pascal, from three hundred years earlier, to support the point that reading must be done at appropriate speeds rather than always at top speed.

questions.q: True or false: According to the Preface, the discussion of Syntopical Reading in Part Four is a revised version of material in the original 1940 edition.
questions.explain: Adler says the discussion of Syntopical Reading in Part Four is wholly new. It was not in the original book at all.

questions.q: In the Preface, the new edition proposes ____ reading as the answer to the speed-reading fad: reading better, sometimes slower, sometimes faster.
questions.explain: The Preface names variable-speed reading as its solution, since different things should be read at different, appropriate speeds.

questions.q: In the Preface, Adler describes a ____ of books to read, broad at the bottom and tapering at the top.
questions.explain: The conception of a pyramid of books, broad at the bottom and tapering at the top, is listed among the new things the first edition did not treat.

questions.q: In the Preface, the four levels of reading are elementary, inspectional, analytical, and ____.
questions.explain: Part One introduces four levels of reading, the highest being syntopical, which Part Four treats as wholly new material.

questions.q: In the Preface, Adler names Charles Van Doren as his associate at the Institute for ____ Research.
questions.explain: Van Doren had for many years been Adler's associate at the Institute for Philosophical Research, and they had worked together on other books such as the Annals of America.

questions.q: Which of these does the Preface give as changes in society since 1940 that led to rewriting the book?
options: Many more high-school graduates now enter and complete college
A shift of interest from reading fiction to reading nonfiction
Many adults have been drawn to the promises of speed-reading courses
Reading instruction is now well carried beyond the elementary level
Radio and television have made the population less literate
questions.explain: Adler lists more college graduates, a shift to nonfiction, and the appeal of speed-reading courses. He says the failure to carry instruction beyond the elementary level has not changed, and that literacy grew in spite of or even because of radio and television.

questions.q: Which of these does the Preface list as new in the rewritten book, not treated adequately or at all in the 1940 version?
options: The discovery and formulation of new rules of reading
The conception of a pyramid of books to read
The flexible application of the basic rules to every variety of reading matter
A program for teaching children their first letters
A system for increasing reading speed to the greatest possible rate
questions.explain: New rules, the pyramid of books, and flexible application of the basic rules to all reading matter are all named as new. The Preface does not offer a program for beginners, and it rejects reading everything at maximum speed.

questions.q: Put these events from the Preface in chronological order, earliest first.
items: James Mursell writes The Failure of the Schools
How to Read a Book is first published
A parody titled How to Read Two Books appears
The Annals of America is published
Adler signs the Preface to the new edition
questions.explain: Mursell wrote in 1939, the book came out in early 1940, the parody appeared the following year, the Annals of America was published in 1969, and the Preface is dated March 26, 1972.

questions.q: In the order of the book's four Parts as the Preface describes them, put these topics first to last.
items: The four levels of reading
The rules of Analytical Reading
Approaches to different kinds of reading matter
Syntopical Reading
questions.explain: The Preface says Part One introduces the levels of reading, Part Two sets out the rules of Analytical Reading, Part Three covers different kinds of reading material, and Part Four treats Syntopical Reading.

questions.q: Match each figure named in the Preface to their role.
pairs: Said reading too fast or too slowly leaves us understanding nothing
Wrote on the schools' failure to teach reading beyond sixth grade
Wrote the serious treatise How to Read a Page
Persuaded the authors to make many important changes
Co-author and associate at the Institute for Philosophical Research
questions.explain: Each person appears in the Preface in exactly this role: Pascal on speed, Mursell on schools, Richards with a serious sequel, Rubin as the friend who urged changes, and Van Doren as co-author.

questions.q: Match each Part of the rewritten book to how the Preface describes its relation to the 1940 edition.
pairs: Introduces the levels of reading, the controlling change
Closely parallels the original but is largely recast
questions.explain: Adler uses comparison with the original Table of Contents to show how much was added: Part Two is the only close parallel, Part Three the largest addition, Part Four wholly new, and Part One's levels the organizing change.

questions.q: Sort these points from the Preface by whether Adler says they changed or stayed the same since 1940.

items.t: More young people complete college
Interest has shifted toward nonfiction
Speed-reading has become a national fad
The need to read different things at appropriate speeds
Reading instruction stops at the elementary level
High-school graduates struggle with closely argued writing

questions.explain: Adler lists social changes such as more college graduates, interest in nonfiction and speed-reading courses, then names constants: reading at appropriate speeds is still the goal, and instruction still stops at the elementary level, as Mursell described.

questions.q: Sort these Mursell claims, quoted in the Preface, by whether they describe what students can or cannot do.

items.t: Follow and enjoy a simple piece of fiction
Improve greatly with special tuition, even as adults
Indicate the central thought of a passage
See levels of emphasis and subordination in an argument
Handle a passage requiring critical consideration

questions.explain: Mursell says the average student can follow simple fiction and that older students and adults can improve enormously with special tuition. But such students are at a loss with close exposition, central thoughts, and the structure of arguments.

questions.q: Why, according to the Preface, did Adler think the book needed rewriting even though the original had sold so well?
questions.a: Society had changed: more people went to college, interest shifted to nonfiction, and speed-reading became a fad. Yet reading instruction still stopped at the elementary level, so the need for the book was even greater. The main motive, though, was new insight into reading: a fuller, better-ordered analysis of the art, new rules, flexible application to all kinds of reading matter, and the pyramid of books.

questions.q: What does the Preface say is wrong with simply reading everything as fast as possible, and what does it offer instead?
questions.a: Adler holds that to achieve all the purposes of reading, one must read different things at different, appropriate speeds, not everything at the greatest speed. He cites Pascal that reading too fast or too slowly leaves us understanding nothing. The book therefore proposes variable-speed reading, aiming to read better, sometimes slower and sometimes faster.

questions.q: Maya, a strong student who sailed through elementary school, finds college philosophy texts baffling and cannot pick out an author's main point. How would the Preface explain her difficulty?
questions.a: Adler, quoting Mursell, says reading is taught well only up to about the sixth grade, after which progress flattens out because little formal training carries students to higher levels of skill. The average graduate can enjoy simple fiction but is at a loss before a closely written argument and cannot find the central thought of a passage. Maya is not at her natural limit: with proper instruction she could improve a great deal.

questions.q: How does the Preface show that the problems behind the titles How to Read Two Books and How to Read a Page are taken up in the rewritten book?
questions.a: Adler mentions the parody and Richards's serious treatise to say both problems are fully treated in the new edition. In particular, it addresses how to read several related books in relation to one another, so that their complementary and conflicting views on a common subject are grasped. This is the syntopical reading of Part Four, which he says is wholly new.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what do Adler and Van Doren say happens when a packaged opinion from the media is accepted?
options: The reader plays it back when needed without having had to think
The reader is forced to weigh the data and statistics against each other
The reader becomes better informed and therefore understands more
The reader rejects it once television replaces print entirely
questions.explain: The authors compare a packaged opinion to a cassette inserted into a player and played back on cue, so the person performs acceptably without thinking. They deny that such packaging produces real understanding.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, how is knowledge related to understanding?
options: Understanding is impossible until one knows every fact about a subject
Knowledge is less of a prerequisite to understanding than commonly supposed
Knowledge and understanding are simply two names for the same thing
Understanding always comes first and makes knowledge unnecessary
questions.explain: The authors grant that knowledge is a prerequisite to understanding but say it is not as much of one as people assume, since too many facts can obstruct understanding as much as too few.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: In the baseball analogy of How to Read a Book, which element corresponds to the passive thing in reading and writing?
options: The catcher
The pitcher
The written material
The umpire
questions.explain: The ball is the only passive thing in the game, and the authors say the thing written and read is like the ball. The catcher stands for the reader, who is active.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Where, according to Adler and Van Doren, does the baseball analogy for reading break down?
options: Writers, unlike pitchers, are trying not to be caught
Readers, unlike catchers, receive the communication passively
Pitchers and catchers do not need to cooperate as writers and readers do
A ball is caught completely or not, while writing can be received in degrees
questions.explain: The ball is a simple unit, but a piece of writing is complex and can be received more or less completely. The authors explicitly deny that the writer is trying not to be caught.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what two things make one person read the same material better than another?
options: Reading it more actively and performing each act involved more skillfully
Reading it faster and remembering more of its facts
Having a better teacher and owning a better edition
Reading it more often and discussing it with more people
questions.explain: Given the same thing to read, one person reads it better first by reading more actively and second by performing each of the many separate acts more skillfully. The two are related.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: In Chapter 1 of How to Read a Book, the authors insist the reader work without outside help, but a footnote points ahead to an exception. Which later chapter discusses it?
options: Chapter 2, The Levels of Reading
Chapter 5, How to Be a Demanding Reader
Chapter 10, Criticizing a Book Fairly
Chapter 18, How to Read Philosophy
questions.explain: The footnote says one situation in which outside help with a difficult book is appropriate is discussed in Chapter 18, which the table of contents lists as How to Read Philosophy.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what follows if a book is completely intelligible to you from start to finish?
options: You have increased your understanding as much as possible
You have shown that the author is inferior to you
You may have gained information but not increased your understanding
You have read it at the highest level of active reading
questions.explain: If you understand everything perfectly, the author and you are like two minds in the same mold, so you may have gained information but your understanding could not have grown.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is the one way to do the job of reading that a challenging book requires?
options: Ask a better reader to explain the hard parts
Consult a commentary or textbook on the book
Decide that you already understand enough of it
Work on the book with only the power of your own mind
questions.explain: Taking the book to someone else or settling for partial understanding both fail to do the job. The book must be worked on without external help, by the reader's own mind.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Which of these is one of the two conditions for reading for understanding named in How to Read a Book?
options: An initial inequality in understanding between writer and reader
A teacher who is present to answer the reader's questions
A book that the reader can understand completely at once
A reader who already shares the writer's opinions
questions.explain: The first condition is initial inequality: the writer must be superior in understanding. The second is that the reader can overcome that inequality in some degree.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say their book will not be much concerned with reading for entertainment?
options: Because entertainment is harmful to serious readers
Because it is least demanding and there are no rules for it
Because good books can never be read for entertainment
Because entertainment reading always becomes reading for information
questions.explain: Reading for entertainment requires the least effort and has no rules; anyone who can read can do it. The authors do not urge readers never to read a good book for entertainment.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what distinguishes being enlightened from being informed?
options: Being enlightened means having read many more books
Being enlightened means remembering the author's exact words
Being enlightened adds knowing why something is so and how it connects to other facts
Being enlightened requires no prior information at all
questions.explain: To be informed is to know that something is the case; to be enlightened is to know also why it is the case, its connections and its similarities and differences. Being informed is a prerequisite, not something enlightenment skips.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is the primary difference between learning by instruction and learning by discovery?
options: Instruction is passive while discovery is active
Instruction needs thinking while discovery needs only observation
Instruction is faster while discovery is more reliable
They differ in the materials the learner works on: discourse versus nature
questions.explain: The difference is primarily in the materials: the instructed learner works on discourse, written or oral, while the unaided discoverer works on nature or the world. The authors reject the idea that instruction is passive.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren place primary emphasis on reading rather than listening?
options: Because reading is learning from an absent teacher who cannot answer questions
Because listening and reading require entirely different arts
Because lectures never contain anything worth learning
Because listening is more difficult than reading
questions.explain: Listening is learning from a present, living teacher, while reading is learning from an absent one. Reading and listening otherwise share the art of being taught.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: How does Chapter 1 of How to Read a Book, "The Activity and Art of Reading," relate to Chapter 2, "The Levels of Reading"?
options: Chapter 2 abandons the idea of active reading introduced in Chapter 1
Chapter 1 lays down that reading is an activity aimed at understanding, and Chapter 2 sets out the levels at which that activity is done
Chapter 1 gives detailed rules for skimming that Chapter 2 then summarizes
Chapter 2 deals only with reading for entertainment
questions.explain: Chapter 1 establishes what reading is and that the book aims at reading for understanding; the next chapter in the table of contents turns to the levels of reading, which later chapters treat one by one.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that radio and television have greatly enhanced our understanding of the world.
questions.explain: They grant that these media serve some functions well, but say it may be seriously questioned whether modern media have much enhanced our understanding.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: True or false: According to How to Read a Book, completely passive reading is impossible.
questions.explain: Since all reading is an activity, the authors say we cannot read with our eyes immobilized and our minds asleep; reading can only be more or less active.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: True or false: The title of Chapter 1 of How to Read a Book, "The Activity and Art of Reading," signals that reading is presented as a passive gift rather than a skill.
questions.explain: The title pairs activity and art: the chapter argues that reading is always an activity and that the art of reading is a skill that can be learned and improved.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that if you learn to read for understanding, reading for information will usually take care of itself.
questions.explain: Their book is about reading for increased understanding, and they add that once you learn that, reading for information usually follows.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: According to How to Read a Book, every book that can be read for entertainment can also be read for understanding.
questions.explain: The authors say the proposition cannot be reversed: a book that can be read for understanding can probably be read for entertainment, but not every entertaining book can be read for understanding.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say thinking takes place both in learning by instruction and in learning by discovery.
questions.explain: If these two ways exhaust how we gain knowledge, thinking must occur in both, though the kinds of thinking differ.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren compare accepting a media-packaged opinion to inserting a ____ into a player and playing it back.
questions.explain: The packaged opinion is inserted like a cassette and played back whenever it seems appropriate, without any thinking.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the reader is said to be much more like the ____ in a game of baseball than like someone receiving a blow.
questions.explain: Catching the ball is as much an activity as pitching or hitting it, so the reader, like the catcher, is active.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that passing from understanding less to understanding more by your own effort is like pulling yourself up by your ____.
questions.explain: The image conveys that lifting one's own understanding is a major exertion done without outside help.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, we can learn only from our ____, those superior to us in understanding.
questions.explain: Reading for understanding requires initial inequality: the writer must be superior to the reader in understanding.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren prefer to call instruction "____ discovery."
questions.explain: Since all learning goes on in the learner, instruction is better described as discovery with the help of a teacher, as opposed to unaided discovery.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Alexander Pope, quoted in How to Read a Book, calls those who have read many books badly bookful ____.
questions.explain: These are the literate ignoramuses who have read widely but not well, showing the doctoral ignorance that comes after knowledge.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, listening is described as learning from a teacher who is present, a ____ teacher, while reading is learning from one who is absent.
questions.explain: A living teacher can answer your questions; an absent one, the author of a book, cannot, which is why reading gets primary emphasis.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, a book you question answers you only to the extent that you do the work of thinking yourself; in this respect a book is like ____ or the world.
questions.explain: Unlike a living teacher, a book cannot answer your questions; you must answer them yourself, just as when you question nature.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Which of these does the opening of How to Read a Book credit radio or television with doing well?
options: Visually communicating news events with great impact
Giving information while we do other things, such as driving
Greatly increasing our understanding of the world
Making it unnecessary to read books at all
questions.explain: The authors admit television conveys news with enormous impact and radio informs us while driving, but they question whether these media have much enhanced understanding.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Which of these are true of the writer and reader in the baseball analogy of How to Read a Book?
options: Both are active, though their activities differ
They succeed only to the extent that they cooperate
The reader's role is passive, like the ball's
The writer is trying hard not to be caught
questions.explain: Pitcher and catcher are both active and succeed only by cooperating. The ball, not the reader, is passive, and the writer is not trying to avoid being caught.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Which of these goals of reading do Adler and Van Doren name?
options: Information
Understanding
Entertainment
Memorization of style
Social prestige
questions.explain: The authors name gaining information and gaining understanding, and also mention entertainment as a further goal that the book will not be much concerned with.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Which of these responses to a book you do not fully understand do Adler and Van Doren say fail to do the job of reading the book requires?
options: Having a better reader explain the troublesome parts
Deciding that what is over your head is not worth bothering about
Working on the symbols with your own mind until you understand more
Reading so that you lift yourself from understanding less to more
questions.explain: Taking the book to someone else and settling for what you already understand both avoid the work. Only working on the book unaided, raising your own understanding, does the job.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Which of these arts does How to Read a Book group with teaching as sharing a special characteristic?
options: Agriculture
Medicine
Architecture
Rhetoric
Law
questions.explain: Teaching shares with agriculture and medicine the feature that the practitioner helps, but the growth must happen in the patient, plant, or student.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Which of these skills of unaided discovery does How to Read a Book say the art of reading also includes?
options: Keenness of observation
Range of imagination
An intellect trained in analysis and reflection
Skill with laboratory instruments
questions.explain: Because reading is discovery with help, it uses the same skills as unaided discovery: observation, memory, imagination and a trained intellect. Laboratory skill is not mentioned.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Put in order the steps of the art of reading as defined in How to Read a Book, from start to finish.
items: The mind has only the symbols on the page
It operates on them with no outside help
It elevates itself by its own operations
It passes from understanding less to understanding more
questions.explain: The definition starts from a mind with nothing but the symbols and no outside help, which elevates itself by its own operations until it understands more.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Put the parts of the baseball analogy in How to Read a Book in the order the ball travels.
items: The pitcher initiates the motion of the ball
The ball travels as the passive object
The catcher terminates the motion
questions.explain: The pitcher, like the writer, starts the motion; the ball, like the written thing, is passive; the catcher, like the reader, ends it.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Put Montaigne's two ignorances and knowledge, as quoted in How to Read a Book, in the order he gives them.
items: Abecedarian ignorance
Knowledge
Doctoral ignorance
questions.explain: Montaigne speaks of an abecedarian ignorance that precedes knowledge and a doctoral ignorance that comes after it, the ignorance of those who have misread many books.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Put these sections of Chapter 1 of How to Read a Book in the order they appear.
items: Active Reading
The Goals of Reading
Reading as Learning
Present and Absent Teachers
questions.explain: The chapter moves from reading as an activity, to its goals, to reading as a kind of learning, and ends with why books, as absent teachers, demand skill.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: In the baseball analogy of How to Read a Book, match each part of the game to what it stands for.
questions.explain: The writer initiates and the reader terminates the communication, the written work is the passive object, and a wild writer is harder to catch.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Match each art to the one who must do the growing, according to How to Read a Book.
questions.explain: In each of these arts the practitioner helps, but the growth must take place in the one being helped.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Match each way of learning in How to Read a Book to the material the learner works on.
questions.explain: Aided discovery works on communication, unaided discovery on nature; listening and reading are both being taught, by present and absent teachers.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Match each goal of reading to how How to Read a Book describes it.
pairs: Adds facts already as intelligible as those you know
Requires reading something initially above you
questions.explain: Information adds to your store without raising understanding; understanding needs a book better than the reader; entertainment needs the least effort.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Sort these into what the baseball analogy of How to Read a Book treats as active or passive.

items.t: The pitcher
The catcher
The reader
The ball
The thing written and read
The writer

questions.explain: Players and their counterparts, writer and reader, are all active; only the ball and the written work are passive.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Sort these reading experiences by whether How to Read a Book would call them reading for information or reading for understanding.

items.t: Reading a newspaper that is at once fully intelligible
Learning more American history facts in the same light
Reading a history that throws new light on all the facts you know
Struggling with a book that at first puzzles you
Reading a magazine you follow with ease

questions.explain: Material equal to your understanding only adds information; material initially above you, which you work to grasp, raises understanding.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Sort these by whether How to Read a Book links them to being informed or being enlightened.

items.t: Knowing that something is the case
Remembering what an author says
Knowing why it is the case
Knowing what the author means and why he says it

questions.explain: Information exercises only memory; enlightenment adds explanation, meaning and connections.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Sort these by whether How to Read a Book places them under learning by instruction or unaided discovery.

items.t: Listening to a lecture
Reading a book
Research and investigation
Reflecting on nature or the world
Learning from discourse

questions.explain: Instruction is learning from discourse by reading or listening; unaided discovery works on nature by research, investigation or reflection.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren think modern media may hinder rather than help understanding?
questions.a: They say we may know more, but too many facts can obstruct understanding as much as too few. The media package positions so effectively, with rhetoric and selected statistics, that the audience does not really make up its own mind but inserts a packaged opinion and plays it back. Thinking only appears unnecessary.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Explain the baseball analogy Adler and Van Doren use to show that reading is active.
questions.a: The writer is like the pitcher who starts the ball's motion, and the reader like the catcher who stops it; both are active, and only the ball, like the written work, is passive. The art of reading is the skill of catching every kind of communication, and success depends on writer and reader cooperating.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: A student reads the same essay as a classmate but gets far less from it. How would Adler and Van Doren explain the difference?
questions.a: Reading is a complex activity made of many separate acts. One person reads better than another first by reading more actively and putting in more effort, and second by performing each of those acts more skillfully. Since writing can be received more or less completely, the amount caught depends on activity and skill.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren mean by the art of reading, and why is it like pulling yourself up by your bootstraps?
questions.a: It is the process by which a mind, with nothing but the symbols on the page and no outside help, elevates itself by its own operations from understanding less to understanding more. It feels like pulling yourself up by your bootstraps because it is a major exertion requiring more varied activity and skill than ordinary reading.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Someone reads ten easy articles a week and says this has deepened their understanding. Using How to Read a Book, why might that be doubtful?
questions.a: If each article was at once thoroughly intelligible, the reader's understanding was already equal to it, so the reading added information but could not improve understanding. Reading for understanding requires material initially above the reader, felt as puzzlement, which the reader works to overcome.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren reject the idea that discovery is active learning and instruction passive?
questions.a: In both cases the learning goes on in the learner; there is no inactive learning, just as there is no inactive reading. That is why they call instruction aided discovery. Like a doctor or farmer, a teacher can help, but the student must do the growing.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: What is the difference between being widely read and being well read, according to Adler and Van Doren?
questions.a: Being widely read may only make one informed, exercising memory; it can produce the doctoral ignorance Montaigne describes, the bookful blockheads or sophomores who have read too widely and not well. Being well read means being enlightened: knowing not only what an author says but what he means and why he says it.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Why does How to Read a Book open with a chapter on the activity and art of reading before setting out any rules?
questions.a: The chapter first establishes that reading is an activity that can be more or less active, and that the book aims at reading for understanding rather than information or entertainment. It also shows why skill matters: books are absent teachers that cannot answer questions. With this foundation set, the following chapters, starting with the levels of reading, can give the rules of the art.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, must people who have left school know how to make books teach them well?
questions.a: A living teacher can answer your questions and give you a lift toward understanding, but a book cannot; you must answer its questions yourself. Since continuing education outside school depends mainly on books read without a teacher, anyone who wants to keep learning must know how to make books teach well, which is the book's primary goal.
questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren call the stages of reading "levels" rather than "kinds"?
options: Because higher levels include the lower ones, so the levels are cumulative
Because each level suits a different kind of book, such as novels or histories
Because readers must finish one level in school before moving to the next
Because the levels differ only in reading speed, not in the reader's skill
questions.explain: Kinds are distinct from one another, but higher levels include lower ones; the fourth level includes all the others and goes beyond them. The levels are not tied to book types or schooling stages.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what question is asked of the reader at the level of elementary reading?
options: What is the book about?
What does the sentence say?
What are the parts of the book?
Is the book true, in whole or in part?
questions.explain: At the elementary level the question is “What does the sentence say?” taken in its simplest sense. "What is the book about?" belongs to inspectional reading.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what mistake do many otherwise good readers make that inspectional reading would prevent?
options: They skim randomly and never read a book through to the end
They read too many books at once and never compare them
They start at page one and plow through without first surveying the book
They chew and digest books that only needed to be tasted
questions.explain: Many readers ignore even the table of contents and plow steadily from page one, so they must gain a superficial knowledge of the book while also trying to understand it, which compounds the difficulty.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what does syntopical reading achieve beyond simply comparing several texts?
options: It lets the reader finish many books in a short, set time
It identifies which of the books is the most accurate on the subject
It lets the reader summarize each book's structure in a few sentences
It lets the reader build an analysis of the subject that may be in none of the books
questions.explain: Mere comparison is not enough; with the help of the books read, the syntopical reader constructs an analysis of the subject that may not be in any of them.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is analytical reading preeminently for?
options: Gaining information quickly
Understanding
Entertainment
Building reading speed
questions.explain: Analytical reading is hardly ever necessary if the goal is information or entertainment; it is preeminently for the sake of understanding.

questions.q: True or false: According to Adler and Van Doren, inspectional reading is the best and most complete reading possible given unlimited time.
questions.explain: That describes analytical reading. Inspectional reading is the best and most complete reading possible given a limited time.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that even capable readers meet the problems of elementary reading again when reading a foreign language they do not know well.
questions.explain: With a poorly known foreign language our first effort must be to identify the actual words before we can try to understand them, so the elementary level's problems return.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren describe inspectional reading as the art of skimming ____, not casual or random browsing.
questions.explain: Inspectional reading is skimming done systematically, to learn everything the surface of the book can teach, not aimless browsing.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say another name for syntopical reading might be ____ reading.
questions.explain: Because the reader reads many books and places them in relation to one another and to a common subject, it might also be called comparative reading.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren note that most speed reading courses concentrate on the level of ____ reading, because overcoming its mostly mechanical difficulties lets us read faster.
questions.explain: The difficulties at the elementary level are mostly mechanical, and overcoming them usually lets us read faster, so speed reading courses focus there.

questions.q: Which of these questions do Adler and Van Doren say a reader should be able to answer after an inspectional reading of a book?
options: What is the book about?
What kind of book is it?
What are its parts?
What does each sentence say?
Is the author's argument sound?
questions.explain: Inspectional reading asks surface questions: what the book is about, its structure or parts, and what kind of book it is. Judging the argument goes beyond the surface.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say about syntopical reading?
options: It is the most complex and systematic type of reading
It makes heavy demands even when the books are easy
It is probably the most rewarding of all reading activities
Its rules are widely known and easily learned
questions.explain: Syntopical reading is the most complex and demanding level, even with easy materials, and probably the most rewarding; but its rules are not widely known and it is not an easy art.

questions.q: Put the four levels of reading in order from lowest to highest, as Adler and Van Doren present them.
items: Elementary reading
Inspectional reading
Analytical reading
Syntopical reading
questions.explain: The levels run from elementary to inspectional to analytical to syntopical; each higher level includes the lower ones.

questions.q: Match each level of reading to the feature Adler and Van Doren give it.
pairs: Recognizing the individual words on the page
Chewing and digesting a book until it becomes your own
Placing many books in relation to a common subject
questions.explain: Elementary reading is about word recognition, inspectional reading about getting the most out of a book in limited time, analytical reading about thorough active work on one book, and syntopical reading about many books on one subject.

questions.q: Sort these activities into the level of reading Adler and Van Doren would assign them.

items.t: Spending fifteen minutes to learn what a book is about
Checking whether a book is a novel, a history or a treatise
Surveying a book's parts from its surface
Asking many organized questions of a book with no time limit
Working at a book until it becomes your own
Reading a hard book to move from understanding less to more

questions.explain: Inspectional reading gets what the surface can teach in limited time; analytical reading is thorough, active work on a book given unlimited time, aimed at understanding.

questions.q: Sort each scenario by the level of reading Adler and Van Doren would say it calls for.

items.t: A tourist working out the words on a menu in a half-known language
A first grader making out the sentence about the cat and the hat
A student building her own account of justice from five books on it
A researcher relating several histories of one war to each other

questions.explain: Recognizing what words and sentences say is elementary reading; relating many books to a common subject and constructing an analysis of it is syntopical reading.

questions.q: Explain how Adler and Van Doren distinguish inspectional reading from analytical reading.
questions.a: Inspectional reading emphasizes time: it is systematic skimming that gets the most out of a book within a limited time by examining its surface, answering what the book is about and what kind of book it is. Analytical reading is thorough, complete reading, the best reading possible given unlimited time. It is intensely active, asks many organized questions, and is mainly for the sake of understanding.

questions.q: Explain how Chapter 2, The Levels of Reading, sets up the structure of the rest of How to Read a Book.
questions.a: Chapter 2 introduces the four cumulative levels, and the authors say these distinctions must be understood before reading skills can improve. Each level then gets its own treatment: elementary reading in Chapter 3, inspectional reading in Chapter 4, analytical reading in Part Two, and syntopical reading in Part Four (Chapter 20).

questions.q: How does Chapter 2 of How to Read a Book build on the distinctions made in Chapter 1, and why do the authors say its points matter more?
questions.a: Chapter 2 recalls Chapter 1's distinctions: the reader's goal of entertainment, information or understanding; effort and skill; and reading as learning from an absent teacher, like unaided discovery. The authors call those distinctions relatively insignificant compared with the levels of reading, because the differences between the levels must be understood before any effective improvement in reading can occur.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Which of these are the three historical trends Adler and Van Doren say converged to produce the modern ferment about reading?
options: The American effort to educate, and so make literate, all citizens
Changes in the methods of teaching reading itself
The American tradition of criticizing the schools
The invention of television and its competition with books
A decline in the number of books published
questions.explain: The authors name universal education, the shifting methods of reading instruction, and the long American habit of attacking the schools. Television and publishing trends are not among the trends named in this chapter.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren call the approach that teaches visual recognition of whole words before letter-names or letter-sounds, advocated by Horace Mann, the ____ method.
questions.explain: This analytical approach, from Germany, taught whole words (and later whole sentences) first and was known as the sight method. It contrasts with the synthetic ABC and phonic methods that start from letters or sounds.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Sort these methods of teaching reading described in Chapter 3 by whether they are synthetic (start from letters or sounds) or analytical (start from whole words or sentences).

items.t: ABC method
Phonic method
Sight method
Whole sentences taught first, then words and letters

questions.explain: The ABC and phonic methods build words up from letter-names or sounds, so they are synthetic. The sight method and its extension to whole sentences are described as analytical rather than synthetic.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to Chapter 3, the problem facing American reading instruction is that teaching every child to read, however unmotivated or deprived, is far harder than teaching a small group of motivated children of literate parents.
questions.explain: The authors sum up the problems of universal education this way: teaching a small, highly motivated group a century ago was a far cry from teaching every child to read.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: According to Chapter 3, why has the problem of poor reading taken on new urgency in recent decades?
questions.a: The effort to educate all citizens has entered a new phase, with ever-growing high school and college populations. A young person who reads poorly but is not in school faces largely a personal problem, but one who stays in school or goes to college becomes a concern for teachers and fellow students as well. This has spurred active research and many new approaches to reading instruction.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Put these emphases in American reading instruction in the order Chapter 3 describes them, earliest first.
items: ABC method dominant through most of the nineteenth century
Sight method advocated by Horace Mann after about 1840
Almost exclusive emphasis on rapid silent reading, about 1920 to 1925
Pendulum swings back toward phonics
questions.explain: The ABC method dominated the nineteenth century, the sight method was advocated after about 1840, silent reading was emphasized around 1920 to 1925, and more recently instruction swung back toward phonics.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: In Chapter 3, the first stage in learning to read, which begins at birth and normally lasts until about age six or seven, is called reading ____.
questions.explain: The authors call the first stage reading readiness, which includes physical, intellectual, language and personal preparation for reading.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Match each kind of reading readiness in Chapter 3 to what it involves.
pairs: Enough visual perception to take in and remember a whole word and its letters
Speaking clearly and using several sentences in correct order
Working with other children, sustaining attention, following directions
questions.explain: Chapter 3 divides reading readiness into these four kinds of preparation, each tied to a different capacity of the child.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: According to Chapter 3, what is the risk of starting reading instruction before a child has reached reading readiness?
options: The child will learn faster but understand less of what he reads
The child is frustrated and may carry a dislike of reading into adult life
The child will skip the second stage and never master sight words
The child will read aloud well but never learn to read silently
questions.explain: The authors warn that jumping the gun is usually self-defeating: the unready child is frustrated and may keep that dislike into later school and adult life. Delaying instruction, by contrast, is not nearly so serious.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: In Chapter 3, what do Adler and Van Doren call possibly the most astounding intellectual feat any human performs?
options: Comparing the views of different writers on the same subject
Building a vocabulary of several hundred sight words in one year
The discovery of meaning in written symbols, usually before age seven
Reading a book independently without the help of a living teacher
questions.explain: During the second stage a child moves, sometimes within weeks, from seeing meaningless symbols to finding meaning in them, and the authors call this discovery of meaning possibly the most astounding intellectual feat. No one really knows how it happens.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Put the four stages of learning to read described in Chapter 3 in order, first to last.
items: Reading readiness
Reading very simple materials and mastering sight words
Rapid vocabulary growth and use of context clues
Refining skills and comparing different writers' views
questions.explain: Readiness comes first, then word mastery with simple books, then vocabulary building and context clues, and finally the mature stage of refining skills and assimilating reading experiences.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Sort these achievements by which stage of learning to read Chapter 3 places them in: the third stage or the fourth stage.

items.t: Unlocking unfamiliar words through context clues
Reading for different purposes and subject areas
Reading on one's own for fun or curiosity
Carrying concepts over from one piece of writing to another
Comparing different writers' views on the same subject

questions.explain: The third stage is about vocabulary, context clues and reading for varied purposes on one's own. The fourth stage is the refinement in which the reader assimilates reading experiences and compares writers.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: According to Chapter 3, which often-overlooked cause helps explain why many young people never reach the mature stage of elementary reading?
options: Too much time spent on silent reading at the expense of phonics
A lack of trained teachers in kindergarten and first grade
The schools' refusal to adopt the Initial Teaching Alphabet
The heavy emphasis on readiness and rudiments, which has slighted the higher levels
questions.explain: Besides deprivation and personal problems, the authors point to a cause not often noted: the stress on readiness and on teaching the rudiments has led the higher levels of reading to be slighted.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A parent worries because her five-year-old cannot yet follow directions or sit still for a story, while a neighbor's child already reads. Applying Chapter 3, what would the authors advise?
options: Wait until the child shows reading readiness, since delay is far less harmful than starting too early
Begin intensive phonics drills now so the child does not fall behind his peers
Switch to the sight method, which works for children who lack readiness
Have the child read aloud daily, since oral reading builds personal readiness
questions.explain: Following directions and sustaining attention belong to personal readiness, and the authors say that pushing an unready child is self-defeating while delaying instruction is not nearly so serious, whatever parents fear about keeping up.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 3, the four stages of learning to read are all stages within the first level of reading, elementary reading.
questions.explain: The authors stress that it is of paramount importance to see that all four stages belong to elementary reading, the first of the four levels described in the previous chapter.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Match each stage of elementary reading in Chapter 3 to the schooling it roughly corresponds to.
pairs: Vocabulary growth and use of context
About the end of fourth grade
Leaving elementary school or junior high
questions.explain: The authors map the stages onto the elementary curriculum, from pre-school readiness to the final stage reached around the end of elementary or junior high school.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Chapter 3 says the third stage of elementary reading produces fourth grade, or ____, literacy, such as reading traffic signs and filling out simple government forms.
questions.explain: Fourth grade literacy is also called functional literacy, defined as the ability to read traffic signs or picture captions and fill out simpler forms.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: In Chapter 3, in what sense is a child who has completed the four stages of elementary reading not yet a mature reader?
options: He has mastered only the first level and cannot read beyond it
He still needs a teacher to explain the meaning of most words
He cannot yet read almost anything placed in front of him
He has not yet discovered meaning in written symbols
questions.explain: Such a child can read almost anything in an unsophisticated way and is ready for high school, but in the book's sense he has only mastered the first level and does not know how to read beyond it.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say they must assume their reader has ninth grade literacy?
questions.a: No one can learn from a how-to-do-it book until he can read it, and a book that teaches reading must have readers who can already read in some sense. So the authors assume the reader has passed through all four stages of elementary reading and mastered the first level. Their book takes over where elementary reading leaves off.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: How does the distinction between aided and unaided discovery apply to elementary reading in Chapter 3?
questions.a: The four stages of elementary reading are typically reached with the help of living teachers, who answer questions and smooth over difficulties. Only after mastering all four stages can a child read independently and learn on his own. That independence is what makes the higher levels, and becoming a really good reader, possible.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
questions.q: According to Chapter 3, what is the main limitation of remedial reading courses in high schools and colleges?
options: They teach syntopical reading before students have mastered analytical reading
They only bring students up to the level they should have reached in elementary school
They are offered to too few students to make any difference
They focus on speed and neglect reading aloud
questions.explain: Remedial instruction, including most speed and effective reading courses, is designed to make up for failures of the lower schools. It is not instruction in the higher levels of reading.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
questions.q: Put these levels of reading competence in the order Chapter 3 says schooling ought to produce them, from earliest to latest.
items: Elementary reading, by the end of elementary school
Competent analytical reading, from a good liberal arts high school
Competent syntopical reading, from a good college
questions.explain: The authors say elementary reading should be mastered in elementary school, a good high school ought to produce analytical readers, and a good college ought to produce syntopical readers.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say a college degree ought to mean a graduate can undertake independent research on almost any subject, which is what ____ reading enables.
questions.explain: They note that independent research on almost any subject is what syntopical reading, among other things, enables you to do, so a good college ought to produce syntopical readers.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
questions.q: True or false: Chapter 3 says the program for teaching the higher levels of reading is arcane and genuinely new, which is why colleges have not adopted it.
questions.explain: The authors say the opposite: there is nothing arcane or even really new about their program, which is largely common sense, and courses based on it could be instituted in many high schools and colleges.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say that something is very wrong with American education's handling of reading?
questions.a: Students often need three or four years of graduate study, on top of twelve years of preparatory school and four of college, before they reach competence in syntopical reading, and sometimes not even then. Twenty years of schooling is far too long to learn to read. The authors argue this can be corrected with high school and college courses based on their program.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
questions.q: A student finishes a college course in speed reading that raises her reading rate but never teaches her to analyze or compare books. Applying Chapter 3, how would the authors judge the course?
options: As instruction in syntopical reading, since it covers many books
As a complete education in reading for a college graduate
As instruction in analytical reading, since it improves efficiency
As largely remedial work that does not take her beyond the first level
questions.explain: The authors say such speed or effective reading courses are, on the whole, remedial: they make up for failures of the lower schools and are not designed to take students beyond elementary reading.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Reading and the Democratic Ideal of Education
questions.q: Which of these positions do Adler and Van Doren take in the section on reading and the democratic ideal of education in Chapter 3?
options: The first task must be to teach new students to read at the elementary level
Educational opportunity limited only by individual desire, ability, and need is society's most valuable service
Becoming a nation of functional literates is not enough
Higher education should be restricted to those who already read well
Elementary reading instruction should be cut back in favor of higher levels
questions.explain: The authors accept that the first task is elementary reading, endorse unlimited educational opportunity, and insist the nation must become truly competent readers, not just functional literates. They never propose restricting access or abandoning elementary instruction.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Reading and the Democratic Ideal of Education
questions.q: What is the conclusion of Chapter 3 about the task facing American education even once everyone can read at the elementary level?
questions.a: Teaching all students to read at the elementary level is the first task, and the authors support unlimited educational opportunity. But even accomplishing that would not accomplish the whole task. The nation must be more than functional literates and become a nation of truly competent readers to meet the needs of the coming world.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Which of these describe how Chapter 3 fits into the structure of How to Read a Book?
options: It takes up the first of the four levels of reading introduced in Chapter 2
It is followed by Chapter 4 on the second level, inspectional reading
It explains elementary reading so the book can assume the reader has already mastered it
It gives the rules for outlining a book's structure
It comes after the chapters on syntopical reading
questions.explain: Chapter 3 treats elementary reading, the first level from Chapter 2, so the authors can assume their readers have mastered it before Chapter 4 turns to inspectional reading. Outlining belongs to Chapter 7, and syntopical reading comes much later.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Chapter 3 is the first of a run of chapters titled by level; its title names the first level of reading, elementary reading, and Chapter 4's title names the second level, ____ reading.
questions.explain: The table of contents shows Chapter 3 on elementary reading followed by Chapter 4, The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading, so the chapters move up the levels in order.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 3 in the order they appear.
items: Stages of Learning to Read
Stages and Levels
Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
Reading and the Democratic Ideal of Education
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the stages of learning to read, to how those stages relate to the levels, to the failure of schools to teach higher levels, and ends on the democratic ideal of education.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what does it mean that the levels of reading are cumulative, as applied to inspectional reading?
options: Inspectional reading contains elementary reading and is itself contained in analytical reading
Inspectional reading replaces elementary reading once a reader has mastered it fully
Inspectional reading is a shortcut that lets a reader skip analytical reading entirely
Inspectional reading must be learned only after analytical and syntopical reading
questions.explain: Each higher level includes the ones below it, so elementary reading is inside inspectional reading, which is inside analytical reading. Nothing is replaced or skipped.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, you cannot read on the inspectional level unless you can already read effectively on the ____ level.
questions.explain: Because the levels are cumulative, inspectional reading presupposes elementary reading: reading steadily without constantly stopping over words, grammar and syntax.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say the experienced reader learns to perform the two steps of inspectional reading simultaneously, though beginners should treat them as separate.
questions.explain: The two types are aspects of a single skill; beginners are advised to treat them as distinct steps, while experienced readers do both at once.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: What must a reader already be able to do, according to Adler and Van Doren, before attempting inspectional reading, and why?
questions.a: Because the levels of reading are cumulative, inspectional reading contains elementary reading. The reader must be able to read the text more or less steadily, without stopping to look up many words or stumbling over grammar and syntax, and make sense of most sentences and paragraphs, though not necessarily the best sense of all of them.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what two assumptions define the situation in which systematic skimming is called for?
options: You know the book well and want to review its main arguments before an exam
You must memorize the book's facts and have unlimited time to read it closely
You want to criticize the book and need to find its weakest arguments quickly
You do not know if the book deserves careful reading, and you have limited time
questions.explain: The authors assume the reader is unsure whether the book deserves an analytical reading and has only limited time to find out. Reviewing, memorizing or criticizing are not the situation described.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is the main aim of skimming or pre-reading a book?
options: To memorize the key terms before reading the book analytically
To discover whether the book requires a more careful reading
To finish the book as fast as possible and move to the next one
To judge whether the author's conclusions are true or false
questions.explain: Skimming's main aim is to find out whether the book deserves more careful reading; it also tells you other things about the book, such as its main contention and kind.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren call skimming a ____ process that helps separate the chaff from the real kernels of nourishment.
questions.explain: They compare giving a book a quick once-over to threshing, which separates chaff from kernels.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: Put the first four steps of systematic skimming in the order Adler and Van Doren give them.
items: Look at the title page and preface
Study the table of contents
Check the index
Read the publisher's blurb
questions.explain: The authors list title page and preface first, then the table of contents, then the index, then the blurb; after these four you may already know whether to read on.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Put the approach to a Shakespeare play that Adler and Van Doren recommend for students in order.
items: Read the play at one sitting
Discuss what you got out of that first quick reading
Study the play carefully and closely
questions.explain: A first quick reading gives enough understanding of the whole to learn more; close study with glossaries and footnotes comes only afterward.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: Match each skimming step in How to Read a Book to what it mainly gives the reader.
pairs: The subject, scope and the author's special angle
A general sense of the book's structure, like a road map
The range of topics covered and the crucial terms
Often the author's own summary of the main points
questions.explain: Each step yields something different: subject and angle from the title page, structure from the contents, topics and terms from the index, and often an author-written summary from the blurb.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how should a skimmer use a book's table of contents?
options: As a list to consult only when looking up a particular topic later
As a marketing device that publishers write to mislead readers
As a road map that gives a general sense of the book's structure
As a replacement for reading the preface and the final pages
questions.explain: The authors say to study the table of contents as you would a road map before a trip. They regret that many people glance at it only to look something up.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, have full analytical tables of contents become less common?
options: Printers found them too expensive to set in type for long books
Readers read them less, and publishers think mysterious titles are more seductive
Authors decided that summaries in advance spoil the pleasure of novels
Scholars objected that summaries distorted the arguments of the chapters
questions.explain: They suggest two reasons: people read tables of contents less than they did, and publishers feel a less revealing contents page attracts readers.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: Match each author in How to Read a Book to the example given about tables of contents.
pairs: Wrote headings he called Arguments for each book of Paradise Lost
Gave each chapter of Decline and Fall an extensive analytical table of contents
Tried to make the table of contents of their own book full and informative
questions.explain: Milton and Gibbon are the authors' examples of the older practice of full tables of contents; they say they made their own as full and informative as they could.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why should a skimmer look up some of the passages cited under crucial-seeming terms in the index?
options: Because those passages may contain the crux or the key to the author's approach
Because the index always lists the author's conclusion on its first page
Because reading the index can replace reading the table of contents
Because the number of index pages shows how difficult the book will be
questions.explain: The passages may hold the crux, the point on which the book hinges, or the new departure that is the key to the author's approach and attitude.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say the publisher's blurb is nothing but sheer puffery and should be skipped when skimming.
questions.explain: They say this impression is quite often not true, since authors frequently write blurbs summarizing their main points; even an empty blurb tells you something about the book.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: In skimming, Adler and Van Doren say not to fail to read the last two or three ____ of the book, where authors often sum up what is new and important.
questions.explain: Few authors can resist summing up their work in the final pages; if these are an epilogue, read the last few pages of the main part instead.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: Which of these does Adler and Van Doren's systematic skimming include?
options: Reading summary statements in the pivotal chapters
Dipping into a paragraph or two here and there
Looking up every unfamiliar word in a dictionary
Reading the last two or three pages
Writing a full outline of every chapter
questions.explain: Skimming includes reading pivotal chapters' summaries, dipping in, and reading the closing pages. Looking up every word is what superficial reading warns against, and outlining belongs to analytical reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren ask the skimmer to think of himself as a ____ looking for clues to a book's general theme or idea.
questions.explain: The detective image captures the alert attitude of skimming: looking for anything that makes the book's theme clearer.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren call inspectional reading a very active sort of reading?
