questions.a: It is impossible to give a book an inspectional reading without being alert, with all one's faculties awake and working. Daydreaming through pages cannot happen if you have a system for following a general thread. The reader acts like a detective looking for clues to the book's general theme.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: Even if you decide after skimming not to read a book further, what have you gained, according to Adler and Van Doren?
questions.a: Skimming may show that what you got is all the book is worth to you, but the time is not wasted. You will at least know the author's main contention and what kind of book he has written. You can also place the book in your mental card catalogue for future reference.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: Sort these actions from How to Read a Book into the two sublevels of inspectional reading they belong to.

items.t: Checking the index for crucial terms
Reading the publisher's blurb
Studying the table of contents
Reading a hard book straight through without stopping
Passing over footnotes you do not understand
Reading a whole Shakespeare play at one sitting

questions.explain: Skimming examines the parts of a book that reveal its subject and structure. Superficial reading means reading the whole text through without stopping at difficulties.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: After the first four skimming steps in How to Read a Book, what choices does the reader have?
questions.a: The first four steps may already tell you that you want to read the book more carefully, or that you do not need to read it at all, and in either case you may put it aside for the moment. If you do not, you go on to skim the book properly speaking: looking at pivotal chapters and dipping through the pages.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is the real mistake when someone struggles fruitlessly with a difficult book?
options: Trying to read such a difficult book in the first place
Choosing a book written for specialists rather than general readers
Expecting too much from the first going over of the book
Reading the book too quickly instead of slowing down
questions.explain: It is natural to think the mistake was attempting the book, but the authors say the mistake was expecting too much from the first reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren's rule: in tackling a difficult book for the first time, read it through without ever stopping to look up or ____ the things you do not understand right away.
questions.explain: The rule tells you to keep going past difficulties and concentrate on what you can understand.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that understanding half of a really tough book is much better than not understanding it at all.
questions.explain: Stopping at the first hard passage leaves you with nothing, while reading through gives you some understanding and prepares a second reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say you will usually puzzle out a hard passage if you stick to it on the first reading.
questions.explain: They say that in most cases you will not puzzle it out by sticking to it; you have a better chance on a second reading, after reading the book through once.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what went wrong for generations of high school students reading Shakespeare?
options: They read the plays in modern translations instead of the originals
They read the plays too quickly to notice their poetry
They watched performances instead of reading the texts
They went scene by scene with glossaries and footnotes and lost the whole
questions.explain: Forced to look up every strange word and footnote, they forgot the beginning by the end and never really read the play; they should have read it at one sitting first.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what happens to a reader of Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations who insists on understanding every page before going on?
options: They miss the big points, missing the forest for the trees
They understand the book fully but take far longer than needed
They become a specialist in economics instead of a general reader
They find the book is only a textbook for specialists
questions.explain: Mastering the fine points first makes you miss Smith's big points on wages, prices, monopoly and free trade. The authors chose the book precisely because it is for the general reader.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which of these big points of The Wealth of Nations do Adler and Van Doren say a page-by-page reader would miss?
options: The role of the market in determining prices
The evils of monopoly
The reasons for free trade
The need for a central bank
The labor theory of surplus value
questions.explain: The authors list the factors entering the cost of things, the market's role in prices, the evils of monopoly and the reasons for free trade. The other two are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which of these did most of us learn to do, according to Adler and Van Doren, that impedes reading when done prematurely?
options: Going to a dictionary for an unfamiliar word
Consulting footnotes and scholarly commentaries
Reading the last pages of the book first
Going to an encyclopedia for allusions we did not grasp
questions.explain: We were taught to consult dictionaries, encyclopedias, footnotes and commentaries; done too early, these impede reading. Reading the last pages is part of skimming, not something they criticize.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: How does reading a difficult book through once, without stopping, help a later reading, according to Adler and Van Doren?
questions.a: What you understand by reading to the end, even fifty percent or less, helps you when you go back to the places you passed by. You have a much better chance of understanding a difficult passage on a second reading, but that requires reading the book through at least once. Even if you never go back, half understanding beats none.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren think Shakespeare students should have done instead of studying the plays scene by scene with glossaries?
questions.a: They should have been encouraged to read the play at one sitting and discuss what they got from that first quick reading. Only then would they be ready to study it carefully and closely, because they would have understood enough of it to learn more.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what do most speed reading courses basically provide?
options: Instruction in analytical reading for difficult books
Training in syntopical reading of many books at once
Remedial instruction, mainly in elementary reading
Practice in criticizing an author's arguments
questions.explain: They had already suggested that such courses are basically remedial, teaching mainly if not exclusively reading on the elementary level.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say a good speed reading course should teach you to read at many ____ speeds, not just one faster speed.
questions.explain: The aim is to vary your rate according to the nature and complexity of the material.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Sort these, as Adler and Van Doren describe them, by whether they deserve fast or slow reading.

items.t: The list of facts in the Declaration of Independence
Interstitial material in a good book
Things not really worth much reading time
The first two paragraphs of the Declaration
The difficult matter that every good book contains
A few books that call for complete comprehension

questions.explain: Speed should fit the material: filler and lists of facts can go fast, while difficult, rewarding matter like the Declaration's opening needs slow reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what are the main obstacles to comprehending a difficult book?
options: Not knowing the rules of reading or what to look for
Physiological limits on how fast the eye can move
Psychological anxiety about reading difficult material
Lack of time to read the whole book at a slow speed
questions.explain: The obstacles are not ordinarily, and perhaps never primarily, physiological or psychological; the reader does not know what to do with a difficult book or how to marshal his resources.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Why is inspectional reading quick, according to Adler and Van Doren, apart from simply reading faster?
questions.a: You do read faster, but inspectional reading is also quick because you read less of the book. You read it in a different way, with different goals in mind. So its speed is not just a matter of eye or reading rate.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: What is the ideal regarding rates of reading, according to Adler and Van Doren, and how does it apply even within an analytical reading?
questions.a: The ideal is not merely to read faster but to read at different speeds and to know when each is appropriate. Even in an analytical reading, which is ordinarily slow, you should not read the whole book at one rate. Every book has interstitial material to read quickly, and every good book has difficult matter to read very slowly.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why are many eye fixations per line wasteful?
options: Because the eye tires quickly when it stops too often
Because the mind can grasp a sentence or paragraph at a glance
Because sub-vocalizing every word is impossible at high speed
Because readers lose their place on the page between stops
questions.explain: The mind, unlike the eye, need not take in only a word or short phrase at a time; it can grasp a sentence or paragraph at a glance if the eyes supply it.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren note that the eye can see only while it is moving across the line.
questions.explain: They say the opposite: the eye is blind while it moves and can only see when it stops, which is why fixations matter.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Put Adler and Van Doren's hand-pointer method for breaking eye fixations in order.
items: Place your thumb and first two fingers together
Sweep this pointer across a line a little faster than is comfortable
Force yourself to keep up with your hand
Keep practicing and increase the speed of your hand
questions.explain: You form the pointer, sweep it slightly faster than comfortable, keep up with it, and gradually speed it up; this can double or treble reading speed.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say most people continue to ____ for years after they are first taught to read.
questions.explain: Speed reading courses rightly stress this habit, together with fixations and regressions.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: What is the primary task of speed reading courses according to Adler and Van Doren, and what is the result once it is done?
questions.a: The primary task is to correct the fixations and regressions that slow readers down, which can be done quite easily, often with nothing more than one's own hand as a pointer. Once done, the student can read as fast as his mind will let him, not as slow as his eyes make him.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that ____ is another name for what they have called activity in reading.
questions.explain: The good reader reads actively, with concentration, which speed reading devices can improve.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what limited kind of comprehension do speed reading courses mainly test?
options: The ability to say whether the book is true
The ability to state the book's unity in a sentence
The ability to compare the book with others on the subject
The elementary ability to answer what does the book say
questions.explain: Answering simple questions of fact is just the elementary question of what a text says; questions implying higher comprehension are seldom asked in such courses.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which of these does Adler and Van Doren's Declaration of Independence example say can be read quickly?
options: The two pages of facts after the second paragraph
The closing pledge of lives, fortunes and sacred honour
The first two paragraphs
Words like inalienable, rights and consent
questions.explain: The list of facts and the rhetorical flourish at the end can be read fast, but the first two paragraphs and their key words need slow, prolonged reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren conclude the problem of speed reading really is, and what does this book aim to improve?
questions.a: The problem of speed reading is the problem of comprehension, which means defining comprehension at levels beyond the elementary, something speed reading courses mostly do not attempt. This book seeks to improve precisely comprehension. You cannot comprehend a book without reading it analytically, since analytical reading is undertaken mainly for understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren's formula: every book should be read no more slowly than it ____, and no more quickly than you can read it with satisfaction and comprehension.
questions.explain: The formula replaces the idea of a single right speed with speed fitted to the book's worth and your comprehension.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: In the summary of How to Read a Book's chapter on inspectional reading, which rule is called the most important of all and the essence of inspectional reading?
options: Always skim the index before the table of contents
Train your hand to move faster than your eyes across the page
Do not try to understand every word or page of a difficult book the first time
Read only books whose blurbs summarize their main points
questions.explain: Not trying to understand everything on the first pass is called the most important rule and the essence of inspectional reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which of these claims appear in Adler and Van Doren's summary of inspectional reading?
options: There is no single right speed at which to read
Great speed in reading is a dubious achievement
It is generally desirable to skim even a book you intend to read carefully
Skimming is unnecessary for books you already plan to read
A good reader reads every book at the same rate
questions.explain: The summary rejects a single right speed, calls great speed dubious, and recommends skimming even books you will read carefully, to see their form and structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say great speed in reading is of value only if what you have to read is not really worth reading.
questions.explain: The summary calls great speed a dubious achievement, of value only for material not really worth reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren recommend skimming even a book you already intend to read carefully?
questions.a: Skimming is always a good idea and is necessary when you do not know whether a book is worth careful reading. Even for a book you plan to read carefully, skimming is generally desirable to get some idea of its form and structure before the closer reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Put the four levels of reading in How to Read a Book in order, from lowest to highest.
items: Elementary reading
Inspectional reading
Analytical reading
Syntopical reading
questions.explain: Inspectional reading is the second level, between elementary and analytical; syntopical reading is the fourth and highest.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Match each stage of inspectional reading to the stage of analytical reading it anticipates, according to Adler and Van Doren.
pairs: The first stage: grasping a book's structure
The second stage: interpreting a book's contents
An important role in syntopical reading, shown in Part Four
questions.explain: Skimming anticipates the comprehension of structure, and superficial reading is the first necessary step in interpretation; Part Four shows inspectional reading's role in syntopical reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Put these chapters of How to Read a Book in the order they appear.
items: The Levels of Reading
The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
How to Be a Demanding Reader
Pigeonholing a Book
questions.explain: Chapter 4 follows the chapters on the levels and on elementary reading, and precedes How to Be a Demanding Reader and the first analytical-reading chapter, Pigeonholing a Book.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: How does the end of How to Read a Book's chapter on inspectional reading lead into the next chapter, How to Be a Demanding Reader?
options: It promises next to explain syntopical reading in full
It announces a pause to consider again the nature of reading as an activity
It says the next chapter will return to speed reading techniques
It says the next chapter will review elementary reading skills
questions.explain: Before explaining analytical reading, the authors pause to reconsider reading as an activity and the actions the demanding reader must perform, the subject of Chapter 5.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Put the sections of How to Read a Book's chapter on inspectional reading in their order.
items: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
Superficial Reading
On Reading Speeds
Fixations and Regressions
The Problem of Comprehension
Summary of Inspectional Reading
questions.explain: The chapter first describes the two sublevels, then turns to speed, its mechanics, its limits in comprehension, and a summary.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Match each idea in How to Read a Book's chapter on inspectional reading with a later chapter where it is developed.
pairs: Placing a book in a mental pigeonhole while skimming
Using the table of contents as a road map of structure
Crucial terms spotted in the index
Coming to Terms with an Author
How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.explain: The skimming steps hint at analytical-reading chapters: classifying (Chapter 6), structure (Chapter 7), terms, which the authors say Part Two treats more fully (Chapter 8), and active reading (Chapter 5).

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Prereading
questions.q: Put these moments of Adler and Van Doren's reading of a difficult book in order.
items: Skim the book systematically
Read it through superficially without stopping
Go back to the places passed by on a second reading
questions.explain: Skimming comes first to decide whether to read; a superficial read-through follows; a second reading then tackles the passages passed by.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Match each part of the Declaration of Independence to how Adler and Van Doren say it should be read.
pairs: Quickly, for a general idea of the kind of facts
Slowly, perhaps over days, weeks or years
questions.explain: The example shows one short document calling for very different speeds.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Sort these points from How to Read a Book by whether they concern the eye or the mind.

items.t: Is blind while it moves
Fixates five or six times per line in untrained readers
Regresses to phrases already read
Can grasp a sentence or paragraph at a glance
Sets the true limit once fixations are corrected

questions.explain: The eye's habits slow reading; the mind can take in far more at once, so after training you read as fast as your mind lets you.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Sort these claims by whether Adler and Van Doren accept or reject them.

items.t: Most people ought to be able to read faster than they do
A few books should be read slowly for complete comprehension
One faster speed is the goal of a good speed course
Comprehension problems are mainly physiological

questions.explain: They favor faster reading and varied speeds, but reject a single speed and locate comprehension problems in not knowing the rules of reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Put the steps of Adler and Van Doren's argument about speed reading and comprehension in order.
items: Speed reading courses claim to increase comprehension
A hand used as a timer improves concentration
Concentration alone has little effect on comprehension
So the problem of speed reading is the problem of comprehension
questions.explain: The authors grant the courses' claim some foundation via concentration, then argue real comprehension goes beyond answering what a text says.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which of these habits do Adler and Van Doren say slow readers down?
options: Sub-vocalizing
Fixating five or six times per line
Regressing to phrases already read
Following a hand pointer across the line
Grasping a whole sentence at a glance
questions.explain: Sub-vocalizing, many fixations and regressions are the wasteful habits; the hand pointer is the cure, and grasping a sentence at a glance is what the mind can do once freed.

questions.q: In the opening of 'How to Be a Demanding Reader', what do the authors say chiefly decides whether you stay awake while reading?
options: How comfortable your chair and lighting are
Your goal in reading, and whether the book makes a difference to you
How difficult or boring the chosen book happens to be
Whether you read in the evening or during the day
questions.explain: The famous candlelight readers stayed awake because it made a great difference to them whether they read the book; staying awake depends largely on your goal. Comfort and dim light do not decide it, since people have read late even in poor light.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: True or false: According to Adler and Van Doren, the rules for staying awake while reading are simply the opposite of the rules for reading yourself to sleep.
questions.explain: The authors say the rules for keeping awake do not consist in doing just the opposite; people stay awake in comfortable chairs and dim light when the book matters to them.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that using a good book as a sedative is conspicuous ____.
questions.explain: The opening states: “To use a good book as a sedative is conspicuous waste.” Good books deserve active reading aimed at profit.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: In the opening of the chapter on demanding reading, why do the authors say many people fail to carry out their reading plans even when they can tell profit from pleasure?
questions.a: They fail not for lack of knowing which books give understanding and which give entertainment, but because they do not know how to be demanding readers. They cannot keep their minds on the book by making the mind do the work without which no profit can be earned.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: According to the opening of 'How to Be a Demanding Reader', reading to grow in mind or spirit requires reading in what way?
options: As quickly as possible, to cover more ground
As relaxed as possible, so the ideas can sink in
As actively as possible, with an effort you expect to be repaid
As selectively as possible, skipping hard passages
questions.explain: If your aim is to profit, you must keep awake, which means reading as actively as possible and making an effort for which you expect to be repaid. Relaxed reading is what the authors associate with falling asleep over a book.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren's one simple prescription for active reading is: ask ____ while you read, which you yourself must try to answer.
questions.explain: The heart of active reading is asking questions in the course of reading and trying to answer them yourself; the art consists in asking the right questions in the right order.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Put Adler and Van Doren's four basic questions a reader asks in the order the authors give them.
items: What is the book about as a whole?
What is being said in detail, and how?
Is the book true, in whole or part?
What of it?
questions.explain: The authors number the questions in this order, and stress that the truth question cannot be answered until the first two are, and that the first three come before the last.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Match each of the four basic questions with what it asks the reader to do.
pairs: What is the book about as a whole?
Find the leading theme and how it is subdivided
What is being said in detail, and how?
Find the main ideas, assertions, and arguments
Is the book true, in whole or part?
Make up your own mind about the author's claims
Ask about the significance and what further follows
questions.explain: Each question targets a different job: the whole and its parts, the detailed message, judging truth, and judging significance.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say you can decide whether a book is true before you know what it is saying.
questions.explain: The authors say you cannot answer the truth question until you have answered the first two; you must know what is being said before deciding whether it is true.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, which of the four basic questions is probably the most important one in syntopical reading?
options: What is the book about as a whole?
What is being said in detail, and how?
Is the book true, in whole or part?
What of it?
questions.explain: The authors say the last question, What of it?, is probably the most important in syntopical reading, though the first three must be answered before it.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, inspectional reading tends to give more accurate answers to which of the four basic questions?
options: The first two, about the whole and the details
The last two, about truth and significance
Only the question of truth
Only the question What of it?
questions.explain: Inspectional reading tends to answer the first two questions more accurately than the last two, though it helps with those too. Analytical reading is not complete until the last two are answered.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren mean by the difference between a demanding and an undemanding reader?
questions.a: Reading beyond the elementary level is essentially an effort to ask a book questions and to answer them as best you can. The demanding reader asks the four basic questions as he reads; the undemanding reader does not, and “The latter asks no questions-and gets no answers.”
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, do people go to sleep over good books?
questions.a: Not because they are unwilling to make the effort but because they do not know how to make it. Good books are over the reader's head, and it is not the stretching that tires but the frustration of stretching unsuccessfully for lack of skill. Active reading needs both the will and the skill, the art of reaching up to a book's level.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say about the four basic questions?
options: They summarize the whole obligation of a reader
They apply even to an article or an advertisement
They are needed only for difficult nonfiction books
Knowing them is enough without remembering to ask them
Stated another way, they become the basic rules of reading
questions.explain: The questions summarize the reader's whole obligation, apply to anything worth reading, and become the rules of Part Two. The authors insist that knowing them is not enough: you must remember to ask them as you read.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that the habit of remembering to ask the four questions is the mark of a ____ reader.
questions.explain: The habit of asking the questions marks the demanding reader; the trained ability to answer them precisely and accurately is the art of reading.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Maya reads a popular book on sleep science, understands its argument, and then asks why the author thinks this matters and whether it should change her own bedtime habits. Which of Adler and Van Doren's basic questions is she asking?
options: What is the book about as a whole?
What is being said in detail, and how?
Is the book true, in whole or part?
What of it?
questions.explain: Asking about the significance of the information, both to the author and to herself, is the fourth question, What of it? She is not judging truth here but importance.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren urge readers not only to read between the lines but also to ____ between the lines.
questions.explain: Unless you write between the lines, the authors say, you are not likely to do the most efficient kind of reading; the pencil becomes the sign of alertness.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, when does full ownership of a book come?
options: When you pay for the book and take it home
When you place your bookplate on the front endpaper
When you have read every page of the book at least once
When you have made the book a part of yourself, best done by writing in it
questions.explain: Purchase is only the prelude to possession; full ownership comes when you make the book part of yourself, and the best way is to write in it. A bookplate expresses only financial ownership.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Which of these are reasons Adler and Van Doren give for why marking a book is indispensable to reading it?
options: It keeps you wide awake, not merely conscious
Active reading is thinking, and thinking tends to express itself in words
Writing your reactions down helps you remember the author's thoughts
It increases the resale value of the book
It lets you skip rereading the book entirely
questions.explain: The authors give exactly three reasons: wakefulness, thinking expressing itself in words, and memory. Neither resale value nor avoiding rereading is mentioned.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say a person who claims to know what he thinks but cannot express it usually does not know what he thinks.
questions.explain: This is their second reason for marking a book: active reading is thinking, and thinking tends to express itself in words, spoken or written.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren describe reading a book as a conversation between reader and author?
questions.a: The author presumably knows more, but understanding is a two-way operation: the learner must question himself and the teacher, and even argue once he understands. Marking a book expresses your agreements or differences with the author, and “It is the highest respect you can pay him.”
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Match each book-marking device recommended by Adler and Van Doren with its purpose.
pairs: Star or asterisk at the margin
Flag, sparingly, the ten or dozen most important passages
Show a sequence of points in an argument
Numbers of other pages in the margin
Tie up related or contradictory points made elsewhere
Emphasize an underlined statement or a long passage
questions.explain: Each device has a distinct job; for example, page numbers marked with Cf link ideas separated by many pages, while margin numbers track the steps of one argument.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Which of these book-marking devices do Adler and Van Doren say serve to emphasize statements?
options: Underlining of major points
Circling of key words or phrases
Vertical lines at the margin
Numbers in the margin to show a sequence of points
A personal index on the back endpapers
questions.explain: Underlining, circling (which serves much the same function as underlining) and vertical margin lines all emphasize. Margin numbers track an argument's sequence, and the back-endpaper index records points in order.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Sort these uses of a book's pages, as Adler and Van Doren describe them, by whether they express financial or intellectual ownership.

items.t: A fancy bookplate on the front endpapers
Buying and paying for the book
An integrated outline of the book on the front endpapers
A personal index of the author's points on the back endpapers
Questions written in the margins

questions.explain: A bookplate and the purchase show only that you paid for the book; outlines, indexes and marginal questions record your thinking and so express intellectual ownership.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Match each place in a book with the use Adler and Van Doren recommend for it.
pairs: A personal index of the author's points in order
An outline of the book as an integrated structure
Structural notes from an inspectional reading
questions.explain: The back holds the page-by-page index, the front the integrated outline that measures understanding, and the otherwise unused contents or title page the structural notes.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say the pencil is so useful when you read actively?
questions.a: Merely asking questions is not enough; you must try to answer them, and although that can be done in your head it is much easier with a pencil in hand. The pencil becomes the sign of your alertness, and writing in the book is how you make it your own.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Sam is reading a long history and notices that a claim on page 210 contradicts one on page 45. Using Adler and Van Doren's marking devices, what should he do?
options: Underline both claims and move on
Write the other page number, perhaps with Cf, in the margin beside each
Put a star on each page and fold its corner
Circle the key word in each claim
questions.explain: Writing other page numbers in the margin ties together points that belong together though separated by many pages, including contradictions. Stars are for the dozen most important passages, not for linking.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Match each level of reading with the kind of note-making Adler and Van Doren associate with it.
pairs: Expert syntopical reading of several books
questions.explain: Inspectional notes concern a book's structure, analytical notes its concepts and your own, and the expert syntopical reader notes the shape of the discussion among authors.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren call notes made during inspectional reading, which concern a book's structure rather than its substance, ____ notes.
questions.explain: These notes record answers about the kind of book, its subject as a whole, and its structural order, so they are called structural.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Notes about the shape of the discussion engaged in by several authors, even unbeknownst to them, are what Adler and Van Doren call ____ notes.
questions.explain: A truly expert syntopical reader can make these notes, often on separate sheets, since they concern several books; the authors return to them in Chapter 20.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, where is the best place to make notes during an inspectional reading?
options: On the back endpapers as a personal index
On separate sheets of paper
On the contents page or the title page
In the margins beside each key passage
questions.explain: Structural notes from inspectional reading go best on the contents page or title page, which are otherwise unused. Separate sheets are for dialectical notes on several books.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren advise judging the truth of a book's statements during an inspectional reading.
questions.explain: They say you should put off judging accuracy or truth until you read the book more carefully; questions of truth and significance belong to analytical reading.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Which of these are the questions Adler and Van Doren say inspectional reading answers?
options: What kind of book is it?
What is it about as a whole?
What is the structural order by which the author develops the subject?
Is the book true, in whole or part?
How does it compare with other books on the subject?
questions.explain: Inspectional reading answers the kind of book, its subject as a whole, and its structural order. Truth belongs to analytical reading and comparing books to syntopical reading.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Sort these notes by whether Adler and Van Doren would call them structural or conceptual.

items.t: What kind of book this is, jotted on the title page
An outline of how the book's parts are ordered
A judgment on whether the author's main claim is true
How the author's idea of freedom deepened your own
The general subject matter, noted on the contents page
A reference to another book's treatment of the same concept

questions.explain: Structural notes record a book's kind, subject and order; conceptual notes concern the author's concepts and your own, including truth and significance, and in syntopical reading may refer to other books.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Why might dialectical notes, in Adler and Van Doren's account, have to be made on separate sheets of paper?
questions.a: Dialectical notes record the shape of the discussion engaged in by several authors, so they concern many books rather than one. They imply a structure of concepts, an order of statements and questions about a single subject, which does not belong in the pages of any single book.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that after practice, an activity becomes as natural as walking, which is what it means to say habit is second ____.
questions.explain: Practice brings almost automatic perfection, so you act as if born to it: “habit is second nature.”
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what do we mean when we call someone skilled?
options: That he possesses the habit of making or doing it
That he knows the rules of making or doing something
That he has an inborn talent no rules can teach
That he can explain the rules to others
questions.explain: Knowing the rules is a condition of getting the skill, but being skilled means having the habit that results from operating by the rules.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter on demanding reading say about forming an art or skill?
options: You learn to do by doing
Knowing the rules is a condition of getting the skill
Knowing the rules is the same as having the habit
You cannot acquire an artistic habit without following rules
Highly original artists follow no rules at all
questions.explain: Habits are formed only by operating, and rules must be known and followed. The authors deny that knowing rules equals having the habit, and argue that even original artists follow rules of technique.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren answer people who say a highly original painter or sculptor follows no rules?
questions.a: They grant there are no final, unbreakable rules for making a painting or sculpture, but say the artist must have followed rules for preparing canvas, mixing and applying paints, or moulding clay and welding steel. However original the result, he must be skilled to produce it, and that skill or craft is the art in question.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Put these phrases into the order in which Adler and Van Doren use them to describe how a habit is formed.
items: One learns to do by doing
Practice makes perfect
Habit is second nature
questions.explain: The authors first say habit comes only from operating, then that practice brings facility and readiness, and finally that the activity becomes as natural as walking or eating.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren distinguish the art as something that can be taught, which consists of rules, from the art as something possessed, which consists of a habit.
questions.explain: The teachable art is the rules to be followed in operation; the learned and possessed art is the habit that results from operating according to them.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: In Adler and Van Doren's skiing analogy, what must the learner do to perform all the separate acts well?
options: Keep thinking about each separate act throughout
Skip the separate acts and practise whole runs from the start
Rely on the instructor to call out each act in turn
Forget the separate acts, after first learning them as separate acts
questions.explain: You must learn to forget the separate acts in order to perform them well, but to forget them you must first learn them separately. Skipping straight to the whole is ruled out.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren compare learning to read well to learning to ____, an activity graceful in experts and humiliating for adult beginners.
questions.explain: “Reading is like skiing.” Both are harmonious when done by experts and awkward, frustrating and slow for beginners.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what does the multiplicity of the rules of reading indicate?
options: Many distinct habits that must each be kept separate
That reading cannot really be taught by rules
The complexity of the one habit to be formed
That only some of the rules need to be learned
questions.explain: The many rules show the complexity of one habit, not a plurality of distinct habits; the parts coalesce as each becomes automatic.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say learning to read well is harder than learning to ski?
questions.a: Reading, especially analytical reading, is more complex than skiing and much more a mental activity. The skier thinks of physical acts, which is relatively easy, while the beginning analytical reader must think of mental acts, in a sense thinking about his own thoughts, which most people are unused to doing.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: Put these stages of learning a complex skill in the order Adler and Van Doren describe in their skiing analogy.
items: Learn each separate act with full attention
Practise the parts until each becomes easier
Put the parts together into a smoothly running whole
Pay attention to the goal rather than the technique
questions.explain: Each act first needs full attention; practice brings facility; the parts then coalesce; and only once they lose their separateness can the learner attend to the goal.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: Priya is learning to drive and at first must consciously check mirrors, signal, and steer, feeling overwhelmed. Months later she drives smoothly while thinking about her route. Which idea of Adler and Van Doren does this illustrate?
options: The separate acts coalesce into one habit once each becomes automatic
Habit is formed by knowing the rules rather than practising
Complex skills are a plurality of distinct habits
Adults cannot learn complex skills they did not start young
questions.explain: As each subordinate act reaches automatic execution, the parts telescope into one habit and the learner can attend to the goal. The authors deny that the rules mark many distinct habits.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: How does 'How to Be a Demanding Reader' relate to the chapters that follow it in Part Two of How to Read a Book?
options: It summarizes rules already fully given in Part Two
Its four basic questions, restated, become the rules of reading Part Two develops
It replaces the rules of analytical reading with a single habit
It introduces syntopical reading, which Part Two then sets aside
questions.explain: The authors say the four questions, stated another way, become the basic rules of reading with which Part Two is mainly concerned, and that they will return to them through the rest of the book.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Put these chapters of How to Read a Book in their order in the book.
items: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
How to Be a Demanding Reader
Pigeonholing a Book
The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.explain: Chapter 4 on inspectional reading leads into Chapter 5 on demanding reading, which prepares for Chapter 6's start on analytical reading; syntopical reading comes in Chapter 20, where dialectical notes are taken up again.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Why does the chapter on being a demanding reader end with the section 'From Many Rules to One Habit' just before the detailed rules of analytical reading begin?
questions.a: The next chapters will enumerate a long list of rules, and the authors want readers not to fear that array. Through the skiing analogy they show that the many rules reflect the complexity of one habit, whose parts coalesce with practice, so the reader should be patient with the instruction to come.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: Sort these topics by whether they appear in 'How to Be a Demanding Reader' or are promised for later chapters of How to Read a Book.

items.t: The four basic questions a reader asks
Devices for marking a book
Adapting the four questions to fiction and poetry
Dialectical note-making in full
The skiing analogy for forming a habit

questions.explain: A footnote sends the adaptation of the questions for fiction and poetry to Chapters 14 and 15, and dialectical notes are promised for Chapter 20.
questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do Adler and Van Doren usually talk about reading whole books when they set out the rules of analytical reading?
options: A whole book, especially a long, difficult one, poses the hardest problems a reader can face
Short pieces such as articles and stories need entirely different rules of their own
Whole books are the only kind of material worth reading analytically at all
Articles and short stories are already covered fully by elementary reading
questions.explain: Reading a whole book poses the severest problems, so rules for books carry over to easier material like articles and short stories, adapted as needed. The authors never say short pieces need wholly different rules.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say reading an article is almost always harder than reading a book on the same subject.
questions.explain: They say the reverse: an article is almost always easier than a book on the same subject, which is why rules worked out for whole books can be adapted to shorter materials.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how do the rules for reading whole books relate to reading shorter materials such as articles, stories or abstracts?
questions.a: Reading a whole book, especially a long and difficult one, is the hardest reading task, so the rules for books also apply to lesser and more easily understood materials. They may not apply in quite the same way or to the same extent, but the reader can easily adapt them.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what does the title of Chapter 6, "Pigeonholing a Book," signal about its job in Part Two?
options: It gives the final rule of analytical reading: judge whether the book is true
It presents the first rule of analytical reading: classify the kind of book you are reading
It explains how to skim a book quickly before deciding whether to buy it
It describes how libraries shelve books so readers can find them
questions.explain: Pigeonholing means placing a book in its category, which is what Rule 1 of analytical reading demands. Judging truth comes much later, in the chapters on criticizing a book.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 6 of How to Read a Book, "Pigeonholing a Book," opens Part Two's account of analytical reading and is followed by "X-raying a Book."
questions.explain: Chapter 6 states Rule 1 of analytical reading; Chapter 7, "X-raying a Book," goes on to stating a book's unity and outlining its parts.

questions.q: Put these sections of Chapter 6 of How to Read a Book in the order they appear.
items: The Importance of Classifying Books
What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
Practical vs. Theoretical Books
Kinds of Theoretical Books
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the rule itself, to titles as clues, to the broad practical/theoretical split, and finally to subdividing theoretical books.

questions.q: How does Chapter 6 of How to Read a Book build on the earlier chapter on inspectional reading?
questions.a: Adler and Van Doren say you follow Rule 1 by first giving the book an inspectional reading: reading the title, subtitle, table of contents, preface, index and blurb, and if needed passages of a summary nature and the beginning and end. Classifying a book thus uses the skimming skills already taught, now put to work as the first step of analytical reading.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, pigeonholing a book is the first rule of ____ reading, the third level of reading.
questions.explain: Chapter 6 opens Part Two by stating Rule 1 of analytical reading: know what kind of book you are reading, as early as possible.

questions.q: Which of these later chapters of How to Read a Book take up kinds of books that Chapter 6 first distinguishes?
options: How to Read Practical Books
How to Read History
How to Read Philosophy
Coming to Terms with an Author
Aids to Reading
questions.explain: Chapter 6 separates practical from theoretical books and theoretical books into history, science and philosophy; later chapters treat each kind. Coming to terms and aids to reading concern other matters.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, Rule 1 of analytical reading says you must know what ____ of book you are reading, preferably before you begin to read.
questions.explain: Rule 1 asks the reader to identify the kind of book as early as possible, ideally before reading begins.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, when do Adler and Van Doren say you should know what kind of book you are reading?
options: Only after finishing the book and reflecting on it
Halfway through, once the main argument is clear
As early as possible, preferably before you begin to read
Whenever you first decide to criticize the author
questions.explain: Rule 1 stresses timing: the earlier the better, ideally before reading. Waiting until the end or until criticism defeats the purpose of guiding how you read.

questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren define an expository book in How to Read a Book?
options: One that contains only proven facts with no opinions or speculation in it
One that tells a story about real people rather than invented characters
One that tries to move the reader's feelings rather than inform the mind
One that primarily conveys knowledge, broadly including opinions and theories claimed to be true
questions.explain: Knowledge is construed broadly: opinions, theories, hypotheses or speculations claimed to be true in some sense count. Proven facts alone would be far too narrow.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say Rule 1, though it applies to all books, applies particularly to works of fiction.
questions.explain: They say the rule applies particularly to nonfictional, expository works, because there the task is telling apart the various kinds of expository book.

questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book say a reader should look at to classify a book during an inspectional reading?
options: The title and subtitle
The table of contents
The publisher's blurb on the dust jacket
Reviews written by other critics
The author's other books
questions.explain: The authors list the title, subtitle, table of contents, preface or introduction, index and blurb as signal flags. Outside reviews and other books are not on the list.

questions.q: Match each book named in How to Read a Book to the classification puzzle the authors raise about it.
pairs: Fiction or a tract against drug abuse?
Romance or a history of the South?
Clearly not fiction, yet almost as readable as a novel
questions.explain: The authors use these books to show that telling fiction from exposition is not always easy, though all the novels did appear on the fiction side of the best-seller lists.

questions.q: Sort these titles from How to Read a Book by whether the authors treat them as novels or as clearly non-fiction.

items.t: Main Street
The Grapes of Wrath
The Andromeda Strain
Middletown
The Universe and Dr. Einstein

questions.explain: Main Street, The Grapes of Wrath and The Andromeda Strain are novels despite their social or physical science; Middletown is social science, and The Universe and Dr. Einstein is clearly not fiction.

questions.q: Put the steps in the classification scheme of How to Read a Book in order, from the broadest split to the narrowest.
items: Separate fiction from expository works
Separate practical from theoretical expository works
Divide theoretical works into history, science and philosophy
questions.explain: The authors start with fiction versus exposition, then make the across-the-board practical/theoretical distinction, then subdivide theoretical books.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the preface, title, contents and blurb are called the signal ____ the author waves to show which way the wind is blowing.
questions.explain: The authors say it is not the author's fault if the reader will not stop, look and listen to these signals.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say Rule 1 matters most for expository books rather than for telling fiction from non-fiction?
questions.a: Most people can tell a work of fiction or an expository work when they see it, though not always easily. The real problem is recognizing that expository books are instructive in different ways: a history and a philosophical work, or a book on physics and one on morals, deal with different problems and use different methods.

questions.q: Why does How to Read a Book mention novels like The Andromeda Strain and the work of Robert Heinlein and Arthur C. Clarke?
options: To show that some fiction contains a good deal of physical science, blurring categories
To argue that science fiction should be classed as expository writing
To give examples of books with misleading and dishonest titles
To show that novels are always easier to read than science books
questions.explain: The authors note that besides social science, physics and chemistry also turn up in novels, which makes classification harder. They still call these books novels.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why is grouping books together as being of the same kind not enough to follow Rule 1?
questions.a: Adler and Van Doren say you must also know what that kind is. Neither the title, the front matter, nor sometimes the whole book will tell you unless you already have categories you can apply, so the rule only becomes intelligible by drawing distinctions that create categories able to stand the test of time.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: In the Darwin example in How to Read a Book, why did more than half of twenty-five well-read people get the title wrong?
options: They confused it with Gibbon's history of the Roman Empire
They assumed it was about the development of the human species and added "the"
They had read the book but forgotten its long subtitle
They thought the book was about natural selection in society
questions.explain: Never having read the book, they supposed it concerned human development and said The Origin of the Species. Darwin treated human beings in a later book, The Descent of Man.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, Darwin dealt with the development of the human species not in The Origin of Species but in a later book, The ____ of Man.
questions.explain: The authors point out that The Origin of Species has little or nothing to do with human development, which Darwin covered in The Descent of Man.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say The Origin of Species is about the proliferation of many species of plants and animals from far fewer species, owing mainly to natural selection.
questions.explain: That is exactly what the title says, which is the authors' point: few readers have read the title carefully and thought about what it means.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why were readers puzzled that Gibbon's first chapter covers the Age of the Antonines?
options: They did not know who the Antonines were or when they had ruled
They thought Gibbon's book was a novel rather than a history
They had silently turned "decline and fall" into "rise and fall" and expected the Republic
They expected the book to start with the fall of the city of Rome
questions.explain: Read carefully, the title implies the story starts at the Empire's high point, the Age of the Antonines. Expecting a rise, readers looked in vain for the Roman Republic.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: What does the Gibbon example in How to Read a Book show about reading titles?
questions.a: The title The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire implies the narrative begins at the Empire's high point and runs to its end. Readers who had unconsciously turned it into "rise and fall" were puzzled that the first chapter is about the Age of the Antonines; reading the title carefully would have given them essential information before they began.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, what is one reason many readers ignore titles and prefaces?
options: Publishers usually make titles misleading to sell more copies
Prefaces are mostly written by editors, not the author
Titles rarely have anything to do with a book's contents
They do not think it important to classify the book they are reading
questions.explain: The authors say readers ignore these signals because they do not follow Rule 1; authors in fact take trouble to make titles and prefaces descriptive.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, Einstein and Infeld supply an ____ table of contents to advise the reader in advance of the details of their treatment in The Evolution of Physics.
questions.explain: Their analytical table of contents, like their preface, helps the reader know the kind of book being given.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book say Einstein and Infeld did to help readers of The Evolution of Physics?
options: Warned in the preface that a popular science book must not be read like a novel
Built an analytical table of contents
Gave the book a title that hid its subject
Asked readers to skip the preface entirely
Placed a glossary of every term at the start
questions.explain: The preface warning and the analytical table of contents are the two aids named; the other options are not mentioned and run against the authors' point about helpful front matter.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Match each pair or group of books in How to Read a Book to what the authors say about classifying them by title.
pairs: Euclid's Elements, Descartes' Geometry, Hilbert's Foundations of Geometry
Titles make it easy to see they are mathematical books
The City of God, Leviathan, Social Contract
Titles do not easily show they are political treatises
Elements of Geometry and Principles of Psychology
Alike only if you know both geometry and psychology are sciences
Aristotle's Politics and The Wealth of Nations
Comparable only if you know what a practical problem is
questions.explain: Titles sometimes make grouping easy and sometimes not; and even when grouped, you need categories such as science or practical problem to see how books are alike and different.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Put these examples in How to Read a Book in the order the authors present them in discussing titles.
items: Darwin's The Origin of Species
Gibbon's The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
Einstein and Infeld's The Evolution of Physics
Euclid's Elements and James' Principles of Psychology
questions.explain: The authors begin with the misremembered Darwin title, then Gibbon, then Einstein and Infeld's helpful preface, then the point that titles need categories already in mind.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, why is reading the title carefully not enough to classify a book?
questions.a: The clearest titles and most explicit front matter will not help unless you already have the broad lines of classification in mind. For example, you cannot see how Euclid's Elements of Geometry and James' Principles of Psychology are alike unless you know both geometry and psychology are sciences, nor tell them apart unless you know there are different kinds of science.

questions.q: What is the next step, according to How to Read a Book, when titles and front matter fail to classify a book as practical or theoretical?
questions.a: You continue the inspectional reading into the body of the book: reading passages that seem to summarize, and the beginning and end of the book and its major parts. By paying attention to the words used and keeping the basic categories in mind, you should be able to classify the book without reading very far.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what distinction do Adler and Van Doren reach by polishing the everyday sense of "theoretical" and "practical"?
options: Knowledge and action as the two ends a writer may have in mind
Truth and falsehood as the two outcomes a book may reach
Fiction and fact as the two materials a writer may use
Visionary dreams and cash returns as two kinds of value
questions.explain: The hardheaded man's view holds a rough truth: the practical concerns what works and the theoretical what is to be understood. Polished, this becomes knowledge versus action.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, theoretical books teach you that something is the case, while practical books teach you ____ to do something.
questions.explain: The authors sum up the distinction as knowing that versus knowing how.

questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, how can practical books still be expository if expository books convey knowledge?
options: Practical books convey no knowledge at all, only commands and exhortations
Intelligent action depends on knowledge, so practical books convey it with a view to its application
Practical books are really a kind of fiction about what might be done
Only theoretical books are expository; practical books form a separate class
questions.explain: The authors answer that intelligent action depends on knowledge; practical writers communicate knowledge too, but always with an emphasis upon its application.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren classify How to Read a Book itself as a theoretical book.
questions.explain: They state plainly that their book is practical, not theoretical, since it teaches how to do something: read better.

questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book count as practical books?
options: A cooking manual
A treatise on ethics
A guidebook
A sociological study that merely reports how people behave
A book on how we in fact know what we know
questions.explain: Manuals, moral treatises and guidebooks tell you what to do or how to do it. A purely reporting sociological study is theoretical, a work of science, and an inquiry into how we know is theoretical too.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, practical books on economic, ethical or political problems are properly called ____ and form a very special category.
questions.explain: The authors call these moral treatises normative and promise to explain later why they form a special category of practical books.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what is wrong with the objection that a book on ethics or economics is not practical because it is not true or would not work?
options: Ethics books are in fact theoretical, so the objection mistakes their class
Only economics books that work are practical, so the objection is half right
Whether a book is true or works is irrelevant to whether it is practical
Books that are not true cannot be classified at all, so the question is empty
questions.explain: A book that tells us what we should do is practical whether or not we agree with it; an untrue economics book is simply a bad practical book.

questions.q: Match each work discussed in How to Read a Book to how the authors classify it.
pairs: Practical, about right conduct and duty
Partly of one sort and partly of another
questions.explain: Kant's first Critique asks what is and how we in fact know it, while the second concerns how people should conduct themselves; the Manifesto is oratory; Spinoza's Ethics mixes kinds.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why is Kant's Critique of Practical Reason still a practical book even for readers who find its stress on duty impractical?
options: Kant labelled it practical in his title, and titles settle a book's kind
Any book about duty is automatically a manual of an art
Modern readers have come to agree that duty is a useful ethical idea
Calling it impractical only means they think Kant is wrong, not that it stops guiding conduct
questions.explain: The book is about how men should conduct themselves, which makes it practical; disagreement with its approach does not change its kind.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say every practical book is somewhat oratorical, yet oratory and exhortation are not coextensive with the practical.
questions.explain: Anyone writing practically tries to persuade, but a political harangue differs from a treatise on politics, as the Communist Manifesto differs from Capital.

questions.q: Sort these words by the kind of book that, according to How to Read a Book, frequently uses them.

items.t: should
ought
good and bad
ends and means
is
these are the facts

questions.explain: A practical book soon betrays itself by words like should, ought, good, bad, ends and means; a theoretical book keeps saying is and tries to show that something is true.

questions.q: Sort these books by how How to Read a Book classifies them.

items.t: Locke's Treatise Concerning the Origin, Extent, and End of Civil Government
Kant's Critique of Practical Reason
A manual of engineering
Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding
Kant's Critique of Pure Reason
A statistical study of economic behavior

questions.explain: Books about government, conduct or how to do things are practical; analyses of understanding, of what can be known, and statistical economic studies are theoretical.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what key difference do the authors find between Locke's stated aim for his Essay and the title of his book on government?
options: One concerns the certainty of knowledge, the other the end or purpose of government
One concerns the origin of knowledge, the other the history of government
One concerns the extent of knowledge, the other the limits of government power
One concerns human feelings, the other the laws of nature
questions.explain: Locke's introduction speaks of the origin, certainty and extent of knowledge, while the government title speaks of origin, extent and end. Questions of validity are theoretical; questions of purpose are practical.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, if a title contains phrases such as "the art of" or "how ____," you can spot at once that the book is practical.
questions.explain: Such phrases, or the name of a practical field like ethics, engineering or business, let you classify a book fairly readily.

questions.q: Put these steps for classifying a book as practical or theoretical, as described in How to Read a Book, in the order a reader would take them.
items: Read the title and other front matter
Read passages of a summary nature and the beginning and end
Watch the main body of the text for words like should or is
questions.explain: The front matter comes first; when it is not enough you read summary passages and beginnings and ends, relying on signs in the main body of the text.

questions.q: Which of these warnings about classification signs does How to Read a Book give?
options: Some books on economics are purely theoretical
Some books claim to teach you how to think
Some authors do not know the difference between theory and practice
Titles never give any clue to a book's kind
Every book belongs wholly to one category
questions.explain: The authors say to mistrust the signs: economics can be theoretical, how-to-think books exist, and some authors confuse theory and practice. Yet titles often help, and some books, such as Spinoza's Ethics, are mixed.

questions.q: Explain the distinction between knowing that and knowing how in How to Read a Book, and its link to practical and theoretical books.
questions.a: To make knowledge practical we must convert it into rules of operation, passing from knowing what is the case to knowing what to do about it. Theoretical books teach you that something is the case; practical books teach you how to do something you want to do or think you should do.

questions.q: A friend says a book of economic policy advice is not practical because its recommendations are wrong. How would Adler and Van Doren reply?
questions.a: They would say truth or workability is irrelevant to whether a book is practical. A work on economics that tells us how to organize economic life and what we should and should not do is practical even if we disagree with it; if it is not true, it is simply a bad book.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, history is called ____, from the Greek words for time and place.
questions.explain: “History is chronotopic.” It always deals with things that existed or events that occurred at a particular date and place.

questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, what is the essence of history?
options: The search for laws that hold at any time or place
Narration of particular past events that underwent changes over time
Reflection on common experience to reach general truths
Experiment and field research beyond everyday experience
questions.explain: “The essence of history is narration.” Seeking laws belongs to science, and appeal to common experience to philosophy.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how does science differ from history?
options: Science studies the distant past while history studies only recent events
Science relies on common experience while history relies on experiment
Science seeks laws about what happens at any time or place, not particular past events
Science tells stories while history states general truths
questions.explain: The scientist wants to know how things happen for the most part or in every case; the historian narrates how particular things happened at a given time and place.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say the title of a scientific work is usually more revealing than the title of a history book.
questions.explain: They say the reverse: in history the title usually does the trick, while scientific titles often name a subject such as physics or psychology that both scientists and philosophers have claimed.

questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, what criterion always works to tell a scientific book from a philosophical one?
options: Whether the word "science" or "philosophy" appears in its title
Whether it deals with past events or with general truths
Whether its author was trained in a laboratory or a university
Whether it relies on experience outside the normal, routine daily experience of the reader
questions.explain: A theoretical book that emphasizes things outside ordinary daily experience is scientific; one that appeals only to common experience is philosophical. Titles are unreliable here, as Aristotle's Physics and Newton's Principia show.

questions.q: Match each work in How to Read a Book to the kind of experience the authors say it relies on.
pairs: Dark rooms, prisms, mirrors and controlled light
Years of observation in the field
Everyone's experience of their own mental processes
questions.explain: Galileo, Newton and Darwin rely on special experience, so their books are scientific; Locke appeals to common experience, so his Essay is philosophical.

questions.q: Match each title in How to Read a Book to the naming puzzle the authors point out.
pairs: Called scientific by its author, philosophical by current usage
Newton's Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy
Called philosophy, now a masterpiece of science
Both scientific and philosophical, but primarily scientific
questions.explain: The words science and philosophy have been used variously, so titles mislead; James takes a middle course between special and common experience.

questions.q: Which of these are traits of philosophy, according to How to Read a Book?
options: It seeks general truths rather than accounts of particular events
It appeals to the ordinary experience of the reader
It requires experiments in the laboratory
It narrates events at a particular date and place
It can solve some important problems in an armchair
questions.explain: Like science, philosophy seeks general truths, but it proves its points by common experience and can settle some problems by armchair thinking. Laboratory work marks science, and narration of dated events marks history.

questions.q: Sort these authors' works by how How to Read a Book classifies them.

items.t: Galileo's Two New Sciences
Newton's Opticks
Many of Freud's writings
Darwin's The Origin of Species
Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding
Aristotle's Physics, by current usage

questions.explain: Works that depend on special experience such as experiments, clinical observation or field work are scientific; Locke's Essay appeals to common experience and is philosophical, and the authors say Aristotle's Physics is now regarded as philosophical.
