questions.q: Sort these features by whether How to Read a Book links them to history or to science.

items.t: Narrative in form
Deals with a particular date and place
Must obey the rules for telling a good story
Seeks laws or generalizations
Treats matters that can happen at any time
Relies on special experience to prove its conclusions

questions.explain: History narrates particular events and so must tell a good story; science looks for laws holding anywhere and proves its points by special experience.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the popular contrast is that science is experimental while philosophy is merely ____ thinking.
questions.explain: The authors accept the contrast but say it should not be invidious: some important problems can be solved in an armchair by someone who thinks about common human experience.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what is true of the philosopher and the scientist?
options: Both observe and think, but they prove conclusions by different kinds of experience
The philosopher only thinks while the scientist only observes
The scientist only thinks while the philosopher only observes
Both rely on exactly the same experiences but argue in different words
questions.explain: The authors deny that the philosopher is a pure thinker and the scientist a mere observer; the scientist points to special experience, the philosopher to experience common to all.

questions.q: Put the kinds of theoretical book in the order How to Read a Book discusses them in its section on kinds of theoretical books.
items: History
Science
Philosophy
questions.explain: The section takes history first, then science, then philosophy, before contrasting science and philosophy by the experience they rely on.

questions.q: Which of these clues does How to Read a Book say reveal a classroom's subject to a visitor?
options: The kind of words the teacher uses
The type of arguments the teacher employs
The kind of responses the teacher expects
The number of students in the room
The time of day the class meets
questions.explain: The authors list the teacher's way of proceeding, words, arguments, problems and expected responses. Class size and timing are not mentioned.

questions.q: A reader picks up a book on the mind that asks readers to check every claim against their own memories and habits of thought, with no lab results. How would Adler and Van Doren classify it, and why?
questions.a: They would call it philosophical, because it appeals to no facts outside the ordinary experience of the reader. Like Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding, it makes every point in terms of the experience we all have of our own mental processes, whereas a scientific work, like much of Freud, relies on special experience such as clinical observation.

questions.q: How does the classroom analogy in How to Read a Book answer the objection that classifying books before reading them is overdone?
questions.a: A visitor to a class could soon tell whether it was history, science or philosophy from the teacher's words, arguments, problems and expected responses, and knowing this helps one listen intelligently. Since the art of being taught must respond to the art of teaching, and books relate to readers as teachers to students, we must learn to read each kind of book in an appropriate manner.

questions.q: Why must a historian write poetically, according to How to Read a Book?
questions.a: The typical history book is narrative in form, and a narrative is a narrative whether it is fact or fiction. So the historian must obey the rules for telling a good story, which is not required of works like Locke's Essay or Newton's Principia, neither of which is a good story.

questions.q: In 'How to Read a Book', what image do Adler and Van Doren use for the structure a reader must find beneath a book's surface?
options: A skeleton hidden beneath flesh and clothes
A map hidden inside a sealed envelope
A foundation buried under a finished building
A melody hidden among an orchestra's notes
questions.explain: The chapter opens with the claim “Every book has a skeleton hidden between its covers.” The reader must see it with X-ray eyes, without tearing off the flesh.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, which books do Rules 2 and 3 of analytical reading apply to?
options: Only expository books such as science and philosophy
Any book, though applied differently to each kind
Only books of fiction, poetry, and drama
Only practical books that aim to guide conduct
questions.explain: The authors stress that the rules apply to any book, poetry as well as science, though their application differs with the kind of book.

questions.q: In explaining Rule 3, why do Adler and Van Doren say a book is like a single house rather than a heap of bricks?
options: It is built according to a fixed architectural standard
Its parts are all of exactly the same size and shape
Its parts are organically connected and serve the whole
It can only be understood by its original builder
questions.explain: A heap of bricks is a mere collection, while a house has rooms connected by a traffic pattern so each contributes to the whole; a good book likewise is an orderly arrangement of related parts.

questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, are the best books also the most readable?
options: They use simpler vocabulary than lesser books
They are shorter and avoid complicated subjects
Their authors always state their plan in the preface
Their parts are better organized and more unified
questions.explain: The best books have the most intelligible structure; their greater complexity is also a greater simplicity because the parts are better organized and unified. Length or vocabulary is not the point.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: In Rule 2, what sense of the word "about" do Adler and Van Doren want the reader to capture?
options: What the author is up to, the book's main point
The kind of subject matter the book treats
The historical period in which the book was written
The audience for whom the author wrote
questions.explain: The colloquial sense of what someone is about, what he is up to, points to the book's theme or main point. Knowing the type of subject matter only tells you what kind of book it is, which was Rule 1.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Whom do Adler and Van Doren cite as showing that the unity of the Odyssey can be summarized in a few sentences?
options: Plato in the Republic
Aristotle in the Poetics
Aquinas in his commentaries
Herodotus in his history
questions.explain: Aristotle, in his Poetics, insists that a single unity of action marks every good story and summarizes the Odyssey to show it.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: In Adler and Van Doren's discussion of plots, what separates a good story from a bad one with the same essential plot?
options: The number of characters the author introduces
Whether the plot follows the boy-meets-girl formula
What the author does with the plot, how he dresses the bones
How faithfully the author copies an older story
questions.explain: Since there are only a few plots, the difference lies in what the author does with the plot, how he dresses up the bare bones.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, how do expository books differ from fiction in helping a reader find the unity?
options: Expository authors usually hide their plan to keep the reader curious
Fiction writers usually summarize the whole story in a preface
Fiction and expository books never reveal their unity in titles
Expository authors often state their plan early, with no reason for suspense
questions.explain: A scientific or philosophical writer has no reason to keep you in suspense, so an expository book may summarize itself in its first paragraph, like a newspaper article.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren say about relying on an author's preface to find a book's unity?
options: Use it as a guide, but the reader must still read the whole book
The preface always contains the definitive statement of unity
Ignore it, since authors usually misdescribe their own books
Read only the preface and the conclusion to save effort
questions.explain: They say not to be too proud to accept the author's help, but not to rely on it too completely; the obligation of finding the unity belongs finally to the reader and is discharged only by reading the whole book.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: In Adler and Van Doren's example of Herodotus, what should a reader do after reading his introductory summary?
options: Stop there, since it states the whole book perfectly
Read all nine parts and elaborate the statement to do justice to the whole
Replace it with a summary of the Persian kings only
List every fascinating detail Herodotus includes
questions.explain: The opening is a good beginning, but after reading the nine parts the reader will probably need to add the main kings, heroes, and battles, while leaving out the many details.

questions.q: What does the title 'X-raying a Book' signal about the rules in that chapter of Adler and Van Doren's book?
options: They teach the reader to judge whether a book's claims are true
They teach the reader to skim a book quickly before buying it
They teach the reader to see the hidden structure beneath a book's surface
They teach the reader to compare several books on one subject
questions.explain: The chapter's rules aim at a book's structure, its skeleton hidden beneath the flesh. Judging truth and comparing books belong to later chapters on criticism and syntopical reading.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren treat Locke's own summary of his Essay Concerning Human Understanding?
options: They reject it and offer a completely different statement
They say it is too long and must be cut to one phrase
They say it describes a different book from the one Locke wrote
They accept it but add two subordinate qualifications for the first and third parts
questions.explain: They would not quarrel with Locke's excellent statement, except to add that there are no innate ideas and that language will be discussed, to do justice to the first and third parts.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what makes one statement of a book's unity better than another?
options: Being brief, accurate, and comprehensive
Matching the author's own words exactly
Being as long and detailed as possible
Agreeing with what most readers have said
questions.explain: One statement is better than another in proportion as it is brief, accurate, and comprehensive; there is no one right wording, and it need not echo the author.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, why are Rules 2 and 3 stated separately rather than as one rule?
options: Because they apply to entirely different kinds of books
Mainly for convenience: a complex structure is easier to grasp in two steps
Because Rule 3 is optional and Rule 2 is required
Because Rule 2 is for the reader and Rule 3 for the writer
questions.explain: The separation is primarily a matter of convenience: Rule 2 directs attention to the unity and Rule 3 to the complexity; also each part has an interior structure of its own.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: In Adler and Van Doren's account of Rule 3, what does outlining the parts involve beyond listing them?
options: Rewriting each part in simpler language
Judging whether each part is true or false
Treating each part as a subordinate whole with its own unity and complexity
Memorizing the chapter titles in order
questions.explain: Rule 3 involves more than enumerating the parts; it means treating them as subordinate wholes, each with a unity and complexity of its own.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren say about how closely a reader must follow the outlining formula of Rule 3?
options: Every book must be outlined in full detail, in writing
Outlining is only for books one plans to teach
The formula should be ignored by skilled readers
A rough approximation is usually enough, varying with the book and purpose
questions.explain: A good rule describes the ideal performance, but you should be satisfied with a very rough approximation; the degree varies with the character of the book and your purpose.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, can no one carry an outline of a book out to the bitter end?
options: Because books are finite and imperfect, and the outline is of the book, not the subject
Because outlines must never be longer than one page
Because authors forbid readers to outline their books
Because only medieval commentators had the necessary training
questions.explain: They say “No book deserves a perfect outline” because no book is perfect; the outline is of the book itself, not of the subject matter, which could be extended indefinitely.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: In Adler and Van Doren's discussion, what does Aquinas do at the start of each section of his commentary on Aristotle?
options: He translates the passage into Latin verse
He gives an outline of Aristotle's points and says how that part fits the whole
He lists objections to Aristotle's conclusions
He summarizes the whole work in one sentence
questions.explain: Aquinas begins each section with an outline of the points Aristotle made and says explicitly how that part fits the whole, especially in relation to the parts before and after.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: In Adler and Van Doren's sample outline of the US Constitution, what does the first Article deal with?
options: The executive department
The judicial department
The legislative department
The relationship between states and the federal government
questions.explain: In their outline, the Second major division is the first Article, dealing with the legislative department; the second and third Articles cover the executive and judicial.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: What point do Adler and Van Doren make by noting that their outline of Aristotle's Ethics does not match its ten books?
options: Aristotle's Ethics is a badly organized book
Chapter divisions should always be ignored
Only the author's divisions are correct
A reader should make his own outline rather than simply follow chapter divisions
questions.explain: They want to show you need not follow the apparent structure given by chapter divisions; the point is to make your own outline, while still using the author's headings as guides.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: In Adler and Van Doren's example of the two-year-old saying "two plus two is four," what is being illustrated?
options: That a correct statement of a book's unity may be a lucky guess without outlining the parts
That children learn mathematics faster than adults
That true statements are always understood by the speaker
That Rule 3 can be skipped for simple books
questions.explain: Like the child who says something true without knowing what it means, a reader might state a book's unity correctly by luck; outlining the parts shows how and why, so Rule 3 supports Rule 2.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, how do readers and writers differ in their relation to a book's skeleton?
options: Both try to hide the skeleton as much as possible
The reader uncovers the skeleton; the author starts with it and covers it up
The reader builds the skeleton; the author removes it
Neither needs to pay attention to the skeleton
questions.explain: The rules are reciprocal but followed differently: the reader tries to uncover the skeleton the book conceals, while the author starts with it and covers it artistically with flesh.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, why shouldn't an expository book be merely an outline of its subject?
options: Outlines are illegal to publish without permission
Outlines are always longer than finished books
The flesh of a book adds an essential dimension, a kind of life
Readers prefer books with no structure at all
questions.explain: Beyond the fact that most readers cannot read outlines, the flesh is as much a part of a book as the skeleton; writing it out from an outline gives the work a kind of life.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: In Adler and Van Doren's discussion, what should a skilled reader conclude if no effort reveals a book's unity or its parts?
options: The reader must always be at fault
The book must be a work of fiction
The book should be reread from the preface only
Very likely the book is a bad one, whatever its reputation
questions.explain: If, with sufficient skill, you still cannot find the unity and parts, the book is very likely badly made; the authors warn against assuming the fault is always in you.

questions.q: What is the intentional fallacy, as Adler and Van Doren describe it?
options: Thinking you can discover what was in the author's mind from the book
Assuming the author had no problems to solve
Believing that every book has a single correct outline
Judging a book only by its title and preface
questions.explain: Critics call the intentional fallacy the error of thinking you can discover what was in an author's mind from the book, such as psychoanalyzing Shakespeare from Hamlet; Rule 4 is not meant to commit it.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what happens to readers who fail to apply Rule 4?
options: They read faster but remember less
Their grasp of the main point is deficient and their outline chaotic
They become too critical of the author
They confuse fiction with history
questions.explain: Without seeing the author's problems, readers do not see why the book has the unity it has, so their idea of its theme is deficient and their outline chaotic.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say a reader who feels a book's unity but cannot express it has probably still grasped it.
questions.explain: They say not to be satisfied with feeling a unity you cannot express; the reader who says he knows it but cannot say it probably does not even fool himself.

questions.q: True or false: According to Adler and Van Doren, if you need too many words to state a book's unity, you have seen a multiplicity rather than the unity.
questions.explain: They say you must state the unity in a few words; if it takes too many, you have not seen the unity but a multiplicity.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say the plot of Tom Jones can be reduced to the formula: boy meets girl, boy loses girl, boy gets girl.
questions.explain: They give this formula for Tom Jones and say it is the plot of every romance, showing there are only a few plots in the world.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that because each reader states a book's unity differently, there is no objective check on such statements.
questions.explain: Readers may state the unity differently, but the book stays the same, so there can be an objective check on the accuracy of what anyone says about it; this does not mean anything goes.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say a good reader habitually does something approximating the outlining formula, even if he does not write it all out.
questions.explain: The good reader does this habitually, easily and naturally; asked to give an account of the structure, he would approximate the formula.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to Adler and Van Doren, a reader's outline should cover the subject matter a book is about, extending beyond what the author put in it.
questions.explain: Your outline is of the book itself, not the subject matter; the rule does not ask you to put into the book things the author did not put there.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say a variorum edition of a Shakespeare play can be many times as long as the play itself.
questions.explain: They note a variorum edition, which includes an exhaustive outline among other things, may be perhaps ten times as long as the original.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say most books are well made, so a reader who cannot find the unity should assume the fault is his own.
questions.explain: They say the very great majority of books are badly made, so although you should not judge too quickly, the fault is usually in the book.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: True or false: According to Adler and Van Doren, a reader can get the idea of Darwin's Origin of Species by reading some parts carefully, but not the idea of a good novel.
questions.explain: Parts of books conveying knowledge are more autonomous; in a good novel the idea is in the whole, so someone who has read enough to get the idea does not know what he is talking about.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say the first stage of analytical reading must be completed by reading the book through before any later rules are applied.
questions.explain: Stage is not meant chronologically except perhaps for beginners; the practiced reader accomplishes all the stages at once.

questions.q: In Adler and Van Doren's Rule 2, the reader must state the ____ of the whole book in a single sentence or a few sentences.
questions.explain: Rule 2 asks you to state the unity of the whole book as briefly as possible, saying what it is about in the sense of its theme or main point.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that sensible things and human productions are not absolutely simple but are all complex ____.
questions.explain: They argue nothing man knows or makes is absolutely simple; all are complex unities, so you must know how a thing is one and how it is many.

questions.q: In Adler and Van Doren's house analogy, the rooms are connected by doors, corridors, and stairways, by what architects call a "____."
questions.explain: The rooms are partly independent but connected by a traffic pattern, so each contributes its share to the usefulness of the whole house, as the parts of a book do.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Aristotle, as quoted by Adler and Van Doren, calls the few-sentence summary of the Odyssey the essence of the plot, and everything else mere ____.
questions.explain: Aristotle says the summary is the essence of the plot and the rest is episode; knowing the plot lets you put the parts in their places.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: In eighteenth-century books, Adler and Van Doren note, sometimes the ____ alone told the reader what the whole book was about.
questions.explain: Writers then composed elaborate titles, like Jeremy Collier's attack on the English stage, that told the reader the whole book's subject.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren's unity statement for Aristotle's Ethics calls it an inquiry into the nature of human ____.
questions.explain: Their statement describes the Ethics as an inquiry into human happiness and the conditions under which it may be gained or lost, with emphasis on the virtues.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren's unity statement for The Wealth of Nations ends by saying the book argues for the beneficence of free ____.
questions.explain: Their summary covers wages, profits, rent, capital, and money, and ends with the argument for the beneficence of free trade.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: For their example of outlining, Adler and Van Doren divide the United States ____ into eight major parts.
questions.explain: They call the Constitution a well-organized practical document and outline it from the Preamble to the later amendments.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say a good rule always describes the ____ performance, though a skilled person can merely approximate it.
questions.explain: A good rule states the ideal case; you can be a good practitioner if you merely approximate it, so a rough approximation should satisfy you.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren recall the old maxim that writing should have unity, clarity, and ____.
questions.explain: The two rules relate to writing that follows this maxim: find the unity, and appreciate clarity and coherence by finding the distinction and order of parts.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say writing and reading are ____, as are teaching and being taught.
questions.explain: The rules of reading are also rules of writing because the two arts are reciprocal, though followed in different ways.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren's Rule 4 tells the reader to find out what the author's ____ were.
questions.explain: Rule 4 says to find out the author's problems: the book starts with questions and ostensibly contains the answers.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren warn against the ____ fallacy, the error of thinking you can discover what was in an author's mind from his book.
questions.explain: Critics call it the intentional fallacy; psychoanalyzing Shakespeare from Hamlet is their example of the grave error.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren head the first four rules: the first stage of analytical reading, or rules for finding what a book is ____.
questions.explain: The first stage gives knowledge of a book's structure and answers the first basic question: what is the book about as a whole.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: The first rule in Adler and Van Doren's review list is: classify the book according to kind and subject ____.
questions.explain: Rule 1, from the chapter on pigeonholing, classifies the book by kind and subject matter; Rules 2 to 4 follow.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren list among things whose unity is more perfect in proportion as they are good?
options: Music and paintings
Novels and plays
Books that convey knowledge
Dictionary entries
questions.explain: They say a good book, as a work of art, has a more pervasive unity, and this holds for music, paintings, novels, plays, and no less for books that convey knowledge. Dictionaries are not mentioned.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Which of these books do Adler and Van Doren use as examples when illustrating how to state a book's unity?
options: Darwin's The Origin of Species
Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations
Homer's Odyssey
Machiavelli's The Prince
Newton's Principia
questions.explain: The unity examples include the Odyssey, Herodotus, Aristotle's Ethics, The Wealth of Nations, The Origin of Species, and Locke's Essay; The Prince and the Principia are not used here.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren give as reasons most readers cannot briefly say what a book is about?
options: A widespread inability to speak concise English sentences
Neglect of the rule in reading
Paying little attention to the author's introductory words and title
Most books having no unity at all
questions.explain: They name inability to speak concise sentences, neglect of the rule, and inattention to introductions and titles. They do not claim books lack unity as the reason here.

questions.q: Which of these earlier ideas does 'X-raying a Book' explicitly build on?
options: Rule 1, classifying the book by kind and subject matter
The first basic question: what is the book about as a whole
Inspecting a book well before reading it
The method of syntopical reading across many books
questions.explain: The chapter refers back to Rule 1, to the first basic question a demanding reader asks, and notes that inspecting a book first helps apply the rules. Syntopical reading comes much later in the book.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren mention as works whose commentaries come close to following Rule 3 perfectly?
options: Medieval commentaries on Aristotle
Modern commentaries on Kant's Critique of Pure Reason
Variorum editions of Shakespeare plays
Newspaper reviews of new novels
questions.explain: They mention medieval commentaries on Aristotle, great modern ones on Kant, and variorum Shakespeare editions as the rule followed close to perfection; newspaper reviews are not mentioned.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Which of these are main parts in Adler and Van Doren's first approximation of the structure of Aristotle's Ethics?
options: Happiness as the end of life
Voluntary action and the formation of habits
Friendship
The ideal constitution of the state
The origin of species
questions.explain: Their six parts are happiness, voluntary action and habits, virtues and vices, states neither virtuous nor vicious, friendship, and pleasure. Constitutions and species do not appear.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Which of these alternative ways of dividing the Constitution do Adler and Van Doren mention?
options: Grouping the first three Articles together in one major division
Grouping the amendments by the problems they dealt with
Dividing the document by the year each part was written
Merging the Preamble into the Bill of Rights
questions.explain: They say the first three Articles could be one division, or the amendments could be grouped by the problems they address; dividing by year is not suggested.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say follow from finding a book's unity and parts, given the maxim of unity, clarity, and coherence?
options: What is clear is so by the distinctness of its outlines
What is coherent hangs together in an orderly disposition of parts
The rules can help tell well made books from badly made ones
A clear book needs no structure at all
questions.explain: They say “What is clear is so by the distinctness of its outlines.” Coherence is orderly disposition of parts, and the rules help distinguish well from badly made books.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren list as theoretical questions an author may be trying to answer?
options: Does something exist?
What caused it to exist?
What means should be chosen to a given end?
What are its relations to other things?
Under these conditions, what is the right thing to do?
questions.explain: Existence, cause, and relations to other things are theoretical questions. Means to an end and the right thing to do are listed as practical questions.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say about the first four rules of analytical reading?
options: They form a group with a single aim
Together they give knowledge of a book's structure
They let a reader judge whether the book is true
They are the only rules of analytical reading
questions.explain: The four rules are connected with one aim, knowledge of a book's structure. Judging truth comes later, and other rules follow.

questions.q: Put Adler and Van Doren's chain from bricks to houses in order, from mere collection to single organized whole.
items: A heap of bricks
A collection of houses
A single house
questions.explain: They contrast a heap of bricks with the house they constitute, and a single house with a collection of houses; a book is like a single house. The ordering here goes from least to most organized unity.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Put the events of Aristotle's summary of the Odyssey, as quoted by Adler and Van Doren, in order.
items: A man is absent from home for many years
Suitors waste his substance and plot against his son
Tempest-tossed, he arrives home
He makes certain persons acquainted with him
He attacks and destroys the suitors
questions.explain: Aristotle's summary runs from the long absence and the plight at home, to the arrival, the recognitions, and the destruction of the suitors.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Put the stages of the romance plot formula that Adler and Van Doren apply to Tom Jones in order.
items: Boy meets girl
Boy loses girl
Boy gets girl
questions.explain: They reduce Tom Jones to this familiar formula and say it is the plot of every romance.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Put the steps of Adler and Van Doren's general formula for applying Rule 3 in order.
items: State what the whole book is about
Name the major parts and what each is about
Divide each major part into its sections
State the points made in each section
questions.explain: After the Rule 2 statement of the whole, the formula names the major parts, then the sections of each part, then the points within each section, and so on.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Put the first four major divisions of Adler and Van Doren's outline of the US Constitution in order.
items: The Preamble
The legislative Article
The executive Article
The judicial Article
questions.explain: Their outline begins with the Preamble, then the first, second, and third Articles covering the legislative, executive, and judicial departments.

questions.q: Put these tasks of analytical reading in the order the book's chapters take them up, starting from 'Pigeonholing a Book'.
items: Classifying the book
Finding its structure and the author's problems
Interpreting the author's terms
Criticizing the book fairly
questions.explain: Chapter 6 classifies, Chapter 7 finds structure and problems, Chapter 8 comes to terms with the author, and Chapter 10 turns to criticism, as the table of contents shows.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Put these parts of Adler and Van Doren's outline of Aristotle's Ethics in their order.
items: Happiness as the end of life
Voluntary action and habits
The virtues and vices
Friendship
Pleasure, completing the account of happiness
questions.explain: Their outline runs happiness, voluntary action, virtues and vices, states neither virtuous nor vicious, friendship, and finally pleasure.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Put these sections in the order Adler and Van Doren outline them for the first Article of the Constitution.
items: Legislative powers vested in a Congress
Composition of the House and Senate
Election and internal organization of Congress
The President's veto power
The powers of Congress
questions.explain: Their outline goes Section 1, Sections 2 and 3, Sections 4 and 5, then Section 7 on the veto and Section 8 on the powers of Congress.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Put the four rules of the first stage of analytical reading in Adler and Van Doren's order.
items: Classify the book by kind and subject matter
State what the whole book is about briefly
Enumerate and outline the major parts
Define the author's problems
questions.explain: The review list gives these four in this order under the heading of rules for finding what a book is about.

questions.q: Put these chapters of 'How to Read a Book' in their order in the book.
items: Pigeonholing a Book
X-raying a Book
Coming to Terms with an Author
Determining an Author's Message
questions.explain: In the table of contents, Chapter 6 is Pigeonholing a Book, Chapter 7 X-raying a Book, Chapter 8 Coming to Terms, and Chapter 9 Determining an Author's Message.

questions.q: Put the sections of the chapter 'X-raying a Book' in their order.
items: Stating the unity of a book
The art of outlining a book
The reciprocal arts of reading and writing
Discovering the author's intentions
The first stage of analytical reading
questions.explain: The chapter moves from Rule 2, to Rule 3, to reading and writing as reciprocal, to Rule 4, and closes by gathering the first four rules into the first stage.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Match each book to the kind Adler and Van Doren use it to illustrate when stating unity.
pairs: A story with a single unity of action
questions.explain: They present the Ethics and The Wealth of Nations as practical, Darwin as theoretical science, Locke as theoretical philosophy, and the Odyssey as a story.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Match each book to the core of Adler and Van Doren's statement of its unity.
pairs: The nature of happiness and how it is gained or lost
The source of national wealth in an economy with division of labor
Variation of living things producing new groupings
The origin, certainty, and extent of human knowledge
questions.explain: Each pairing restates the opening of the summary the authors give for that book.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Match each author to how Adler and Van Doren say he helps the reader see his book's unity.
pairs: A statement of the plan of the work at the start
His own summary, which they accept with additions
questions.explain: Collier's title, Herodotus' opening, Smith's plan of several pages, and Locke's summary are their examples of authors helping the reader.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Match each part of Adler and Van Doren's outline of Constitution Article I to what it covers.
pairs: Relation of Congress to the executive and the veto
Limitations on the powers of Congress
Limitations on the powers of the states
questions.explain: These match the outline items II,4 through II,8 in their sample outline of the first Article.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Match each part of Aristotle's Ethics in Adler and Van Doren's outline to where it falls in the ten books.
pairs: Happiness as the end of life
Book II and the first half of Book III
The rest of Book III through Book VI
End of Book VII and start of Book X
questions.explain: They map their parts onto Aristotle's books to show the outline need not follow the chapter divisions.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Match each quality in the old maxim of good writing to how Adler and Van Doren say the reader recognizes it.
questions.explain: If the writing has unity we must find it; clarity and coherence are appreciated by finding the distinction and the order of the parts.

questions.q: Match each question to its type in Adler and Van Doren's list of questions authors try to answer.
pairs: What kind of thing is it?
What things must one do to gain an objective?
questions.explain: Questions about existence, kind, cause, properties, relations, and behavior are theoretical; questions about ends, means, and what to do are practical.

questions.q: Match each chapter of 'How to Read a Book' to its role around 'X-raying a Book'.
pairs: Coming to Terms with an Author
Begins the next stage, interpreting terms
questions.explain: Chapter 6 classifies, Chapter 7 completes the first stage, and the following chapters move to interpretation and then criticism, as the table of contents shows.

questions.q: Sort these by whether Adler and Van Doren's house analogy treats them as a true whole or a mere collection.

items.t: A single house
A good book with connected parts
A heap of bricks
A group of separate houses

questions.explain: Organically related parts make a whole; without that relation there is merely a collection, like a heap of bricks or a set of houses.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Sort these by whether Adler and Van Doren treat them as practical or theoretical books in their unity examples.

items.t: Aristotle's Ethics
The Wealth of Nations
The Origin of Species
Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding

questions.explain: They introduce the Ethics and Smith as practical books, and Darwin and Locke as theoretical books in science and philosophy.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Sort these by whether Adler and Van Doren connect them to Rule 2 or to Rule 3.

items.t: Directs attention to the book's unity
Stated in a sentence or a short paragraph
Directs attention to the book's complexity
Treats parts as subordinate wholes
Could in theory run longer than the book

questions.explain: Rule 2 concerns the unity and is brief; Rule 3 concerns complexity, outlines parts as wholes, and could in theory be longer than the original.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Sort these by whether Adler and Van Doren describe them as the reader's or the writer's task.

items.t: Uncover the skeleton the book conceals
Find the unity of the book
Start with the skeleton and cover it
Put flesh on the bare bones

questions.explain: The reader uncovers the skeleton and finds the unity; the author starts with the skeleton and conceals it artistically with flesh.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Sort these by whether Adler and Van Doren say a reader can get the idea from careful reading of some parts.

items.t: Aristotle's Ethics
Darwin's Origin of Species
A good novel
A play

questions.explain: Parts of books conveying knowledge are more autonomous; in poetical works, plays, and novels the idea is in the whole.

questions.q: Sort these questions into Adler and Van Doren's two types of questions.

items.t: What purpose does it serve?
What are its characteristic properties?
What means should be chosen to a given end?
Under what conditions would it be better to do this rather than that?

questions.explain: Purpose and properties appear in the theoretical list; means to ends and better choices under conditions are practical questions.

questions.q: Sort these rules by whether Adler and Van Doren state them in 'Pigeonholing a Book' or in 'X-raying a Book'.

items.t: Classify the book by kind and subject matter
State the unity of the whole book
Set forth the major parts and their order
Find out what the author's problems were

questions.explain: Rule 1 was covered earlier, as the chapter itself notes; Chapter 7 states Rules 2, 3, and 4.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say a reader needs X-ray eyes when reading a book?
questions.a: Every book has a structure hidden under its surface, like a skeleton under flesh and clothes. The reader does not tear the book apart but must see through it to grasp that structure, since apprehending a book's structure is essential to apprehending the book.

questions.q: Explain Adler and Van Doren's claim that a good book's greater complexity is also a greater simplicity.
questions.a: The best books are usually more complex than poor ones, but their parts are better organized and more unified. So their structure is more intelligible, which makes them more readable; lesser books are more bothersome because their plan is less clear.

questions.q: How does Rule 2 differ from Rule 1 in Adler and Van Doren's account?
questions.a: Rule 1 says what kind of book it is, by its type of subject matter. Rule 2 says what the book is about in the sense of what the author is up to, its theme or main point, stated in a sentence or short paragraph.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: What does Aristotle's summary of the Odyssey show, according to Adler and Van Doren?
questions.a: It shows that a complex story full of episodes still has a single unity of action that can be stated in a few sentences. Once you know this essential plot, you can put the many episodes into their proper places.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren mean by saying there are only a small number of plots in the world?
questions.a: Many stories share the same essential plot, as with boy meets girl, boy loses girl, boy gets girl in every romance. What distinguishes good from bad stories is what the author does with that plot, how he dresses up the bare bones.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: How should a reader use an author's own statement of his plan, according to Adler and Van Doren?
questions.a: Accept the help, since authors of expository books often summarize themselves early. But do not rely on it completely, because authors' plans go awry; the obligation of finding the unity belongs finally to the reader and can be met only by reading the whole book.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren warn readers not to treat their sample unity statements as final?
questions.a: A unity can be stated in many ways and there is no one right wording; statements are better as they are brief, accurate, and comprehensive. Yet anything does not go: the book is the same for all readers, so statements can be checked objectively against it.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: What does Adler and Van Doren's treatment of Locke's Essay show about using an author's own summary?
questions.a: They accept Locke's statement of plan as excellent but add two qualifications so it covers the whole: that there are no innate ideas and knowledge comes from experience, and that language is discussed. A good author's summary can be a base for the reader's own fuller statement.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, does Rule 3 involve more than listing a book's major parts?
questions.a: The major parts may be seen when you grasp the unity, but they are themselves complex with an interior structure. So Rule 3 means outlining them, treating each part as a subordinate whole with its own unity and complexity.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say readers should not worry that Rule 3 demands an impossible amount of work?
questions.a: The formula describes the ideal performance, and a rough approximation is usually enough; the degree depends on the book and your purpose. Good readers do it habitually without writing everything out, and no book is perfect enough to deserve a perfect outline anyway.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say a reader should make his own outline instead of following a book's chapter divisions?
questions.a: The apparent structure of chapters may be better or worse than the real one; the author made his outline to write well, and you must make yours to read well. Chapter headings are guides to use actively, not to rely on passively, because “The surface can be deceiving.”

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Explain why Adler and Van Doren call Rule 3 a necessary complement to Rule 2.
questions.a: Without outlining the parts, a correct statement of unity would be only a good guess or lucky hit, like a toddler saying two plus two is four without understanding it. Showing how the parts exemplify and develop the main theme supports and verifies your statement of the unity.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Your friend skims a long report and sums it up in one good sentence. Using Adler and Van Doren's argument, what is still missing?
questions.a: The summary may be right, but from the friend's point of view it is only a lucky guess. To know it is adequate, the friend must also set forth the major parts and show how they develop the main point, as Rule 3 requires.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: In what sense are the rules of reading also rules of writing, according to Adler and Van Doren?
questions.a: Reading and writing are reciprocal: if authors did not unify and order their work, there would be no point in readers seeking its unity and structure. But they are followed differently, since the author covers the skeleton with flesh while the reader uncovers it.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: How can Rules 2 and 3 help a reader judge the quality of a book, according to Adler and Van Doren?
questions.a: If a skilled reader, after real effort, still cannot grasp a book's unity or discern its parts and their relations, the book is very likely bad, whatever its reputation. The reader should not judge too quickly, but should not always blame himself either, since most books are badly made.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren think Rule 4 is useful even though it repeats the work of Rules 2 and 3?
questions.a: Stating the author's main and subordinate questions throws the whole and its parts into another light and can help with finding the unity and parts. Readers who neglect it do not see why the book has the unity it has, so their view of its theme is deficient and their outline chaotic.

questions.q: A student reading a book on how to save for retirement wants to apply Rule 4. Using Adler and Van Doren's ideas, what should she do?
questions.a: She should state the main question the author is trying to answer and the subordinate questions, in an intelligible order of which come first. Since the book is practical, the questions will be about ends and means, such as what ends to seek and what to do, in what order, to reach them.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren mean by calling the first four rules the first stage of analytical reading?
questions.a: Together the four rules give a knowledge of a book's structure and answer the first basic question, what the book is about as a whole. Stage is not meant chronologically: a practiced reader does all the stages at once, though the answer improves as the other rules are applied.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what does Chapter 8, Coming to Terms with an Author, begin?
options: The second stage of analytical reading, which interprets a book's contents
The first stage of analytical reading, which outlines a book's structure
The third stage of analytical reading, which criticizes a book fairly
The inspectional level of reading, which skims a book quickly
questions.explain: Chapter 7 closed the first stage with four rules for classifying and outlining a book; Chapter 8 opens the second stage, whose aim is interpreting the book's message rather than outlining its structure.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do Adler and Van Doren say the title phrase 'coming to terms' is a twist on its usual business meaning?
options: In business it settles a dispute, but in reading it starts one with the author
In business it is the last step, but in reading it is the first step beyond the outline
In business it is a first step, but in reading it is the final step of criticism
In business it needs a lawyer, but in reading it needs only a good dictionary
questions.explain: In a negotiation, coming to terms is the last thing before signing, whereas in analytical reading it is the first step after outlining. It is not the final step of criticism, which comes in later chapters.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, put these chapters of the analytical-reading sequence in the order they appear.
items: X-raying a Book
Coming to Terms with an Author
Determining an Author's Message
Criticizing a Book Fairly
questions.explain: Outlining a book (Chapter 7) comes first, then coming to terms (Chapter 8) and finding propositions and arguments (Chapter 9), and only then fair criticism (Chapter 10).

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the rule of coming to terms is the fifth rule of analytical reading and the first rule of its second stage.
questions.explain: The four rules of the first stage end in Chapter 7, so coming to terms is Rule 5 and opens the interpretive stage.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how does Chapter 8 on coming to terms prepare for Chapter 9, Determining an Author's Message?
questions.a: Chapter 8 gives only the first rule of the interpretive stage; the other rules, on propositions and arguments, follow in the next chapter. All these rules share a pattern of two steps, one dealing with the language as such and one going beyond it to the thought behind it. Coming to terms with words comes first because propositions and arguments are built out of terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what do the authors call the basic element of communicable knowledge?
options: A proposition
An argument
A term
A key sentence
questions.explain: The chapter opens by saying that unless the reader comes to terms with the author, knowledge is not communicated, because a term is the basic element of communicable knowledge. Propositions and arguments belong to the next chapter.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors say that unless the reader comes to ____ with the author, the communication of knowledge does not take place.
questions.explain: Coming to terms is the condition of communication: shared words are not enough without shared meanings.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do Adler and Van Doren say coming to terms is necessary for any communication of knowledge?
questions.a: A term is the basic element of communicable knowledge. If the reader does not grasp the author's words in the meanings the author gives them, words pass between them but no knowledge does. Coming to terms is therefore the first step of interpreting a book after outlining it.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book say about the point where Chapter 8 picks up the reader?
options: The reader has applied the four rules of the first stage
The reader can tell what the book is about
The reader has already judged whether the book is true
The reader has finished all rules of analytical reading
The reader can outline the book's structure
questions.explain: The first stage lets the reader say what the book is about and outline it. Judging truth belongs to the later critical stage, and many rules remain.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how do the authors finally define a term?
options: A word that has only one meaning in the dictionary
A technical word coined by the author
A word printed in italics or quotation marks
A word used unambiguously
questions.explain: They first say a term is an unambiguous word, then correct this: strictly there are no unambiguous words, so a term is a word used unambiguously.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say terms can be found in a good dictionary.
questions.explain: They say “You cannot find terms in dictionaries”, though the materials for making them are there; terms occur only in the process of communication.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors say that where there is unresolved ____ in communication, there is no communication, or at best incomplete communication.
questions.explain: If the author uses a word in one meaning and the reader takes it in another, only the words are shared, not the meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why is finding an author's important words not enough to come to terms with him?
questions.a: A term is not just a word, because a word, especially an important one, can have many meanings. If the author uses a word in one sense and the reader reads it in another, words have passed between them but no meaning is shared. The reader must also determine the meaning in which the author uses each important word.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, to which kind of writing do the authors say the rule of coming to terms chiefly applies?
options: Expository writing that conveys knowledge
Poetry, where words carry layered meanings
Fiction, where dialogue must be read closely
Newspaper writing for everyday readers
questions.explain: They say they are speaking exclusively of expository books; poetry and fiction are not nearly so concerned with the unambiguous use of words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, Rule 5 says: find the important ____ and through them come to terms with the author.
questions.explain: The rule has two parts: locate the words that make a difference, then determine their meanings as used.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which of these are the two parts of Rule 5 in How to Read a Book?
options: Locate the important words
Look up each word in a dictionary
Determine the meaning of those words, as used, with precision
Find the author's key sentences
Judge whether the author's terms are true
questions.explain: The rule's first part locates the words that make a difference and the second fixes their meanings. Key sentences belong to the next rule, and terms are not true or false.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what would happen if language were a perfect, 'diaphanous' medium in which every word was an ideal term?
options: Poetry would become the only form of writing
Interpretation would be unnecessary
Readers would still need a dictionary at every page
Outlining a book would become impossible
questions.explain: The reader would see straight through the words to the writer's mind, so the second stage of analytical reading would not be needed.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what image do the authors use for writer and reader overcoming the barrier of language?
options: Two climbers roped together on one mountain
Two ships signalling across a foggy harbour
Two teams tunnelling from opposite sides of a mountain
Two builders laying bricks on the same wall
questions.explain: Like tunnellers who meet only if they calculate by the same engineering principles, reader and writer meet only if both work by shared skills. The reader must meet the writer halfway.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do the authors say a good writer cannot achieve communication by himself?
questions.a: Language is an imperfect medium and so acts as a barrier between minds. The writer does his best to reach through it, but the reader must meet him halfway with a reciprocal skill, just as teaching avails only if there is reciprocal activity of being taught. A meeting of minds depends on both working together.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each aspect of the rules of interpretive reading to what it deals with.
questions.explain: Each interpretive rule has a grammatical step dealing with words and a logical step dealing with terms, and both are indispensable for communication.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors say each rule of interpretive reading has a grammatical aspect and a ____ aspect.
questions.explain: The grammatical step deals with words; the logical step deals with their meanings, that is, with terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors symbolize the word 'reading' as X and three meanings as a, b and c. What are Xa, Xb and Xc?
options: Three words but one term
Three words and three terms
One word and one term
Three terms but one word
questions.explain: X stays the same, so there is one word, but there are three terms provided writer and reader know which sense is in use. Minds meet in Xa, Xb or Xc, not in X alone.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each letter in the authors' 'reading' scheme to what it stands for.
questions.explain: The scheme shows one word carrying three meanings, each of which becomes a term only when both parties know which is meant.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort each statement by whether it is true of a word or of a term.

items.t: Can be found in a dictionary
Usually has many meanings
Exists only in the process of communication
Has one meaning shared by writer and reader at a time
Can pass between two people without shared meaning
Is the basic element of communicable knowledge

questions.explain: Words are the dictionary's material and are mostly ambiguous; a term is a word used unambiguously by writer and reader in communication.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, if the authors write 'reading' in the sense of reading for information and you read it as reading for entertainment, what has happened?
options: The same word passed between you, but you have not come to terms
You have come to terms, since the word is the same
You have found a synonym for the author's term
You have discovered the author's technical vocabulary
questions.explain: Writing Xa while the reader reads Xb shares the word but not the meaning, so the ambiguity impedes communication.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what is the authors' main point about the relation between words and terms?
questions.a: One word can be the vehicle for many terms, and one term can be expressed by many words. The word 'reading', for example, carries the terms reading for entertainment, for information and for understanding. Communication happens only when reader and writer use the same word with the same meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say most of the words an author uses are important for interpreting the book.
questions.explain: They say you can be sure most of an author's words are not important; only words used in a special way matter.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors say Eddington cannot use the word '____' lightheartedly because he uses it in a special sense in discussing causation.
questions.explain: Unlike 'reading', 'cause' is used in a definitely special sense in his theory of causation, so its meaning matters to both author and reader.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book say make it harder to tell ordinary words from special ones?
options: Reading books written in the past
Authors who deliberately use archaic words or senses
Books translated from foreign languages
Books written by contemporary authors
Words used as the man in the street uses them
questions.explain: Words are not equally familiar in every time and place, and archaic usage and translation complicate matters; contemporary writers use words as you do today.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, which word do the authors call clearly the most important one in Chapter 8 up to that point?
options: Word
Term
Ambiguity
Communication
questions.explain: They list 'word', 'term', 'ambiguity' and 'communication' as the few important words, with 'term' clearly the most important and the others important in relation to it.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what paradox do the authors note about locating the key words in a passage?
questions.a: You cannot locate the key words without trying to understand the passage, yet if you understood it you would already know which words matter. If you do not understand it, it is probably because you do not know how the author is using certain words. So marking the words that trouble you is likely to hit the ones the author uses specially.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say that from the reader's point of view the most important words are those that give you trouble.
questions.explain: Words that trouble you are likely to be the ones the author uses specially, since ordinary words should give no trouble, though they may not always be important for the author.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors say most of the words in any book can be read just as one would use them in talking to one's ____.
questions.explain: Prepositions, conjunctions, articles and most nouns and verbs are used ordinarily, so only a few words need special effort.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, put the steps the authors suggest for spotting key words by trouble in the order they occur.
items: Try to understand the passage
Notice the words that give you trouble
Mark those words
Work out the terms they convey
questions.explain: Effort to understand reveals the troubling words; marking them locates the places where the work of coming to terms must be done.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort these words by whether the authors treat them as used ordinarily or specially in the book being discussed.

items.t: 'reading' in Eddington's 'pointer-readings'
'cause' in Eddington's theory of causation
Prepositions and articles in How to Read a Book
'term' in Chapter 8 of How to Read a Book
'reading' in How to Read a Book

questions.explain: Eddington uses 'reading' ordinarily but 'cause' specially; in How to Read a Book itself, 'reading' and 'term' are special while function words are ordinary.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how do the authors suggest a reader first tells important words from ordinary ones?
questions.a: Most words are used as the man in the street uses them, with a range of meanings and shifts the context makes clear, so the reader has no trouble with them. Only words the author uses in a special way are important. By eliminating the ordinary words, the reader is left with the words that give trouble, which are likely the special ones.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book list as positive signs that an author stresses a word?
options: Quotation marks or italics around it
Explicitly discussing its various senses
Defining the thing the word names
Using it in the book's first sentence
Repeating it in every paragraph
questions.explain: Typographical devices, explicit discussion of senses, and defining the thing named are the signs given; placement or mere repetition are not.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how do the authors say you know 'equals', 'whole' and 'part' are important in Euclid?
options: Euclid defines them at the start
They are printed in italics
They occur in his axioms
He quarrels with other geometers about them
questions.explain: Unlike 'point' or 'line', these words name nothing Euclid defines; their importance shows because they occur in the axioms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors say: Every field of knowledge has its own technical ____.
questions.explain: They write “Every field of knowledge has its own technical vocabulary.” Euclid makes his plain at the start; elsewhere the reader must discover it.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say the geometrical method of exposition used in mathematics works in every field of knowledge.
questions.explain: Some men thought any subject could be expounded geometrically, but the authors say that method is not applicable in every field.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each author to a technical word the authors say belongs to him.
questions.explain: Each word is used in a special sense by its author: wealth for Smith, species for Darwin, point for Euclid, and cause in Eddington's theory of causation.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort these words by whether the authors list them as important words of Adam Smith or of Darwin.

items.t: capital
rent
commodity
variety
selection
adaptation
wages
hybrid

questions.explain: Smith's list includes labor, capital, land, wages, profits, rent and commodity; Darwin's includes variety, genus, selection, survival, adaptation and hybrid.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, when the author has not pointed out his technical words, what can help the reader find them?
options: Counting how often each word occurs in the book
Reading reviews of the book by other critics
Checking which words appear in the index only
Prior knowledge of the subject and the rules for analyzing structure
questions.explain: Knowing something of biology or economics, and knowing the book's kind, unity and parts through title, chapter headings and preface, helps separate technical from ordinary words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors say ____ are notorious for having private vocabularies.
questions.explain: They write “Philosophers are notorious for having private vocabularies.” Philosophy is a field without a well-established technical vocabulary.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, which practice of philosophers do the authors call most likely to mislead a reader?
options: Taking a word from common speech and making it technical
Coining entirely new words
Using words from other languages
Refusing to define any words at all
questions.explain: A reader who supposes he knows the common word may treat it as ordinary; good authors usually warn explicitly when they do this.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what do the authors mean by an author's special vocabulary, and why is it broader than technical vocabulary?
questions.a: It is the relatively small set of words that express the author's main ideas and leading concepts, the words that carry his analysis and argument. Some may be used in a very special way, others in a way traditional in the field. For the reader, any other word whose meaning is not clear is also important.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what is the outstanding fault of the non-active or undemanding reader?
options: Reading too slowly to finish books
Inattention to words, and so failure to come to terms
Disagreeing with the author too quickly
Taking too many notes in the margins
questions.explain: The authors say “Most of us are addicted to non-active reading.” Its chief fault is inattention to words and the resulting failure to come to terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do the authors say a reader who fails to mark the words he does not understand is headed for disaster?
questions.a: A book that can increase your understanding must contain words that are not completely intelligible to you at first. All the aids for finding key words are useless without a deliberate effort to note the words that need work. Treating every word as ordinary means making no headway toward interpreting the book.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, a student starts an economics text and sees 'utility' italicized and explained as differing from its everyday sense. What should she conclude?
options: It is an ordinary word she can skim past
It is a typographical habit with no meaning
It is probably one of the author's important words
It is a synonym for every other italic word
questions.explain: Italics and explicit discussion of a word's senses are the first positive signs of an important word, especially when an everyday word is made technical.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what is the first thing to do with a troubling word once it is marked?
options: Look it up in a specialized dictionary
Replace it with a simpler synonym
Find the key sentence that contains it
Determine whether it has one or many meanings
questions.explain: The procedure is to determine whether the word has one or many meanings, see how they relate, and note where each is used and why the context shifts it.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, put the authors' procedure for a marked word in order.
items: Determine whether the word has one or many meanings
If many, see how the meanings are related
Note where the word is used in each sense
Look for clues in the context to the reason for the shift
questions.explain: Following this order lets the reader track the word's changes of meaning with the same flexibility as the author.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors say you discover the meaning of a word you do not understand by using the meanings of all the other words in the ____ that you do understand.
questions.explain: There is no other way, however circular it seems at first: the surrounding familiar words are the context for the strange one.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, which definition do the authors use to show how meanings are acquired?
options: Euclid's definition of a point
Darwin's definition of a species
Smith's definition of wealth
Eddington's definition of a cause
questions.explain: Euclid says “A point is that which has no part.” The reader understands it from words he already knows, such as part, whole and simple.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors infer from Euclid's definition that, if no physical things lack parts, a Euclidean point cannot be physical.
questions.explain: Since a point is that which has no part, and if every physical thing has parts, a point as Euclid speaks of it cannot be physical.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do the authors say a reader can acquire new meanings from a book despite the apparent circularity?
questions.a: You operate with meanings you already possess: if every word in a definition had itself to be defined, nothing could be defined. Most words in any English book are familiar, and they surround and give context to the strange words. So the reader has all the materials needed to interpret the difficult words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors compare finding meanings to putting together a ____ puzzle.
questions.explain: Each piece put in place makes the next easier, and words already in place are terms shared by author and reader.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, completing the jigsaw comparison, the authors write: A word in place is a ____.
questions.explain: They write “A word in place is a term.” It is fixed by the meaning reader and author share.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say there is a reliable rule of thumb for finding an author's meanings.
questions.explain: They say there is no rule of thumb; the process is like trial and error in a jigsaw puzzle.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, where does the jigsaw comparison fail, according to the authors?
options: Books have no picture to complete
No book is ideally good, with all its parts fitting perfectly
Readers can never correct their errors
Jigsaw pieces have meanings but words do not
questions.explain: A good puzzle fits perfectly, as would an ideally good book, but there is no such book; the better the book, the more fruitfully its terms can be interpreted.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say the rules of reading work on bad books only to show how bad they are.
questions.explain: If an author uses words ambiguously you cannot find what he means, only that he has not been precise.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what do the authors say it means to use a word ambiguously?
options: To use a word in more than one sense anywhere in a book
To use a technical word that readers do not know
To use a word in several senses without distinguishing or relating them
To use synonyms in place of a key word
questions.explain: Using a word in several senses is usual and not ambiguous if the author distinguishes them; ambiguity is failing to distinguish or relate the senses.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, is an author who uses an important word in several senses using it ambiguously? Explain the authors' answer.
