questions.a: No. Authors usually do use their most important words in several senses, but ambiguity means using a word in several senses without distinguishing or relating their meanings. An author who distinguishes the senses and lets the reader make a responsive discrimination is offering terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors suggest listing an author's important words in one column and their important meanings in another, to see the relation between his vocabulary and his ____.
questions.explain: Vocabulary is the set of words; terminology is the set of terms, and one word may carry several terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each usage of 'reading' to its symbol in the authors' scheme.
pairs: Reading books that instruct rather than entertain
Reading that enlightens rather than informs
questions.explain: Related meanings let a word stand for all, some or only one of them; so long as each usage is definite, the word is a term.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book list as further complications in the relation of words and terms?
options: A word can be used in a combination of its senses
Synonyms: one term expressed by different words
Phrases can express terms just as words do
Every word has exactly one correct dictionary sense
Terms can be found by counting word frequency
questions.explain: The three complications are combined senses, synonyms and phrases. The authors deny that words have only one meaning, and frequency is not their method.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, which pair of words do the authors use to illustrate synonyms expressing one term?
options: 'Information' and 'entertainment'
'Point' and 'line'
'Word' and 'term'
'Enlightenment' and 'insight'
questions.explain: As X and Y they both express a gain in understanding, so reading for insight and reading for enlightenment name one kind of reading.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say that whenever an author changes his words, you can assume he has shifted his terms.
questions.explain: Assuming that every change of word shifts the term is as great an error as assuming the same word always carries the same term.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each relationship to an example the authors give.
pairs: Word, short phrase, long phrase for one term
'reading', 'reading for enlightenment', and a long phrase
questions.explain: The authors' examples show the two-way relation between vocabulary and terminology, extended to phrases, and Euclid's restriction of words to a single meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do the authors say a phrase is generally less likely to be ambiguous than a single word?
options: Each word in a phrase is in the context of the others, restricting its meaning
Phrases are always defined in the author's preface
Phrases are usually technical terms from science
Readers pay more attention to longer expressions
questions.explain: Because the words of a phrase restrict each other's meanings, writers often substitute an elaborate phrase for a word to make sure of their meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors' long phrase for the kind of reading the book is about is the process of passing from understanding less to understanding ____ by the operation of your mind upon a book.
questions.explain: One term is expressed by the single word 'reading', the short phrase 'reading for enlightenment', and this longer phrase.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book name as further interests the practice of coming to terms may lead a reader to?
options: The literal and metaphorical use of words
The distinction between abstract and concrete words
The emotive use of words
The history of printing and typography
The rules of English spelling
questions.explain: The authors mention literal and metaphorical use, abstract and concrete words, proper and common names, definition, and the emotive use of words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how do the authors sum up the payoff of the rule of coming to terms at the end of the chapter?
questions.a: Even a reader who never studies grammar and logic further will find comprehension of any book greatly increased by finding its important words, identifying their shifting meanings, and coming to terms. The authors write “Seldom does such a small change in a habit” have such a large effect.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do the authors say the study of grammar and logic is best taken up after practising analytical reading?
options: Because it is too difficult for beginners
Because you then bring questions born of your own reading experience
Because the rules of reading replace the need for it
Because grammar and logic change over time
questions.explain: The study of these sciences is practical only insofar as it relates to practice; you profit more when you come with your own questions.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, a reader of a history book sees 'liberty' used for national independence in one chapter and for freedom of speech in another, with the author noting the difference. What does the author's practice show?
options: He is using the word ambiguously and cannot be understood
He is using two synonyms for one term
He is offering two terms through one word
He is using liberty in its ordinary sense only
questions.explain: One word can carry several terms; because the author distinguishes the senses, he is not ambiguous but offering terms the reader can follow.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, apply the authors' advice: a reader keeps meeting 'freedom', 'liberty' and 'independence' in one essay. What should she check, and why?
questions.a: She should check whether the author uses these different words with the same meaning, since one term can be expressed by several words used synonymously. It would be as great an error to assume every change of word shifts the term as to assume the same word always keeps the same term. Listing the vocabulary and terminology in two columns shows the relations.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how does a reader use context to grasp a technical word, and why does this make reading for understanding possible?
questions.a: The reader uses the meanings of the familiar surrounding words to fix the meaning of the strange word, much as pieces already placed in a jigsaw make the next easier. If readers could not come to understand new words by their own efforts, it would be impossible to pass from understanding less to understanding more through a book.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors say a single term can be expressed by a word or by a ____, which can serve as the subject or predicate of a sentence.
questions.explain: A phrase that is a unit works like a single word, so all the relations between words and terms hold for phrases too.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, put the four sections of Chapter 8 in the order they appear.
items: Words vs. Terms
Finding the Key Words
Technical Words and Special Vocabularies
Finding the Meanings
questions.explain: The order follows the two parts of Rule 5: first distinguishing words from terms and locating the important words, then determining their meanings.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort these tasks by whether they belong to the first or the second stage of analytical reading.

items.t: Classifying the book by kind and subject
Stating what the whole book is about
Outlining the major parts
Coming to terms with the author
Finding the key sentences and propositions
Finding the arguments

questions.explain: The first stage, in Chapter 7, outlines a book's structure; the second stage, begun in Chapter 8 and continued in Chapter 9, interprets its contents.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, put these points of the opening of Chapter 8 in the order the authors make them.
items: The first stage of analytical reading is complete
The next stage also has four rules
The first of them is called coming to terms
Without terms, knowledge is not communicated
questions.explain: The chapter links back to the first stage, announces the second, names its first rule, and then says why terms matter.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each situation to what coming to terms means in it.
pairs: The first step beyond the outline
The basic element of communicable knowledge
questions.explain: The authors contrast the business sense of coming to terms, which ends a negotiation, with its role in reading, where it begins interpretation.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, put the stages of the authors' account of communication in logical order.
items: Writer and reader exchange words
Ambiguity leaves only words in common
Both use the same words with the same meanings
They come to terms and share a single thought
questions.explain: Communication succeeds only when it results in something common; shared words alone are not enough until the meanings are shared too.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book say about language as a medium for knowledge?
options: It is imperfect and acts as an obstacle to communication
The rules of interpretive reading aim to overcome that obstacle
Readers must meet the writer halfway
A skilled writer can communicate without any effort from readers
Inventing an ideal language is the only remedy
questions.explain: The authors call language an imperfect barrier both parties must work through; they reject both the lone skilled writer and the ideal-language scheme.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort these by whether they make spotting an author's ordinary words easier or harder.

items.t: Reading a contemporary writer
Words you use with friends every day
A book written centuries ago
Deliberately archaic senses of words
A translation from a foreign language

questions.explain: You know today's ordinary usage because you live today; older books, archaic senses and translation complicate the matter.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book say help a reader separate technical words from ordinary ones when the author does not point them out?
options: Some prior knowledge of the subject matter
Knowing what kind of book it is and what it is about
The title, chapter headings and preface
The length of each word
How often the publisher reprinted the book
questions.explain: Prior knowledge and the structural rules of the first stage, aided by title, headings and preface, help; word length and reprints are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, order these fields from the most to the least well-established technical vocabulary, as the authors describe them.
items: Euclid's geometry, with words defined at the start
Darwin's biology or Smith's economics, found with some prior knowledge
Philosophy, notorious for private vocabularies
questions.explain: Euclid makes his vocabulary plain at the outset; in established fields the reader can spot technical words from acquaintance with them; philosophers often coin or adapt words of their own.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each Euclidean word to how the authors say its importance is shown.
pairs: Names a geometrical entity Euclid defines
Occurs in the axioms but names nothing defined
Known important from the axioms, though common words
questions.explain: Euclid defines points, lines and parallels; words such as equals, whole and part are known to be important because they occur in his axioms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort these by whether the author is offering terms or using words ambiguously.

items.t: Distinguishing the several senses of a key word
Using synonyms with one clear meaning
Restricting a key word to one defined sense
Shifting a word's sense without signalling it
Blurring 'important for the author' with 'important for the reader'

questions.explain: Ambiguity means using several senses without distinguishing or relating them; signalled distinctions, clear synonyms and fixed definitions all offer terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book say about the jigsaw-puzzle comparison for finding meanings?
options: The more parts in place, the easier the rest
A book comes with many words already in place
Errors force readjustments of other words
Every book's pieces fit perfectly
The first piece placed decides the whole picture
questions.explain: Placed words make later placements easier and errors get corrected; but no book is ideally good, so not every piece fits perfectly.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do the authors say Chapter 8 was a hard chapter to write and to read?
questions.a: The rule of coming to terms cannot be made fully intelligible without grammatical and logical explanations about words and terms. Even so, they say they have only touched on the most essential points, since an adequate account would take many chapters. They hope it is enough to make the rule a useful guide in practice.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how does a proposition in a book differ from a proposition made by a trader?
options: It declares the author's judgment about what is true, not an intention to act.
It declares an intention to act, just as a trader's offer does.
It is a proposal the reader may accept or refuse, like a deal.
It states the author's purpose, which is normally given in the preface.
questions.explain: A trader's proposition is an offer declaring how he intends to act, but a book's proposition is a declaration of knowledge, not intentions. The author's intentions belong to the preface, not to his propositions.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say a proposition in an expository book is a declaration of ____, not of intentions.
questions.explain: The author affirms what he thinks true and denies what he judges false, so his proposition declares knowledge rather than a plan of action.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that, like businessmen, readers usually find out what the proposition is before they come to terms.
questions.explain: The authors say the order of reading reverses the order of business: the reader must come to terms with the author first, and only then can he find what the author proposes.

questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, does the seventh rule of analytical reading (about arguments) follow the rule about propositions?
options: Arguments are simpler units than propositions and so are easier to find later.
Without supporting reasons, an author's propositions are only expressions of personal opinion.
Propositions cannot be identified until the whole argument of the book is known.
Readers interested in the author's personality need to know his reasoning style.
questions.explain: If we care about the subject and not just the author, we want to know why he thinks we should accept his propositions; unsupported, they are nothing but personal opinion.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what do words such as "because", "since ... therefore" and "if ... then" signal to a reader?
options: That the author is about to define one of his key terms.
That a sentence is interrogative and states a problem.
That statements are being related so that one gives a reason for another.
That the author is expressing a wish rather than knowledge.
questions.explain: These connecting words indicate the presence of arguments: one thing is said because of another, and "because" signifies a reason being given.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren call books, from which adults out of school must keep learning, absent ____.
questions.explain: Their sample argument runs: if we want to go on learning after school, we must know how to learn from books, which are absent teachers.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that if an argument is valid, its conclusion follows from the premises, but the conclusion may still be false.
questions.explain: Validity means the conclusion follows from the premises; if one or all of the premises are false, the conclusion need not be true.

questions.q: Put the logical units of interpretation in How to Read a Book in the order the rules of interpretation deal with them, from simplest to most complex.
items: Terms
Propositions
Arguments
questions.explain: The rules go from terms to propositions to arguments, building up from simpler to more complex units of thought.

questions.q: Put the grammatical units in How to Read a Book in the order that matches the movement from terms to propositions to arguments.
items: Words and phrases
Sentences
Collections of sentences or paragraphs
questions.explain: The grammatical side of the order runs from words (and phrases) to sentences to collections of sentences, matching terms, propositions and arguments.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, where do the two processes of outlining a book and interpreting it meet?
options: At the level of the book's unity and its title.
At the level of single words and key terms.
At the level of the author's stated problems.
At the level of propositions and arguments.
questions.explain: You work down to propositions and arguments by dividing the book into parts, and up to arguments from propositions and terms, so the two movements meet there.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort each activity into the stage of analytical reading it belongs to.

items.t: Dividing the book into its major parts
Moving from the whole book down to subordinate divisions
Building up from words to sentences to paragraphs
Working up to arguments from propositions and terms

questions.explain: Outlining moves from the book as a whole to its parts and their divisions; interpretation moves the opposite way, from terms to propositions to arguments.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why must the reader reverse the businessman's usual order of terms and propositions?
questions.a: Businessmen usually find out what the proposition is and then come to terms. A reader cannot find out what an author is proposing until he understands the author's words, so he must come to terms first. That is why the fifth rule concerns words and terms and the sixth concerns sentences and propositions.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how do the rules of interpretation have both a grammatical and a logical side?
questions.a: The logical units are terms, propositions and arguments; the grammatical units that express them are words, sentences and collections of sentences or paragraphs. Interpretation builds up from the simpler to the more complex unit on both sides. The active reader must attend to words, sentences and paragraphs because there is no other way to discover the author's terms, propositions and arguments.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what point do Adler and Van Doren make with the buttons and buttonholes of a well-made coat?
options: Elements of language and of thought do not stand in a one-to-one relation.
Every sentence in a good book corresponds to exactly one proposition.
Readers should match each key word to one definition in a glossary.
Arguments and paragraphs fit together as neatly as buttons and holes.
questions.explain: Buttons and holes illustrate a one-to-one relation, and the point is that words and terms, and sentences and propositions, are not related that way. Assuming they are is called the greatest error in applying the rules.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren call the supposition that language and thought correspond one-to-one the greatest error a reader can make in applying these rules.
questions.explain: They write that the greatest error is to suppose a one-to-one relationship exists between the elements of language and those of thought or knowledge.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren call sentences that express propositions ____ sentences.
questions.explain: Propositions are declarations of knowledge or opinion, which is why sentences expressing them are called declarative.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren call sentences that ask questions ____ sentences.
questions.explain: Sentences that ask questions state problems rather than answers, and the authors distinguish them as interrogative.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, propositions are the ____ to questions.
questions.explain: Questions state problems; propositions are the answers, declarations of knowledge or opinion.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each kind of sentence to what it does.
pairs: States a problem rather than an answer
Expresses a proposition, a declaration of knowledge or opinion
Sentence expressing a wish or intention
May show the author's purpose but not the knowledge he expounds
Expresses two or more propositions even with unambiguous words
questions.explain: Only declarative sentences express propositions; questions and wishes do not, and a compound sentence is really a collection of sentences carrying several propositions.

questions.q: Which of these are reasons Adler and Van Doren give why a declarative sentence cannot always be read as expressing exactly one proposition?
options: Its words may be ambiguous, so the same sentence can express different propositions
It may be compound, joining several propositions with words like "if ... then"
It may really be a question disguised as a statement
It may be part of a paragraph that is too long
questions.explain: The two reasons given are ambiguity of words and complexity of sentences. Questions are a separate case of sentences that express no proposition, and paragraph length is a different issue.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, even when its words are used unambiguously, a ____ sentence expresses two or more propositions.
questions.explain: A compound sentence is really a collection of sentences joined by words like "and" or "if ... then", so it carries several propositions.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why is it important to separate the propositions in Machiavelli's sentence about a prince inspiring fear?
options: The sentence is grammatically faulty and must be rewritten first.
A reader may agree with some of its claims and disagree with others.
Machiavelli hid his real meaning so that only experts could find it.
Each proposition must be translated from Italian separately.
questions.explain: Machiavelli says three things in one sentence; you might reject his recommendation of fear yet accept his other claims. Unless you see the distinct propositions, you cannot judge discriminatingly.

questions.q: Put the propositions Adler and Van Doren find in Machiavelli's sentence from The Prince in the order the sentence states them.
items: A prince ought to inspire fear in such a way that he avoids hatred
The reason is that he can endure being feared while he is not hated
He avoids hatred by keeping his hands off his citizens' property and women
questions.explain: The first proposition comes before the semicolon; after "because" come the reason for it and then the condition for not being hated.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what do Adler and Van Doren use the sentence "John Doe signed the lease on March 24" to show?
options: Lawyers use technical terms that ordinary readers cannot follow.
A sentence containing a date is always a statement of fact.
Even a grammatically simple sentence can express more than one proposition.
Complex sentences are harder to interpret than simple ones.
questions.explain: John Doe may have signed the lease but not on March 24, so the sentence asserts several things, some of which could be true and others false.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, why is some knowledge of grammar indispensable to a reader?
options: Authors expect readers to correct the grammar of their sentences.
Grammar is the main subject that expository books try to teach.
Without grammar a reader cannot read at more than one speed.
Until words and sentences are analyzed, they block communication instead of carrying it.
questions.explain: So long as words, sentences and paragraphs remain opaque and unanalyzed, they are a barrier to, rather than a medium of, communication; you read words but receive no knowledge.

questions.q: Rule 6 in How to Read a Book tells the reader to mark the most important sentences in a book and discover the ____ they contain.
questions.explain: Rule 6 joins the grammatical unit, the sentence, to the logical unit it expresses, the proposition.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort each item as a unit of language or a unit of thought.

items.t: Word
Sentence
Paragraph
Term
Proposition
Argument

questions.explain: Sentences and paragraphs are units of language; propositions and arguments are logical units, or units of thought and knowledge, as terms are to words.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do Adler and Van Doren say that not every sentence in a book expresses a proposition?
questions.a: Some sentences are interrogative: they ask questions and state problems, while propositions are the answers. Other sentences express the author's wishes or intentions, which may tell us his purpose but not the knowledge he is expounding. Only declarative sentences express propositions, and even they may express more than one or a shifting one.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, explain in what two directions sentences and propositions fail to be related one-to-one.
questions.a: A single sentence can express several propositions, either through ambiguity, when its words shift in meaning, or through complexity, as in a compound sentence like Machiavelli's. In the other direction, one and the same proposition can be expressed by two or more different sentences, as with the two ways of saying that teaching and being taught are related.

questions.q: From the reader's point of view, which sentences in a book do Adler and Van Doren call the important ones?
options: Those that require an effort of interpretation because they are not clear at first sight.
Those that state surprising facts the reader did not know before.
Those the reader finds most interesting or most enjoyable.
Those that the reader can understand completely on first reading.
questions.explain: The important sentences for you are the ones you understand just well enough to know there is more to understand. Interesting or surprising sentences are a different thing.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how are the sentences important to the reader related to the sentences important to the author?
questions.a: For the reader, the important sentences are those that need an effort of interpretation because they are not perfectly intelligible at first. For the author, they are those expressing the judgments his whole argument rests on. The two may not be the same, but they are likely to be, because readers tend to have the greatest difficulty with the most important things an author has to say.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren mention as ways authors themselves help readers find the leading sentences?
options: Telling the reader that a point is important when they make it
Using a typographical device to make leading sentences stand out
Labeling every proposition to be proved, as Euclid does
Placing the key sentences in footnotes
Repeating every key sentence word for word in each chapter
questions.explain: Authors may say a point is important, use typography, or, like Euclid, label each proposition. Footnotes and word-for-word repetition are not among the aids described.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each author or book to the point Adler and Van Doren use it to make.
pairs: States definitions, postulates and axioms first and labels each proposition to be proved
Marks where his own argument begins with the phrase I answer that
Summarizes the whole argument in a final chapter
One complex sentence contains at least three propositions
questions.explain: Euclid and Aquinas put leading sentences in high relief, Darwin supplies a closing summary, and Machiavelli's sentence shows how many propositions one sentence can hold.

questions.q: Put the parts of a section of Aquinas's Summa Theologica in the order Adler and Van Doren describe them.
items: A question heading the section
A series of objections opposing his answer
His own argument, introduced by the phrase I answer that
questions.explain: Each section is headed by a question, objections opposing Aquinas's answer are stated, and his own argument begins at the words "I answer that".

questions.q: In the Summa Theologica, Aquinas marks the place where he begins to argue his own point with the words "I ____ that."
questions.explain: The phrase "I answer that" makes his leading sentences easy to locate, after the opening question and the objections.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, why do some readers still find even Aquinas's clearly marked Summa "all a blur"?
options: Aquinas hides his conclusions among the objections he states.
They treat everything as equally important and read it all at one speed.
The book contains no indication of the answer being defended.
Aquinas's terms are too technical for the general reader.
questions.explain: The format leaves no excuse; the trouble is readers who read everything at the same speed, which usually means everything is equally unimportant.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren write that ____ is the beginning of wisdom in learning from books as well as from nature.
questions.explain: Being perplexed and knowing it helps locate the important sentences: “Wonder is the beginning of wisdom in learning from books”.

questions.q: Which of these are clues Adler and Van Doren give for locating a book's important sentences yourself?
options: Noticing the passages you cannot understand readily
Following the important words you have already marked
Detecting sentences that form a sequence with a beginning and an end
Pausing over the sentences that interest you most
Looking for the facts that most surprise you
questions.explain: Perplexity, key words, and sequences of premises and conclusions are the clues. Pausing over what interests or surprises you is the mistake the authors warn against.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say the reader must always mark the important words before looking for the important sentences.
questions.explain: The rules are stated in a fixed order, but you need not follow them in that order: you may mark certain words only after being puzzled by a sentence.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why can finding terms and finding propositions be done in either order?
questions.a: Terms constitute propositions and propositions contain terms. If you know the terms the words express, you have caught the proposition in the sentence; if you understand the proposition, you have arrived at the terms too. So important words can lead you to important sentences, but a puzzling sentence can also lead you to mark its words.

questions.q: Maya reads a 17th-century travel book and lingers over the odd prices and customs, skimming the passages where the author explains why nations rise and fall. What mistake do Adler and Van Doren say she is making?
options: Reading the whole book at a single uniform speed.
Failing to come to terms before finding the propositions.
Pausing over sentences that interest her rather than the ones that puzzle her.
Treating a book of practical advice as if it were theoretical.
questions.explain: Many readers pause over sentences that interest them rather than those that puzzle them; old books invite this with surprising facts, but reading for understanding seeks the author's ideas.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why are old books a special obstacle for readers who believe they read well because they vary their speed?
questions.a: Such readers slow down over the wrong sentences, pausing over what interests them rather than what puzzles them. Any old book contains surprising facts that differ from what we know, and these attract attention. But curiosity about the author, his language or his world is one thing; the concern to understand his ideas is another, and that is what the rules serve.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort each kind of sentence by how Adler and Van Doren say a reader should treat it.

items.t: A sentence you understand just well enough to know there is more
A sentence that seems to be a premise in a sequence of reasoning
A sentence containing a key word you have already marked
A digression or side remark
A sentence that causes you no difficulty

questions.explain: Puzzling sentences and those in the main line of argument deserve slow reading; most sentences cause no difficulty, and digressions are of secondary importance.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is one difference between finding terms and finding propositions?
options: Finding propositions requires no knowledge of grammar.
Finding terms proceeds from what is unclear to what is clear.
Finding terms requires separating several units out of one word.
Finding propositions uses a larger context: the surrounding sentences.
questions.explain: You bring the surrounding sentences to bear on a sentence just as you used surrounding words for a word; the other difference is that complicated sentences carry more than one proposition.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what are the two differences between finding the terms in words and the propositions in sentences?
questions.a: First, in finding propositions you use a larger context, bringing the surrounding sentences to bear, as surrounding words were used for terms. Second, complicated sentences usually express more than one proposition, so you have not finished interpreting an important sentence until you have separated out all its propositions. In both cases you proceed from what you understand to what is at first unclear.

questions.q: Put the steps Adler and Van Doren suggest for practicing with a complicated sentence into order.
items: Locate an important, complicated sentence
Separate out the different propositions it asserts
State each proposition in your own words
Number the propositions and relate them
questions.explain: They suggest taking complicated sentences, stating in your own words each thing asserted, and then numbering and relating them.

questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren call the best test of whether you have understood the proposition in a sentence?
options: Being able to state it in your own, quite different words.
Being able to repeat the author's sentence exactly.
Being able to find where the author defines its words.
Being able to agree or disagree with it at once.
questions.explain: If all you can do is repeat the author's words with minor changes, you should suspect you do not know what he means; only words, not thought, have passed to you.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that producing a faithful English translation of a French sentence proves you understand what its writer meant.
questions.explain: Even a faithful English replica may remain only on the verbal level, so you may still not know what the French writer was trying to convey.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, how does failing to see through language to propositions harm syntopical reading?
options: The reader will spend too long on each individual book.
The reader may think authors disagree because of verbal differences, or miss real differences.
The reader cannot find books on the same subject.
The reader will mistake expository books for poetry.
questions.explain: Different authors say the same thing in different words or different things in similar words, so a reader stuck on words misreads agreement and disagreement.

questions.q: Besides restating it in other words, what second test of understanding a proposition do Adler and Van Doren propose?
options: Finding the same proposition in another author's book.
Proving the proposition from axioms and postulates.
Pointing to an actual or imagined experience that the proposition describes.
Locating the sentence where the author first states it.
questions.explain: Can you exemplify the general truth by a particular instance? Imagining a possible case is often as good as citing an actual one.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, explain the exemplification test and why Adler and Van Doren think it matters.
questions.a: The test asks whether you can point to some experience, actual or imagined, that a proposition describes or is relevant to. Propositions do not exist in a vacuum; they refer to the world we live in. If you cannot illustrate a proposition at all, you are playing with words, not dealing with thought and knowledge, though some scientific propositions may need laboratory experience.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, which restatement of the metaphysical proposition "Nothing acts except what is actual" shows that a student understood it?
options: Everything that exists is always acting on something.
Only what can be observed is actually real.
What is possible will sooner or later become actual.
If something does not exist, it cannot do anything.
questions.explain: The authors give this as an immediately apparent translation; the other options add claims the proposition does not make.

questions.q: Put in order the steps Adler and Van Doren took with students who recited "Nothing acts except what is actual".
items: Students repeat the words with satisfied wisdom
They are asked to state the proposition in other words
Failing that, they are asked for an example of it
questions.explain: The sham showed when students could not restate the proposition; failing a translation, the authors asked for an exemplification.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren call the bad habit of using words without regard for the thoughts they should convey ____.
questions.explain: Verbalism is playing with words, without awareness of the thoughts or the experiences to which they refer.

questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren answer the charge by certain modern educators that the liberal arts tend toward verbalism?
options: The opposite is true: lack of training in grammar and logic produces slavery to words.
They agree, and propose more practical subjects instead.
They say verbalism is harmless if a reader remembers the words.
They say only science teaching can cure verbalism.
questions.explain: They write that the omnipresent verbalism of those untrained in grammar and logic shows how lack of such discipline results in “slavery to words rather than mastery of them”.

questions.q: Sam can recite his textbook's definition of opportunity cost word for word but cannot explain it differently or give an example from his own life. What would Adler and Van Doren say about him?
options: He has fully understood the proposition, since his memory is exact.
He has fallen into verbalism: he knows the words, not the author's mind.
He has understood it but simply lacks grammar.
He is reading syntopically rather than analytically.
questions.explain: He fails both tests, restating and exemplifying, so only words have passed to him, not thought or knowledge.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren offer as tests of whether you understand a proposition?
options: Stating it in totally different words
Giving an actual or imagined example of it
Repeating the author's sentence with a few words rearranged
Memorizing the sentence exactly
questions.explain: Translation into other words and exemplification are the two tests; repeating or memorizing the author's words is the sign of verbalism.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each idea about understanding propositions to its description.
pairs: Say the same thing in different words
Point to an experience the proposition describes
Using words without regard for thoughts or experiences
May stay merely verbal and miss the writer's meaning
questions.explain: The two tests guard against verbalism; translating from a foreign language can be a faithful verbal replica without true understanding.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say an author may himself express the same proposition in different words in the course of a book.
questions.explain: They warn that a reader who has not seen through the words may treat such equivalent sentences as if they stated different propositions.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what is verbalism and why do Adler and Van Doren call it the besetting sin of those who do not read analytically?
questions.a: Verbalism is the bad habit of using words without regard for the thoughts they should convey and without awareness of the experiences they refer to. Readers who fail the tests of restating and exemplifying never get beyond the words; they hold what they read as a verbal memory to recite emptily. Without training in grammar and logic, they become slaves to words rather than masters of them.

questions.q: Why did Adler and Van Doren avoid telling readers in Rule 7 simply to find the most important paragraphs?
options: Paragraphs are too long to be marked in the margin.
Important arguments are always stated in single sentences.
Writers follow no settled conventions about how to construct paragraphs.
Most good books have no paragraphs that state arguments.
questions.explain: Some great writers write very long paragraphs and others short ones, and an argument is not uniquely tied to any unit of writing.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each writer or influence to what Adler and Van Doren say about paragraphs.
pairs: Leads writers to cut paragraphs for quick, easy reading
Come close to making one paragraph one argument
questions.explain: The variety of paragraph practice is why Rule 7 is not stated in terms of paragraphs; mathematical writers come nearest the ideal.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say about how arguments relate to paragraphs?
options: An argument may be expressed in a single complicated sentence
An argument may run through several or many paragraphs
Some paragraphs express no argument at all
Each well-made paragraph expresses exactly one argument
An argument is always longer than one paragraph
questions.explain: The argument is not uniquely related to any unit of writing: it may be one sentence, part of a paragraph, a whole paragraph or many paragraphs, and some paragraphs only detail evidence.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why is the argument harder to locate in the text than the term or the proposition?
questions.a: Terms are related to words and phrases and propositions to sentences, but the argument, a sequence of propositions some of which give reasons for another, is not uniquely related to any unit of writing. It may be one complicated sentence, part of a paragraph, a whole paragraph, or run through many paragraphs. Many paragraphs also express no argument at all, only evidence or side remarks.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, an argument is a sequence of propositions, some of which give ____ for another.
questions.explain: The logical unit Rule 7 points to is the argument, in which some statements provide the grounds or reasons for what is concluded.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren's revised Rule 7 says that if a book's arguments are not stated in paragraphs, the reader must construct them from sentences in different paragraphs.
questions.explain: The reformulated rule says to find the paragraphs that state the arguments if you can, and otherwise construct them by gathering a sentence from this paragraph and one from that.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what tends to happen to paragraphs as a book becomes more loosely constructed?
options: They become shorter, each stating one clear argument.
They become fewer, since the author omits evidence.
They become more mathematical in style.
They become more diffuse, so arguments must be searched for across a chapter.
questions.explain: In proportion as a book is more loosely constructed, paragraphs grow diffuse, and you may have to search through a whole chapter to build one argument.

questions.q: Darwin summarizes his whole argument in The Origin of Species in a last chapter titled "Recapitulation and ____".
questions.explain: The authors cite this chapter as an example of a good book summarizing itself; the reader who has worked through the book deserves that help.

questions.q: Priya finds a two-page summary at the end of a chapter in a history of economics. How do Adler and Van Doren suggest she use it?
options: Look back over the preceding pages to find the material the summary brings together.
Read only the summary, since it replaces the chapter.
Ignore it, since summaries distort the author's arguments.
Use it to decide whether to agree with the author.
questions.explain: A good book summarizes itself as its arguments develop, and the reader should be able to find in earlier pages what the summary gathers; inspectional reading shows where such summaries are.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren describe as signs of a bad or loosely constructed book?
options: Diffuse paragraphs that make you search a chapter for one argument
Steps omitted from an argument
Summaries of the argument at the end of chapters
Arguments stated in single paragraphs
questions.explain: Diffuse paragraphs and omitted steps mark loose construction. Summaries and paragraph-length arguments are marks of good, helpful authors.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that leaving relevant steps unstated is a familiar trick of the orator or propagandist.
questions.explain: Such a writer leaves out things relevant to the argument that might be challenged if made explicit, which is why a careful reader makes every step explicit.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that any good argument can be put into a ____.
questions.explain: Whatever the book, a reader must know its arguments and be able to state them briefly; the units of reasoning are single arguments.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say a reader needs considerable logical training to find the arguments in books written for the general reader.
questions.explain: They say no great logical competence is needed to read such books; if the mind works during reading, it will see the arguments.

questions.q: Which of these are among the helpful hints Adler and Van Doren give for carrying out Rule 7?
options: If you find the conclusion first, look for the reasons
Distinguish arguments from particular facts from arguments from general statements
Observe what the author assumes, what he proves and what he takes as self-evident
Learn the formal names of every type of argument first
Skip any paragraph that reports evidence
questions.explain: The three hints are about conclusions and reasons, the two kinds of reasoning, and assumptions versus proofs. The authors say the names of the kinds of reasoning are not what is important.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say an argument that points to particular facts as evidence for a generalization is usually called ____.
questions.explain: Reasoning from particular facts to a generalization is inductive; reasoning from general statements to further generalizations is deductive.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say an argument offering general statements to prove further generalizations is usually called ____.
questions.explain: The authors stress that being able to discriminate the two kinds of reasoning matters more than the names.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each item to its role in the discussion of kinds of argument.
pairs: Particular facts offered as evidence for a generalization
General statements offered to prove a further generalization
Illustrates by experiment conclusions reached by mathematical demonstration
Harvey's On the Motion of the Heart
Says the circulation of blood is shown by reason and experiment
questions.explain: Science observes the distinction whenever proof by reasoning is set against establishment by experiment; Galileo and Harvey are the authors' examples.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book's terms, sort each way of supporting a claim by the kind of argument it is.

items.t: Several observed cases are cited as evidence for a general rule
An experiment establishes the proposition
The proposition is proved from axioms and earlier theorems
General truths are used to prove a further generalization

questions.explain: Pointing to particular facts, including experimental evidence, is inductive; proving by reasoning from general statements is deductive.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do Adler and Van Doren want readers to tell inductive from deductive arguments, and how does science show the difference?
questions.a: One kind points to particular facts as evidence for a generalization; the other offers general statements to prove further generalizations. The names matter less than the ability to discriminate. Science observes the distinction when it separates proof by reasoning from establishment by experiment, as Galileo and Harvey do, and some propositions can be supported both ways.

questions.q: Put these stages in the building of proofs into the order Adler and Van Doren describe.
items: Axioms, assumptions or postulates are taken without proof
Other propositions are proved from them
Those proved propositions serve as premises in further proofs
questions.explain: Not everything can be proved; axioms and postulates are needed to begin, and once other propositions are proved they can be used as premises in further proofs.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren name as the places where a line of argument can start?
options: Assumptions agreed on between writer and reader
Self-evident propositions that neither writer nor reader can deny
The author's personal opinions
Propositions proved later in the book
questions.explain: Every line of argument must start with agreed assumptions or with self-evident propositions; opinions and later conclusions cannot serve as starting points.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each kind of starting point or label to its description.
pairs: Can be anything, so long as writer and reader agree
Neither writer nor reader can deny it
Truth contained in the definition of the words
questions.explain: Assumptions rest on agreement, self-evident propositions on undeniable understanding, and a true tautology only conceals a verbal stipulation.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say "the whole is greater than its parts" is not a mere tautology?
options: It can be proved from the definitions of "whole" and "part".
It expresses our understanding of how things are related, whatever words we use.
It belongs to mathematics rather than to common sense.
It is a verbal stipulation like naming a grandparent.
questions.explain: Unlike the grandparent statement, it concerns existing finite wholes and parts; "whole" and "part" cannot even be defined, so the truth is not put in by definition.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort each statement as a mere tautology or an instructive self-evident truth.

items.t: A father of a father is a grandfather
Let us call the parent of a parent a grandparent
The whole is greater than its parts
A page before cutting is not less than half of it

questions.explain: The grandparent statement only conceals a verbal stipulation; the whole-and-part statement expresses our understanding of things and teaches something.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say are true of self-evident propositions such as "the whole is greater than its parts"?
options: They are indemonstrable but undeniable
They rest on common experience alone
They belong to no organized body of knowledge
They belong properly to mathematics
They are true only because of how words are defined
questions.explain: Such truths are common-sense knowledge, belonging no more to mathematics than to history, which is why Euclid called them common notions; they are not true by definition.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say Locke saw the difference between a tautology like the grandparent statement and an instructive truth like the whole-and-part statement.
questions.explain: They say Locke could see no difference between the two and did not think such propositions instructive; modern writers who call them all tautologies make the same mistake.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what mistake do Adler and Van Doren say Locke and certain moderns make about self-evident propositions?
questions.a: They treat all self-evident propositions as tautologies that teach nothing, rabbits pulled out of a hat after being put in by definition. Some, like "a father of a father is a grandfather", really are verbal stipulations. But others, like "the whole is greater than its parts", express our understanding of how things are related and teach us something we would not otherwise know.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what does it mean that a reader must be able to put a book's arguments into a nutshell, and why is that enough?
questions.a: Whatever kind of book it is, if it contains arguments the reader must know what they are and be able to state them briefly. Books may build arguments on arguments, proving one thing to prove another. But the units of reasoning are single arguments, and a reader who finds these is not likely to miss the larger sequences.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do Adler and Van Doren say that good expository authors still differ in how plainly they show their arguments?
questions.a: Good expository authors try to reveal, not conceal, their thought, but they do not all do it the same way. Mathematical writers like Euclid, Galileo and Newton come close to making each paragraph one argument, while most non-mathematical writing puts two arguments in a paragraph or runs one through several. The looser the book, the more the reader must search and construct the arguments.

questions.q: Rule 8 of analytical reading in How to Read a Book says: find out what the author's ____ are.
questions.explain: Rule 8 brings the rules about terms, propositions and arguments to a head and completes the interpretation of the book's content.

questions.q: Which of these are questions Adler and Van Doren tell the reader to ask in applying Rule 8?
options: Which of the problems he tried to solve did the author succeed in solving?
In solving these, did he raise any new problems?
Of the problems he failed to solve, which did he know he had failed on?
Which of his solutions do other experts accept?
questions.explain: The three questions check the author's success, the new problems raised and his awareness of failure; what other experts think is outside the interpretation of this book.

questions.q: Put the questions Adler and Van Doren pose for Rule 8 in the order they give them.
items: Which problems did the author succeed in solving?
Did he raise new problems while solving them?
Which of his failures did the author know about?
questions.explain: They first ask which problems were solved, then whether new ones arose, then which failures, old or new, the author recognized.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, why does Rule 8 tie together the first and second stages of analytical reading?
options: It replaces the outline made in the first stage with a new one.
It asks the reader to judge whether the author is right.
It returns to the major problems found in Rule 4 and checks the author's answers to them.
It requires rereading the book from the beginning.
questions.explain: Rule 4 ended the first stage by finding the author's major problems; Rule 8 asks which of them he solved, linking structure and interpretation. Judging him belongs to the next stage.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what changes for the reader once Rules 5 through 8 have been applied?
options: The reader can stop reading, since the book is understood.
The reader must begin outlining the book's structure.
The reader should look up what critics say about the book.
Having followed the author so far, the reader may now argue with him.
questions.explain: Up to this point the reader has kept eyes and mind open and mouth shut, following the author; from here he gets a chance to argue and express himself.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what does Rule 8 ask of the reader, and what do Adler and Van Doren say it accomplishes?
questions.a: Rule 8 asks the reader to find out what the author's solutions are: which of his problems he solved, whether he raised new ones, and which failures he knew about. It brings the rules on terms, propositions and arguments to a head and ties the outlining stage to the interpreting stage. Once it is applied, the reader can feel reasonably sure he understands the book and is ready to argue with the author.

questions.section: The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: The second basic question a reader asks about a book, answered by Rules 5 to 8, is: What is being said in ____, and how?
questions.explain: Coming to terms, finding propositions and arguments, and identifying solutions tell you what the author says in detail.

questions.section: The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Put the rules of the second stage of analytical reading in How to Read a Book in their numbered order.
items: Come to terms by interpreting key words
Grasp leading propositions through the most important sentences
Know the arguments by finding or constructing them from sequences of sentences
Determine which problems the author solved and which he did not
questions.explain: Rules 5 to 8 move from terms to propositions to arguments to solutions.

questions.section: The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each rule of the second stage to what it deals with.
pairs: The author's solutions to his problems
questions.explain: The second stage, interpreting a book's contents, runs from terms through propositions and arguments to solutions.

questions.section: The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren call the second stage of analytical reading the rules for finding what a book says, or interpreting its contents.
questions.explain: The summary at the end of the chapter heads Rules 5 to 8 as the rules for finding what a book says, interpreting its contents.

questions.section: The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how do Rules 5 through 8 answer the second basic question a reader asks about a book?
questions.a: The second basic question is what is being said in detail, and how. When you have come to terms with the author, found his key propositions and arguments, and identified his solutions to the problems he faced, you know what he is saying. You are then prepared to ask the final two basic questions about the book.

questions.q: Put the sections of the chapter "Determining an Author's Message" in How to Read a Book in order.
items: Sentences vs. Propositions
Finding the Key Sentences
Finding the Propositions
Finding the Arguments
Finding the Solutions
The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.explain: The chapter clarifies sentences and propositions, then follows Rules 6, 7 and 8 in turn, and ends by summarizing the second stage.

questions.q: Put these chapters of How to Read a Book in their order in the book.
items: X-raying a Book
Coming to Terms with an Author
Determining an Author's Message
Criticizing a Book Fairly
questions.explain: Outlining a book (X-raying) comes first, then the interpretive chapters on terms and on propositions and arguments, then criticism.

questions.q: Put the stages of analytical reading in How to Read a Book in order.
items: Outlining the book's structure
Interpreting its contents
Arguing with the author
questions.explain: Rule 8 ties the first stage (outlining) to the second (interpreting); after that the reader gets a chance to argue with the author.

questions.q: Why does the chapter "Determining an Author's Message" come right after "Coming to Terms with an Author" in How to Read a Book?
options: A reader must come to terms with an author before finding what he proposes.
Propositions are simpler than terms and should be learned second.
Coming to terms is part of criticizing, which precedes interpretation.
The order is arbitrary, since the rules can be applied in any order.
questions.explain: The chapter opens by saying the reader must come to terms first, which is why Rule 5 concerns terms and Rule 6 propositions. The rules can overlap in practice, but terms are the building blocks.

questions.q: What does the title "Determining an Author's Message" signal about the chapter's place in How to Read a Book?
options: It turns from reading to judging whether the author is right.
It moves from the author's words to what he actually asserts and argues.
It describes how to decide which books are worth reading.
It explains how to classify a book by its subject matter.
questions.explain: The author's message is his propositions, arguments and solutions, built on the terms of the previous chapter; judging and classifying belong to other chapters.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, which chapter takes up the stage the reader is ready for after "Determining an Author's Message"?
options: Pigeonholing a Book
Aids to Reading
Criticizing a Book Fairly
X-raying a Book
questions.explain: Having followed the author through Rules 5 to 8, the reader now gets a chance to argue with him, which is the subject of the next chapter, on criticism.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say the rules about propositions and arguments differ for novels, plays and poems. Where in How to Read a Book is that taken up?
options: In the earlier chapter on pigeonholing a book.
In the chapter on inspectional reading.
In the chapter on reading science and mathematics.
In the later chapters on reading imaginative literature.
questions.explain: The rules apply primarily to expository works, and the authors promise to discuss the changes for poetical works later, in the chapters on imaginative literature and on stories, plays and poems.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each rule or question to where it fits in the plan of analytical reading.
pairs: Discover the major problems the author tried to solve
Find out what the author's solutions are
What is being said in detail, and how?
questions.explain: Rule 4 closes the first stage and Rule 8 closes the second by returning to those problems; together Rules 5 to 8 answer the second basic question.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how does the chapter "Determining an Author's Message" connect the chapters before and after it?
questions.a: It continues the interpretive work begun with coming to terms in the previous chapter, moving on to propositions, arguments and solutions. Through Rule 8 it links back to Rule 4 and the outlining of the book's structure in the first stage. Having followed the author through the second stage, the reader is ready for the next chapter, where he may criticize the book fairly.

questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book give as words that indicate the presence of an argument?
options: because
since this, therefore that
it follows from this that
for instance
in the preface
questions.explain: Words that relate statements so that one is a reason for another signal an argument; "for instance" introduces an example and a preface states intentions.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book's terms, sort each sentence by whether it expresses a proposition.

items.t: The whole is greater than its parts.
Teaching and being taught are correlative functions.
What makes a sentence important?
We hope this book will help you read better.

questions.explain: Declarative sentences express propositions; questions state problems, and wishes or intentions tell the author's purpose rather than knowledge.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort each description by whose point of view makes a sentence important.
groups: Important from the author's point of view
Important from the reader's point of view

items.t: Expresses a judgment on which the whole argument rests
States one of the major affirmations or denials
Is not perfectly intelligible at first sight
Must be read more slowly than the rest

questions.explain: For the author, key sentences carry the judgments his argument rests on; for the reader, they are the ones needing an effort of interpretation. The two usually coincide.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do Adler and Van Doren say it is essential to reading to be perplexed and know it?
questions.a: Sensitivity to the difference between passages you understand readily and those you cannot is the first clue to the sentences that carry the main burden of meaning. Wonder is the beginning of wisdom in learning from books as well as from nature. If you never ask yourself questions about a passage's meaning, you cannot expect the book to give you any insight you do not already have.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each item from the "Nothing acts except what is actual" example to its role.
pairs: Nothing acts except what is actual
A sham showing only verbal memory
If something does not exist, it cannot do anything
An apparent translation into other words
Merely possible showers do not make grass grow
An exemplification showing the proposition is grasped
questions.explain: The example shows both tests: a restatement in other words and a particular instance reveal understanding that mere repetition does not.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort each feature as a mark of a helpful book or of a loosely constructed one.

items.t: Summarizes itself as its arguments develop
Comes close to one paragraph per argument
Diffuse paragraphs that hide the argument
Steps of the argument left out in misleading ways
Makes the reader search in vain for arguments

questions.explain: Good expository authors reveal their thought, through summaries and tight paragraphs; loose books have diffuse paragraphs and omitted steps.

questions.q: In Adler and Van Doren's picture of reading as a conversation, who has the last word?
options: The reader, once the author has had his say
The author, since the reader cannot interrupt him
The critics who review the book in public
Neither, because a book is a monologue
questions.explain: The authors say the reader has the last word: the author has had his say, and then it is the reader's turn. Thinking a book is a one-sided monologue is exactly the mistake they warn against.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what makes ordinary conversation profitable rather than mere bickering?
options: Following the conventions of social politeness
Observing an intellectual etiquette
Letting the more learned party speak first
Avoiding serious subjects that cause disagreement
questions.explain: They say conventions of social politeness are not really important; what matters is an intellectual etiquette, without which conversation is bickering. The profit of good conversation is something learned.

questions.q: How, according to Adler and Van Doren, does the undemanding reader damn a book?
options: By attacking it angrily in a hostile review
By agreeing with it without understanding it
By putting it aside and forgetting it, with no critical consideration
By reading only its first few pages
questions.explain: The undemanding reader dismisses a book by putting it aside and forgetting it; worse than faint praise, he gives it no critical consideration at all.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how is the virtue of teachability best described?
options: Passive and pliable acceptance of what an author says
Deference to authors as one's intellectual superiors
Sheer amount of effort spent on a book
An active virtue that requires independent judgment
questions.explain: Teachability is often confused with subservience, but the authors call it an extremely active virtue: no one is really teachable who does not freely exercise independent judgment.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, when does a reader become fit to criticize a book that is superior to him?
options: Once he understands it, which raises him almost to the author's level
Only after experts have reviewed it first
As soon as he has finished an inspectional reading
Never, since readers are not the author's peers
questions.explain: A book that can enlighten its readers should not be criticized by them until they understand it; when they do, they have raised themselves almost to equality with the author and owe him critical engagement.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, which art underlies the third stage of analytical reading?
options: Grammar
Rhetoric
Logic
Dialectic
questions.explain: Skill in the first two stages comes from grammar and logic; skill in the third stage, criticism, rests on the principles of rhetoric in the broadest sense.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, a serious communicator seeks to convince about which kind of matters?
options: Matters that affect action
Matters that affect feeling
Theoretical matters
Matters of taste and opinion
questions.explain: They distinguish convincing about theoretical matters from persuading about matters that ultimately affect action or feeling.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what is the error that the authors call a popular misconception about criticism?
options: That criticism must always give reasons
That criticism should wait for understanding
That suspending judgment is a critical act
That to criticize is always to disagree
questions.explain: The authors hope readers have not supposed that to criticize is always to disagree; agreeing and suspending judgment are equally critical positions.

questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren recommend as the polite response to a critic who challenges your position without understanding it?
options: Ask him to state your position for you in his own words
Answer each of his objections point by point
Concede the point to avoid contentiousness
Suspend judgment on his criticism
questions.explain: There is no point answering such critics; the only polite thing is to ask them to state the position they claim to challenge. If they cannot, their criticism is irrelevant.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, when does saying "I don't understand" reflect on the book rather than on the reader?
options: Whenever the book uses technical words
Only after the reader has tried his hardest
Whenever the book is a great book
As soon as the first reading is finished
questions.explain: Saying "I don't understand" is a critical judgment, but only after you have tried your hardest does it reflect on the book; with good books the presumption favors the book.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren call some literary critics brash in their judgments of Aristotle's Poetics?
options: They judged it only from translations
They read it as practical rather than theoretical
They ignored that its principles depend partly on his other works
They disagreed with it before finishing the first chapter
questions.explain: Its main principles depend in part on Aristotle's treatises on psychology, logic and metaphysics, so critics who judged it alone agreed or disagreed without understanding it.

questions.q: In the Symposium exchange quoted in How to Read a Book, what does Socrates tell Agathon to say instead of "I cannot refute you"?
options: That Socrates has won the argument
That the question cannot be settled
That they should suspend judgment
That he cannot refute the truth
questions.explain: Socrates replies that Agathon should say he cannot refute the truth, since Socrates himself is easily refuted. The point is that truth, not winning, is what matters.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, how does a reader win in a conversation with a book?
options: Only by gaining knowledge
By finding the author's first mistake
By disagreeing successfully
By having the last word
questions.explain: The only profit in conversation with living or dead teachers is what one learns from them; you win only by gaining knowledge, not by knocking the other fellow down.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is the source of most disagreements among men?
options: Their rationality
Their animality and the imperfections of reason it brings
Disagreements buried in the body of reason itself
The fact that everything is a matter of opinion
questions.explain: Rationality is the source of the power to agree; animality, with the imperfections of reason it entails, causes most disagreements. Deeply buried disagreements in reason itself are mentioned only as hard to be sure about.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say a reader who is not convinced by a book still owes the author a considered judgment.
questions.explain: Even if the reader is not convinced or persuaded, the author's intention and effort deserve respect, and the reader owes him a considered judgment, with grounds for disagreeing or suspending judgment.

questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the most teachable reader is said to be the least critical one.
questions.explain: The authors say the opposite: the most teachable reader is the most critical, the one who makes the greatest effort to make up his own mind.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that the third stage of analytical reading can be carried on at the same time as the first two by an expert reader.
questions.explain: The first two stages interpenetrate and an expert combines them, but the third must always follow them in time; the expert no less than the beginner must wait until he understands.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren hold that when reading only part of a book, a reader should be more hesitant to criticize.
questions.explain: Reading only part of a book makes it harder to be sure you understand, so you should be more hesitant to criticize.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say a reader who feels whipped at having to agree with an author has a problem that is intellectual rather than emotional.
questions.explain: Such a reader is inveterately disputatious, and the authors say his problem is emotional rather than intellectual.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that disagreement owing to inequality of knowledge is curable by instruction.
questions.explain: The relatively ignorant often wrongly disagree with the relatively learned, but this can be corrected: inequality of knowledge is always curable by instruction.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say teachability is often confused with ____, as if a teachable person were passive and pliable.
questions.explain: They warn that teachability is often confused with subservience, whereas it is in fact an extremely active virtue.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say a serious listener must be not only responsive but also ____, which means taking a position of his own.
questions.explain: You are responsive when you follow what is said; you are responsible when you take a position, which is yours and not the author's.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that to agree without understanding is inane, and to disagree without understanding is ____.
questions.explain: Both agreement and disagreement require understanding first; disagreeing without it is called impudent.

questions.q: Rule 9 in How to Read a Book says you must be able to say, with reasonable certainty, "I ____," before you agree, disagree, or suspend judgment.
questions.explain: The ninth rule requires that you can honestly say "I understand" before taking any of the three critical positions.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that suspending judgment is also an act of ____, since it takes the position that something has not been shown.
questions.explain: Suspending judgment is a critical position: the reader says he is not convinced or persuaded one way or the other.

questions.q: Rule 10 in How to Read a Book says that when you disagree, do so reasonably, and not disputatiously or ____.
questions.explain: The second general maxim of critical reading is to disagree reasonably, not disputatiously or contentiously.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren compare conversation among people who think everything is a matter of opinion to a ____ game in which no one keeps score.
questions.explain: On the view that everything is opinion, conversation is hardly better than a ping-pong game of opposed opinions where everyone ends up holding the opinions he started with.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren define ____, in their sense, as unsupported judgment, which is why they call it mere or personal.
questions.explain: Opinion in their sense is unsupported judgment, held on personal feeling or prejudice; knowledge consists of opinions that can be defended with evidence.

questions.q: Which of these are the critical positions that Adler and Van Doren say a reader can take once he understands a book?
options: I agree
I disagree
I suspend judgment
I reject the author's terms
I refuse to judge the man
questions.explain: The three remarks agree, disagree and suspend judgment exhaust the critical positions. The other choices are not among them.

questions.q: Which of these are the two reasons Adler and Van Doren give for stating Rule 9 so explicitly?
options: Many people identify criticism with disagreement
Few people observe the rule in practice
The rule is not obvious common sense
Authors cannot be trusted to write clearly
questions.explain: They state the rule explicitly because many identify criticism with disagreement, and because, though it seems obviously sound, few observe it in practice. They grant it does seem obvious common sense.

questions.q: Which of these situations do Adler and Van Doren say call for special care before saying "I understand"?
options: Reading only part of a book
Reading a book that depends on other books by the same author
Reading a book by a living author
Reading a book in translation
questions.explain: The authors name two conditions: reading only part of a book, and a book that depends on the author's other works for its full significance.

questions.q: Which of these kinds of disagreement do Adler and Van Doren say are curable?
options: Apparent disagreement resulting from misunderstanding
Disagreement owing to inequality of knowledge
