Disagreements deeply buried in the body of reason itself
Disagreements that are pure matters of taste
questions.explain: Misunderstanding and ignorance can be removed, so those disagreements are curable. Disagreements buried in reason itself are hard to be sure about and almost impossible for reason to describe.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren describe as aims of a serious communicator?
options: To be understood
To be agreed with in some sense
To convince or persuade
To win the argument whether right or wrong
questions.explain: A serious talker wishes to be understood and agreed with, that is, to convince or persuade. Winning regardless of truth is the contentious attitude the chapter rejects.

questions.q: Which of these does Rule 11 in How to Read a Book require of a reader?
options: Respect the difference between knowledge and mere personal opinion
Give reasons for any critical judgment
Treat the author's personality as the main object of interest
Accept only self-evident propositions as knowledge
questions.explain: Rule 11 says to respect the difference between knowledge and mere personal opinion by giving reasons for any critical judgment. Judging the man instead of the book is what it warns against.

questions.q: Put the sections of the chapter Criticizing a Book Fairly in the order in which they appear.
items: Teachability as a Virtue
The Role of Rhetoric
The Importance of Suspending Judgment
The Importance of Avoiding Contentiousness
On the Resolution of Disagreements
questions.explain: The chapter first establishes the reader's right and duty to criticize, grounds it in rhetoric, then sets out the three general maxims in turn.

questions.q: Put the three liberal arts in the order in which, according to Adler and Van Doren, they govern the stages of analytical reading, from the first stage to the critical stage.
items: Grammar and logic for finding the structure and terms
Grammar and logic for interpreting the message
Rhetoric for criticizing
questions.explain: Skill in the first two stages comes from mastery of grammar and logic; skill in the third depends on rhetoric.

questions.q: Put these in the order in which Adler and Van Doren say a reader should proceed with a good book.
items: Do the work of understanding the book
Honestly be able to say I understand
Agree, disagree, or suspend judgment
questions.explain: Rule 9 requires understanding first; only then may the reader take one of the three critical positions.

questions.q: Put these steps in the order Adler and Van Doren give for a reader who finds himself disagreeing with a book.
items: Make sure the disagreement is not owing to misunderstanding
Distinguish genuine knowledge from mere opinion
Treat the issue as resolvable and give reasons for the disagreement
questions.explain: The reader first checks for misunderstanding, then separates knowledge from opinion, and regards an issue of knowledge as resolvable by reasons.

questions.q: Put the general maxims of criticism in Criticizing a Book Fairly in the order in which they are stated.
items: Understand before you criticize
Do not disagree contentiously
Regard disagreements as resolvable and give reasons
questions.explain: The chapter summary gives the maxims in this order: complete understanding, avoid disputatiousness, view disagreement as remediable and give reasons.

questions.q: Match each rule of reading in Criticizing a Book Fairly to its content.
pairs: Be able to say I understand before agreeing, disagreeing, or suspending judgment
When you disagree, do so reasonably, not contentiously
Respect knowledge versus opinion by giving reasons for critical judgments
questions.explain: These are the three general maxims of critical reading treated in this chapter.

questions.q: Match each work to the other work by the same author that Adler and Van Doren say should be read before judging it.
pairs: His treatises on psychology, logic and metaphysics
questions.explain: Each of these writers could not say everything in one work, so judging one work alone risks judging what one does not fully understand.

questions.q: Match each writer to the remark about reading quoted in Criticizing a Book Fairly.
pairs: Warns against those who read to doubt or to scorn
No book so bad but something good may be found in it
questions.explain: Bacon and Scott are cited for the reverent view of books; the authors then reverse Cervantes, saying no book is so good that no fault can be found with it.

questions.q: Match each kind of disagreement in How to Read a Book to how it is resolved.
pairs: Removed by coming to terms and a meeting of minds
Resolved in the long run by appeals to fact and reason
questions.explain: The authors hold that most disagreements can be resolved by removing misunderstanding or ignorance, or in the long run by fact and reason.

questions.q: Sort these according to Adler and Van Doren: is each a critical judgment, or not a valid critical judgment because it lacks understanding?

items.t: Agreeing after honestly understanding the book
Suspending judgment because something has not been shown
Disagreeing with reasons after understanding
Saying I don't know what you mean, but you're wrong
Agreeing with a position you cannot state in your own words
Doubting a book without knowing what you doubt

questions.explain: Agreement, disagreement and suspended judgment are all critical acts, but only when based on understanding; without it, affirmations and denials are equally meaningless.

questions.q: Sort these into knowledge or mere opinion as Adler and Van Doren use the words.

items.t: A judgment supported by evidence others are likely to accept
An opinion that can be defended
A belief held subject to correction because the weight of evidence supports it
A judgment based only on personal feeling
A statement with no reason except prejudice
An author's proposition given without any reasons

questions.explain: Knowledge consists in opinions that can be defended with evidence; opinion in their sense is unsupported judgment based on feeling or prejudice.

questions.q: Sort these into the speaker's side or the listener's side of rhetorical skill as Adler and Van Doren describe it.

items.t: Knowing how to convince or persuade
Writing clearly and intelligibly as a means to an end
Knowing how to react to someone trying to persuade
Taking a position for which one is responsible

questions.explain: On the writer's side rhetoric is knowing how to convince or persuade; on the reader's side it is knowing how to react to such efforts.

questions.q: Sort these attitudes into the reasonable critic and the contentious critic as Adler and Van Doren describe them.

items.t: Is as prepared to agree as to disagree
Admits a point when he sees it
Is moved only by the truth about the case
Reads only to find something to disagree with
Treats conversation as a battle
Feels whipped when he has to agree

questions.explain: The contentious reader treats conversation as a battle and seeks a bone to pick; the reasonable reader is motivated by the facts alone.

questions.q: Sort these into the opportunity or the obligation of the reader to talk back, as Adler and Van Doren describe them.

items.t: Nothing can stop a reader from pronouncing judgment
The author cannot defend himself against the reader
The author's effort to teach deserves respect
The reader owes the author a considered judgment

questions.explain: The opportunity is clear since nothing stops a reader from judging; the obligation is rooted in the author's effort to teach, which deserves a considered judgment.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say that reading a book is a kind of conversation, and what does that imply for the reader?
questions.a: The author has his say and then it is the reader's turn, so the reader has the last word. Because the author cannot defend himself or protest that he is misunderstood, the reader must observe an intellectual etiquette. A good book deserves active reading that is completed by criticism, the work of judging.

questions.q: Explain why Adler and Van Doren reject the view that a good book is above the criticism of the average reader.
questions.a: They grant that readers should not criticize a book until they understand it. But once they understand, they have raised themselves almost to equality with the author, and failing to criticize would do him an injustice. They add that there is no book so good that no fault can be found with it.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say the most teachable reader is the most critical?
questions.a: Teachability is not subservience but an active virtue; a person who does not exercise independent judgment can be trained, perhaps, but not taught. The teachable reader fully hears and understands the teacher and then makes the greatest effort to make up his own mind on the matters discussed.

questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren connect rhetoric to the reader's responsibility for his own judgments?
questions.a: Rhetoric is involved in all communication, since a serious speaker wants to convince or persuade. The serious reader must be responsive, following what is said, and also responsible, taking a position that is his own. To regard anyone except yourself as responsible for your judgment is to be a slave, which is where the liberal arts get their name.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren insist that the third stage of analytical reading must follow the first two in time?
questions.a: The first two stages can interpenetrate, and an expert combines them, but criticism is only relevant if it rests on understanding. Agreeing without understanding is inane and disagreeing without it is impudent, so even the expert must wait until he understands before he criticizes.

questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren mean by watching your tone of voice when you say "I don't understand" about a good book?
questions.a: Saying you don't understand is a critical judgment, but with good books the presumption is in favor of the book, and failure to understand is usually the reader's fault. Only after the reader has tried his hardest does it reflect on the book, so his tone should concede that it may not be the author's fault.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren think contentious reading is futile, even though the reader can easily seem to win?
questions.a: In private the author cannot defend himself, so a reader can get the empty satisfaction of showing him up by glancing at a few pages. But the only profit in conversation is what one learns; you win only by gaining knowledge. Following Plato and Aristotle, the reader should honor truth and be as ready to agree as to disagree.

questions.q: Explain how Adler and Van Doren use human nature to explain both why people disagree and why they can agree.
questions.a: Men are rational animals. Their rationality is the source of their power to agree, while their animality and the imperfections of reason it entails cause most disagreements, through passion, prejudice and language clouded by emotion. To the extent men are rational, these obstacles can be overcome.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren reject the view that everything is just a matter of opinion?
questions.a: On that view communication cannot increase knowledge, and conversation is a ping-pong game where everyone ends with the opinions he started with. The authors hold that knowledge can be communicated and discussion can result in learning, so disagreements about knowledge are either apparent or can be resolved in the long run by fact and reason.

questions.q: How does Criticizing a Book Fairly fit into the structure of analytical reading, and how does it relate to the following chapter?
questions.a: It opens the third and last stage of analytical reading, after the first two stages of outlining and interpreting a book. This chapter gives general maxims of intellectual etiquette, Rules 9 to 11, while the next chapter, Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author, gives more specific criteria for points of criticism.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what must a reader be able to say before he may agree or disagree with a book?
options: That he understands it
That he has read every chapter of it
That he has consulted other critics
That he finds the author likable
questions.explain: The chapter opens by saying the reader must say he understands in order to say more. Merely having read the whole book is not the same as understanding it.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: When can the reader's remark "I don't understand" count as a genuine critical remark, in How to Read a Book?
options: When the reader feels the book is too long
When the reader can show the fault lies in the book itself
When the reader has read it only once
When the reader disagrees with its conclusions
questions.explain: The remark becomes criticism only if the reader can support it by locating the trouble in the book, such as disorderly structure or equivocal use of important words. Otherwise he should go back to work on the book.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that if a reader understands a book and agrees thoroughly with it, the analytical reading is completely done.
questions.explain: If the reader understands and agrees fully, he has been enlightened and convinced, so the work is over. Further steps arise only with disagreement or suspended judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that suspended judgment is a more usual outcome than disagreement once a reader understands a book.
questions.explain: The authors say further steps arise in the case of disagreement or suspended judgment, and that disagreement is the more usual case.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren call the error of supposing that understanding makes disagreement impossible a failure to distinguish two senses of "____".
questions.explain: Some people wrongly think all disagreement is owing to misunderstanding because they confuse agreement about the use of language with agreement about the facts.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: In the "all men are equal" example in How to Read a Book, why was the first disagreement irrelevant?
options: Because equality cannot be debated rationally
Because the facts about human abilities are unknown
Because the disagreement rested on a misreading of what the speaker meant
Because political rights are a matter of taste
questions.explain: The reader took the words to mean equal natural endowment when the speaker meant equal political rights. Once the misunderstanding is corrected, a disagreement becomes a real issue.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Explain why, according to Adler and Van Doren, understanding an author is the condition for genuinely agreeing or disagreeing with him rather than an obstacle to it.
questions.a: Understanding is an agreement about the use of language, a meeting of minds through words. Only when reader and author share an understanding of what is being said can there be a real issue about facts or policy, since the author is making judgments about the world that may be right or wrong. So it is because of, not in spite of, sound interpretation that the reader can concur or dissent.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which of these can a reader point to, according to Adler and Van Doren, to support the charge that a book is unintelligible?
options: Its structure is disorderly
Its parts do not hang together
The author equivocates in the use of important words
The reader dislikes its conclusions
The book has very few illustrations
questions.explain: The authors list disorderly structure, parts that do not hang together, irrelevance, and equivocation as faults in the book. Disliking the conclusions is a reaction of the reader, not a fault of intelligibility.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Put the three ideal conditions for well-conducted controversy in the order Adler and Van Doren give them.
items: Acknowledge the emotions you bring to the dispute
Make your own assumptions explicit
Attempt impartiality by taking the other's point of view
questions.explain: The authors first ask for acknowledgment of emotions, then explicit assumptions or prejudices, and finally an attempt at impartiality as an antidote to partisanship.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say you must acknowledge the emotions you bring to a dispute?
options: Because emotions always weaken an author's case
Because authors expect readers to share their feelings
Because emotions are forbidden in analytical reading
Because otherwise you may be venting feelings while thinking you have reasons
questions.explain: Since men are animals as well as rational, unacknowledged emotion can masquerade as argument: you may think you have reasons when you have only strong feelings.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors explain that your prejudices are your ____, which you must make explicit.
questions.explain: The second condition asks you to know your prejudices, that is, your prejudgments, so you can admit your opponent may be equally entitled to different assumptions.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren hold that controversy without partisanship is possible if both sides are careful enough.
questions.explain: They say controversy without partisanship is impossible; what they recommend is an attempt at impartiality as an antidote to the blindness partisanship brings.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: If an author explicitly asks you to take something for granted, what do Adler and Van Doren say you should do?
options: Honor the request even though the opposite could also be assumed
Refuse unless you already share the assumption
Stop reading until he proves the assumption
Replace it with your own assumption
questions.explain: Good controversy should not be a quarrel about assumptions, so the fact that the opposite can be taken for granted should not prevent you from honoring the author's request.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren replace their three ideal conditions of controversy with four prescriptions for adverse criticism?
questions.a: The three conditions are an ideal that can only be approximated, and the authors admit they too have violated them. They still believe critical reading can be disciplined, so they substitute four ways a book can be adversely criticized that are easier to follow. If a reader confines himself to these points, he is less likely to indulge in expressions of emotion or prejudice.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Apply Adler and Van Doren's idea: Maya finishes a book on diet that rests on an assumption she has always rejected, and she immediately dismisses the book. What has she failed to do, and what would they advise?
questions.a: She has not made her own assumptions explicit and recognized them as prejudgments, so she cannot give the author's case a fair hearing. The authors say good controversy should not be a quarrel about assumptions; she should grant the author's stated assumption and try to read sympathetically, taking his point of view, before judging whether he can be shown to be wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say a reader must do when making any of the four adverse remarks about a book?
options: Specify the precise respect in which the author fails
Give reasons supporting the remark
Show the book is wrong about everything
Get the author to concede the point
Read at least two other books on the subject first
questions.explain: The remark must be definite, specifying the respect, and supported with reasons. A book cannot be uninformed or illogical about everything, so a total charge is not what is required.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Match each adverse remark in How to Read a Book with what it charges the author with.
pairs: Lacking some knowledge relevant to his problem
Asserting what is not the case
Not solving all his problems or using his materials fully
questions.explain: These are the authors' definitions of the four remarks. The first three concern soundness; the fourth concerns the completeness of the author's execution of his plan.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Match each author with the defect Adler and Van Doren use him to illustrate.
pairs: Uninformed about the mechanism of inheritance
Misinformed that democracy is more primitive than monarchy
A non sequitur about good laws and arms
An inconsistency about bodies and sensory qualities
questions.explain: Darwin lacked genetics, Spinoza asserted a falsehood of political history, Machiavelli's conclusion does not follow from his premise, and Hobbes contradicts his own position on qualities.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: What must a reader be able to do to support the charge that an author is uninformed, according to Adler and Van Doren?
options: Show the author was careless in his research
State the missing knowledge and show how it changes the conclusions
Prove the author wrote before key discoveries
Find another author who disagrees
questions.explain: The reader must be able to state the knowledge the author lacks and show how it is relevant to his conclusions. Without relevance, the remark has no point.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: How does Adler and Van Doren's discussion of uninformed authors contrast philosophy with science and history?
options: In philosophy knowledge only accumulates over time
In philosophy no author can be uninformed
In philosophy there may be loss as well as gain over time
In philosophy gaps are found by later experiments
questions.explain: In science and history later research usually reveals what an author lacked, but in philosophy there is as likely to be loss as gain, as when Hume ignored the ancient distinction between images and ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say David Hume revealed his ignorance of the distinction between images and ____, a distinction earlier philosophers had well established.
questions.explain: Their example of philosophical loss over time: the ancients distinguished what men can sense and imagine from what they can understand, yet Hume ignored it.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say Aquinas's error about the matter of the heavenly bodies has limited relevance to his metaphysics.
questions.explain: Modern astrophysics corrects his error, but making it does not affect his metaphysical account of all sensible things as composed of matter and form.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which example do Adler and Van Doren give of an author who was misinformed?
options: Gibbon on facts bearing on the fall of Rome
Euclid on postulates about parallel lines
Dewey on thinking in learning by instruction
Aristotle on the female role in animal reproduction
questions.explain: Aristotle asserted what is not the case about reproduction and drew unsupportable conclusions. Gibbon illustrates being uninformed, while Euclid and Dewey illustrate incompleteness.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren distinguish being misinformed from being uninformed?
options: Misinformation is a positive error, not merely a lack of knowledge
Misinformation concerns logic, uninformation concerns facts
Misinformation is always deliberate
Misinformation affects only minor points
questions.explain: Being uninformed is a negative defect, a lack; being misinformed is positive as well, asserting as true what is false, which leads to wrong conclusions and untenable solutions.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that taken together, the charges of being uninformed and misinformed accuse an author of defects in his ____.
questions.explain: Both charges say his evidences and reasons are not good enough in quantity or quality, so they fall on his premises rather than his reasoning.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which of these are the two sorts of fallacy Adler and Van Doren name when an author is illogical?
options: Non sequitur
Inconsistency
Equivocation
Incompleteness
Misinformation
questions.explain: A non sequitur draws a conclusion that does not follow from the reasons; an inconsistency says two incompatible things. Incompleteness and misinformation are separate points of criticism.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, a conclusion that simply does not follow from the reasons offered is called a non ____.
questions.explain: The authors name the non sequitur as one of the two general sorts of fallacy, the other being inconsistency.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: What is the fallacy in Machiavelli's argument about good laws, as Adler and Van Doren analyze it?
options: He assumes laws are unnecessary in old states
From good laws needing arms, he concludes well-armed states have good laws
He contradicts himself about the power of princes
He lacks historical knowledge of ancient states
questions.explain: It does not follow from good laws depending on adequate force that adequate force guarantees good laws, just as health does not guarantee happiness.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Explain the inconsistency Adler and Van Doren find in Hobbes's Elements of Law.
questions.a: Hobbes holds that all bodies are only quantities of matter in motion with no qualities, and that man is just a collection of bodies in motion. Yet he concludes that sensory qualities like colors and tastes are the motions of atoms in the brain. Since what is said of all bodies in motion must apply to the atoms of the brain, this conclusion contradicts his first position.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Sort these examples from How to Read a Book by which defect they illustrate.

items.t: Darwin's ignorance of genetics
Gibbon lacking facts on the fall of Rome
Hume ignoring images versus ideas
Spinoza on democracy as more primitive
Aristotle on the female factor in reproduction
Aquinas on the matter of heavenly bodies

questions.explain: The uninformed examples involve a lack of relevant knowledge; the misinformed examples involve asserting what is false or less probable.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Apply Adler and Van Doren's criteria: a reviewer says a 1950s book on nutrition is flawed because it does not mention a vitamin discovered in 1980. When is this a fair criticism?
questions.a: It is a charge that the author is uninformed, which is fair only if the missing knowledge is relevant to the problem the author is trying to solve. The reviewer must state the knowledge the author lacked and show how it makes a difference to his conclusions. If the vitamin would not change those conclusions, there is no point in making the remark.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say a reader need not bother with every lapse in an author's facts or logic?
questions.a: Each of the soundness criticisms matters only when it is relevant to the author's conclusions. A misinformation should be pointed out only if it bears on the conclusions, and lack of cogency matters only to the extent that major conclusions are affected; as they put it, a book “may safely lack cogency in irrelevant respects.” The Aquinas example shows an error with limited relevance.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that if you understand a book but cannot show the author is uninformed, misinformed, or illogical, you must ____ with him as far as he has gone.
questions.explain: Failing to support any of the first three remarks obligates you to agree; you have no freedom of will about this.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren say a reader really means when he finds no fault in an author.s premises or reasoning yet says he rejects the conclusions?
options: That he has found a hidden fallacy
That the book is incomplete
That he does not like the conclusions
That he needs more evidence
questions.explain: Such a person is not disagreeing but expressing emotions or prejudices. If still honestly unconvinced, perhaps he should not have claimed to understand.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say the first three adverse remarks bear on the structure of the whole book, while the fourth bears on terms and propositions.
questions.explain: It is the reverse: the first three relate to the author's terms, propositions, and arguments, while the remark that the book is incomplete bears on the structure of the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which of these count as an incomplete analysis, according to Adler and Van Doren's definition?
options: Not solving all the problems the author started with
Failing to see all the implications of his materials
Failing to make distinctions relevant to his undertaking
Asserting what is contrary to fact
Drawing a conclusion that does not follow
questions.explain: Incompleteness concerns unsolved problems, underused materials, and missing relevant distinctions. Asserting falsehoods is being misinformed, and an unsupported conclusion is a non sequitur.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say it is not enough simply to call a book incomplete?
options: Because incompleteness is never a fault
Because only experts may judge completeness
Because authors always state their own limits
Because every finite human work is incomplete in some way
questions.explain: Men and their works are finite, so anyone can say that of any book. The remark has a point only if the reader defines the inadequacy precisely.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Match each work with why Adler and Van Doren call it incomplete.
pairs: Cannot conceive democracy based on universal suffrage
Did not consider other postulates about parallel lines
Omits thinking in reading or learning by instruction
Incomplete on happiness for a believer in immortality
questions.explain: Each illustration shows an analysis that would need extending: to new political forms, other geometries, other kinds of thinking, or a view of personal immortality.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say the measure of a book's completeness is the number of valid and significant ____ it contains.
questions.explain: The profoundest comparison between books concerns completeness, measured by distinctions, which is why grasping the author's terms matters: terms are correlative with distinctions.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: How, according to Adler and Van Doren, does the fourth critical remark tie together the three stages of analytical reading?
questions.a: Structural outlining ends by knowing the problems the author tries to solve, and interpretation ends by knowing which he solved and which he did not. The point about completeness, the final step of criticism, touches outlining by considering how adequately he stated his problems, and interpretation by measuring how satisfactorily he solved them.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren say related books in the same field can be compared, and which comparison is profoundest?
questions.a: Books can be compared using the four criteria: one is better as it speaks more truth and makes fewer errors, has more information, fewer erroneous suppositions, and more cogent reasoning. The profoundest comparison concerns the completeness of each analysis, measured by the number of valid and significant distinctions each contains.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Sort these remarks from How to Read a Book by what they concern.

items.t: You are uninformed
You are misinformed
You are illogical
You did not solve all your problems
You failed to make relevant distinctions

questions.explain: The authors say the first three points deal with soundness, while the fourth deals with the adequacy with which the author discharges his chosen task.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Put these rules of analytical reading in the order Adler and Van Doren list them.
items: Classify the book according to kind and subject matter
Define the problems the author has tried to solve
Come to terms with the author
Determine which problems the author has solved
Do not begin criticism until you have outlined and interpreted
Show wherein the author's analysis is incomplete
questions.explain: The list runs from the structural rules (1 to 4), through interpretation (5 to 8), to criticism (9 to 15).

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Put these rules for the third stage of analytical reading in the order Adler and Van Doren give them.
items: Do not say you agree or disagree until you understand
Do not disagree disputatiously or contentiously
Present good reasons for any critical judgment
Show wherein the author is uninformed
Show wherein the author is illogical
questions.explain: The three general maxims of intellectual etiquette (rules 9 to 11) come before the special criteria for points of criticism (rules 12 to 15).

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Put the four basic questions a reader asks in the order the rules of analytical reading answer them, according to Adler and Van Doren.
items: What is the book about as a whole?
What is being said in detail, and how?
Is it true?
What of it?
questions.explain: The first four rules answer the first question, the interpretive rules answer the second, and the last seven rules help answer the third and fourth.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Sort these rules from the third stage in How to Read a Book into their two groups.
groups: Special criteria for points of criticism

items.t: Do not begin criticism until you can say you understand
Do not disagree disputatiously
Give good reasons for any critical judgment
Show wherein the author is uninformed
Show wherein the author is misinformed
Show wherein the analysis is incomplete

questions.explain: Rules 9 to 11 are the maxims of etiquette; rules 12 to 15 are the four criteria for adverse criticism.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren title the third stage of analytical reading: rules for criticizing a book as a communication of ____.
questions.explain: The third stage treats the book as a communication of knowledge, which is why truth is its central concern.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren's note on the last four rules, what follows if a reader fails to show any of the first three defects?
options: He must agree, at least in part
He may still disagree on grounds of taste
He must reject the book as incomplete
He should start the reading over
questions.explain: The note says the first three are criteria for disagreement; failing in all of them, you must agree at least in part, though you may suspend judgment on the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Match each feature of human discourse with the reading task it makes necessary, according to Adler and Van Doren.
pairs: Language is a relatively opaque medium
questions.explain: The first three questions correspond to the nature of discourse: without complexity, opacity, and error, outlining, interpretation, and criticism would be unnecessary.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say the question "Is it true?" applies only to scientific and historical writing.
questions.explain: They say it can be asked of anything we read, in one or another sense of truth: mathematical, scientific, philosophical, historical, and poetical.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: What distinction does the fourth question, What of it?, turn on, according to Adler and Van Doren?
options: Between fact and fiction
Between information and understanding
Between author and reader
Between speed and comprehension
questions.explain: When material is informational, the reader is challenged to go further and seek enlightenment, and even when enlightened to keep searching for significance.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Which of these standards do Adler and Van Doren say many reviewers now use instead of truth?
options: Novelty
Sensationalism
Seductiveness
Clarity
Power to enlighten
questions.explain: They list novelty, sensationalism, seductiveness, force, and power to bemuse, contrasting these with truth, clarity, and power to enlighten, which reviewers neglect.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren say "well-read" should mean?
options: Having read the books on every required list
Having read many books quickly
Reading well rather than merely reading widely
Being able to quote famous authors
questions.explain: Too often the phrase means quantity rather than quality; a person who has read widely but not well deserves to be pitied rather than praised.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: What point do Adler and Van Doren make with Hobbes's remark about reading as many books as most men do?
questions.a: They use it to show that quantity of reading is not the measure of being well-read; quality is. A person who reads widely but not well deserves pity rather than praise. Great writers often read fewer books than colleges now require, but read them well and so became peers of their authors.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say the rules of analytical reading describe an ____ performance that few readers ever fully reach.
questions.explain: The ideal remains the measure of achievement: you are a good reader to the degree in which you approximate it.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Apply Adler and Van Doren's fourth question: Raj reads a news digest full of statistics on rising rents and stops once he has noted the numbers. What does the book say he is missing?
questions.a: He has the information but has not asked What of it? The authors say facts seldom come without some interpretation, and digests select facts by some principle of significance. Reading for information intelligently means determining what significance is, or should be, attached to the facts, and going on to seek understanding.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say a chapter on agreeing and disagreeing is needed in a book on reading?
options: Because most books are written to be refuted
Because readers rarely understand what they read
Because disagreement is the goal of reading
Because authors argue with readers and expect readers to argue back
questions.explain: Since authors argue and expect replies, a good reader must know the principles of argument and carry on civil, intelligent controversy, meeting the author's arguments and not just following them.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which of these does the final section of Chapter 11 of How to Read a Book do?
options: Sets out all fifteen rules of analytical reading in order
Links the last seven rules to the questions Is it true? and What of it?
Introduces the rules of syntopical reading
Stresses that the rules describe an ideal performance
Explains how to use a dictionary
questions.explain: The section titled The Third Stage of Analytical Reading assembles all the rules, ties the criticism rules to the third and fourth questions, and stresses the ideal. Dictionaries come in the next chapter, Aids to Reading.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, Chapter 11 follows a chapter on criticizing a book fairly, whose maxims it presupposes when it discusses disagreement.
questions.explain: Chapter 10, Criticizing a Book Fairly, gives the maxims of etiquette; Chapter 11 assumes a reader who has tried to abide by them and turns to the specific grounds for disagreement.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: How does the order of the sections in Chapter 11 of How to Read a Book reflect its argument?
options: It moves from the reader's attitude, to soundness, to completeness, to a summary of all the rules
It moves from examples to definitions to attitudes
It begins with the full rule list and then explains each rule
It treats completeness before soundness because it matters most
questions.explain: Prejudice and Judgment sets the reader's attitude and the four remarks, the next two sections take the first three and then the fourth remark, and the last gathers all the rules of analytical reading.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Chapter 11 of How to Read a Book completes the ____ stage of analytical reading, after the stages of outlining and interpretation.
questions.explain: Its last section is titled The Third Stage of Analytical Reading, matching the earlier sections on the first and second stages in Chapters 7 and 9.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: How does the end of Chapter 11 of How to Read a Book prepare for what follows it?
questions.a: Having completed and listed all the rules of analytical reading, the authors stress, before proceeding to Part Three, that the rules describe an ideal performance and that being well-read means reading well. The next chapter, Aids to Reading, turns to extrinsic help such as experience and other books, which the completeness criterion already points to when it allows a reader to define inadequacy through the help of other books.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say a reader may do after failing to show the author is uninformed, misinformed, or illogical?
options: Agree with the author as far as he has gone
Suspend judgment on the whole because the analysis is incomplete
Disagree because he dislikes the conclusions
Disagree on the strength of strong feelings
questions.explain: The reader must agree at least in part, though he may suspend judgment on the whole in light of incompleteness. Disliking the conclusions is expressing emotion or prejudice, not disagreeing.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Put the four adverse remarks in the order Adler and Van Doren number them.
items: You are uninformed
You are misinformed
You are illogical
Your analysis is incomplete
questions.explain: The authors list these four remarks in this order and discuss the first three under soundness before turning to the fourth.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Match each stage of analytical reading in How to Read a Book with its heading.
pairs: Rules for finding what a book is about
Rules for interpreting a book's contents
Rules for criticizing a book as a communication of knowledge
questions.explain: These are the headings under which the authors gather all fifteen rules at the end of Chapter 11.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Sort these examples from How to Read a Book by where the defect lies.

items.t: Darwin lacking knowledge of genetics
Spinoza calling democracy more primitive
Aristotle on the female factor in reproduction
Machiavelli on good laws and arms
Hobbes on bodies without qualities

questions.explain: Being uninformed or misinformed charges the author with defects in his premises; the Machiavelli and Hobbes cases are fallacies, a non sequitur and an inconsistency.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Sort these situations by whether Adler and Van Doren would count the disagreement as a real issue.

items.t: Both sides agree on what equal means and differ on political rights
A reader shows the author lacks relevant knowledge
A reader took equal to mean equal natural abilities when equal rights were meant
A reader dislikes conclusions but finds no error in premises or reasoning

questions.explain: A genuine disagreement needs a common understanding of what is said plus a supportable ground. Misreadings make disagreement irrelevant, and mere dislike is emotion, not disagreement.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Sort these by which basic question Adler and Van Doren tie them to at the end of Chapter 11 of How to Read a Book.

items.t: Applicable to mathematical, historical and poetical writing alike
The highest praise a work can earn
Asked only once a work is true in some sense
Turns on information versus understanding
Renewed at every stage of learning

questions.explain: The authors say truth can be asked of anything read and earns the highest commendation; What of it? follows only if the work is true, concerns significance, and is renewed at every stage.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, reading a book in the light of other books, rather than by itself, is called ____ reading.
questions.explain: Adler and Van Doren call reading a book by itself intrinsic reading and reading it in the light of other books extrinsic reading; any aid lying outside the book is an extrinsic aid.

questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, what is the main reason the authors avoided discussing extrinsic aids until Chapter 12?
options: Extrinsic aids were rarely available to ordinary readers in 1972
Extrinsic aids only matter for syntopical reading, which comes later
The rules of extrinsic reading contradict the rules of analytical reading
Many readers depend on such aids too slavishly, and the authors wanted to show this is unnecessary
questions.explain: The authors say the main reason was that many readers lean on outside aids too slavishly. They do not claim the aids contradict intrinsic rules; in fact they say the two kinds of reading tend to fuse.

questions.q: Put the four categories of extrinsic aids in the order How to Read a Book discusses them in Chapter 12.
items: Relevant experiences
Other books
Commentaries and abstracts
Reference books
questions.explain: The chapter announces and follows this order: relevant experience, other books, commentaries and abstracts, and finally reference books.

questions.q: True or false: How to Read a Book advises seeking outside help as soon as any passage of a book feels difficult.
questions.explain: The common-sense maxim is to seek outside help only when a book stays unintelligible after you have done your best with the rules of intrinsic reading. Doing all you can alone first means you need less help over time.

questions.q: Why does How to Read a Book say that no book can be read entirely in isolation, even though its rules so far have been rules of intrinsic reading?
questions.a: Intrinsic and extrinsic reading tend to fuse in the actual work of understanding and criticizing a book. Every reader has read other books before and brings experience of books and of life to bear, measuring an author's statements against what is known from other sources. So it is common sense that no book should, because no book can, be read completely in isolation.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what is the general rule for when to reach for an extrinsic aid?
options: Before starting a book, so you know what to look for
Whenever a single unfamiliar word appears
After doing your best with the intrinsic rules, if the book is still unintelligible
Only when reading syntopically on several books at once
questions.explain: The authors' maxim is to seek outside help when a book remains unintelligible, in whole or part, after you have read it as well as you can by the rules of intrinsic reading.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, experience that must be actively sought, such as a laboratory experiment, is called ____ experience.
questions.explain: Special experience is available only to those who take the trouble to acquire it; the laboratory experiment is the authors' best example. Common experience comes simply from being alive.

questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, an experience must be shared by every human being to count as common experience.
questions.explain: The authors stress that common is not the same as universal. Family life counts as common even though some people are orphans from birth, because most people share it.

questions.q: Match each kind of book to the type of experience How to Read a Book says is mainly relevant to reading it.
pairs: Common experience, appealed to as common sense
Special experience behind the reported evidence
questions.explain: Fiction and philosophy draw on common experience, science on special experience, and history on both because it partakes of the fictional and the scientific.

questions.q: Why does How to Read a Book say both common and special experience are relevant to reading history?
options: History is a story with plot and characters, yet the historian also relies on special research
Historians write mainly for specialists who have done fieldwork
History books are usually read alongside novels of the same period
History is a branch of philosophy and so appeals to common sense
questions.explain: History partakes of both the fictional and the scientific: narrative history has a plot like a novel, while the historian's documents and research are special experience most readers lack.

questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, how can you test whether you are making proper use of your experience to understand a book, and what example do the authors give?
questions.a: The surest test is to ask whether you can give a concrete example of a point you feel you understand. Students who seemed to grasp a point but could supply no example had not really understood it. With Aristotle's claim in the Ethics that virtue is a mean between excess and defect, you should be able to supply examples beyond his own; if you cannot, reread his discussion.

questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book give as examples of special experience?
options: An anthropologist traveling to study people in an unexplored region of the Amazon basin
Astronauts experiencing life on the moon
The experience of being a child of parents
The experience of being taught in school
A laboratory experiment
questions.explain: Fieldwork in an unexplored region, the astronauts' experience on the moon, and laboratory experiments are the authors' examples of special experience. Family life and being taught are their examples of common experience.

questions.q: Sort each experience into the category How to Read a Book assigns it.

items.t: Family life
Sexual love
Being taught
A laboratory experiment
Living on an airless planet
Studying an unexplored people firsthand

questions.explain: Family life, sexual love and being taught are shared by most people, though not all, so they are common. The others must be sought out and are available only to a few, so they are special.

questions.q: Martha cannot judge whether a physics book's argument is sound because she cannot picture the experiments it reports. In How to Read a Book's terms, what is she lacking?
options: Common experience of everyday life
A good dictionary for technical terms
Special experience relevant to scientific evidence
A commentary to read before the book
questions.explain: The authors say special experience is mainly relevant to scientific works, because judging inductive arguments means following the evidence the scientist reports. Common experience is what fiction and philosophy rely on.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, judgments about the ____ of a novel, whether it is true to life as most people lead it, rest almost wholly on common experience.
questions.explain: The authors say judgments concerning the verisimilitude of a novel are almost wholly based on common experience of life as most people, including ourselves, live it.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, why do enthusiastic readers of the great books often soon feel hopelessly inadequate, and what is the remedy?
questions.a: Partly they do not know how to read a single book well, but also they expect to understand the first book they pick up without reading the books it is closely related to, such as trying The Federalist Papers before the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution. The remedy is to read related books in relation to one another, in an order that makes the later ones more intelligible.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how is reading other books as extrinsic aids related to the earlier rules of intrinsic reading?
options: It replaces the rule of finding key words
It is an extension of the value of context: related books form a larger context for the book
It is the opposite of context, since it takes you away from the text
It applies only once you have finished criticizing the book
questions.explain: Just as the whole book is the context for its parts, related books provide an even larger context for interpreting the book you are reading.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: True or false: How to Read a Book says the need to read books in relation to one another is most important for philosophy.
questions.explain: Philosophers are great readers of each other, so the authors call this need most important in philosophy and probably least important for novels and plays.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: How to Read a Book says the great books are involved in a prolonged ____, which readers join by reading them in relation to one another.
questions.explain: The great authors were great readers who carried on a conversation with earlier authors; to join it, we read the great books in relation to one another in an order that respects chronology.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book say about the order in which related great books should be read?
options: The order should somehow respect chronology
Reading from past to present is the only acceptable direction
Reading from past to present has advantages through being more natural
The order does not matter as long as all related books are read
questions.explain: Time is of the essence in the conversation of the books, so chronology should be respected. It can be observed either from present to past or past to present, though the latter is more natural.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: Put the readings How to Read a Book suggests for The Federalist Papers in the order the authors imply, from earliest background to the book itself.
items: Montesquieu, Rousseau and Locke on government
The Articles of Confederation and the Constitution
The Federalist Papers
questions.explain: The authors say readers try The Federalist Papers without first reading the Articles and the Constitution, or try all of these without having read Montesquieu, Rousseau and Locke, which lie further back.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: Sort these kinds of books by how much, according to How to Read a Book, they need to be read in relation to other books.

items.t: Philosophy
History
Novels
Plays
Science

questions.explain: The authors say the need applies more to history and philosophy than to science and fiction, and that good novels or plays can be read in isolation.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Which of these are reasons How to Read a Book gives for using commentaries sparingly?
options: Commentators are not always right
Commentaries are always too long to finish
Even a correct commentary may not be exhaustive, limiting what you discover
Commentaries are illegal to use in college courses
Habitual dependence makes you a worse reader in general
questions.explain: The two stated reasons are that commentators may be wrong and, even when right, may not be exhaustive. The authors add that a habit of depending on them leaves you lost without one and a worse reader overall.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: What rule does How to Read a Book give about when to read a scholarly or critical introduction written by someone else?
options: Read it first, as you would the author's own preface
Read it halfway through, once the plot is clear
Never read it at all
Read it only after you have read the book yourself
questions.explain: Unlike the intrinsic rule of reading the author's own preface first, the extrinsic rule is to read someone else's commentary only after the book; read first, it is likely to distort your reading.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Why does How to Read a Book say reading a commentary after the book, rather than before, is both safer and more pleasurable?
questions.a: Read first, a commentary distorts your reading: you tend to see only the critic's points and miss others just as important. Read afterwards, you have your own understanding of the book and approach the commentator on essentially equal terms. Read beforehand, the authors say, “you are at his mercy.”

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Match each claim in How to Read a Book about handbooks and commentaries to its point.
pairs: Even correct ones may not be exhaustive
You will be lost if you cannot find one
questions.explain: The authors concede handbooks help with exams, give two reasons for sparing use, and warn that habitual dependence makes you a worse reader.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Which of these are the uses How to Read a Book allows for abstracts and plot digests?
options: Jogging your memory of a book you have already read
Replacing the reading of a book you lack time for
Judging, in syntopical reading, whether a work is relevant to your project
Preparing you to understand a book before you open it
questions.explain: The authors say abstracts are useful in two connections only: refreshing memory of a book already read, and deciding during syntopical reading whether a work is germane. An abstract can never replace reading the book.

questions.q: Match each example in How to Read a Book's discussion of facts to what it illustrates.
pairs: An outdated theory describable in an article on its school
questions.explain: The authors say facts are either informational singulars or relatively unquestioned generalizations, and allow one exception for theories tied to a topic, person or school.

questions.q: Put the four kinds of knowledge How to Read a Book says you need to use a reference book well in the order the authors list them.
items: Know what you want to know
Know in what reference work to find it
Know how to find it in that work
Know that it is considered knowable
questions.explain: The authors sum up the four requirements in this order: what you want, which work, how the work is organized, and whether the compilers consider it knowable.

questions.q: How to Read a Book says that to use a reference book well, your ignorance must be like a circle of ____ surrounded by light.
questions.explain: You must have some idea of what you want to know; light must surround the dark circle so that you can ask the reference book an intelligible question.

questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, what kinds of things are found in reference books?
options: Only things about which people generally and conventionally agree
The editors' best judgments on moral questions
Predictions about the future from leading experts
Answers to every question a reader can ask
questions.explain: Only matters of general, conventional agreement belong in reference books; moral questions and the future, on which we do not agree, are not found there.

questions.q: What does How to Read a Book mean by saying reference books cannot cure total ignorance and are not guides to the perplexed?
questions.a: A good deal of knowledge is required before you can use a reference book: what you want to know, which work answers that kind of question, how the work is organized, and whether the matter is considered knowable. Someone wandering in a fog of ignorance cannot ask an intelligible question. So reference books cannot do your thinking for you; they are “useless to people who know nothing.”

questions.q: True or false: How to Read a Book says one reference book can be found that answers questions of all kinds.
questions.explain: The authors say no reference book answers all questions; all such works are specialists, so you need a fair knowledge of the major types to use any one well.

questions.q: Why does How to Read a Book say the history of reference books is interesting in itself?
options: It reveals which publishers dominated each era
It shows how alphabetical order was invented
It records changes in men's opinions about what is knowable
It proves that the physical world has always been orderable
questions.explain: Because reference books contain what is considered knowable, their history tells us much about changing opinions as to what is knowable; the orderability of the physical world was not always assumed.

questions.q: How to Read a Book says a reference book's compiler should anticipate readers' needs, so before using one you should read its introduction and ____ for the editor's advice.
questions.explain: The rule to read a book's introduction and preface first applies particularly to reference books: do not use one before getting the editor's advice on how to use it.

questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, what was the purpose of the first dictionaries?
options: To help Romans read Homer and other Greek literature with archaic vocabulary
To fix the spelling of Latin for Roman schools
To record every usage of English, worst and best
To list the technical terms of medieval universities
questions.explain: The first dictionaries were glossaries of Homeric words for Romans who went to school to Greek teachers. The full record of usage describes the much later Oxford English Dictionary.

questions.q: How to Read a Book says that, however it is constructed, the dictionary is primarily an ____ instrument.
questions.explain: From the beginning the educational motive dominated dictionary making; the conflict between the lexicographer as arbiter and as historian is called a side-issue.

questions.q: True or false: How to Read a Book says the Oxford English Dictionary set out to dictate correct usage rather than record usage.
questions.explain: The authors present the OED as a new departure precisely because it did not try to dictate usage but to give an accurate historical record of every type, worst as well as best.

questions.q: Match each of How to Read a Book's four ways of looking at words to what it covers.
pairs: Grammatical role in a phrase or sentence
Many related meanings, synonyms and antonyms
A history of roots and shifting meanings
questions.explain: Each way of looking at words corresponds to a kind of question a good dictionary answers: form, grammar, meaning, and history.

questions.q: Put How to Read a Book's four ways of looking at words in the order the authors number them.
items: Physical things
Parts of speech
Signs
Conventional
questions.explain: The authors number them: words are physical things, parts of speech, signs, and finally conventional, man-made signs with a history.

questions.q: Which of these are negative rules for dictionary use in How to Read a Book?
options: Do not settle arguments about justice or freedom by quoting the dictionary
Do not read the dictionary's explanatory notes
Do not try to get word-rich quick by memorizing word lists
Do not look up every unfamiliar word on a first reading of a difficult book
Do not attend to the order of meanings listed under a word
questions.explain: The authors warn against settling arguments by dictionary, swallowing the dictionary, and looking up too many words on a first reading. They urge reading the explanatory notes and noting the order of meanings.

questions.q: Lena reads a hard philosophy book for the first time with a dictionary open, looking up every new word. What does How to Read a Book say she risks?
options: Learning too many synonyms at once
Losing track of the book's unity and order
Misjudging the author's verisimilitude
Reading the book's commentary too early
questions.explain: Looking up too many words at the beginning makes you lose track of the book's unity and order; on a first reading, look up only words that seem important to the author's general meaning.

questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, what single fact about dictionaries yields all the rules for using one intelligently, and how?
questions.a: The dictionary is a book about words, not about things. Remembering this lets you ask the four kinds of questions about words: as physical things, parts of speech, signs, and conventional man-made signs. The art of using a dictionary is knowing which questions to ask, and the dictionary itself, through its explanatory notes and abbreviations, tells you how to find the answers.

questions.q: Sort these uses of a dictionary by how How to Read a Book values them.
groups: Uses according to its primary intention

items.t: Understanding archaic words in an old text
Following literary allusions
Tracing the order and relation of a word's meanings
Treating it merely as a spelling guide
Settling an argument about justice
Memorizing fancy word lists

questions.explain: The primary intention is to help read books whose vocabulary is technical, archaic, allusive or obsolete. Using it only for spelling, to settle arguments, or to get word-rich quick is criticized.

questions.q: Why does How to Read a Book say you should use a dictionary according to its primary intention rather than as a spelling and pronunciation guide?
questions.a: A dictionary is primarily an educational instrument and contains a wealth of historical information crystallized in the growth of language. Used only for spelling or pronunciation, it is not used well. Its primary intention is to help you read books whose vocabulary includes technical or archaic words, literary allusions, or familiar words in obsolete senses, so you should attend to the order and relation of meanings too.

questions.q: Match each period in How to Read a Book's history of dictionaries to its typical dictionary.
pairs: Encyclopedias of the technical terms of learned discourse
The OED's historical record of all usage
questions.explain: The authors trace dictionaries from Roman glossaries of Homer through medieval and Renaissance works to the Oxford English Dictionary.

questions.q: How to Read a Book warns that someone who knew an encyclopedia by heart risks being called an idiot savant, a "learned ____".
questions.explain: Trying to read an encyclopedia through is as vain as reading a dictionary through; the person who memorized one would risk the title idiot savant.

questions.q: Why, according to How to Read a Book, did the Greeks have no encyclopedia?
options: They had not yet invented alphabetical order
To them the word meant knowledge itself, not a book holding knowledge
Their libraries were destroyed before one could be compiled
Their philosophers rejected the idea of collected facts
questions.explain: For the Greeks, the word meant all the knowledge an educated man should have, not a book in which it reposed. The Romans first needed encyclopedias, the oldest surviving being Pliny's.

questions.q: Match each item to what How to Read a Book says about it in the history of encyclopedias.
pairs: Author of the oldest extant encyclopedia
Ordered by the seven liberal arts
Divided into specialties like university departments
questions.explain: The authors trace the ordering of encyclopedias from the Romans through the liberal arts to modern specialist fiefs masked by alphabetical arrangement.

questions.q: Sort the seven liberal arts into the two groups named in How to Read a Book.

items.t: Grammar
Rhetoric
Logic
Arithmetic
Geometry
Astronomy
Music

questions.explain: The trivium was grammar, rhetoric and logic; the quadrivium was arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and music. Medieval encyclopedias reflected this ordering of knowledge.

questions.q: What does How to Read a Book describe as the ideal encyclopedia?
options: One arranged entirely by topic, like a medieval set
One without any index, so readers browse freely
One limited to dates, places and simple facts
Alphabetical articles plus a topical key or outline, like a table of contents
questions.explain: The ideal would combine alphabetical articles with a topical key, since an alphabetical arrangement obscures the relations among facts that a topical one highlights.

questions.q: Why does How to Read a Book tell encyclopedia users to start with the index and to look for the work's infra-structure?
questions.a: The understanding an encyclopedia can give, as opposed to mere information, depends on seeing facts in relation to other facts. Those relations, which reflect how knowledge is divided into specialties, are masked by alphabetical arrangement. The index gathers related discussions under one heading and its breakdowns are topically arranged, so it partly reveals the arrangement of knowledge.

questions.q: Put How to Read a Book's four points about facts in the order the authors number them.
items: Facts are propositions
Facts are true propositions
Facts are reflections of reality
Facts are to some extent conventional
questions.explain: The authors list the points about facts in this order, as the analogue of their four ways of looking at words.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how should an encyclopedia handle a moral question on which there is no consensus?
options: Give the editors' considered verdict
Omit any mention of the topic
Present the majority view as fact
Report only the disagreements among men about it
questions.explain: Because facts are generally agreed true propositions, an encyclopedia cannot properly settle matters without consensus; if it treats them, it can only report the disagreements, clearly labeled.

questions.q: Which of these does How to Read a Book say about using encyclopedias?
options: Use them to end disputes about matters of fact
Use them to settle arguments based on differences of opinion
Consult more than one, preferably from different times, on a subject you care about
Rely on one encyclopedia, since encyclopedias agree as dictionaries do
questions.explain: Encyclopedias should end factual disputes quickly. But they should not settle differences of opinion, and because they often disagree about facts, you should read more than one.

questions.q: True or false: How to Read a Book says an encyclopedia may properly describe a theory no longer held correct, such as Aristotle's views on celestial matter, in an article on that thinker's school.
questions.explain: This is the authors' one exception to the rule that an explanation is not a fact until generally agreed; an outdated theory may be described when tied to a topic, person or school.

questions.q: What does How to Read a Book mean by saying facts are to some extent conventional?
questions.a: Some propositions taken as facts in one epoch are not in another, because almost any proposition we take as true can be falsified by more careful observation, especially in science. Facts are also partly culturally determined: an atomic scientist and a primitive share some facts, like two plus two is four, yet each may reject the other's facts. Truth and reality themselves do not change, but our grasp of them does.

questions.q: According to How to Read a Book, what two striking omissions make an encyclopedia an unsatisfying tool for pursuing understanding?
options: Arguments and imaginative literature
Dates and biographies
Indexes and tables of contents
Definitions and pronunciations
questions.explain: An encyclopedia contains no arguments, beyond reporting accepted ones, and no poetry or imaginative literature; since understanding needs both reason and imagination, it falls short.

questions.q: How does How to Read a Book draw a parallel between using a dictionary and using an encyclopedia?
questions.a: Just as a dictionary is about words, an encyclopedia is about facts. The authors give four points about facts to match their four ways of looking at words, and in both cases the art of use lies in asking the proper questions; they suggest the questions and the reference work supplies the answers. Both invite playful reading, should not be read through, and should not be used to settle differences of opinion.

questions.q: Where does How to Read a Book's Chapter 12, Aids to Reading, fall in the book's structure?
options: It opens the discussion of inspectional reading
It follows the rules of analytical reading and comes just before chapters on reading different kinds of books
It closes the book after syntopical reading
It sits between elementary and inspectional reading
questions.explain: Chapter 12 follows Chapters 6 to 11 on intrinsic analytical reading and precedes Chapter 13, How to Read Practical Books, which begins the treatment of different kinds of reading matter.

questions.q: Why does How to Read a Book place its discussion of extrinsic aids only after the chapters on the rules of analytical reading?
questions.a: The authors wanted readers first to do all they could with their own minds, because many readers depend too slavishly on outside aids. The rules up to that point are rules of intrinsic reading. Once those are established, the chapter admits that extrinsic aids can help and are sometimes necessary, provided they are used after one's own best effort.

questions.q: How to Read a Book's Chapter 12 builds on the distinction between common and special experience first drawn in Chapter 6, titled ____ a Book.
questions.explain: The section on relevant experience says the distinction was already mentioned in Chapter 6, Pigeonholing a Book, and builds on it.

questions.q: How does How to Read a Book's Chapter 12 link its discussion of other books and abstracts to a later chapter?
options: It previews the practical books of Chapter 13
It sets up the rules for criticizing a book fairly
It looks ahead to syntopical reading, where several books on one subject are read
It recalls the levels of reading from Chapter 2
questions.explain: The chapter says more will be said later about syntopical reading, treated in Chapter 20, and notes that abstracts help decide whether a work is germane to a syntopical project.

questions.q: Match each idea in How to Read a Book's Chapter 12 to the earlier rule or idea it extends.
pairs: The use of context to interpret a book's words and sentences
Reading a reference book's preface first
Reading an author's preface and introduction before the book
Giving a concrete example of a point you understand
questions.explain: Chapter 12 presents its extrinsic advice as extensions of earlier intrinsic rules: context, prefaces first, and the concrete-example test of understanding.

questions.q: In the opening of How to Read Practical Books, what drawback do the authors see in very general rules of reading?
options: They are remote from the intricacies of the actual situation in which you follow them
They are too numerous to remember when reading a particular book
They are harder to understand than specific rules for each kind of book
They apply only to theoretical books and never to practical ones
questions.explain: The authors grant that general rules are fewer and more intelligible, but say the more general they are, the more remote they are from the actual situation. That is why the reader needs flexibility with particular books; generality actually makes rules fewer and easier to understand, not more numerous or harder.

questions.q: True or false: According to Adler and Van Doren, the fifteen rules of analytical reading from Chapter 11 apply just as they stand to novels, plays, and poems.
questions.explain: The authors say the fifteen rules do not apply to fiction and poetry, because imaginative works do not proceed by terms, propositions, and arguments. A parallel set of rules for imaginative literature comes in the next chapter.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say the rules for reading imaginative literature, like those for expository works, are developed from the ____ every reader must ask of any book.
questions.explain: The link between the two sets of rules is that you must ask four particular questions of whatever you read, whether fiction or nonfiction.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort these into the two main divisions of expository books.

items.t: History
Science and mathematics
Philosophy
A cookbook
A driver's manual
A book about how to read
