questions.explain: Theoretical books are concerned only with something to be known and divide into history, science and mathematics, and philosophy; practical books are concerned with problems of action. Rule books like cookbooks and driver's manuals, and this book on reading, are practical.

questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, do the rules of analytical reading not simply carry over to fiction and poetry, and what still connects the two kinds of reading?
questions.a: Novels, plays, and poems do not proceed by terms, propositions, and arguments; their fundamental content is not logical, so outlining and criticizing them rests on different premises. Yet the rules for both kinds of book grow out of the same four questions a reader must ask of anything. So there is a parallel set of rules for imaginative literature rather than a wholly new system.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is the most important thing to remember about any practical book?
options: It must always be read more quickly than a theoretical book
It contains only rules and never any principles
It can never solve the practical problems with which it is concerned
It is less worth reading than a great theoretical book
questions.explain: A theoretical book can solve its own problems, but a practical problem is solved only by action. As the authors put it, “nothing but action solves practical problems”.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say a practical problem, such as how to earn a living, can only be solved by ____ itself, never by a book.
questions.explain: A book may suggest things to do, but nothing short of the doing solves the problem; action occurs only in the world, not in books.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Why, in How to Read Practical Books, can the author of a practical book not give the reader concrete practical advice?
options: Because practical authors deliberately avoid committing themselves
Because concrete advice would make the book too long to read
Because only principles, not rules, can be written down
Because he cannot envisage the particular situations in which readers must act
questions.explain: Every action happens here and now under particular circumstances, and the practical judgment just before action must be highly particular. Only someone in exactly the same situation could give such concrete advice.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Which of these, according to Adler and Van Doren, must the reader himself add to a practical book to make it applicable in practice?
options: Knowledge of the particular situation
Judgment of how the rule applies to the case
A summary of the author's life and times
A list of the book's key terms
Agreement with every principle the author states
questions.explain: Since books give only general rules, the reader must add his knowledge of the particular situation and his judgment of how the rule applies. Knowing the author's life matters for judging practical books, but it is not what makes the rules applicable.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Put these steps in the order Adler and Van Doren describe for getting from a practical book to a solved practical problem.
items: The book states a general rule
The reader adds knowledge of his particular situation
The reader judges how the rule applies to the case
The reader acts, which alone solves the problem
questions.explain: Practical books can only give general rules, so the reader must add his knowledge of the situation and his judgment of how the rule applies. The problem itself is solved only by action, which occurs in the world, not in books.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say the principles underlying practical rules, taken together, are the ____ of the thing, as in the theory of bridge building.
questions.explain: Principles that underlie rules are usually items of theoretical knowledge; together they make up the theory of a practice, such as bridge building or contract bridge.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Match each item from How to Read Practical Books with the kind of practical book or element it belongs to.
pairs: Great books in economics, politics, and morals
Primarily concerned with principles that generate rules
The principles that make rules of good procedure what they are
A stitch in time saves nine
questions.explain: Rule books like cookbooks present rules; most great books in economics, politics, and morals deal with principles. A theory is the set of principles behind the rules, and a rule can be put in declarative as well as imperative form.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say there are many great books of the rule-book kind, such as cookbooks and manuals.
questions.explain: The authors say there are few great books of the rule-book sort; most great practical books, in economics, politics, and morals, deal with principles.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Which of these kinds of argument do Adler and Van Doren say to look for in a rule book, as attempts to show the rules are sound?
options: Appeals to the principles behind the rules
Illustrations of how the rules work in concrete cases
Appeals to the author's personal authority
Statistics on how many readers follow the rules
questions.explain: The writer may appeal to principles or show the rules working in concrete cases, and the reader should look for both. Appeals to principles are usually less persuasive but explain the reasons for the rules better.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: In How to Read Practical Books, sort these features into the kind of practical book they mainly describe.

items.t: Major propositions are imperatives or recommendations
Immediately recognizable as practical
Arguments try to show the rules are sound
Propositions say that something is the case
May look at first like a theoretical book
Reader must derive unstated rules between the lines

questions.explain: In a rule book the main propositions are rules and the arguments defend them. A book of principles reads like theory, so the intelligent reader works out the rules the principles imply and how to apply them.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what does an intelligent reader do when reading a book of practical principles, and why is that necessary?
questions.a: He reads between the lines or in the margins, trying to see the rules that are not stated but can be derived from the principles, and to figure out how they should be applied in practice. This is necessary because the ultimate problems are problems of action. A practical book not read as practical is read poorly, since the significance of practical principles lies in the rules and actions they lead to.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say a rule of conduct is practically true on two conditions: it ____, and its working leads to the right end.
questions.explain: Practical truth differs from theoretical truth: a rule must work, and its working must lead you to an end you rightly desire.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: According to How to Read Practical Books, when you judge a practical book, on what does everything finally turn?
options: The soundness of the author's means
The author's character and life
Whether the author's basic assumptions match your own
The ends or goals the author proposes
questions.explain: In judging a theoretical book you compare your basic principles with the author's, but in judging a practical book everything turns on the ends. We have no practical interest in even sound means to ends we reject.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren suggest that a reader who, like Edmund Burke, prizes preserving the status quo is likely to find The Communist Manifesto practically false.
questions.explain: The authors use Marx and Burke to show that judgment of a practical book turns on ends: someone who values the status quo above removing capitalism's inequities will find Marx's recommendations preposterously false.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Explain how practical truth differs from theoretical truth in How to Read a Book, using the authors' example of a reader who does not value careful reading.
questions.a: Theoretical truth concerns whether what is said accords with the way things are. A rule of conduct is practically true only if it works and if its working leads to an end you rightly desire. So if you do not think careful and intelligent reading is worth doing, this book has little practical truth for you, however sound its rules may be.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A friend says a dieting book's advice clearly works but rejects the book because she has no wish to lose weight. How would Adler and Van Doren describe her judgment?
options: She is judging it as practically false because she does not share its end
She has misread it, since sound means make a practical book true
She is judging it as a theoretical book rather than a practical one
She is showing too much sales resistance to its oratory
questions.explain: Practical truth requires both that the rules work and that they lead to an end you rightly desire. Sound means alone do not make a practical book true for a reader who rejects its goal.

questions.q: Which of these are the two major questions Adler and Van Doren say you must ask yourself in reading any practical book?
options: What are the author's objectives?
What means for achieving them is he proposing?
Is the author an expert in his field?
How long will the advice take to follow?
Is the book theoretically true?
questions.explain: The discussion of ends and means yields the two questions: the author's objectives and the means he proposes. Answering both is needed to understand and criticize any practical book.

questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, must the author of a practical book always be something of an orator or propagandist?
options: Because practical books are written mainly to sell copies
Because the reader's judgment turns on accepting his goal, so he must win the reader to his ends
Because practical matters cannot be argued about rationally
Because readers of practical books are less educated than readers of theory
questions.explain: Since your final judgment depends on accepting the goal, the author has to win you to his ends, appealing to the heart as well as the mind. The authors insist this is not wrong or vicious.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say no one makes serious practical judgments or acts without being moved somehow from below the ____.
questions.explain: Their point is that practical thinking and action are not affairs of the mind alone; the emotions are always involved.

questions.q: In How to Read Practical Books, what is 'sales resistance', and why do the authors say it should not be one hundred percent?
questions.a: Sales resistance is the reader's ability, from knowing a book's terms, propositions, and arguments, to spot its emotive use of words and weigh its appeals instead of buying hastily and thoughtlessly. But a practical reader must be open to persuasion, since practical books exist to move us to act. A reader who thinks he should be totally deaf to all appeals might just as well not read practical books.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren compare undetected propaganda to a drug, and what follows for the reader?
questions.a: Oratory that reaches the heart without going through the mind is likely to bounce back and put the mind out of business. Like a drug you do not know you are swallowing, its effect is mysterious: afterwards you do not know why you feel or think as you do. So the reader must recognize the oratory in practical books for what it is, which a reader who knows their terms, propositions, and arguments can do.

questions.q: Match each practical book named by Adler and Van Doren with the background they say throws light on it.
pairs: Greek society was based on slavery
The Italian political situation and his relation to the Medicis
He lived during the English civil wars and dreaded social disorder
questions.explain: Each example shows that the author's character, life, and times matter more for practical books than for theoretical ones like a mathematical treatise.

questions.q: A reader notices that a political pamphlet keeps calling its opponents 'parasites' and 'traitors'. Which reading habit from How to Read Practical Books is he using?
options: Spotting the emotive use of words in the author's oratory
Finding the author's key terms by their technical vocabulary
Suspending judgment until he has understood the book
Reading between the lines to derive unstated rules
questions.explain: A reader who knows a practical book's terms, propositions, and arguments can detect its oratory and spot passages that make an emotive use of words. Deriving unstated rules is what one does with books of principles, not how one detects persuasion.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say Rule 4, adapted for practical books, becomes: find out what the author wants you to ____.
questions.explain: For a practical work, knowing what the author wants to do comes down to knowing what he wants you to do. Rule 8 is adapted in parallel: find out how he proposes that you do it.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Match each of the four questions with how Adler and Van Doren say it changes for a practical book.
pairs: Discerning the author's objectives becomes dominant
What is being said, and how?
Discovering the means the author recommends looms largest
Do his ends and means accord with what you think right?
Agreement implies action on your part
questions.explain: The first two questions change little, the third somewhat more, and the fourth most of all, since agreeing with a practical book commits you to act.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Put the four basic questions in order from the one Adler and Van Doren say changes least for a practical book to the one that changes most.
items: What is the book about?
What is being said in detail, and how?
Is it true?
What of it?
questions.explain: The authors say the first two questions do not change very much, the third changes somewhat more, and the fourth, What of it?, is changed most of all.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what does it mean if a reader claims to accept both a practical author's ends and his means but does not act?
options: He is simply too lazy or tired to act
He has found a flaw in the author's argument
He does not really agree with the ends or accept the means
He has read the book theoretically, which is equally valid
questions.explain: If he truly agreed with the ends and accepted the means, he could not reasonably fail to act. The authors say failing to read analytically after Part Two is not just laziness or tiredness but a sign of not really meaning the agreement.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that, for a theoretical book, the changes in your view that follow from reading need not imply any action on your part.
questions.explain: After a theoretical book you adjust your general view of things, but such adjustments need not be earth-shaking and do not necessarily imply action. Agreement with a practical book, by contrast, does.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Which of these does Adler and Van Doren's chocolate mousse example illustrate?
options: Some practical ends apply only to a certain class of people
A reader who declines to act may be fooling himself about whether the end applies to him
Practical books about cooking cannot be read analytically
Recipes are theoretical rather than practical books
Inaction may mean we want someone else to do the work
questions.explain: The mousse reader shows that selective ends bind only those in the relevant class, but also that deciding one is outside it may mask a wish that someone else, perhaps his wife, make it. Nothing in the example says cooking books are theoretical or cannot be read well.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: In How to Read Practical Books, sort these ends by whether the authors treat them as universal or selective.

items.t: That all persons should read better
The goal of How to Read a Book itself
Making a chocolate mousse
An end applying only to a certain class of people

questions.explain: This book's end, that everyone should read better, is universal, so its implication for action applies to every reader. An end like making a mousse applies only to some, and the reader must decide whether he belongs to that class.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Explain the distinction between universal and selective ends in How to Read Practical Books, and why the authors say a reader outside the class 'may not be' obligated to act.
questions.a: A universal end applies to all human beings, as this book's aim that everyone read better does, so agreement obliges every reader to act. A selective end applies only to a certain class, so the reader must decide whether he belongs to it. The authors hedge because the reader may be fooling himself about his motives, conceding the end and means but wanting someone else to do it.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: After reading a persuasive book on saving money, Priya agrees that saving is worthwhile and that the book's budgeting method works, yet she never budgets. What would Adler and Van Doren conclude?
options: She has shown that agreement with a practical book never implies action
She has read the book correctly as theoretical knowledge
She was right to resist its oratory completely
She does not really agree with its ends or accept its means
questions.explain: Agreement with a practical book's ends and means implies action; if both were genuine she could not reasonably fail to act. Treating the book as mere knowledge would be reading a practical book poorly.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say the fourth question, What of it?, is changed most of all for a practical book?
questions.a: After a theoretical book, agreement means adjusting your general view of things, which need not imply action. But if a practical author persuades you that his ends are worthy and that his means will achieve them, it is hard to see how you can refuse to act as he wishes. So agreement with a practical book does imply action on your part.

questions.q: Put these chapters of How to Read a Book in the order in which they appear.
items: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
Aids to Reading
How to Read Practical Books
How to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.explain: Chapter 11 finishes the rules of analytical reading and Chapter 12 covers aids to reading; Chapter 13 opens the treatment of particular kinds of books, and Chapter 14 turns to imaginative literature.

questions.q: Why does How to Read Practical Books come right after the general rules of analytical reading and before the chapter on imaginative literature?
options: Because practical books are the easiest kind and need no adaptation of the rules
Because the authors begin adapting their general rules to particular kinds of books, starting with practical expository books
Because it summarizes the rules of Chapter 11 for readers who skipped them
Because practical books must be read before any other kind of book
questions.explain: The chapter opens by noting that rules stated generally must be adapted to particular books. It treats practical books because the practical division cuts across all boundaries, and the next chapter takes up the parallel rules for imaginative literature.

questions.q: Sort these sections and topics by whether they belong to How to Read Practical Books or to the chapter that follows it.

items.t: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
The Role of Persuasion
What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature

questions.explain: Chapter 13 moves from kinds of practical books to persuasion to agreement; Chapter 14 then gives the parallel rules for fiction and poetry promised in Chapter 13's opening.

questions.q: In Adler and Van Doren's paradox about imaginative literature, what is said to be strange?
options: Reading fiction is harder to master, yet the skill seems more widely possessed
Reading fiction is easier to master, yet few people ever acquire the skill
Fiction is read less than nonfiction, yet it is taught more often in schools
Fiction teaches more than nonfiction, yet readers value it far less highly
questions.explain: The authors say knowing how to read imaginative literature is inherently more difficult than reading expository books, yet the skill seems more widely possessed. The reverse claim, that fiction is easier, inverts the paradox.

questions.q: True or false: According to Adler and Van Doren, imaginative literature primarily teaches rather than pleases.
questions.explain: The authors say imaginative literature primarily pleases rather than teaches. It is easier to be pleased than taught, but much harder to know why one is pleased.

questions.q: Explaining why fiction is hard to read well, Adler and Van Doren write that ____ is harder to analyze than truth.
questions.explain: The authors say it is easier to be pleased than taught but harder to know why one is pleased: “Beauty is harder to analyze than truth.”

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren doubt that people who cannot say what they liked about a novel are nevertheless good readers of fiction?
questions.a: They grant it might seem that such people are good readers but poor critics, but call this at best a half-truth. A critical reading of anything depends on the fullness of one's apprehension, so readers who cannot account for their enjoyment have probably not read the novel below its most obvious surfaces.

questions.q: Put in order the three ways Adler and Van Doren say they will approach reading imaginative literature, starting with Chapter 14.
items: The way of negation: stating the obvious don'ts
The way of analogy: translating the rules for nonfiction
Examining specific kinds: novels, plays, and lyric poems
questions.explain: The authors first state the don'ts, then translate the expository rules by analogy, and leave the specific types of imaginative literature to the next chapter.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say they postponed imaginative literature until Chapter 14 of How to Read a Book?
options: Fiction is less important than expository writing and so comes last
Explaining rules for both kinds of literature at once would have been confusing
Fiction needs no rules and could be dealt with in a short appendix
Readers must first learn to read history before they can read fiction
questions.explain: The authors say they had limited themselves to serious nonfiction because expounding the rules for imaginative and expository literature at the same time would have been confusing. They do not rank fiction as less important.

questions.q: Which of these accurately describe how Chapter 14 of How to Read a Book connects to other chapters?
options: It translates the structural, interpretive, and critical rules set out earlier for expository books
It leaves novels, plays, and lyric poems as specific types for Chapter 15
It replaces the earlier rules with a wholly separate method owing nothing to them
It opens the book's discussion of how to use dictionaries and encyclopedias
questions.explain: The chapter builds its constructive rules by analogy from the three groups of expository rules and promises that the next chapter will examine novels, plays, and lyric poems. Aids such as dictionaries were covered in Chapter 12.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is the most obvious difference between expository and imaginative books?
options: Expository books are longer, while imaginative books are usually shorter
Expository books use prose, while imaginative books are written in verse
Expository books convey knowledge, while imaginative ones communicate an experience
Expository books are about the past, while imaginative books are about the future
questions.explain: The difference lies in purpose: expository books try to convey knowledge about experience, while imaginative ones try to communicate an experience itself, one the reader can have only by reading.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say fiction appeals primarily to the ____, whereas science and philosophy are intellectual.
questions.explain: We experience things through sense and imagination and know things through judgment and reasoning. Fiction appeals mainly to the imagination, which is one reason it is called imaginative literature.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say the most important negative rule for imaginative literature is not to resist the effect a work has on you.
questions.explain: They call this probably the most important of their negative injunctions: “Don't try to resist the effect that a work of” imaginative literature has on you.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Match each authority Adler and Van Doren cite in Chapter 14 with the point they use him to support.
pairs: Poetry must be read as having several distinct but related meanings
In poetry and drama, statement is one of the obscurer mediums
The standard of correctness differs between poetry and politics
We must grant the artist his subject and judge what he makes of it
questions.explain: Dante and Mark Van Doren support the point about poetic language, Aristotle the rule against judging fiction by standards of truth, and Henry James the corollary that we do not question the author's world.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren answer the charge that imaginative literature is merely escapist?
questions.a: They deny it is always or essentially escapist and call escapism in the ordinary sense contemptible. If we must escape from reality, it should be to a deeper or greater reality, that of our inner life and our own unique vision of the world. The rules for reading should aim at this profound experience and clear away whatever stops us from feeling as deeply as we can.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, how does the imaginative writer use the ambiguity of words?
options: He removes ambiguity so every word carries a single sharp meaning
He avoids metaphors because they make the meaning too uncertain
He states everything explicitly so nothing is left between the lines
He maximizes latent ambiguities to gain the force of multiple meanings
questions.explain: The imaginative writer tries to maximize the latent ambiguities of words and builds with metaphors. Sharpening words to a single meaning and stating everything explicitly is what the logical writer does.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Sort these features into those Adler and Van Doren assign to expository writing and those they assign to imaginative writing.

items.t: Words sharpened to a single meaning
Aims at unambiguous explicitness
Nothing left between the lines
Metaphors as units of construction
Relies on what is implied
Several related meanings, as Dante said

questions.explain: Expository logic aims at explicit, single-meaning statement, while imaginative writing multiplies metaphors and relies as much on what is implied as on what is said.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren warn: don't look for terms, propositions, and arguments in imaginative literature, because these are logical, not ____, devices.
questions.explain: Terms, propositions, and arguments belong to logic. As Mark Van Doren put it, in poetry and drama statement is one of the obscurer mediums.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how do imaginative books teach, compared with expository books?
options: They teach primarily, by commenting on experiences we already have
They do not teach at all and serve only to give pleasure
They teach more directly than science because their lessons are stated plainly
They teach only derivatively, by creating experiences from which we can learn
questions.explain: Expository books teach primarily by commenting on experience we have or can get, while imaginative books teach derivatively through vicarious experiences we must think about ourselves.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what must the reader do to learn from a novel, and how does this differ from learning from a philosopher?
questions.a: A novel creates a vicarious experience in our imagination, and we learn from it as we learn from ordinary experience, by doing our own thinking about it. To learn from scientists and philosophers, by contrast, we must first try to understand the thinking they have already done.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: For Adler and Van Doren, the "truth" of a good story is its ____, its intrinsic probability or plausibility.
questions.explain: A story must be a likely story, not one verifiable by research: “The "truth" of a good story is its verisimilitude”.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A reader complains that a historical novel misplaces a river by fifty miles. By Adler and Van Doren's rule, what should decide whether this flaw matters?
options: Whether the novelist checked an atlas before writing the scene
Whether the misstatement is surrounded with enough plausibility
Whether most readers would notice the geographical mistake
Whether the river is mentioned in other books about the region
questions.explain: Misstatements of fact do not mar a story if the teller surrounds them with plausibility. Geographic errors deserve criticism only when a book offers itself as a treatise on geography.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say we cannot test Othello against our own experience the way we test a philosophical book?
questions.a: A philosophical book is tested against the common experience that inspired it: we ask whether it is true and whether we have felt this. Othello cannot be tested so, since few of us are Moors married to Venetian ladies we suspect, and even then Othello is not every Moor and most couples never meet an Iago. The character and the play are unique.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which of these questions do Adler and Van Doren say we ask when testing a philosophical book against common experience?
options: Is this true?
Have we felt this?
Is the plot plausible?
Is the theory simpler than our previous chaotic opinions?
Do we like the characters?
questions.explain: We test philosophy by asking whether it is true, whether we have felt or always thought it, and whether it is simpler than our earlier opinions. Plausibility of plot and liking characters belong to judging fiction.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Put Adler and Van Doren's negative rules for imaginative literature in the order they present them.
items: Don't resist the effect the work has on you
Don't look for terms, propositions, and arguments
Don't criticize fiction by standards of truth and consistency
questions.explain: The first follows from fiction's appeal to imagination, the second from its different use of language, and the last one concerns criticism by the standards of knowledge.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Match each group of rules for expository books with what Adler and Van Doren say it is for.
pairs: Discovering the unity and part-whole structure
questions.explain: These three groups are translated by analogy into constructive rules for reading poems, novels, and plays.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, should you classify a work of imaginative literature by its kind?
options: Because each kind is governed by a different standard of factual truth
Because only novels need to be read actively, while plays need not be
Because differences in the manner of writing call for differences in the reader's receptivity
Because a lyric always contains more characters than a novel or a play
questions.explain: Lyrics, novels, and plays differ in how they tell their stories, and these differences call for different receptivity. A lyric in fact centres on a single emotional experience.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say a playwright, unlike a novelist, can never speak in his own person.
questions.explain: A play narrates entirely through actions and speeches, while the novelist can and frequently does speak in his own person.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren hold that the unity of a story is always in its ____.
questions.explain: Because the fiction writer's problem is conveying a concrete experience, the unity is in the plot, summarized in a brief narration rather than a proposition.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren reconcile saying a story's unity lies in its plot with saying the experience a work conveys cannot be put in words?
questions.a: They say there is no real contradiction. The plot is not the concrete experience re-created in the reader but only its framework or occasion. It stands for the unity of the work, which properly lies in the experience itself, just as a logical summary stands for the argument of an expository book.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Put in order the stages Adler and Van Doren say you must know to grasp the structure of a narrative.
items: Where it begins
The crises leading up to the climax
The climax
The aftermath
questions.explain: You must know where a story begins, what it goes through, its crises and climax, and what happens within the narrative after the climax.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say the parts of a novel are more likely to be independently readable than the parts of an expository book.
questions.explain: It is the reverse: the first book of Euclid's Elements can be read by itself, but the chapters of a novel or acts of a play often become relatively meaningless when wrenched from the whole.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Match each interpretive rule for expository books with its fictional analogue in How to Read a Book.
pairs: Becoming acquainted with characters and incidents
Becoming at home in the imaginary world
Following the unraveling of the plot
questions.explain: Elements of fiction are like terms, the scene or background is a static connection like propositions, and the plot's unraveling is the dynamic connection, like reasoning.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Sort these elements of fiction by whether Adler and Van Doren treat them as a static or a dynamic connection.

items.t: The scene or background
The social setting
The unraveling of the plot
Following characters through their adventures

questions.explain: The scene, background, or social setting is a static connection like a proposition, while the unraveling of the plot is the dynamic connection like an argument.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren report that Aristotle said ____ is the soul of a story.
questions.explain: Aristotle called plot the soul of a story, its life; to read well you must have your finger on the pulse of the narrative.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren caution against pressing the analogy between expository and fictional rules too hard, and what should the rules do for enjoyment?
questions.a: An analogy of this sort is like a metaphor that will disintegrate if pressed too hard. The three steps only outline how one becomes progressively aware of the writer's artistic achievement. Far from spoiling enjoyment, they should enrich it, so that you know not only what you like but why you like it.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say hold true of even a short non-narrative lyric?
options: It represents a concrete experience and tries to re-create it in the reader
It has a beginning, middle, and end
It always has at least one character, the speaker
It has a complicated plot with many characters
It states its meaning in a single proposition
questions.explain: A lyric re-creates a concrete experience with a temporal sequence and at least the speaker as a character. Complicated plots belong to novels and plays, and a lyric's meaning is never confined to propositions.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: What is Adler and Van Doren's critical maxim for imaginative writing, translated from the rule for expository books?
options: Don't criticize it until you fully appreciate what the author tried to make you experience
Don't criticize it until you have checked its facts against history
Don't criticize it until you have read the author's other works
Don't criticize it until you can state its main argument in propositions
questions.explain: Just as you must understand an expository book before agreeing or disagreeing, you must fully appreciate a work of fiction before criticizing it. Checking facts and stating propositions misapply the standards of exposition.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A reader dislikes a novel because the author set it in Paris rather than a city the reader prefers. How would Adler and Van Doren judge this complaint?
options: Fair, since readers may question the world the author creates
Unfair, since we must grant the artist his subject and judge what he makes of it
Fair, since a setting must be verifiable by research to be convincing
Unfair, since no aspect of a novel may ever be criticized by a reader
questions.explain: Quoting Henry James, they say we must grant the artist his subject; we may criticize what the writer does with his Parisians and the city, but not the choice of Paris itself.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Put in order the steps Adler and Van Doren describe for criticizing a work of fiction.
items: Make an honest effort to appreciate the work
State whether you like or dislike it and why
Point to the things in the book that caused your reactions
Say what is good or bad about the book and why
questions.explain: After appreciation comes a judgment of taste, which is then objectified by pointing to causes in the book, passing from liking to saying what is good or bad.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say about a reader's first judgment of taste on a novel?
options: Its reasons are likely to be more about the reader than about the book
It must be objectified by pointing to what in the book caused it
It is the final and complete act of criticism
It concerns chiefly whether the novel's statements are true
questions.explain: The first reasons tend to reflect the reader's preferences and prejudices, so criticism is completed only by pointing to causes in the book. Truth is the standard for expository works, not fiction.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Sort these claims by whether Adler and Van Doren apply them to criticizing expository books or to criticizing imaginative literature.

items.t: Judgment concerns chiefly truth
First say you understand before you agree
Judgment concerns chiefly beauty
Grant the author his subject
We like it or we do not

questions.explain: Expository works are judged for truth after understanding; belles-lettres are judged mainly for beauty after appreciation, granting the artist his subject.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren say happens as a reader learns to discern the causes of pleasure in reading fiction?
questions.a: The better a reader reflectively discerns the causes of pleasure, the nearer he comes to knowing the artistic virtues in the work itself. He gradually develops a standard of criticism and will likely find many people of similar taste to share his judgments. The authors think good taste in literature is acquired by anyone who learns to read.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Someone says that reading a novel needs no effort because stories simply wash over you. How would Adler and Van Doren reply?
options: Agree, since fiction should be read passively for pure relaxation
Agree, since appreciation needs no effort, unlike understanding
Disagree, since a novel must be read actively to be appreciated
Disagree, since a novel should be outlined as a logical argument
questions.explain: They say you cannot appreciate a novel by reading it passively any more than you can understand philosophy that way; you must read actively, even passionately. Outlining a novel as an argument misapplies the rules for exposition.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 15 of How to Read a Book in the order they appear.
items: How to Read Stories
A Note About Epics
How to Read Plays
A Note About Tragedy
How to Read Lyric Poetry
questions.explain: Each note follows the genre it belongs to: epics after stories, tragedy after plays, and lyric poetry comes last.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Put these chapters of How to Read a Book in the order they appear.
items: How to Read Practical Books
How to Read Imaginative Literature
Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
How to Read History
questions.explain: Chapter 15 follows the general rules of Chapter 14 and precedes Chapter 16 on history.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each topic by the chapter of How to Read a Book where it is treated.
groups: Chapter 14: How to Read Imaginative Literature
Chapter 15: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems

items.t: How not to read imaginative literature
General rules for reading imaginative literature
A note about epics
A note about tragedy

questions.explain: Chapter 14 gives the general rules; Chapter 15 adapts them to particular kinds, with notes on epics and tragedy.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: How does Chapter 15 of How to Read a Book relate to Chapter 14?
questions.a: Chapter 14 gave general rules for reading all imaginative literature, parallel to the rules for expository books. Chapter 15 adapts those general rules to particular kinds: stories, plays, and lyric poems, with notes on epics and Greek tragedy. It also takes up the fourth question, "What of it?", which the previous chapter had not covered for imaginative works.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what does the fourth question, "What of it?", require of a reader who has read a novel or poem well?
options: Strictly speaking, no action at all is called for
Adjusting one's views to match the author's conclusions
Going out and acting on the work's moral point
Writing a reasoned critique of the work's statements
questions.explain: Strictly speaking, the reader has discharged all responsibilities once the first three questions are answered. Adjusting one's views is what a convincing theoretical expository book demands, not a story.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, is a work of fine art called "fine"?
options: Because it is refined in style and taste
Because it is polished and fully finished
Because it is an end in itself, not a means
Because it is reserved for cultivated readers
questions.explain: The authors trace "fine" to the Latin finis, meaning end: the work does not move toward any result beyond itself. They explicitly reject the readings "refined" and "finished."

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren hold that imaginative works such as Animal Farm can lead readers to action, but that such practical consequences are not of the essence of the matter.
questions.explain: They grant that stories have often moved readers to act, citing Orwell, Huxley, and Solzhenitsyn. But imaginative writing belongs to fine art and does not have to lead to action.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that a work of imaginative literature belongs to the realm of ____ art, being an end in itself.
questions.explain: A work of fine art is "fine" because it is an end in itself, from the Latin finis.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: The fourth question a reader asks of any book, which Adler and Van Doren say must be interpreted quite differently for imaginative literature, is "What ____?"
questions.explain: The fourth question is "What of it?" For expository books it implies action; for stories and poems, strictly speaking, no action is called for.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which of these works do Adler and Van Doren cite as imaginative writings that make a political or moral point powerfully?
options: George Orwell's Animal Farm
Aldous Huxley's Brave New World
Solzhenitsyn's The First Circle
Fielding's Tom Jones
Sherwood Anderson's I Want to Know Why
questions.explain: Orwell, Huxley, and Solzhenitsyn are cited as attacks on totalitarianism, technological tyranny, and Soviet bureaucracy. Tom Jones is cited for addressing the reader directly, and Anderson's title for the wish to know why.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Put the four questions a reader asks of any book in the order Adler and Van Doren give them.
items: What is the book about as a whole?
What is being said in detail, and how?
Is the book true, in whole or part?
What of it?
questions.explain: The first three are applied to imaginative literature in the previous chapter; this chapter opens with the fourth.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Match each author to the target of the work Adler and Van Doren cite.
pairs: The cruelty of the Soviet bureaucracy
questions.explain: These are the authors' examples of stories that make a political or moral point more powerfully than expository works.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each item by the kind of book for which Adler and Van Doren say it follows from answering "What of it?"

items.t: Acting on ends you agree with
Adjusting your views to its conclusions
Simply experiencing the work
No action, strictly speaking

questions.explain: Practical and theoretical books call for outward or mental action; a story or poem, read well, need only be experienced.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say the reader of imaginative literature should apply the question "What of it?" with caution?
questions.a: Imaginative works belong to fine art, which is an end in itself and does not have to lead to action. If a story makes you want to act, it is probably some implied statement in it that moves you, and you are then reacting to something other than the story itself. To read the story well, all you have to do is experience it.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What is the first piece of advice Adler and Van Doren give for reading a story?
options: Read it slowly, savoring each scene
Read it quickly and with total immersion
Read a summary first, then the story
Read it twice, once aloud and once silently
questions.explain: The first advice is to read a story quickly and with total immersion, ideally at one sitting. Savoring and drawing out the reading is, they say, more about indulging feelings than reading.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: In discussing War and Peace, what do Adler and Van Doren compare the reader's confusion over its many characters to?
options: Learning a foreign language from scratch
Studying a complicated family tree
Moving to a new town, school, job, or party
Reading a crowded historical chronicle
questions.explain: Just as individuals soon emerge from the crowd at a new job or party, the important characters of a big novel become clear. Readers do not give up in those everyday situations, so they should not give up on the novel.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, in what way does a story cease to be like life?
options: Its events are always explained as they occur
It ends on its last page while life goes on
Its characters are more complex than real people
It contains no background persons
questions.explain: A story is like life in that events become clear only looking back, but on its last page it stops being like life: life goes on, the story does not. So speculating about what happens after the ending is meaningless.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren say about writing preludes to Hamlet or asking what happens to Pierre and Natasha after War and Peace ends?
options: Such speculations are meaningless
They are a good test of understanding
They reveal the author's hidden intentions
They help the reader judge poetic truth
questions.explain: Characters have no vitality outside the book, so such speculations are meaningless and preludes to Hamlet are "ridiculous." We are satisfied with the works partly because they are limited in time.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is one of the most irritating things about a bad story?
options: Its characters have too many strange names
It is too long to read at one sitting
Its people are rewarded or punished with no rhyme or reason
It contains political or moral statements
questions.explain: Good stories satisfy our wish for justice: people get what they deserve. In a bad story, rewards and punishments seem arbitrary, so poetic justice is not achieved.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren distinguish the great stories that live on for centuries?
options: They satisfy the deep unconscious needs of almost everybody
They satisfy the particular needs of one reader
They contain the most explicit moral statements
They are the most realistic about an unjust world
questions.explain: We must separate books that satisfy our own particular unconscious needs from those that satisfy the deep needs of nearly everyone, such as a belief in justice and the allaying of anxiety. The latter are the great stories.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren advise readers who love a novel to draw out its reading for as long as they can.
questions.explain: They say such readers are probably not so much reading as satisfying unconscious feelings about the events and characters. Their advice is to read a story quickly, ideally at one sitting.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say the great storyteller convinces us that a kind of justice, which we call ____ justice, has been done.
questions.explain: In a satisfying story people are rewarded or punished according to their true merit; the authors call this poetic justice.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say the terms of a story are its characters and its ____.
questions.explain: The terms of a story are its characters and incidents, which the reader must get to know and sort out.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, fiction is important because it touches not only the conscious mind but also the ____.
questions.explain: Fiction satisfies many unconscious as well as conscious needs, which is one reason it is a human necessity.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which of these unconscious needs or wishes do Adler and Van Doren say stories can satisfy?
options: The wish to come into good fortune, such as an inheritance
The wish to love more richly than we do
The wish to see justice done in an unjust world
The wish to memorize every character's name
questions.explain: The authors discuss inheritance, love, unconscious sadism and masochism, and the desire for justice. They say explicitly that we should not expect to remember every character.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Match each part of the four questions to how Adler and Van Doren say it is answered for a story.
pairs: What is it about as a whole?
Describe the unity of the plot
Discern the characters' roles and recount key incidents
Judge its poetical truth with reasons
Strictly speaking, no action is required
questions.explain: The opening of the chapter restates how the questions apply to imaginative literature.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each reading habit by whether Adler and Van Doren recommend it for stories.

items.t: Reading at one sitting where possible
Suspending disbelief about the events
Living in the character's world
Disapproving of a character before understanding him
Speculating about events after the last page
Giving up because of the many characters

questions.explain: Read quickly and with total immersion; do not judge too soon, abandon a big novel, or speculate beyond its pages.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren urge reading a story quickly and with total immersion?
questions.a: Reading quickly lets you see the unity of the plot, which you would otherwise forget, and so answer what the story is about as a whole. Reading with total immersion means letting the characters into your mind and heart and living in their world, which lets you see the details. Unless you read both quickly and intensely you miss either the unity or the details.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren explain why fiction seems to be a human necessity?
questions.a: Fiction satisfies unconscious as well as conscious needs. We enjoy seeing sympathetic characters prosper, identifying with lovers, and indulging hidden feelings, and above all we find in stories a justice the real world seems to lack. A great story gives us a belief in justice and understanding and allays our anxiety.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, is high tragedy satisfying even though terrible things happen to good men?
questions.a: The tragic hero, even if he does not wholly deserve his fate, comes to understand it, and we deeply want to share that understanding. If we knew why, we could withstand what the world brings. We share his insight without sharing his suffering.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, where does the main difficulty of reading the great epic poems lie?
options: In their being written in verse
In their unfamiliar ancient languages
In their great number of characters
In their elevation and approach to their subject
questions.explain: Verse is not the main problem, since prose translations exist for all but Paradise Lost. The difficulty lies in their elevation, which demands attention, involvement, and imagination.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which of the five great epics named by Adler and Van Doren is the one with no prose translation available?
options: The Iliad
The Aeneid
The Divine Comedy
Paradise Lost
questions.explain: The authors note that in every case except Paradise Lost prose translations are available. So verse alone cannot explain the difficulty of the epics.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren call the major epic poems perhaps the most honored and also the most widely read books of the Western tradition.
questions.explain: The paradox they note is that the epics are perhaps the most honored but probably the least read books in the great tradition.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren name among the five major epic poems?
options: Homer's Odyssey
Virgil's Aeneid
Wordsworth's Prelude
Byron's Don Juan
Dante's Divine Comedy
questions.explain: The five are the Iliad, Odyssey, Aeneid, Divine Comedy, and Paradise Lost. Wordsworth's Prelude and Byron's Don Juan are cited as epics that grew long without being finished.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Match each epic poem to its author as named by Adler and Van Doren.
questions.explain: With the Bible, these authors form the backbone of any serious reading program.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What paradox about the great epics do Adler and Van Doren discuss, and what do they urge the reader to do?
questions.a: The major epics are perhaps the most honored but least read books of the Western tradition, because their elevation makes great demands of attention, involvement, and imagination. Yet the rewards of reading them analytically are as great as from any fiction. The authors urge readers to read all five, since every good poet has read these authors and, with the Bible, they form the backbone of a serious reading program.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is the one important difference between reading a play and reading a story?
options: A play has no plot unity to discover
A play read in a book is not a complete work
A play cannot be read at one sitting
A play has fewer characters to sort out
questions.explain: The complete play is apprehended only when acted on a stage; like music that must be heard, it lacks a physical dimension in a book. The reader must supply it.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: In the Hamlet example, what question do Adler and Van Doren say the reader, acting as director, must decide?
options: Whether Hamlet truly loves Ophelia
Whether the ghost is real
Whether Hamlet overheard Polonius plotting to spy on him
Whether Polonius is mad
questions.explain: If Hamlet overheard the plan to spy on him, his talks with Polonius and Ophelia mean one thing; if not, another. Shakespeare left no stage directions, so the reader must decide.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say it is a mistake to read a Shaw play without its preface?
options: Shaw's prefaces explain the plays' meaning and how to understand them
Shaw's plays cannot be staged without them
The prefaces contain the plays' missing endings
Shaw required them to be read aloud before performance
questions.explain: Shaw hoped his plays would be read and wrote long prefaces explaining their meaning. Skipping them is to turn one's back on an important aid to understanding.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren recommend reading a puzzling passage of Shakespeare out loud before turning to the glossary or notes.
questions.explain: Reading slowly and with expression, as if to an audience, clears up many difficulties. Only after that fails should you turn to the glossary or notes.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: To supply the missing physical dimension of a play, Adler and Van Doren advise the reader to imagine ____ the play with actors awaiting commands.
questions.explain: Once you know what the play is about, try directing it: tell imagined actors how to say lines and play scenes.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Put Adler and Van Doren's advice for reading a play in order.
items: Discover what the play is about as a whole and in detail
Answer the other questions you ask of any story
Imagine directing the play with actors before you
questions.explain: Only once you know what the play is about and have answered the usual questions should you try directing it in imagination.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Match each playwright to the device Adler and Van Doren associate with him.
pairs: Actor steps out of character to give a political speech
No stage directions, leaving the reader to decide
questions.explain: Aristophanes and Shaw are exceptions to the rule that a playwright cannot address the reader directly; Shakespeare leaves the staging to the reader.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each statement about reading plays by whether Adler and Van Doren make it.

items.t: A play read in a book is incomplete
Most plays are not worth reading
Reading aloud helps with puzzling Shakespeare
Plays need less imagination than novels
Shaw's prefaces can safely be skipped

questions.explain: The reader of a play must work harder to create its world, and Shaw's prefaces are an important aid.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren advise readers to imagine directing a play?
questions.a: A play is complete only when acted on a stage; read in a book, it lacks a physical dimension, as music must be heard. The reader must supply that dimension by pretending to see it acted, telling imagined actors how to say lines and play scenes. Their Hamlet example shows that such staging decisions are central to understanding the play.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is the essence of tragedy?
options: Fate decreed by the gods
Time, or rather the lack of it
The hero's pride
The conflict of love and duty
questions.explain: No problem in a Greek tragedy could not have been solved given enough time, but there is never enough, so decisions are made in a moment and turn out wrong. Pride and fate are not what the authors name.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren advise imagining the chorus of a Greek tragedy as giants and the protagonists as persons of your own stature.
questions.explain: It is the reverse: tragic actors wore buskins that raised them above the chorus. So imagine the chorus as your own size and the protagonists as larger than life.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren note that Greek tragic actors wore ____ on their feet, raising them several inches above the ground.
questions.explain: The buskins made the protagonists taller than the chorus, so they should be imagined as larger than life.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: The only surviving Greek trilogy of tragedies, according to Adler and Van Doren, is the ____ of Aeschylus.
questions.explain: Three tragedies were presented together, but except for the Oresteia only single plays survive.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren give as reasons Greek tragedy is hard for beginning readers?
options: Mostly single plays survive from trilogies with a common theme
We know almost nothing about how Greek directors staged the plays
The stories were familiar to the audience but are known to us only through the plays
The plays were written without any chorus
questions.explain: The authors list lost trilogies, unknown staging, and unfamiliar background stories. The chorus did exist, and they discuss how to imagine it.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Match each figure in Greek tragedy to how Adler and Van Doren advise imagining its words.
pairs: Spoken by persons of your own stature
Spoken by giants, larger than life
Made in a moment, with no time to weigh them
questions.explain: Buskins raised the protagonists above the chorus, and lack of time drives the tragic decisions.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren mean by saying that the essence of tragedy is time?
questions.a: In Greek tragedy every problem could have been solved with enough time, but there is never enough. Choices must be made in a moment, and fallible heroes choose wrongly. The reader should always ask whether he would have seen the right course in time.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What is the first rule Adler and Van Doren give for reading a lyric poem?
options: Look up every difficult word first
Read about the poet's life and times
Read it aloud slowly, line by line
Read it through without stopping, whether you understand it or not
questions.explain: The first rule is to read the poem through without stopping, because its unity can be grasped only from the whole. Readers who stall on the first line and puzzle over it soon give up.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what kind of questions do you mainly ask of a lyric poem, as opposed to an expository work?
options: Grammatical and logical questions
Historical and biographical questions
Moral and practical questions
Rhetorical, and sometimes syntactical, questions
questions.explain: Expository works are questioned grammatically and logically; lyrics usually rhetorically. You find the key words by asking why rhythm, rhyme, or repetition makes certain words stand out.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that a vast knowledge of a poem's context is no guarantee that the poem itself will be understood.
questions.explain: Facts about the author and times may help, but to be understood a poem must be read “over and over”.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that in most good lyric poems there is some kind of ____, often between love and time.
questions.explain: Sometimes two antagonists are named, but often the conflict is only implied, as between love and time or life and death.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that when reading a lyric you do not come to terms with it, but you must discover the key ____.
questions.explain: Key words are found not by grammatical but by rhetorical discernment: what rhythm, rhyme, or repetition makes them stand out.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which of these definitions of poetry do Adler and Van Doren consider too narrow?
options: Poetry must praise
Poetry must be written in rhyme
Poetry must use a specialized poetic diction
Poetry is what poets write
questions.explain: Praise, rousing to action, rhyme, and poetic diction are all called too narrow. "What poets write" is their own simplest definition.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which of these poems do Adler and Van Doren use to show the conflict between love (or life) and time?
options: Shakespeare's 138th sonnet
Marvell's To His Coy Mistress
MacLeish's You, Andrew Marvell
Milton's Paradise Lost
Shaw's Heartbreak House
questions.explain: Shakespeare's sonnets, Marvell's lyric, and MacLeish's poem all turn on love or life against time. Paradise Lost is an epic and Heartbreak House a play.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Put Adler and Van Doren's steps for reading a lyric poem in order.
items: Read it through without stopping
Read it through again, out loud
Ask it rhetorical questions to find key words
Return to it again and again over the years
questions.explain: The first two rules come before anything else; once the unity is grasped you can question the poem, and a great poem deserves many return visits.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Match each poem to how Adler and Van Doren say its love-and-time theme appears.
pairs: Time is explicitly said to take love away
Stated at the start: world enough, and time
Invoked through its title and the coming night
questions.explain: The examples move from explicit to implied treatments of the same conflict.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Match each definition of poetry to Adler and Van Doren's verdict on it.
pairs: A spontaneous overflowing of the personality
Poetry must be written in rhyme
Words arranged in an orderly, disciplined way
questions.explain: The authors reject an over-broad and several over-narrow definitions, settling on words arranged in a disciplined way.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether Adler and Van Doren hold it about lyric poetry.

items.t: A good lyric has a unity
Reading aloud is essential for lyrics
Almost everyone can read any poem
A poem's essence is in its first stanza
You must understand each line before going on

questions.explain: The essence of a poem lies in the whole, never conclusively in any part, so read it through without stopping.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren insist on reading a lyric poem straight through without stopping?
questions.a: A good lyric has a unity that can be grasped only by reading all of it at once. Its essence is almost never in its first line or stanza, but only in the whole. Readers who stall on the first line, thinking they must understand it at once, are the ones who conclude poetry is too hard.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say reading a lyric aloud is essential?
questions.a: Speaking the words forces you to understand them better, since you cannot glide over a misunderstood line when saying it. Your ear catches misplaced emphasis that your eye misses, and rhythm and rhyme place the emphasis where it belongs. It also opens you to the poem so that it can work on you.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren use MacLeish's "You, Andrew Marvell" to show that a poem's conflict may be implied rather than stated?
questions.a: The poem never uses the word time and mentions no lover; it describes someone lying in the noon sun feeling the night's shadow come on. But its title recalls Marvell's lyric about having world enough and time. Poem and title together invoke the same conflict between love or life and time.

questions.q: In 'How to Read History', which sense of the word history do Adler and Van Doren use?
options: Essentially narrative accounts, more or less formal, of past events
Any collection of documents from a period of interest
History as the actual events of the past themselves
Personal diaries and letters written during a past period
questions.explain: They restrict themselves to formal narrative accounts of past periods or events, since in their sense of read you cannot read facts. Documents, diaries and letters are wider uses they set aside.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say the essence of history is ____, and the last five letters of the word, story, help show this.
questions.explain: They hold that the essence of history is narration, so even a collection of documents tells an implicit story.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say their meaning of history is both narrower and broader than other uses of the word?
questions.a: It is narrower because they restrict it to essentially narrative accounts of past events, presented in a more or less formal manner, rather than every document, diary or letter from a period. It is broader because they hold that the essence of history is narration, so even a collection of documents tells an implicit story. Not all historians agree, but the authors say this does not matter for the reader.

questions.q: In 'How to Read History', why do Adler and Van Doren use the example of a jury deciding a car accident?
options: To show that courts are more reliable than historians
To show how hard it is to reconstruct even one recent event from witnesses
To argue that historians should adopt the rules of evidence
To show that juries usually reach the wrong verdict
questions.explain: Even with recent events, living witnesses and strict rules of evidence, a juror is rarely sure what happened. The point is the difficulty of reconstruction, not a call for historians to copy courts.

questions.q: Which of these does the book list as disadvantages a historian has compared with a jury?
options: The witnesses are usually dead
The testimony is not governed by strict rules of evidence
The witnesses are not cross-examined
The historian is forbidden to estimate or suppose
The events are usually recent
questions.explain: The historian's witnesses are long dead, their evidence is not governed by careful rules, and they cannot be cross-examined. It is the court witness who may not guess or estimate, and the historian's events are usually long ago.

questions.q: In 'How to Read History', the authors say that a historical ____, despite the feeling of solidity the word gives, is one of the most elusive things in the world.
questions.explain: They conclude that if a jury struggles with a simple recent matter, it is far harder to know what really happened in history, so a historical fact is one of the most elusive things.

questions.q: The law tells a juror that a doubt affects the verdict only if it is ____, meaning enough to trouble the conscience.
questions.explain: The law assumes jurors will never be absolutely sure, so it says the doubt must be reasonable, sufficient to trouble the conscience, to count.

questions.q: True or false: In 'How to Read History', the authors say the date of the firing on Fort Sumter is a kind of historical fact we can be pretty certain about.
questions.explain: They grant that about some facts, such as the dates of Fort Sumter and Appomattox, we can be pretty certain; the harder questions are what the dates mean and why things happened.

questions.q: Which of these views about the American Civil War do Adler and Van Doren mention to show that even its dates are disputed?
options: It began with Lincoln's election in 1860
It ended with Lincoln's assassination
It was still being fought in outlying places months after Lee's surrender
It will not be over until certain lasting issues are settled
It actually began with the surrender at Appomattox
It was decided entirely by calendar errors
questions.explain: The book cites claims that the war began with Lincoln's election, ended with his assassination, and is not over yet. Fighting in outlying areas is mentioned, but as a known fact, not a rival dating; the other options are not in the book.

questions.q: In 'How to Read History', what point do the authors make by asking whether the firing on Fort Sumter would still be a significant historical fact if we did not care about it?
questions.a: They suggest that knowing an exact date teaches us little; what matters is why the event happened and what followed from it. Many attacks on forts have occurred that we know nothing about. A fact becomes historically significant through the questions and interest that connect it to a larger story, which is why historical facts are so elusive.

questions.q: In 'How to Read History', is history said to be closer to fiction or to science?
options: Closer to science, because it deals with facts
Exactly midway, belonging to neither
Closer to fiction, though it is placed in between
Closer to philosophy than to either
questions.explain: The authors say history is more often classed under fiction, and if it rests between the two it is usually admitted to be closer to fiction. This does not mean the historian makes up his facts.

questions.q: True or false: In 'How to Read History', the authors say a good historian makes up the past just as a novelist makes up a world.
questions.explain: A good historian does not make up the past; he is bound by a criterion of accuracy. But he must still make up something: a pattern or the motives behind actions.

questions.q: Which of these does 'How to Read History' say a historian must do, since he must always make up something?
options: Find or impose a general pattern on events
