Suppose he knows why people acted as they did
Assign causes to events if he rejects an outside pattern
Invent events where records are missing
Avoid any point of view
questions.explain: The historian must either find or impose a pattern, or else assign causes and motives. Inventing events is what a good historian does not do, and the book says every narrative has some point of view.

questions.q: According to 'How to Read History', what was Tolstoy's theory of history?
options: Providence rules all human affairs
Economic self-interest explains every event
Great men alone determine the course of events
The causes of human actions are so complex and hidden that we cannot know why anything happened
questions.explain: Tolstoy thought the causes of every action were so manifold and hidden in unconscious motives that it is impossible to know why anything happened. Providence is cited as a different kind of general theory.

questions.q: The first rule of reading history in 'How to Read History' is to read more than one ____ of the event or period you want to understand.
questions.explain: Because theories of history differ and shape a historian's account, the authors say we must read more than one account, which is the first rule of reading history.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say that a reader of history must recognize which way the historian is operating?
questions.a: Every historian must make up something: either he finds or imposes a general pattern on events, such as a theory that Providence rules human affairs, or he claims merely to report events and then must assign causes and motives. Since this choice shapes the whole account, the reader has to see which one the historian is making. The only way to avoid both positions is to deny that history has any pattern at all.

questions.q: Why do the authors find it odd that a Civil War history called itself impartial and objective while written from the point of view of the South?
options: Because every narrative has a point of view, so it cannot be both impartial and one-sided
Because Southern historians are never accurate
Because the Civil War has no point of view
Because objectivity is only possible in science books
questions.explain: They admit every narrative history is written from some point of view, which is why one must look from more than one viewpoint to get at the truth; a book claiming impartiality from one side shows the problem.

questions.q: True or false: In 'How to Read History', the authors say that reading more than one account matters all the more when the event has practical significance for us.
questions.explain: They say the rule is all the more important for events of practical significance, like the Civil War for Americans, who still live in the world it helped make.

questions.q: According to 'How to Read History', why is Thucydides still worth reading?
options: Because his account of the Peloponnesian War can be checked against many others
Because his view of the war shaped later history and helps us understand the present
Because the war still directly affects life in Greece today
Because he described perfectly what happened before he wrote
questions.explain: Later leaders used Thucydides as a justification and pattern of conduct, so he partly determined what happened afterward. We read him not because he described events perfectly but to know what is happening now.

questions.q: Aristotle wrote that poetry is more ____ than history, meaning more general and universal.
questions.explain: The book quotes Aristotle saying poetry is more philosophical than history, meaning more universal; history is tied to events, though any good history is also universal.

questions.q: True or false: In 'How to Read History', the authors say history is just as universal as poetry.
questions.explain: They say history is not quite so universal as poetry because it is tied to events, though any good history is still universal in some way.

questions.q: What is the second suggestion for reading history in 'How to Read History', and how does Thucydides illustrate it?
questions.a: The second suggestion is to read a history not only to learn what really happened at a particular time and place but also to learn how men act in all times and places, especially now. Thucydides wrote so that future men would not repeat the mistakes he had seen, and similar errors have been made again and again since. So a reader who seeks only what really happened misses the main thing a good historian teaches.

questions.q: In 'How to Read History', the authors define history as the story of what led up to ____.
questions.explain: They say history is the story of what led up to now, and that it is the present, and the future it partly determines, that interests us.

questions.q: In 'How to Read History', why is a reader who cannot check Thucydides against other sources still not wasting time?
questions.a: Reading more than one account is the way to learn what really happened, but that is not the only reason to read history. Thucydides wrote the only major contemporary history of the Peloponnesian War, so there is little to check him against. Yet his account shaped how later leaders acted and shows the kinds of human mistakes that recur, so it teaches us about the present and even the future.

questions.q: Sort these according to the two suggestions for reading history summed up in 'How to Read History'.
groups: Read for how men act in all times

items.t: Every narrative is written from some point of view
Theories of history differ and shape the account
Check Civil War histories written by different factions
Thucydides wrote so future men would not repeat mistakes
Good history, like poetry, has something universal
History is the story of what led up to now

questions.explain: The first suggestion answers the problem of differing theories and viewpoints; the second rests on the universal in history, illustrated by Thucydides.

questions.q: Lena can find only one surviving account of an ancient siege. Following 'How to Read History', what should she get from reading it?
options: Nothing, since a single account cannot be trusted
Certain knowledge of exactly what happened
Insight into how people act in such situations, including today
Only entertainment, as an amateur would
questions.explain: When only one history exists we have little chance of learning what really happened, but we can still learn the way men act in all times and places, as with Thucydides.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: In 'How to Read History', why should a reader find out precisely what a history is not about?
options: Because the authors should cover everything in a period
Because subjects outside the history are always more important
Because limitations reveal the historian's bias
Because an author cannot be blamed for not doing what he did not try to do
questions.explain: Every history has a particular and limited subject; to criticize it fairly we must know its limits, since an author cannot be blamed for not doing what he did not try to do.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: According to 'How to Read History', what should a reader look for when asking how a history is organized?
options: How the historian chose to tell the story and which aspect seems most fundamental to him
Its index and footnotes
Its general outline, which must be searched for carefully
Whether it follows strict chronological order
questions.explain: Since the story occurs in time, its general outline is already given; what matters is how the historian tells it and which aspect, such as economics or wars, he treats as basic.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: Match each criticism of a historian in 'How to Read History' to what it means.
pairs: People just do not act the way the historian says
He judged or read his sources wrongly
He has the facts of the matter wrong
Too much nobility for the hero
questions.explain: The book names two forms of criticism: lack of verisimilitude, shown by doubts such as over-noble heroes, and misuse of sources or misinformation about facts.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: In 'How to Read History', a good historian must combine the talents of the storyteller and the ____.
questions.explain: The authors say he must know what is likely to have happened, the storyteller's sense, as well as what witnesses said, the scientist's care with evidence.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: According to 'How to Read History', what is the main answer to the question 'What of it?' for history, and why does it make reading history well important?
questions.a: The main answer lies in the direction of practical, political action. History tells what people have actually done, so it suggests what is possible, things that might be done again or avoided, and it often moves people to try to better their lot. Since leaders have often acted with some knowledge of history but not enough, and the world is small and dangerous, all of us should read history better.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: Put the questions a reader asks of a historical book in the order 'How to Read History' discusses them.
items: What is the history's limited subject?
How has the historian chosen to tell the story?
Is it true, judged by verisimilitude and use of sources?
What of it?
questions.explain: The section follows the four questions for any expository book: subject, organization, truth through criticism, and significance.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A reader is irritated that a Civil War history says nothing about the American West in the 1860s. What would 'How to Read History' advise?
options: Reject the book as incomplete
Check the limits the author set himself before blaming him
Read only histories of the whole nineteenth century
Assume the author was misinformed
questions.explain: Readers must note the limits an author sets; a Civil War history probably will not be a history of the West, and he cannot be blamed for what he did not try to do.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Match each kind of biography in 'How to Read History' to its description.
pairs: Final, exhaustive scholarly work, never about a living person
Commissioned by heirs or friends to show the subject in the best light
Neither final nor commissioned; expected to be accurate and lifelike
Written with a moral purpose, to help readers be great
questions.explain: The book distinguishes definitive, authorized, ordinary and didactic biographies by their purpose and trustworthiness.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Match each work to the kind of biography it exemplifies in 'How to Read History'.
pairs: A definitive biography that is also fascinating
A didactic biography with a moral purpose
Izaak Walton's Lives of Donne and Herbert
An ordinary biography that is good reading
Often called the first real autobiography
questions.explain: Boswell shows a scholarly book need not be dull; Plutarch wrote to help readers be great; Walton and Tyndall are ordinary biographies; Rousseau is customarily called the first autobiography.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: According to 'How to Read History', what can an authorized biography tell us even though it cannot be trusted like a definitive one?
options: The real private life of its subject
The final scholarly verdict on its subject
Much about the time it was written and what was thought acceptable then
Nothing of value at all
questions.explain: An authorized biography shows how friends want the subject known, and so tells much about the customs and acceptable attitudes of its time, but not what the private life really was.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: True or false: In 'How to Read History', definitive biographies cannot be written about living persons.
questions.explain: The book states that definitive biographies cannot be written about living persons and usually follow several earlier, non-definitive ones.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Sort these statements by whether 'How to Read History' applies them to the definitive biography or the authorized biography.

items.t: Should be read as history
Has already gathered all sources and made sense of them
Not always easy reading
May be biased toward the subject
Author gets access to material from those who control it
Most biographies of living persons are this kind

questions.explain: The definitive biography is exhaustive history; the authorized one is commissioned by heirs or friends, may be biased, and is the usual kind for living persons.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Why does 'How to Read History' say we read Plutarch's Lives today?
options: Mainly for its biographical information
Because it was written for children
Because it is a definitive biography of each man
Mainly for its view of life in general
questions.explain: Although many of its accounts are the only ones we have, we read it less for its biographical information than for its view of life in general.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: In 'How to Read History', the authors say that much of what anyone writes on any subject is ____.
questions.explain: They argue there is a great deal of Plato in the Republic and Milton in Paradise Lost, so formal autobiography being a new genre matters little.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Which of these reasons does 'How to Read History' give for doubting that anyone has written a true autobiography?
options: It is even harder to know one's own life than another's
Autobiographies are written about lives not yet complete
With no one to contradict, people are tempted to tell less or more than the truth
Autobiographies contain no truth at all
Autobiography is too new a genre to judge
questions.explain: The book gives self-knowledge, incompleteness and the temptation to distort as reasons. It denies that an autobiography can contain no truth, since every one reveals something, if only what the author hides.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: What warning do Adler and Van Doren give about reading books, including autobiographies, partly to discover their authors' character?
questions.a: Within reasonable limits we tend to read any book partly to discover its author, since words are written by a living person and no one keeps himself entirely out of his book. But this should never be the primary consideration, and overdoing it leads to the pathetic fallacy. We should not spend so much time hunting a writer's secrets that we miss what he says plainly.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Mark reads one admiring biography of a famous inventor, written with help from her family. Following 'How to Read History', what should he do if he wants the truth about her life?
options: Read as many biographies of her as he can, including any she wrote herself
Accept it, since the family knew her best
Read only her autobiography
Stop reading biography, since none can be trusted
questions.explain: The authors advise reading as many biographies as you can find, including the subject's own account, and treating an authorized biography as possibly biased.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Put these biographical works in the order 'How to Read History' discusses them.
items: Boswell's Life of Johnson
Walton's Lives and Tyndall's Faraday the Discoverer
Plutarch's Lives
Rousseau's Confessions
questions.explain: The section moves from the definitive biography, to ordinary biographies, to didactic ones, and then to autobiography.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: In 'How to Read History', how does Plutarch's Lives illustrate the claim that history and biography can shape later history?
questions.a: Plutarch shows Alexander the Great modeling his life on Achilles, whom he knew from Homer. In turn, many later conquerors tried to model their lives on Plutarch's Alexander. So Plutarch's work, like Thucydides', has had a profound influence on subsequent history, which is why the authors say to read biography as history and as a cause of history.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Put the kinds of biography in the order 'How to Read History' introduces them.
items: Definitive biography
Authorized biography
Ordinary biography
Didactic biography
Autobiography
questions.explain: The section starts with the definitive biography, contrasts the authorized kind, adds ordinary and didactic biographies, then turns to autobiography.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Put the five questions about current-events material from 'How to Read History' in the order the authors give them.
items: What does the author want to prove?
Whom does he want to convince?
What special knowledge does he assume?
What special language does he use?
Does he really know what he is talking about?
questions.explain: The book lists these five questions in this order, and notes the last is probably the hardest to answer.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: In 'How to Read History', the authors' warning for reading contemporary material is Caveat lector, meaning let the ____ beware.
questions.explain: Rather than a set of rules, they sum up with Caveat lector, since a contemporary author or his sources may have an interest in your understanding something a certain way.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: According to 'How to Read History', what is the most important thing to know when reading any report of current happenings?
options: When it was published
Who is writing the report, meaning the kind of mind he has
How many sources it cites
Whether it agrees with other reports
questions.explain: The authors say the most important thing is who is writing the report, not as personal acquaintance but as knowing what kind of filter his mind is.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say the reporter's mind is not a clear glass?
options: Because reporters deliberately lie
Because reporters lack education
Because it filters reality, separating out what it thinks untrue, and may be mistaken
Because reality cannot be reflected at all
questions.explain: Ideally a reporter would be a clear glass, but the mind filters out what it considers untrue; that is proper, yet the reporter may be mistaken.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Why does 'How to Read History' say it is hard to discover the assumptions an author of current events shares with his readers?
questions.a: The book quotes Basil Willey that it is almost insuperably difficult to become critically conscious of one's own habitual assumptions, the doctrines felt as facts. These are easier to see in an age different from our own. In reading about our own time we lack that distance, so we must see through the filter of our own mind as well as the author-reporter's.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: True or false: In 'How to Read History', the authors say the four questions must always be asked of anything you read, even though analytical reading is not always necessary.
questions.explain: They qualify their earlier claim: the full rules need not always be applied, but the four questions must always be asked, including of newspapers and magazines.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Match each current-events question in 'How to Read History' to what it helps the reader discover.
pairs: What does the author want to prove?
The thesis, often stated in the blurb or preface
Whom does he want to convince?
Whether you belong to the intended audience
What special knowledge does he assume?
Opinions or prejudices he expects you to share
What special language does he use?
Words that provoke special responses, like Communist
questions.explain: Each question exposes a part of the reporter's filter: thesis, audience, assumptions and loaded words.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Which of these does 'How to Read History' say about the question 'Does he really know what he is talking about?'
options: It is probably the hardest of the five to answer
Even well-meaning reporters may be uninformed about secret actions
Management of the news affects reporters as well as the public
Bias is the only thing a reader needs to consider
It can be answered by reading the blurb
questions.explain: The authors say bias is not the only issue: a reporter with good will may still be uninformed about secret matters, perhaps without knowing it, which is especially perilous for readers.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Priya, a strong supporter of one party, picks up a book about current politics written for readers of the other party. What does 'How to Read History' suggest she may experience?
options: She will be easily persuaded
She will find no assumptions at all
She will understand it better than its intended readers
She may only be irritated, since many authors write for readers who agree with them
questions.explain: The authors say many writers write only for readers who agree with them, and if you disagree sharply with a reporter's assumptions you may only be irritated.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: True or false: In 'How to Read History', the authors say readers must be just as wary when reading Aristotle or Shakespeare as when reading a contemporary book.
questions.explain: They say readers do not have to be wary with Aristotle, Dante or Shakespeare; it is the contemporary author, or his sources, who may have an interest in how you understand him.

questions.q: According to 'How to Read History', why is reading digests sometimes the most demanding reading you can do?
options: Because you must infer from the condensation itself what was left out
Because digests use difficult language
Because digests are longer than the originals
Because digests contain no information
questions.explain: The more condensed a digest, the more selection has occurred, and since you cannot check the original you must read between the lines to infer what was left out.

questions.q: In 'A Note on Digests', the greater the condensation, the more important it is to know the character of the ____.
questions.explain: The book says the caveat about reporters applies with even greater force to the condensor of a digest.

questions.q: Which of these does 'How to Read History' say about digests such as news magazines and Reader's Digest?
options: Their makers are primarily skilled readers
For the average informational article, a condensation is often adequate or better
The very best articles cannot be condensed without loss
Digests spare us the trouble of reading altogether
A summary of Montaigne would satisfy us as well as the original
questions.explain: The editors are expert readers, and condensation works for average articles but not the best. Digests save us extent of reading but not the trouble of reading, and a summary of Montaigne would serve only if it sent us to the original.

questions.q: In 'A Note on Digests', what does it mean that we sometimes have to read for information about understanding?
questions.a: It follows from the basic distinction between reading for information and reading for understanding. Sometimes we read to find out how others have interpreted the facts, as when we read digests made by skilled readers. To profit from them we must read the digest as well as its editors read the originals, which involves reading for understanding as well as information.

questions.q: Sort these readings by whether 'A Note on Digests' says a condensation can serve well or would leave us unsatisfied.

items.t: An average, mainly informational magazine article
The week's news reduced to essentials
The essays of Montaigne
The very best articles, like the best books

questions.explain: The book says the best writing cannot be condensed without loss, while average informational articles are often served well or even better by a condensation.

questions.q: Why does 'How to Read History' come right after the two chapters on imaginative literature in Part Three?
options: Because history is a kind of practical book
Because history is said to lie between fiction and science, so it bridges imaginative literature and the science chapter that follows
Because history requires no analytical reading
Because history is a branch of philosophy
questions.explain: The chapter places history between fiction and science, closer to fiction; it follows the chapters on stories, plays and poems and precedes How to Read Science and Mathematics.

questions.q: Put these chapters of 'How to Read a Book' in their order in the table of contents.
items: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
How to Read History
How to Read Science and Mathematics
How to Read Philosophy
questions.explain: Chapter 15 is on stories, plays and poems, 16 on history, 17 on science and mathematics, and 18 on philosophy.

questions.q: Put these sections of 'How to Read History' in the order they appear.
items: The Elusiveness of Historical Facts
Theories of History
The Universal in History
Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
How to Read Biography and Autobiography
How to Read About Current Events
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the difficulty of facts, to the historian's theories and the universal in history, to the four questions, then to biography and current events, ending with a note on digests.

questions.q: How does 'How to Read History' reuse the four questions developed earlier in the book for expository works?
questions.a: The authors say that although histories are closer to fiction than to science, they can and should be read as expository works, so the same four questions apply, asked a little differently. They then reshape them for current events into five questions, noting these are only variations, such as special language being coming to terms with the author. This links the chapter back to the rules of analytical reading.

questions.q: Which of these topics does 'How to Read History' treat as kinds of reading related to history?
options: Biography and autobiography
Newspapers and books on current events
Digests of news and articles
Lyric poetry
Mathematical proofs
questions.explain: The chapter extends history to biography and autobiography, current events and digests. Lyric poetry belongs to the previous chapter and mathematics to the next.

questions.q: Why does 'How to Read History' end with sections on current events and digests rather than staying with books about the past?
questions.a: The authors say history did not stop long ago; the world goes on and people keep writing about it, and we have an obligation as citizens to understand the world around us. Knowing what is happening now poses the same problem as history, since we cannot be sure we have the facts. So reading newspapers, current-events books and digests is an extension of reading history, with the added warning Caveat lector.

questions.q: Match each historian's approach in 'How to Read History' to what it involves.
pairs: Fits the history to a pattern imposed from above
Is forced to assign causes and motives
Holds that causes are too hidden for anyone to know why things happen
questions.explain: A historian either imposes a pattern or must assign causes and motives; the only escape is Tolstoy's view that history has no knowable pattern.

questions.q: Match each Civil War claim in 'How to Read History' to how the authors treat it.
pairs: Fort Sumter was fired on April 12, 1861
A fact we can be pretty certain about
The war began with Lincoln's election
A disputed view of when it started
Fighting went on into mid-1865 in outlying areas
Shows word of the end had not reached everyone
The war is not over yet
A claim that its issues remain unsettled
questions.explain: The dates are agreed, but when the war began and ended is disputed, which shows how little a bare date teaches.

questions.q: Match each idea from 'The Universal in History' to its source or example.
pairs: Poetry is more philosophical than history
Writing so future men would not repeat mistakes
Leaders comparing their position to Athens or Sparta
questions.explain: Aristotle supplies the contrast with poetry; Thucydides wrote to warn the future, and later leaders used his story as a pattern of conduct.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Sort these by whether 'How to Read History' presents them as a problem with the reporter or with the reader.

items.t: His mind filters out what he thinks untrue and may be mistaken
He may be uninformed about secret actions and treaties
Our own habitual assumptions feel like facts
Loaded words provoke special responses in us

questions.explain: The authors say we must see through the filter of the author-reporter's mind and also of our own.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Sort these statements by whether 'How to Read History' makes them about biography or about autobiography.

items.t: A story about a real person, so it has a mixed character
Should be read as history and as a cause of history
Always written about a life not yet complete
Should be taken with a grain of salt
Montaigne said his book had made him

questions.explain: Biography is read as history; autobiography is incomplete, tempts its author to distort, and, as Montaigne said, is co-substantial with its author.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: In "How to Read a Book", which two kinds of scientific writing do Adler and Van Doren say Chapter 17 will confine itself to?
options: The great scientific and mathematical classics, and modern scientific popularizations
Specialized research monographs, and current scientific journal articles
Science textbooks for students, and laboratory manuals for experiments
Biographies of great scientists, and histories of scientific institutions
questions.explain: The authors limit the chapter to the classics of the tradition and modern popularizations. They say they cannot help with specialized monographs, partly because they are not qualified to.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, roughly when did major scientific books stop being written for a lay audience?
options: Around the end of the seventeenth century
Around the end of the nineteenth century
Around the middle of the eighteenth century
Around the start of the Second World War
questions.explain: The authors say that until approximately the end of the nineteenth century, major scientific books such as those of Galileo, Newton, and Darwin were written for lay readers.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, has the history of science become a respectable field, as shown by the "Newton industry"?
options: Because science departments now need more teaching staff
Because Newton's papers were recently discovered and published
Because scientists are more concerned than ever about the nature of the scientific enterprise
Because laymen now demand easier books about famous scientists
questions.explain: The authors explain the surge of Newton research by scientists' growing concern with the nature of the scientific enterprise itself, not by teaching needs or newly found papers.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: In "How to Read a Book", what do Adler and Van Doren say is the layman's purpose in reading classical scientific books?
options: To become expert in their subject matter in a contemporary sense
To pass examinations in the sciences they treat
To judge whether their conclusions are still correct today
To understand the history and philosophy of science
questions.explain: The layman reads the classics not to master their subjects in a modern sense but to understand the history and philosophy of science, chiefly by grasping the problems the great scientists tried to solve.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, how is scientific objectivity attained?
options: By frank confession of the author's initial bias
By eliminating every presupposition before beginning
By relying only on deductive proofs
By avoiding all technical vocabulary
questions.explain: The authors write: “Scientific objectivity is not the absence of initial bias.” It comes from openly stating what the author asks the reader to take for granted.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: In "How to Read a Book", what kind of argument do Adler and Van Doren call characteristic of science?
options: Deductive argument from propositions already established
Inductive argument from observable evidence
Rhetorical argument aimed at persuading the reader
Narrative argument tracing events in time
questions.explain: Science uses deduction too, and there it differs little from philosophy, but the authors say the inductive argument, establishing a general proposition from observable evidence, is characteristic of science.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say Lavoisier's Elements of Chemistry is still worth a layman's reading?
options: It remains the best textbook for passing chemistry exams
It contains no technical terms at all
Its method was revolutionary and its conception of an element largely survives
It was the first chemistry book written in the form of a dialogue
questions.explain: The authors say a student would be unwise to use it to pass even a high school exam, but its method was revolutionary and its idea of a chemical element is still, on the whole, ours.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, why does mathematics have to be learned only once, while our own language must be learned twice?
options: Because mathematics uses fewer symbols than ordinary language
Because mathematics is taught earlier in school
Because mathematics has no grammar or syntax
Because mathematics is almost wholly a written language
questions.explain: We learn our own language once to speak and again to read it, but mathematics is almost wholly written, so it is learned only once. The authors stress that it does have its own vocabulary, grammar, and syntax.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: In Euclid's Elements, what do the letters Q.E.F. at the end of a proposition signal, according to Adler and Van Doren?
options: That a construction problem has been done
That a theorem has been proved
That a postulate has been assumed
That a definition has been stated
questions.explain: Q.E.F. stands for Quod erat faciendum, what it was required to do, and closes a construction problem. Q.E.D., what it was required to prove, closes a theorem.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, are the first three propositions in Book I of Euclid's Elements construction problems?
options: Because Euclid thought constructions were easier for beginners
Because they are needed in the proof of the theorem in Proposition 5
Because theorems cannot appear before Book II
Because they replace the postulates Euclid omitted
questions.explain: The authors show that Proposition 5 on the isosceles triangle uses Proposition 3, which uses 2, which uses 1, so the constructions are needed for the sake of Proposition 5.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: In "How to Read a Book", what exactly does a proven Euclidean proposition such as Proposition 5 assert, according to Adler and Van Doren?
options: That the hypothesis is true
That the conclusion is true in all cases
That an if-then connection between hypothesis and conclusion holds
That isosceles triangles really exist
questions.explain: The proposition asserts an if-then relationship and does not assert the truth of the hypothesis, or of the conclusion except when the hypothesis is true. It is the connection that is proved.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, how should a reader handle the mathematics in a scientific work like Newton's Principia on a first reading?
options: Work through every proof with pencil and scratch pad
Skip the whole book until calculus has been mastered
Read only the diagrams and ignore the text
Read the statements of propositions, glance at proofs, and read the scholiums
questions.explain: Reading a mathematical book for itself needs pencil in hand from start to finish, but with a scientific work containing mathematics, the authors say skipping is often the better part of valor.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say Galileo's Two New Sciences is particularly difficult for modern readers?
options: Because it is presented as a dialogue rather than primarily mathematically
Because it is full of advanced calculus
Because it reports experiments no one can repeat
Because it was written only for specialists
questions.explain: The authors note that the absence of mathematics can cause more trouble than its presence: the dialogue form suits the stage and Plato's philosophy but is not really appropriate to science.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what problem do popular science magazines such as Scientific American share with the reading discussed at the end of Chapter 16?
options: They are written in a dialogue form
We are at the mercy of reporters who filter the information
They contain too much mathematics
They report only the history of science
questions.explain: Like reports of current events, these publications leave us dependent on reporters who filter information; if the reporters are poor, we have almost no recourse.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that most modern scientists write mainly for lay readers.
questions.explain: The authors say the opposite: most modern scientists do not care what lay readers think, and science tends to be written by experts for experts.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that science, unlike history, is not chronotopic because a scientist tries to get away from locality in time and place.
questions.explain: The main propositions of science are general; the scientist tries to say how things generally are and behave, unlike the historian.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that Lavoisier improved chemistry by improving its language.
questions.explain: The authors say Lavoisier did exactly what his Preface describes, improving chemistry by improving its nomenclature, as Newton had improved physics by ordering its language.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that learning to read mathematics is theoretically much harder than learning to read English or French.
questions.explain: They say it is no more difficult, theoretically, than learning to read English or French or German, and at the elementary level may even be easier.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren describe Newton's Optics as heavily mathematical, with diagrams that require advanced proofs.
questions.explain: The authors say there is very little mathematics in the Optics; its diagrams merely illustrate experiments with prisms and sunbeams that readers can repeat themselves.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that Whitehead's Introduction to Mathematics shows the attentive reader that the mathematician is an ordinary man, not a magician.
questions.explain: The authors praise Whitehead's eloquence on mathematical reasoning and say that, if nothing else, it shows the mathematician is an ordinary man, not a magician.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say the central aim of education, from Socrates' day to ours, is the freeing of the mind through the discipline of ____.
questions.explain: The authors close the section by tying the historical study of science to education, whose aim is freeing the mind through the discipline of wonder.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say the general reader, unable to become expert in all fields, must fall back on scientific ____.
questions.explain: Since no one can be expert in every field, the lay reader must rely on popularizations, and must learn to tell good ones from bad and read the good ones with understanding.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Some psychologists, Adler and Van Doren report, think fear of mathematics comes from "symbol ____", an inability to follow the controlled shifting of symbols.
questions.explain: The authors grant there may be something to symbol blindness, but note that words shift too, and less controllably.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren recommend starting with Euclid, whose ____ of Geometry they call one of the most lucid and beautiful works ever written.
questions.explain: They suggest the reader start with Euclid's Elements to see how beautiful and satisfying mathematics can be.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that, unlike ordinary discourse, mathematical terms and equations properly used carry no ____ connotations.
questions.explain: Ordinary discourse is mainly about emotional facts not fully shared between persons; mathematics treats things outside both, free of emotional connotations.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that when reading a scientific work that contains mathematics, ____ is often the better part of valor.
questions.explain: Reading a mathematical book for itself needs a full, pencil-in-hand reading, but in a scientific work with mathematics the reader can often skip.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren call the closing passage of Newton's Principia the General ____, which states the great problem of almost all later physics.
questions.explain: Scholiums discuss how propositions relate to each other and to the whole; the General Scholium at the end of Book III sums up the work.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren report that Hippocrates viewed medicine as the art of keeping people ____ rather than curing them when sick.
questions.explain: The authors note that this view of medicine as keeping people well is unfortunately an uncommon idea nowadays.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Which of these reasons do Adler and Van Doren give for not helping readers with specialized scientific monographs?
options: They are not qualified to do it
Science today is written by experts for experts
Such monographs contain only false conclusions
Monographs are never worth reading
Specialized works are always written as dialogues
questions.explain: They give two reasons: they are not qualified, and modern science assumes so much specialized knowledge that lay readers are left out. They do not dismiss monographs as false or worthless.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Which of these benefits do Adler and Van Doren attribute to the historical study of science?
options: It engages reason where it has operated with the most success
It dispels in some measure the apparent unintelligibility of science
It qualifies the reader to do original research
It is an activity of the mind essential to education
It replaces the need to read popular science
questions.explain: The authors list reason's greatest success, dispelling science's apparent unintelligibility, and its essential place in education. They never claim it makes the reader a researcher.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren suggest when a scientific book alone cannot make its evidence clear?
options: Witness a laboratory demonstration
Handle apparatus like that described in the book
Observe specimens or models in a museum
Accept the author's conclusions without the evidence
Stop reading and turn to a textbook
questions.explain: The reader's one recourse is first-hand experience, through demonstrations, apparatus, or museum specimens; there are classical experiments as well as classical books.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Which of these features of Euclid's Proposition 5 make it beautiful, according to Adler and Van Doren?
options: The clarity of its logical exposition
The limited nature of its problem
Its rich emotional connotations
Its dependence on facts about real animals
questions.explain: The authors praise a really logical exposition of a really limited problem; ordinary and philosophical discourse find such limiting difficult.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Which of these scientific classics do Adler and Van Doren name as not mathematical?
options: The works of Hippocrates
Harvey's discourse on the circulation of the blood
Gilbert's book on magnets
Newton's Principia
Euclid's Elements
questions.explain: Hippocrates, Harvey, and Gilbert can be read without much difficulty; the Principia and the Elements are full of propositions and proofs.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Which of these does Adler and Van Doren's note on popular science say popularizations generally avoid?
options: Detailed descriptions of experiments
Much mathematics
Any need for active reading
Reports of experimental results
questions.explain: Popularizations contain few descriptions of experiments, merely reporting results, and little mathematics. Yet the authors insist active reading matters more here than almost anywhere.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Put the propositions of Euclid's Book I in the order of dependence Adler and Van Doren trace, from the most basic to the theorem that needs them.
items: Proposition 1
Proposition 2
Proposition 3
Proposition 5
questions.explain: Proposition 5 uses Proposition 3, which depends on the construction in Proposition 2, which involves Proposition 1.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Put these sections of Chapter 17 of "How to Read a Book" in the order they appear.
items: Understanding the Scientific Enterprise
Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
Facing the Problem of Mathematics
Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
A Note on Popular Science
questions.explain: The chapter moves from why laymen should read science, to how to read the classics, to the mathematics difficulty, and ends with popularizations.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Put the suggested course of mathematical reading in the order Adler and Van Doren propose for a beginner.
items: Spend several evenings with Euclid's Elements
Glance at Archimedes, Apollonius, and Nicomachus
Read a scientific work with mathematics, such as the Principia, skipping as needed
questions.explain: They suggest starting with Euclid to overcome fear, then glancing at other Greek mathematicians, and then handling scientific works by skipping where useful.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Put these chapters of "How to Read a Book" in the order they appear in Part Three's sequence of kinds of reading matter.
items: How to Read History
How to Read Science and Mathematics
How to Read Philosophy
How to Read Social Science
questions.explain: The table of contents places Chapter 17 between history (Chapter 16) and philosophy (Chapter 18), with social science following in Chapter 19.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Match each classic to what Adler and Van Doren say about reading it.
pairs: Read statements, glance at proofs, read the scholiums
Diagrams merely illustrate experiments you can repeat
Hard because it is a dialogue, not mathematical
Medicine as the art of keeping people well
questions.explain: Each classic illustrates a different point: skipping mathematics, repeatable experiments, the trouble with dialogue in science, and a non-mathematical classic.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Match each popular science book to the reason Adler and Van Doren give for reading it.
pairs: Theoretical work on the environmental crisis with practical consequences
Barnett's The Universe and Dr. Einstein
Atomic physics, a great achievement posing great perils
Mathematics as a leading modern mystery
questions.explain: Commoner's subject implicates us in a crisis, Barnett's treats atomic physics with its promise and perils, and Whitehead's demystifies mathematical reasoning.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Match each term from Adler and Van Doren's discussion of Euclid to its meaning.
pairs: What it was required to do
What it was required to prove
questions.explain: Construction problems end with Q.E.F. and theorems with Q.E.D.; the first demands doing, the second proving.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Match each element of Lavoisier's account of a physical science, as quoted by Adler and Van Doren, to its description.
questions.explain: Lavoisier says every branch of physical science consists of facts, the ideas representing them, and the words expressing them, so improving the language improves the science.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Match each field to the audience Adler and Van Doren say its writers now mostly address.
questions.explain: The authors say the experts-for-experts situation is most extreme in science but obtains in philosophy and economics too, and is spreading to history.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Match each figure to the remark Adler and Van Doren attach to them.
pairs: Called the pre-specialist era the happy childhood of science
Those who can, do; those who can't, teach
Education as freeing the mind through wonder
questions.explain: Einstein's phrase describes the era before specialization; Shaw's quip summed up scientists' old disdain for historians of science; Socrates anchors the aim of education.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Sort each description into the kind of argument Adler and Van Doren say it fits.

items.t: Establishes a general proposition from observable evidence
May rest on a single case created by an experiment
May rest on many cases from patient investigation
Proves a proposition by others already established
Where science differs little from philosophy

questions.explain: Induction argues from evidence and is characteristic of science; deduction proves from established propositions, where science resembles philosophy.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Sort each feature into Euclid's Proposition 5 or the syllogism about mortal men, as Adler and Van Doren contrast them.

items.t: Does not matter whether its objects really exist
Conclusion holds absolutely, now and forever
Assumes something about real things
Its assumptions must be examined against reality

questions.explain: Both follow with certainty from their premises, but the syllogism makes assumptions about real animals and men that may be false, while Euclid's if-then claim needs no such check.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Sort each reading practice by the intention Adler and Van Doren tie it to.
groups: Reading a mathematical book for itself
Reading a scientific work that has mathematics

items.t: Read from beginning to end
Keep a pencil in hand and use a scratch pad
Glance at proofs to see how they are done
Avoid the diagrams if they trouble you

questions.explain: A mathematical book read for itself demands a complete, pencil-in-hand reading; a scientific work with mathematics can be read selectively.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether Adler and Van Doren apply it to short popular science articles or to excellent popular science books.

items.t: Usually primarily informational
Often need only following the author's account
Have implications the careful reader will not miss
Require something more than following the account

questions.explain: Short articles ask less active thinking beyond understanding; books like Commoner's demand more because their theoretical conclusions have consequences.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren open Chapter 17 of "How to Read a Book" by warning that its title may be misleading, and how does this shape the rest of the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter does not teach how to read every kind of science, only the great scientific and mathematical classics and modern popularizations. Since science is now written by experts for experts, the lay reader is left out of specialized work and must rely on the classics and on popularizations. The chapter therefore treats the classics first, with their difficulties of evidence and mathematics, and ends with a note on popular science.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren call the most helpful advice for reading the scientific classics, and why does it fit the layman's responsibility?
questions.a: The reader should state as clearly as possible the problem the author tried to solve, a rule of analytical reading that is especially relevant to science and mathematics. The layman reads the classics to understand the history and philosophy of science, not to become competent in the subject. So the main task is to become aware of the problems the great scientists faced and their background.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: How, according to Adler and Van Doren, should a reader deal with bias in a great scientific work?
questions.a: Great scientific works contain no oratory or propaganda, but they may have bias in the sense of initial presuppositions. The reader detects it by distinguishing what the author assumes from what he establishes by argument. The more objective the author, the more openly he asks the reader to take things for granted, since objectivity is attained by frank confession of bias.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: What is the first main difficulty Adler and Van Doren identify in reading scientific books, and how can a reader overcome it?
questions.a: Science is primarily inductive, so understanding its arguments requires following the evidence the scientist reports, which the book alone may not make possible. The reader may need first-hand experience: watching a laboratory demonstration, handling apparatus, or seeing specimens in a museum. There are classical experiments as well as classical books.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren argue that reading mathematics is no harder in principle than reading any other language?
questions.a: Mathematics is a language with its own vocabulary, grammar, and syntax, which a beginner must learn at the elementary level, much as with English or French. Because it is almost wholly written, it has to be learned only once. At the elementary level it may even be easier, since its terms carry no emotional connotations when properly used.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: What two purposes do Adler and Van Doren see for the construction problems at the start of Euclid's Elements?
questions.a: First, the constructions are needed in proving theorems, as Proposition 5 depends on Propositions 3, 2, and 1. Second, constructions resemble postulates, since both assert that geometrical operations can be performed; postulates assume this, while constructions prove it. Proposition 1, for example, shows that if there are straight lines and circles, there are equilateral triangles.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren contrast Euclid's Proposition 5 with the syllogism that all men are mortal?
questions.a: Both conclusions follow with certainty from their premises, and the syllogism can be treated like mathematical reasoning. But the syllogism assumes something about real animals and men that may or may not be true, so its assumptions must be examined. Euclid's proposition asserts only an if-then connection, so it does not matter whether isosceles triangles exist.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say the absence of mathematics can sometimes trouble a reader more than its presence?
questions.a: Mathematics is used in science because of its preciseness, clarity, and limitedness, so readers can often grasp the matter without going deeply into it. Galileo's Two New Sciences is hard for modern readers because it is presented as a dialogue rather than mathematically. The dialogue form suits the stage and Plato's philosophy but not science, so it is hard to discover what Galileo is saying.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say active reading matters with particular force for scientific popularizations?
questions.a: Popularizations are never easy reading the way a story seems to be; even a short article on DNA with no experiments or formulas demands considerable effort. So the familiar rules apply with particular force: identify the subject, relate whole and parts, come to terms, and plot propositions and arguments. The reader must understand before criticizing or judging significance.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren explain that Commoner's The Closing Circle, though theoretical, has practical significance?
questions.a: Commoner's subject is the environmental crisis, and the environment is our own, so we are necessarily involved in the crisis. In a crisis, the usual thing is to act in a certain way or to stop acting in a certain way. So the book, though not a practical work in the sense of Chapter 13, has a significance that reaches into the practical.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren cite Aristotle's view that philosophy begins in ____.
questions.explain: The chapter opens with children's questions and recalls that, according to Aristotle, philosophy begins in wonder, which certainly begins in childhood.

questions.q: Sort these kinds of questioning into those Adler and Van Doren link with children and those they link with adults.

items.t: Why are people?
Did God have a reason for creating the earth?
Asking why something is so
Asking only whether something is so
Questions an encyclopedia can answer
Asking only for information

questions.explain: The authors say adult curiosity does not vanish but deteriorates in quality, seeking whether something is so and mere information, while children ask profound why questions.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that adults lose the curiosity that children naturally have.
questions.explain: The authors say adults do not lose their native curiosity; rather, it deteriorates in quality, turning to questions of fact instead of why.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren suggest help dull a child's natural inquisitiveness?
options: The dead weight of rote learning in school
Parents telling a child there is no answer when one exists
Parents demanding that the child ask no more questions
Children's natural lack of capacity for deep questions
Too much reading of philosophy in early childhood
questions.explain: The authors blame school's rote learning and, even more, parents who say there is no answer or demand no more questions. They insist children are born with inquisitive minds, so a lack of capacity is not the cause.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what rare combination of qualities marks the great philosophers, and how should readers follow them?
questions.a: The great philosophers retain the child's view of the world while maturely understanding what it means to retain it, and so ask the same profound questions children ask. They clear away the complexities of adult life to see simple distinctions. To follow them, readers must see, wonder, and ask as children do while answering with mature wisdom.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that to follow the great philosophers we must be childishly simple in our questions and maturely ____ in our replies.
questions.explain: The opening ends by asking readers to combine the child's simple, profound questioning with mature wisdom in answering.

questions.q: A parent, irritated by a child's question "What's the world's first name?", tells the child to stop asking. According to Adler and Van Doren, what is the likely long-term effect?
options: The child's inquisitiveness is debased into asking only for information
The child's inquisitiveness is killed entirely and never returns
The child learns to ask better and deeper philosophical questions
The child turns to encyclopedias and finds the true answers there
questions.explain: The authors say human inquisitiveness is never killed but is soon debased, so that people come to ask only for information, like most college students.

questions.q: Match each branch of philosophy with the kind of question Adler and Van Doren say it mainly deals with.
pairs: Becoming: the kinds, conditions, and causes of change
The causes, extent, and limits of human knowledge
The good life and right conduct of the individual
The good society and the individual in the community
questions.explain: The first three are subdivisions of theoretical philosophy; ethics and politics are the two spheres of normative philosophy.

questions.q: Sort these questions into the two main divisions of philosophy that Adler and Van Doren describe.

items.t: What is common to all things that exist?
Is anything immutable?
How many kinds of change are there?
What are the limits of human knowledge?
Is there a universal distinction between good and evil?
Can the many goods be ordered?
How should the state relate to the individual?
What about war and peace?

questions.explain: Theoretical questions concern what is or happens in the world; normative questions concern what ought to be done or sought.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say epistemology is just another name for theory of ____.
questions.explain: A work of theoretical philosophy mainly concerned with what is involved in knowing, and the extent and limits of knowledge, is a work in epistemology.

questions.q: In what sense do Adler and Van Doren call the philosophers' questions "childishly simple"?
options: They are easy to answer once a person has enough experience
They are basic or fundamental, though enormously difficult to answer
They are the questions children answer better than adults
They are trivial questions that serious science has outgrown
questions.explain: The authors say the questions do not look simple because answering them is so hard, but they are simple in the sense of being basic or fundamental.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren call philosophers' questions about being and becoming both simple and difficult?
questions.a: The questions, such as what is common to all existing things or what is involved in any change, are not difficult to state or understand and begin with a childishly simple attitude toward the world. Yet they are enormously difficult to answer, so difficult that some recent philosophers have held they cannot be answered satisfactorily.

questions.q: Match each kind of change Adler and Van Doren mention with its example or description.
pairs: Coming to be and passing away
Moving from one place to another
Becoming larger or smaller, heavier or lighter
questions.explain: The authors list these kinds of change when describing the questions asked in the philosophy of nature, and ask whether birth and death resemble the less fundamental changes.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say the practical division of philosophy is more accurately called ____ philosophy.
questions.explain: Questions about what ought to be done or sought belong to the division sometimes called practical and more accurately called normative.

questions.q: Sort these features into those Adler and Van Doren give to how-to books, such as cookbooks and driving manuals, and those they give to books of normative philosophy.

items.t: Assume you already want to make or do something
Need not argue that you ought to pursue the goal
Tell you how to succeed in your efforts
Concern the goals all men ought to seek
Deal with leading a good life or a good society
Prescribe means only in the most universal terms

questions.explain: How-to books take the goal for granted and give practical steps; normative philosophy argues about the goals themselves and goes no further than universal prescriptions of means.

questions.q: Match each pair of terms from Adler and Van Doren's account of philosophy with what it concerns.
pairs: What is or happens in the world
What ought to be done or sought
The world itself or what men ought to do
Our knowledge, our thinking, and the language expressing it
questions.explain: The theoretical and normative divisions together cover first-order questions; second-order questions are about our first-order knowledge and its expression.

questions.q: Which of these claims about goods do Adler and Van Doren make?
options: Even if whatever is right is good, we probably do not feel that whatever is wrong is evil
There are many goods, and some may depend on others
Goods can conflict, forcing a choice of one at the expense of another
Good and evil mean exactly the same as right and wrong
Good is a technical term with no place in everyday speech
questions.explain: The authors say good and evil are not the same as right and wrong, and that good is important in everyday vocabulary too. They raise questions about ordering many goods and their possible conflicts.

questions.q: What two main divisions of philosophy do Adler and Van Doren identify, and what distinguishes them?
questions.a: Questions about being and becoming, about what is or happens in the world, belong to theoretical or speculative philosophy. Questions about good and evil, right and wrong, concern what ought to be done or sought and belong to the division sometimes called practical and more accurately called normative.

questions.q: A reader picks up a book asking what is involved in knowing anything and how certain human knowledge can be. In Adler and Van Doren's scheme, what kind of work is it?
options: A work in metaphysics
A work in the philosophy of nature
A work in epistemology
A work in ethics
questions.explain: Questions about the causes, extent, limits, and certainties of human knowledge define epistemology. Metaphysics deals with being, and the philosophy of nature with change.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say a work of speculative philosophy mainly concerned with questions about being or existence is ____.
questions.explain: Within theoretical philosophy, the authors call a work metaphysical if it is mainly concerned with questions about being or existence.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren call questions about our first-order knowledge and the language expressing it ____ questions.
questions.explain: First-order questions concern the world and human conduct; second-order questions concern our knowledge, thinking, and language about them.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren say most professional philosophers of their day devote themselves to?
options: First-order questions about being, change, and the good life
Popular essays written mainly for ordinary intelligent readers
Experimental research meant to settle old metaphysical disputes
Second-order questions, very often about the language of thought
questions.explain: The authors report that most professional philosophers no longer believe first-order questions can be answered by philosophers and turn exclusively to second-order questions, often about language.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren consider modern philosophers' attention to second-order questions harmful in itself.
questions.explain: The authors call it all to the good, since it is never harmful to be critical. What troubles them is the wholesale abandonment of first-order questions.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren call "the trouble" with recent philosophy?
options: The wholesale giving up of first-order questions that interest lay readers
Its excessive attention to questions of everyday good and evil
Its reliance on experiments instead of careful reflection
Its tendency to write for lay readers rather than for other experts
questions.explain: The authors approve of critical, second-order work but object that first-order questions, those most likely to interest lay readers, have been abandoned wholesale.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: Put in order the changes in philosophy's audience that Adler and Van Doren describe, from earliest to latest.
items: Plato and the classical philosophers write for ordinary intelligent readers
Philosophical books still aimed at the general reader up to about 1930
Most professional philosophers write on second-order questions for other experts
questions.explain: All the great classical works from Plato onward were written for lay readers, a pattern that lasted until about 1930, after which philosophy, like science, came to be written only for experts.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say modern philosophy is very hard for non-philosophers to read?
questions.a: Most professional philosophers now deal exclusively with second-order questions, which are almost by definition of narrow appeal. Like scientists, they care only about the views of other experts and no longer write for lay readers, so their work is as difficult for non-philosophers as science is for non-scientists.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say about the great classical works of philosophy?
options: They were written for ordinary, intelligent men and women as well as peers
They ask the kinds of questions the authors call first-order
They are accessible to the lay reader who wishes to read them
They were written exclusively for other professional philosophers
They are concerned mainly with the language in which thought is expressed
questions.explain: The authors say the classics from Plato onward ask first-order questions and were written for the general reader, so a lay reader can succeed with them. Writing only for experts and focusing on language describe recent philosophy.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: A reader finds a recent professional journal article on the logic of the word "know" impenetrable. What would Adler and Van Doren say?
options: It should be read with special care because it is the heart of philosophy
It addresses second-order questions for experts; read the first-order classics instead
It is a first-order work and the chapter's rules will make it easy
It is really science, so the rules for reading science should be used
questions.explain: The authors say they can give no advice on reading philosophy concerned exclusively with second-order questions, but urge lay readers toward the classics that ask first-order questions.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, how must a philosopher proceed with a question such as what all existing things have in common?
options: By designing an experiment to test a proposed answer
By observing a special range of carefully chosen phenomena
By reflecting on the question, since there is nothing to do but think
By searching out and reading documents from the past
questions.explain: Unlike scientific or historical questions, philosophical ones cannot be settled by experiment, observation, or documents; as the authors put it, there is “nothing to do but think.”

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren deny that good philosophy is "pure" speculation?
questions.a: Good philosophy is not thinking divorced from experience; ideas cannot be put together just any way. There are stringent tests of the validity of philosophical answers, but these tests rest on common experience alone, the experience everyone has as a human being rather than as a specialist.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say the tests of philosophical answers are based on ____ experience alone.
questions.explain: Philosophical answers are tested against the experience everyone has as a human being, not special experience obtained by research.

questions.q: What distinguishes the greatest philosophers from the rest of us, according to Adler and Van Doren?
options: They gathered far more experience than ordinary people have
They carried out careful investigations of special phenomena
They had access to instruments that others did not possess
They thought more profoundly about the same experience everyone has
questions.explain: The authors say the great philosophers succeeded not by investigation or more experience but by thinking more profoundly about common experience.

questions.q: Put in order the steps in Adler and Van Doren's story of the matter of the heavenly bodies.
items: Ancients observe that heavenly bodies change only in place
They conclude celestial bodies are made of a different matter
Galileo uses the telescope and finds the moons of Jupiter
Kepler asserts celestial and earthly matter are the same
Newton formulates one celestial mechanics for all bodies
questions.explain: The ancients answered by philosophy a question later settled by science, beginning with Galileo's telescope, leading to Kepler's assertion and then Newton's mechanics.

questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren use the ancients' view of celestial matter to illustrate?
options: A philosopher taking up a question that should have been left to science
A philosophical question that science can never hope to answer
A scientist wrongly trying to answer a normative question
A philosophical truth later confirmed by Galileo and Kepler
questions.explain: The ancients treated as philosophical a question that later scientific investigation answered, which shows why readers must separate truly philosophical questions from others.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say the scientific misinformation in classical philosophers is, on the whole, irrelevant to reading them.
questions.explain: Apart from the confusions it may cause, such misinformation is irrelevant because we read a philosophical work for its philosophical questions, not scientific or historical ones.

questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren show that scientists, too, can mistake what kind of question they face?
questions.a: They imagine a scientist troubled by what kind of life a man ought to lead, a question of normative philosophy answerable only by thinking. If he instead surveys many people about the life they would like and bases his answer on theirs, his answer is as irrelevant as Aristotle's speculations about celestial matter.

questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, can no instrument help answer a philosophical question?
questions.a: Philosophical questions, such as what existence is or why things change, are not about special phenomena that could be observed more closely. If we could build a telescope or microscope to examine the properties of existence we would, but no such instruments are possible, so thinking is the only way to answer them.

questions.q: Sort these questions by how Adler and Van Doren say they can be answered.

items.t: Whether celestial matter differs from earthly matter
Whether Jupiter has moons
What happened in a past event, from documents
What all existing things have in common
What change is and why things change
What kind of life a man ought to lead

questions.explain: Scientific and historical questions call for experiment, observation, or documents; philosophical questions, theoretical or normative, can be answered only by reflection.

questions.q: Someone wants to settle whether the will is free and plans to ask a thousand people whether they feel free. How would Adler and Van Doren judge this plan?
options: As sound, because common experience is gathered most reliably by surveys
As misguided, since a philosophical question can be answered only by thinking
