As the proper scientific method for any question about human nature
As acceptable only if the people surveyed are professional philosophers
questions.explain: Freedom of the will is listed among philosophical questions, and the authors say a survey-based answer to such a question would be as irrelevant as Aristotle's view of celestial matter.

questions.q: Put Adler and Van Doren's five philosophical styles of exposition in the order they present them.
items: The philosophical dialogue
The philosophical treatise or essay
The meeting of objections
The systemization of philosophy
The aphoristic style
questions.explain: The authors begin with Plato's dialogue, first in time, then Aristotle's treatise, Aquinas' meeting of objections, the mathematical systems of Descartes and Spinoza, and finally the aphoristic style.

questions.q: Match each philosophical style with the philosopher Adler and Van Doren most associate with it.
questions.explain: Plato wrote dialogues, Aristotle originated the treatise, Aquinas perfected the meeting of objections, Spinoza wrote his Ethics in strict mathematical form, and Nietzsche used aphorisms.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say Plato's dialogue style is ____, meaning it leads the reader to discover things for himself.
questions.explain: In a master's hands, the dialogue is heuristic: it allows, indeed leads, the reader to discover things for himself.

questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren suggest may be a sign that the dialogue style is inappropriate for philosophy?
options: Plato himself abandoned it in favor of the treatise
It cannot report the views and objections of others
No one except Plato has ever been able to handle it effectively
It was used mainly by the later Greeks for comedy
questions.explain: Cicero and Berkeley tried dialogues with little success, and the authors suggest the fact that only Plato succeeded may show the style's inappropriateness.

questions.q: Match each figure with what Adler and Van Doren report about Plato or the dialogue form.
pairs: Called all Western philosophy a footnote to Plato
Said that everywhere in their heads they met Plato coming back
Wrote dialogues the authors call flat and dull
questions.explain: The authors cite Whitehead and the later Greeks on Plato's influence, and Cicero and Berkeley as failed imitators of his dialogue form.

questions.q: Why do scholars suggest that Aristotle's surviving treatises were originally notes, according to Adler and Van Doren?
options: Because the treatises are written as dialogues with missing speakers
Because Aristotle said in them that he was recording his lectures
Because they survive only on a papyrus recovered in 1890
Because the works are curiously difficult although Aristotle was clearly a clear thinker
questions.explain: The authors say the difficulty of the surviving works, set against Aristotle's evident clarity of thought, led to the suggestion they were lecture notes. The 1890 papyrus held the constitution of Athens.

questions.q: Which of these kinds of writing do Adler and Van Doren attribute to Aristotle?
options: Popular works, mostly dialogues, surviving only in fragments
Documentary collections, such as 158 constitutions of Greek states
Major treatises such as the Physics and the Ethics
Works in strict geometrical form with propositions and lemmas
Collections of short, enigmatic aphorisms
questions.explain: The authors list Aristotle's popular works, documentary collections, and major treatises. Geometrical form belongs to Spinoza and aphorisms to Nietzsche.

questions.q: Put in order the parts of an article in Aquinas' Summa Theologica as Adler and Van Doren describe it.
items: A question is posed
The opposite, wrong answer is given
Arguments are offered for the wrong answer
An authoritative text counters them
Aquinas gives his own answer, introduced by I answer that
He replies to each argument for the wrong answer
questions.explain: Every article follows the same form, moving from the question and the wrong answer with its arguments, through an authoritative text and Aquinas' own solution, to his replies to the objections.

questions.q: Sort these authors by whether Adler and Van Doren say a reader can skip parts of their work.
groups: You can skip a great deal

items.t: Spinoza
Newton
Kant
Aristotle
Plato

questions.explain: Spinoza's mathematical form, like Newton's, allows skipping; in Kant and Aristotle the reasoning is continuous, and skipping Plato would be like skipping part of a play or poem.

questions.q: Why, according to Adler and Van Doren, was the medieval style of meeting objections suited to its time?
questions.a: The idea that truth evolves out of opposition and conflict was common in the Middle Ages, and philosophers expected to defend their views in open public disputes. Because the civilization was essentially oral and books were few, a proposition was not accepted unless it met the test of open discussion, so the Summa is imbued with the spirit of debate.

questions.q: What did Descartes and Spinoza attempt in the style Adler and Van Doren call the systemization of philosophy?
options: To organize philosophy with the certainty and formal structure of mathematics
To replace philosophical argument with experiments on nature
To present philosophy through conversations among many speakers
To compress philosophy into short and enigmatic statements
questions.explain: Fascinated by mathematics' success in organizing knowledge of nature, they tried to give philosophy the structure Euclid had given geometry.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say a reader can skip a great deal in Spinoza, as in Newton, but nothing in Kant or Aristotle.
questions.explain: Spinoza's mathematical form allows skipping, while the continuous line of reasoning in Kant and Aristotle does not.

questions.q: Which of these writers do Adler and Van Doren say chose a form that was likely a major reason they failed to communicate fully?
options: Spinoza, writing philosophy in mathematical form
Galileo, writing science in dialogue form
Plato, writing philosophy in dialogue form
Kant, writing philosophy as finished treatises
questions.explain: The authors doubt a satisfactory philosophical work can be written in mathematical form or a scientific one in dialogue, citing Spinoza and Galileo. Plato is praised as the master of dialogue, and Kant's treatises as finished works of art.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren compare the author in the aphoristic style to a hit-and-run ____.
questions.explain: The aphorist touches on a subject, suggests an insight, and runs off to another subject without properly defending what he said.

questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren see as both the great advantage and the great disadvantage of the aphoristic style?
questions.a: Its advantage is that it is heuristic: the reader feels more is said than is said, because he does much of the thinking, making connections and constructing arguments himself. That same feature is its disadvantage, since the style is not really expositional and the author never properly defends his insights, which irritates serious philosophers who want to follow and criticize a line of thought.

questions.q: Match each item with what Adler and Van Doren say about it in discussing the aphoristic style.
pairs: Used aphorisms in Thus Spake Zarathustra
Left in fragments because he died before writing it as an essay
Possible source of the style's recent popularity
Lucretius' On the Nature of Things
Originally in verse, yet no different in style from other essays
questions.explain: Nietzsche exemplifies the style; Eastern wisdom books and Pascal's unfinished work may have influenced it; Lucretius is noted as not being a sixth style.

questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren compare the treatise of Kant and Aristotle with Plato's dialogue?
questions.a: Like the dialogue, the treatise, especially Aristotle's, gives accounts of the views and objections of others. But the element of drama is missing: the treatise develops a philosophical view through straightforward, orderly exposition with a beginning, middle, and end, rather than through the conflict of positions and opinions as in Plato.

questions.q: Put in order the tasks Adler and Van Doren set for a reader working through a philosophical book.
items: Find the question or questions the book tries to answer
Discover the author's controlling principles
Decide whether he adheres to those principles throughout
Listen to other philosophers on the same problem
Make up your own mind about what is true
questions.explain: The authors first stress finding the questions, then the controlling principles and their consistency, and finally urge reading other philosophers before judging for oneself.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say how a philosopher answers his questions is deeply affected by his controlling ____.
questions.explain: Every great philosopher has controlling principles underlying his work, which may be stated, reserved for another book, or left implicit throughout.

questions.q: Match each philosopher with the controlling principle or insight Adler and Van Doren attribute to him.
pairs: Conversation about philosophy is perhaps the most important human activity
Happiness is the whole of the good, not the highest good
The limitation of the mind must be surveyed first
The basic principles of logic from the Organon are assumed
questions.explain: The authors give these as examples of principles that govern a philosopher's work even where they are not stated explicitly.

questions.q: True or false: According to Adler and Van Doren, Aristotle's controlling insight in the Ethics is that happiness is the highest good.
questions.explain: The controlling insight is that happiness is the whole of the good, not the highest good, which would make it only one good among others.

questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren take Plato to be suggesting when Cephalus leaves the discussion in Book I of the Republic?
options: That older men are wise to avoid philosophical arguments
That refusing to join the search for truth betrays man's deepest nature
That practical business matters more than conversation
That Socrates' questioning drives honest people away
questions.explain: The authors read the episode, like Protagoras' unwillingness to keep talking, as expressing Plato's unstated principle that philosophical conversation is supremely important.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say Kant contrasted his critical philosophy with ____, the presumption that the intellect can reach the most important truths by pure thinking without knowing its limits.
questions.explain: Kant imputed dogmatism to many earlier philosophers and required first a critical survey of the mind's resources and powers.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren recommend reading books about philosophers' lives and opinions as a shortcut to finding their controlling principles.
questions.explain: The authors do not recommend that shortcut, saying the discovery you come to on your own is much more valuable than someone else's ideas.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what must a reader do when a philosopher is inconsistent?
options: Ignore the inconsistency, since consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds
Accept the conclusions, since they are what the book was written for
Decide whether he really means his first principles or his conclusions, or neither
Reject the whole book, since no inconsistent work deserves reading
questions.explain: The authors say inconsistency is a serious problem: the reader must decide which set of propositions the author really means, or that neither is valid. Emerson's remark is quoted but not followed.

questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren distinguish the philosophical problem from the scientific one?
options: Philosophy describes phenomena, while science explains their ultimate causes
Philosophy uses abstract terms, while science avoids abstractions
Philosophy relies on special experience, while science uses common sense
Philosophy seeks to explain the ultimate causes of things, while science describes
questions.explain: The authors say philosophy explains rather than describes, penetrating beyond connections of phenomena to ultimate causes. They add that science, too, uses abstract terms.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren warn that a philosopher's terms are usually expressed in words taken from common ____ but used in a very special sense.
questions.explain: Because the words are familiar, readers who use them in their familiar way will make gibberish and nonsense of the book.

questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren explain the difference between abstract and concrete, and why does it matter for reading philosophy?
questions.a: What we perceive through the senses is always concrete and particular, while what we think with the mind is always abstract and general. To understand an abstract word is simply to have the idea it expresses, a general aspect of things we experience concretely. Since no general knowledge is expressible except in abstract terms, abstractions are nothing to fear, but trying to imagine what ideas refer to only befuddles the reader.

questions.q: Sort these statements according to the kind of philosophical principle Adler and Van Doren say they describe.

items.t: Things the author asks you to assume with him
Make them to see what follows
Accept them even against contrary presuppositions
Drawn directly from experience
Not proved by other propositions
Tested by your common sense and daily observation

questions.explain: Assumptions cause no trouble: grant them and see what follows. Self-evident propositions may cause trouble; they come from common experience, which the reader can consult.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say a reader needs in order to test a philosopher's leading principles?
options: Your own common sense
Daily observation of the world you live in
Laboratory work or field research
The testimony of scientific experts
questions.explain: The philosopher refers the reader to the common experience of mankind, so no extrinsic aid of special, methodically obtained experience is needed.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say the rules of analytical reading apply more directly to philosophy than to any other kind of book?
questions.a: A philosopher facing a problem can do nothing but think about it, and a reader facing a philosophical book can do nothing but read it, which means thinking about it, with no aids but the mind. This essential loneliness of reader and book is exactly the situation imagined at the start of the discussion of the rules of analytical reading.

questions.q: A reader of a metaphysical treatise takes the word "substance" to mean any kind of stuff, as in everyday talk, and the argument seems absurd. What would Adler and Van Doren say went wrong?
options: The reader used a familiar word in its familiar way instead of the author's special sense
The author failed to use technical terms that differ from common speech
The reader tried to imagine what abstract ideas refer to
The author's argument depends on special experience the reader lacks
questions.explain: The authors warn that philosophical terms are usually common words used in a special sense, and readers who keep the familiar sense make nonsense of the book.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say Kant states the limitation of the mind explicitly in the Critique of Judgment.
questions.explain: The principle is explicitly stated in the Critique of Pure Reason; in the Critique of Judgment it is assumed rather than stated, though it still controls the work.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: Which of these are reasons Adler and Van Doren give for not being troubled that philosophers disagree?
options: Persistent disagreement may point to a great unsolved problem
Your responsibility is only to make up your own mind
Disagreement proves that philosophical questions have no answers
Experts will eventually settle the disagreement for you
questions.explain: The authors say it is good to know where the true mysteries are, and that the disagreements of others matter less than your own judgment. They also say you cannot depend on experts in philosophy.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren call the most distinctive mark of philosophical questions?
options: That only professional philosophers can answer them
That everyone must answer them for himself
That they can be answered by the testimony of experts
That they are answered once and for all by the classics
questions.explain: The authors say taking others' opinions is not solving philosophical questions but evading them; each reader must answer them, with solid arguments.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say a reader of a good theoretical work in philosophy need not investigate the author's social and economic background.
questions.explain: A good theoretical work is as free from oratory and propaganda as a good scientific treatise, so the author's personality and background are not the reader's concern.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that taking the opinions of others on philosophical questions is not solving them but ____ them.
questions.explain: Because everyone must answer philosophical questions for himself, borrowing others' answers only evades them.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say you cannot depend on experts for philosophical questions as you may in science?
questions.a: Philosophical questions must be answered by each person for himself, and the answers must be solidly grounded with arguments. Taking others' opinions evades the questions rather than solving them, and the authors add that these questions are simply more important than those asked by anyone else, except children.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: A student finishes Aristotle's account of change and plans to judge it before reading anything else. What would Adler and Van Doren advise?
options: First read a biography to learn Aristotle's social background
First consult an expert and adopt the expert's verdict
First read other great philosophers who dealt with the same problem
First check the account against modern laboratory findings
questions.explain: The authors say philosophers have carried on a long conversation, and readers should listen in on it, reading others on the same subject, before making up their minds.

questions.q: Sort these features into natural theology and dogmatic theology as Adler and Van Doren describe them.

items.t: A branch of philosophy
The last chapter of metaphysics
Reached by the unaided working of the mind
First principles are articles of faith
Depends on the authority of a church
Adhered to by the communicants of a religion

questions.explain: Natural theology is philosophy arriving at conceptions such as an uncaused cause by unaided reason; dogmatic theology rests on dogmas proclaimed by a church.

questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren use the idea of an uncaused cause to illustrate?
options: How dogmatic theology depends on the authority of a church
How science later replaced a philosophical conclusion
How an article of faith differs from a tentative opinion
How natural theology reaches its conceptions by the unaided effort of the mind
questions.explain: Asking whether everything is caused may lead to an infinite regress and so to positing an uncaused cause, a conception reached by the natural working of the mind.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren note that Aristotle called the uncaused cause an unmoved ____.
questions.explain: In the note on theology, the authors say one could call this originating cause by other names, even God, but Aristotle called it an unmoved mover.

questions.q: Which of these are the mistakes Adler and Van Doren say readers typically make with dogmatic theology?
options: Refusing to accept the articles of faith even temporarily
Assuming the reasoning and conclusions are dogmatic just as the principles are
Accepting the first principles as true while reading the book
Treating the dogmas with the respect given to a mathematician's assumptions
questions.explain: The authors name these two mistakes. Accepting the principles while reading and treating them like a mathematician's assumptions is what they recommend.

questions.q: True or false: According to Adler and Van Doren, an article of faith is, for the faithful, a tentative opinion that they assume.
questions.explain: The authors stress that an article of faith is not something the faithful assume; for them faith is the most certain form of knowledge.

questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren say a non-believer should read a work of dogmatic theology?
questions.a: He should treat its dogmas with the same respect he gives a mathematician's assumptions, accepting the first principles as true while reading, and then read with all the care any good expository work deserves. He must remember that for the faithful these are not assumptions but the most certain knowledge, and must still judge whether the reasoning from them is cogent.

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what happens if the reasoning in a theological book is defective?
options: Even the most acceptable first principles will lead to invalid conclusions
The conclusions remain valid because the principles are dogmas
The reader must reject the articles of faith themselves
The book becomes a work of natural rather than dogmatic theology
questions.explain: Conclusions must be accepted only if the principles are accepted and the reasoning is cogent; defective reasoning yields invalid conclusions whatever the principles.

questions.q: Which of these features of an institution do Adler and Van Doren say make its members read some books canonically?
options: It is a teaching institution
It has a body of doctrine to teach
It has a faithful and obedient membership
It elects its leaders democratically
It forbids its members to read any other books
questions.explain: The authors extend the notion of canonical books to any church, party, or society with these three features. The other options are not mentioned.

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren sum up canonical reading in the word ____, from Greek roots meaning "right opinion."
questions.explain: Canonical books are those for which there is one and only one right reading, and any other interpretation is fraught with peril.

questions.q: What obligation do Adler and Van Doren say the faithful reader of a canonical book has?
options: To question its authorized reading and find its errors
To make sense of it and find it true, seeking help if he cannot
To compare it with rival books before accepting it
To read it only as literature rather than as doctrine
questions.explain: The faithful reader must make sense of the text and find it true; if he cannot, he must go to someone who can and accept the resolution offered.

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say the reader of a canonical book reads essentially without freedom but gains a satisfaction rarely found in reading other books.
questions.explain: The authors say the faithful reader gives up freedom of interpretation, but in return gains a kind of satisfaction possibly never obtained in other reading.

questions.q: Match each group of readers with a text Adler and Van Doren say they read canonically.
pairs: The works of Marx and Lenin
questions.explain: The authors list these among examples showing that canonical reading extends well beyond sacred scripture.

questions.q: A law student studies a set text exactly as the examiners expect in order to pass the bar exam. How would Adler and Van Doren classify this reading?
options: As syntopical reading across several related books
As inspectional reading meant to skim the text
As an approach to canonical reading, with one right interpretation
As critical reading that judges the author's truth
questions.explain: The authors say a fledgling lawyer, like students bound to a professor's interpretation, approaches the situation of reading canonically.

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren stop short of giving rules for reading the Holy Book?
questions.a: They call reading the Holy Book, for one who has faith that it is the Word of God, the most difficult problem in the whole field of reading. More books have been written about how to read Scripture than about all other aspects of reading together, and the Bible, though the most difficult writing, is for believers also the most important to read.

questions.q: Why is it fitting that Adler and Van Doren close the section on making up your own mind with the words "Except children"?
options: It introduces the next chapter's discussion of social science
It warns that philosophy is unsuitable for young readers
It shows that children answer philosophical questions best
It returns to the opening claim that philosophers ask the same questions children ask
questions.explain: The chapter opens with children's magnificent questions and says great philosophical books ask the same sort; the closing words echo that theme.

questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 18 of How to Read a Book with its main content.
pairs: The theoretical and normative divisions and their branches
There is nothing to do but think about common experience
Five styles from dialogue to aphorism
Natural theology contrasted with dogmatic theology
questions.explain: The chapter moves from what philosophy asks and how it answers, through how it is written, to hints for reading and notes on theology and canonical books.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part Four of How to Read a Book in their order.
items: How to Read History
How to Read Science and Mathematics
How to Read Philosophy
How to Read Social Science
questions.explain: The table of contents places philosophy after science and mathematics and before social science, followed by the chapter on syntopical reading.

questions.q: Put these sections of Chapter 18 of How to Read a Book in the order they appear.
items: The Questions Philosophers Ask
Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
On Philosophical Method
On Philosophical Styles
Hints for Reading Philosophy
questions.explain: The chapter first defines philosophy's questions, then explains why modern philosophy is set aside, then covers method and style before giving hints for reading.

questions.q: Match each kind of reading in How to Read a Book with what Adler and Van Doren say deserves the reader's closest attention.
pairs: Articles of faith accepted while reading
questions.explain: In Chapter 18 the authors contrast the focus on inductive arguments in science with the focus on principles in philosophy, and treat theological dogmas like assumptions to be accepted while reading.

questions.q: In Chapter 18 of How to Read a Book, which three sections follow the hints for reading philosophy? Put them in sequence.
items: On Making Up Your Own Mind
A Note on Theology
How to Read Canonical Books
questions.explain: After the advice on judging for oneself, the chapter adds a note on theology and then turns to canonical books, ending with the Bible as the most carefully read book.

questions.q: How does Chapter 18 of How to Read a Book reuse the earlier distinction between theoretical and practical works?
questions.a: The authors say the speculative questions about being and becoming are theoretical in the sense of the terms they used earlier to distinguish the theoretical and practical realms. They then divide philosophy into theoretical or speculative and practical, more accurately called normative, and contrast normative philosophy with practical books such as cookbooks and driving manuals.

questions.q: Which of these ideas from elsewhere in How to Read a Book does Chapter 18 explicitly draw on?
options: The distinction between theoretical and practical works
The essential loneliness of reader and book assumed by the rules of analytical reading
Basil Willey on discovering an author's hidden assumptions
The five steps of syntopical reading
The advice on reading digests
questions.explain: The chapter recalls the theoretical-practical distinction, the situation imagined at the start of analytical reading, and the earlier quotation from Basil Willey. Syntopical reading comes in Chapter 20, and digests were discussed in Chapter 16.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what do Adler and Van Doren say journalists usually do with facts, beyond the bare front-page news story?
options: They wrap the facts in interpretation and analysis drawn from social science concepts
They report the facts only, leaving all interpretation to specialists
They test the facts against the methods of the hard sciences
They present the facts as fiction to make them more readable
questions.explain: The authors say journalists commonly enmesh facts in interpretation, commentary and analysis, and these draw on social science concepts and terminology. Bare fact-reporting is limited to the shorthand who-what-why-when-where story.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, novels, plays and stories that build artificial models of society to explore, for example, the social effects of new technology are called social-science ____.
questions.explain: The authors name a large category of contemporary writing “social-science fiction,” whose aim is to create artificial models of society.

questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors report that enrollments in social science courses run far behind those in traditional literature and language courses.
questions.explain: The authors say the reverse: social science enrollments run far ahead of literature and language courses and greatly exceed those in the pure sciences.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren give as signs of how pervasive the social sciences have become?
options: Journalism interprets the news using social science concepts
Social criticism on crime, poverty and education borrows its language
Specialists are called in to help formulate and deal with public problems
Social science has replaced history in most universities
Most novels are now written by trained sociologists
questions.explain: The chapter opens by citing journalism, social criticism, and specialists advising on social problems, along with school enrollments. It says nothing about replacing history or sociologists writing novels.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do Adler and Van Doren open the chapter on social science by stressing how pervasive its concepts are?
questions.a: They point out that social science concepts and terminology run through journalism, social criticism, social-science fiction, public policy and school courses. Because almost everything we read today draws on them, readers meet social science constantly, often without noticing. This makes learning how to read it well a practical necessity.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, which fields do the authors treat as the central core of social science that almost all social scientists would include?
options: Law, education, business and public administration
Anthropology, economics, politics and sociology
Psychology, psychiatry, biology and geography
History, philosophy, statistics and demography
questions.explain: The authors name anthropology, economics, politics and sociology as a central core of social science. Law, education and the like are only partly included, and history is excluded as a science of laws.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what reason is commonly given for keeping schools of law, education and business out of university social science divisions?
options: They do not use the concepts or methods of the social sciences
They are older than the social science departments
Their main purpose is training for professional work outside the university
They rely on mathematics more heavily than the core departments
questions.explain: The usual reason given is that these schools train people for professional work outside the university, while the core departments pursue systematic knowledge of human society. The authors note these schools do draw on social science concepts and methods.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the science of elections and polling, studied in interdisciplinary centers, is called ____.
questions.explain: The authors list psephology, which they gloss as the science of elections and polling, among the studies of the new interdisciplinary centers.

questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, strict social scientists exclude psychology because it concerns individual and personal characteristics rather than cultural and institutional factors.
questions.explain: The authors report that strict interpreters exclude psychology for focusing on the individual, while less strict ones include it because the individual cannot be separated from his social environment.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each field to how the authors place it in relation to social science.
pairs: Part of the central core of social science
Supplies data but does not yield laws of behavior
Much, though not all, of their literature falls within it
questions.explain: The authors build their working definition from a core (anthropology, economics, politics, sociology), partial inclusions such as law and education, and exclusions such as physiological psychology and history as a science.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what did the term behavioral science originally emphasize, and how has its use changed?
questions.a: Originally it covered sociology, anthropology and the behavioral aspects of fields like biology, economics, psychology and political science. Its accent on behavior stressed observable, measurable behavior that could be systematically investigated and yield verifiable findings. Recently it has come to be used almost as a synonym for social sciences, though many purists object.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort these fields by whether the authors place them in the central core of social science or treat them as only partly or doubtfully included.

items.t: Anthropology
Economics
Politics
Sociology
Business
Public administration
Psychology
Social service

questions.explain: The core is anthropology, economics, politics and sociology. Fields like business, social service, public administration and much of psychology are included only in part.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren give as reasons social science seems easy to read?
options: Its data often come from experiences familiar to the reader
Its style is usually narrative, like fiction and history
Its jargon is already part of everyday talk
Its authors stipulate their terms at the outset
Its arguments are usually set out in mathematical form
questions.explain: Familiar data, narrative style and everyday jargon all make it seem easy. Stipulating terms and mathematical form belong to the hard sciences, which the authors contrast with social science.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors call the word society ____-like, because so many adjectives can be placed before it while it still means people living together.
questions.explain: The authors call society a “chameleon-like word” and run through adjectives from aberrant to zymotic society.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say readers usually hold strong opinions on philosophical questions but are rarely committed on matters social science deals with.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: we are not ordinarily committed on philosophical questions, but on social science matters we are likely to have strong opinions.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how do the reader's feelings contribute to the deceptive ease of reading social science?
questions.a: Social science writing deals with matters the reader hears about almost daily, and it is often imbued with deep feeling. The reader's attitudes and feelings about these matters are usually firmly developed. Unlike philosophy, where we are not ordinarily committed, social science touches subjects on which we already hold strong opinions, so the reading feels easy and familiar.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: Maya reads a magazine essay full of words like alienation, status and in-group and finishes it feeling she understood everything at once. In How to Read a Book, what would the authors warn her about?
options: Familiar jargon can make reading feel easy while hiding unclear meanings
She should first check the essay's mathematical proofs
Essays using such words are fiction and need no analysis
She must read the author's philosophical predecessors first
questions.explain: The authors say the jargon and metaphors of social science make for deceptively easy reading. Familiar terms may not be clearly understood by reader or writer.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the hard scientist is said to ____ his usage, telling the reader at the start which terms are essential and how he will use them.
questions.explain: The hard scientist “stipulates his usage,” usually through definitions, postulates and axioms at the beginning of the book.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do the authors compare the hard sciences to games such as poker or bridge?
options: Because scientific results depend partly on chance
Because scientists compete with one another for discoveries
Because stipulated terms, like game rules, are accepted rather than disputed
Because both reward the reader who memorizes the most rules
questions.explain: Stipulating usage is like setting the rules of a game: you do not dispute that three of a kind beats two pairs, and you do not dispute a hard scientist's stipulations. You accept them and go on.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren give as reasons social scientists have stipulated their usage less than hard scientists?
options: The social sciences were typically not mathematicized
Terms like economic depression or mental health are hard to define
Readers tend to question a social scientist's definitions
Social scientists are forbidden by convention to define terms
Social science has no key terms at all
questions.explain: The authors cite the lack of mathematics, the difficulty of defining terms like depression or mental health, and readers' tendency to question such definitions. There is no rule against defining terms.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, what do the authors call the most important source of difficulty in reading social science?
options: Its heavy use of mathematical notation
Its lack of any familiar subject matter
Its narrow focus on a single classic text
Its being a mixed rather than pure kind of expository writing
questions.explain: The most important difficulty is that social science is a mixed kind of expository writing, a shifting blend of science, philosophy and history, sometimes with fiction. It is not mathematical in the way hard science is.

questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say social science is harder to read than history partly because its mixture of strands shifts from book to book.
questions.explain: History is a mixture we are used to, but social science is not always the same mixture: it shifts from book to book and even within one book.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each kind of writing to how the authors describe its makeup.
pairs: A mixture of fiction and science
A shifting mixture of science, philosophy and history, sometimes fiction
Stipulates terms and assumptions clearly at the outset
questions.explain: The authors contrast history's familiar mixture of fiction and science, social science's changing mixture, and the hard sciences' stipulated usage.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the authors use the concept of ____ as an example of an economic term that journalists make do too much work.
questions.explain: Some social scientists complain that reporters use the Gross National Product too widely, without really understanding its relatively limited sense in serious economic writing.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why must the reader of social science check his opinions at the door?
questions.a: Readers are often committed to a view of the matter the author discusses and fear it would be disloyal to stand apart and question it impersonally. Yet analytical reading, especially structural outlining and interpretation, requires that impartial stance. As the authors put it, “You cannot understand a book if you refuse to hear what it is saying.”

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort these steps of analytical reading by whether the authors say they pose special difficulty for social science or no special problem.

items.t: Saying what kind of book it is
Coming to terms with the author
Answering What of it?
Outlining the work
Finding propositions and arguments in a good book

questions.explain: Outlining poses no special problem, nor do propositions and arguments in a good book. Classifying the book, coming to terms, and the restraint needed for What of it? are the hard steps.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, put these steps of analytically reading a social science work in the order the authors discuss them.
items: Identify what kind of book it is and its strands
Outline the work
Come to terms with the author
Find the propositions and arguments
Ask What of it? with restraint
questions.explain: The authors walk through the analytical rules in their usual order, noting where social science adds difficulty: classifying, terms, and the final critical question.

questions.q: Raj reads a careful study on school funding and admits he cannot fault its reasoning, yet he still rejects its conclusions. In How to Read a Book, what explains his reaction?
options: The study failed to stipulate its terms as a game does
Prejudgments he already holds about the author's approach and conclusions
The study is a mixture of fiction and history he cannot separate
He has not yet read the philosophers the author read
questions.explain: The authors say What of it? requires restraint, because readers of social science may say they cannot fault the conclusions but still disagree, owing to prejudgments about the author's approach.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why do the authors speak of social science literature rather than a social science book?
options: Because social science readers usually read several works on one problem
Because social science is mostly written as imaginative literature
Because one classic text covers each social science subject
Because social science books are too short to read alone
questions.explain: In social science we usually read several works on a matter such as law enforcement or taxation, because there is typically no single authoritative work. Classic texts are few.

questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren give as reasons readers of social science must read several works rather than one?
options: The field is relatively new and has few classic texts
Readers focus on a problem rather than on one author
New editions and works quickly make older ones obsolete
Social science books contradict their own definitions
Analytical reading rules forbid reading one book alone
questions.explain: The authors cite the field's newness, readers' focus on a problem, and the rapid obsolescence that forces new editions. Analytical rules still apply to each book read.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, the fourth level of reading, which the need to read several social science works introduces, is called ____ reading.
questions.explain: Passing from analytical reading to the fourth level, syntopical reading, requires new rules for reading several works on the same subject.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how does the need to read several books differ in social science from philosophy and history?
questions.a: In philosophy you should read the philosophers your author read, and in history you should read several books to discover the truth of the past. But in those fields you were much more likely to find one major, authoritative work. In social science that is less common, so reading several works rather than one is much more urgent.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, put the kinds of reading discussed in Part Three in the order the authors treat them.
items: Practical books
Fiction and poetry
History
Science and mathematics
Philosophy
Social science
questions.explain: The authors began with practical books, then imaginative literature, and then the theoretical, expository kinds, ending with social science; history comes between imaginative literature and science in the table of contents.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, why is the social science chapter placed last in Part Three?
options: Because social science is the least important kind of book
Because it serves as an appendix on technical vocabulary
Because it is the easiest kind of reading and so can be quick
Because its need to be read syntopically leads into Part Four
questions.explain: The authors say social science came last because of the need to read it syntopically, so the chapter both ends Part Three and introduces Part Four. They do not rank it as less important or easier.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, put these sections of the chapter How to Read Social Science in their order.
items: What Is Social Science?
The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
Difficulties of Reading Social Science
Reading Social Science Literature
questions.explain: The chapter defines its subject, shows why it seems easy, explains why that ease is deceptive, and ends by pointing to reading many works, which leads into syntopical reading.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, how does the chapter How to Read Social Science connect to Chapter 20, The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading?
questions.a: The chapter ends by showing that social science is typically read as a literature of several works on one problem, not one book for its own sake. The rules of analytical reading apply to each work but are not enough for reading several together. This need prepares for the fourth level, syntopical reading, so the chapter is both the end of Part Three and an introduction to Part Four.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, sort these Part Three subjects by whether the authors group them as theoretical expository writing or not.
groups: Other kinds treated in Part Three

items.t: Science and mathematics
Philosophy
Social science
Practical books
Fiction
Poetry

questions.explain: The authors say they dealt last with three types of theoretical, expository writing: science and mathematics, philosophy, and social science. Practical books carry an obligation to act, and fiction and poetry pose their own problems.

questions.q: In How to Read a Book, match each level of reading to what the chapter says about it.
pairs: Its rules apply to each social science work read
Needs new rules for reading several works on one subject
The level the reader is passing from here
questions.explain: Analytical reading, the third level, still governs each book, but reading several works together requires the new rules of the fourth level, syntopical reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is the first requirement in any project of syntopical reading?
options: Knowing that more than one book is relevant to a particular question
Knowing exactly which books on the question should be read
Having read every relevant book analytically beforehand
Owning a topical index such as the Syntopicon
questions.explain: The authors say the first requirement is knowing that more than one book is relevant to a question. Knowing which books to read is the second requirement, and a much harder one.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say War and Peace and The Charterhouse of Parma are not really books on the same subject for someone studying war?
options: Both novels describe different wars, so they cannot be compared at all
War is only the background of both stories; the authors rivet our attention on the stories themselves
Novels never contain any accurate information about battles or history
Tolstoy denied that Stendhal had written truthfully about Waterloo
questions.explain: Both novels use the Napoleonic Wars as context, but neither is about war as such. Tolstoy even said he learned about battles from Stendhal, so the point is not that novels contain nothing about war.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Tolstoy once said he had learned much of what he knew about battles from Stendhal's account of the Battle of ____.
questions.explain: The authors mention that Tolstoy credited Stendhal's account of Waterloo, yet still argue we do not go to novels if our main aim is to study war.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Using the example of the statements about loving cheese, football and mankind, explain what problem the authors raise about identifying the same subject.
questions.a: One eats cheese, plays football and does something quite different when loving mankind, yet all three use the same word. The authors ask whether the word has any common sense in these uses, or some deeper reason for being shared. Until that is answered, it is doubtful that one has identified the same subject to read about.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which of these conceptions of love do Adler and Van Doren report finding even within the literature on human love alone?
options: Love as wholly acquisitive, usually sexual, desire
Love as pure benevolence with no acquisitive desire
Love as cognitive, an intellectual act rather than an emotional one
Love as a purely chemical reaction that science has fully explained
Love as an illusion that no serious author defends
questions.explain: The authors list acquisitive desire, pure benevolence and a cognitive conception of love. They do not report a settled scientific explanation or a view that love is an illusion.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren describe a curious ____ in syntopical reading: the subject must seemingly be identified before the reading, yet in a sense can only be identified after it.
questions.explain: They call it a paradox: the level is defined as reading books on the same subject, yet the identification of the subject must in a sense follow the reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Sort these questions into those the authors list about who or what can be loved, and those about whether love changes over time or relationships.
groups: Who or what can be loved

items.t: If humanoid robots existed, could human beings love them?
Can we love someone we have never met, like a movie star?
If we discovered intelligent beings on another planet, could we love them?
Is a couple's love the same in their twenties as in their seventies?
Does a mother's love for her children change as they grow up?
Is love the same when courting as when married?

questions.explain: The authors pile up both kinds of question to show how many problems arise from reading even part of the literature of love.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say that, in syntopical reading, identifying the subject matter must in a sense follow the reading rather than precede it?
questions.a: Syntopical reading is defined as reading two or more books on the same subject, which seems to assume the subject is known first. But as the love example shows, the range of reference is so wide that you may need to read many works before you can decide what you are reading about. Only then can you tell which books are really on the subject.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each step of inspectional reading with the step of analytical reading it chiefly prepares for, as Adler and Van Doren recall it.
pairs: First step: identify subject, kind of book and outline its structure
Second step: come to terms, state propositions, follow arguments
questions.explain: The authors recall that skimming anticipates the first step of analytical reading and superficial reading chiefly the second; in a similar way inspection prepares for syntopical reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren estimate that reading a hundred books analytically might well take ____ years.
questions.explain: They say a hundred books read analytically might take ten years, or many months even full time, so a short cut is needed.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which of these are the two essential functions the authors say inspecting all the books on a bibliography performs in syntopical reading?
options: It gives a clear enough idea of the subject to make later analytical reading productive
It cuts the bibliography down to a more manageable size
It acquaints the reader with all the intricacies of the subject
It tells the reader which author is right on each issue
It replaces the need for any analytical reading
questions.explain: Inspection clarifies the subject and trims the list. The authors say plainly it will not acquaint you with all the intricacies of the subject, nor does it judge truth.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What do the authors say makes the reading of many graduate and research students enormously wasteful?
options: They cannot get at the meat of any book they read
They read only summaries instead of whole books
They spend the same amount of time and effort on every book or article they read
They refuse to read anything outside their own field
questions.explain: The authors grant that some advanced students read actively and analytically, but say they waste effort because they do not know how to read some books faster than others.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors advise reading the most promising books on a bibliography analytically first and inspecting the rest afterwards.
questions.explain: They advise the opposite: you should not read any book analytically before inspecting all of them.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what does the skilled inspectional reader learn about each book in a short time?
options: Precisely what the book says about his subject
Whether the author's conclusions are true or false
How the book compares in style with others on the list
Whether the book is one to return to for light or one that need not be read again
questions.explain: He learns whether the book says something important about his subject; what that something is precisely usually waits for another reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren reject the idea that inspecting all the books on a list can be done at the same time as reading them analytically?
questions.a: Skilled analytical readers do perform some steps concurrently, so it may seem that inspection could merge with analytical reading. But the authors say no reader, however skilled, can do this. Researchers who try to collapse the two steps end up reading everything at the same rate, too fast or too slow for most of the books.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Once relevant books have been identified by inspection, the authors say you proceed to read them ____, not simply analytically.
questions.explain: They point out they did not say analytically, because analytical reading aims at understanding a single book, while the aim of syntopical reading is quite different.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Explain how inspectional reading offers a short cut around the paradox of syntopical reading.
questions.a: Reading every title on a long bibliography analytically to find the real subject would take years. Inspecting all the books first gives a clear enough idea of the subject to make later analytical reading productive, and lets you cut the list down. It shows which books you must return to for light and which need not be read again.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Jo has twenty books on remote work and plans to read the first one cover to cover before opening the others. What would Adler and Van Doren advise?
options: Read the first book analytically, since it will define the subject for the rest
Inspect all twenty first, to sharpen the subject and drop irrelevant books, before reading any analytically
Read all twenty analytically at an even pace to be fair to each
Read only the most recent book, since it summarises the others
questions.explain: The authors say you should not read any book analytically before inspecting all of them; reading at one even rate is the mistake they attribute to younger researchers.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put the five steps of syntopical reading in the order Adler and Van Doren give them.
items: Finding the relevant passages
Bringing the authors to terms
Getting the questions clear
Defining the issues
Analyzing the discussion
questions.explain: The authors discuss the five steps roughly in the order in which they occur, though in a sense all must take place for any of them to.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: In step 1 of syntopical reading, whose needs come first, according to the authors?
options: The individual books, each to be understood on its own terms
The authors' intentions in writing their books
The reader's own problem and concerns, not the individual books
The needs of whoever will read the final report
questions.explain: Reading each book thoroughly would put the books first and your problem second; in syntopical reading the order is reversed.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say the books you read syntopically are read for an ____ purpose, namely the light they may throw on your own problem.
questions.explain: You read each book quickly, not for its own sake, but for the ulterior purpose of illuminating your own problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren advise that, at the start of a syntopical project, finding relevant books and finding relevant passages be kept as separate steps?
questions.a: The first inspection aims partly at zeroing in on the subject itself, and an adequate understanding of the problem often comes only after inspecting many books. Trying to pick out relevant passages at the same time is therefore perilous and leads to mistakes that must be corrected later. With later books, once the problem is clear, the two steps can coalesce.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What relationship to the book do the authors say the reader has in syntopical reading, compared with analytical reading?
options: In both kinds of reading the reader is a disciple to the author as master
In analytical reading the reader is master; in syntopical reading a disciple
In syntopical reading author and reader are equal partners in a dialogue
In analytical reading the reader is disciple to master; in syntopical reading the reader must be master of the situation
questions.explain: Because the books serve the reader, the authors call syntopical reading the most active reading you can do; the reader must be the master of the situation.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren call syntopical reading the most ____ reading you can do, since the books serve you rather than the other way around.
questions.explain: Analytical reading is active too, but in syntopical reading the reader masters the situation, making it the most active reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which step do Adler and Van Doren call probably the most difficult step in syntopical reading?
options: Bringing the authors to terms
Finding the relevant passages
Defining the issues
Analyzing the discussion
questions.explain: Bringing the authors to terms means forcing each author to use your language rather than his, which runs against all normal reading habits.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Explain how step 2 of syntopical reading, bringing the authors to terms, differs from coming to terms in analytical reading.
questions.a: In analytical reading you identify the author's key words and discover how he uses them, accepting his terms. In syntopical reading the authors will not all have used the same words or terms, so the reader must establish the terms and bring the authors to them. It means forcing an author to use your language rather than his.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say a coincidence of terminology between the reader and one of the authors is merely accidental and may even be inconvenient.
questions.explain: If you adopt one author's term, you may be tempted to adopt his others, and these may get in the way rather than help.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that syntopical reading is, to a large extent, an exercise in ____.
questions.explain: Not from one natural language to another, but by imposing a common terminology on authors who may not have created ideal terms for the reader's problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which of these are the two things the authors say the reader's built-up set of terms must do in syntopical reading?
options: Help the reader understand all of the authors, not just one or a few
Help the reader solve the problem
Match the terminology of the greatest author on the list
Avoid every word the authors themselves used
Translate the books into a different natural language
questions.explain: The terms must help with all the authors and with the problem. Adopting one great author's terminology is exactly what the authors warn against.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: In step 3 of syntopical reading, what is the best way to establish a set of neutral propositions, according to Adler and Van Doren?
options: Copy each author's key sentences word for word into a common list
Frame a set of questions that shed light on the problem and to which each author gives answers
Summarise each book in a single sentence of its own
Choose the propositions of the most respected author as a standard
questions.explain: Since the reader sets the terms, he must also set neutral propositions, and the best way is to frame questions all or most authors can be read as answering.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to How to Read a Book, when an author gives no answer to one of the reader's questions, the reader must invent the answer the author would most likely have given.
questions.explain: The reader records him as silent or indeterminate. An implicit answer may sometimes be found in the book, but restraint is needed: we cannot put words into authors' mouths.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What balance do the authors ask the syntopical reader to strike between an author's explicit statements and implicit answers?
questions.a: Sometimes an author does not discuss a question explicitly, yet his book yields an implicit answer showing how he would have answered it. The reader must show restraint and not put thoughts into authors' minds or words into their mouths. But he cannot depend entirely on explicit statements either, for if he could, he would probably have no problem to solve.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put in order the general sequence of questions Adler and Van Doren suggest for a syntopical inquiry.
items: Whether the phenomenon exists or what character the idea has
How the phenomenon is known or how the idea manifests itself
What consequences follow from the earlier answers
questions.explain: The authors say the first questions usually concern existence or character, then how it is known or manifests itself, and a final set concerns consequences.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: When a question is clear and authors answer it in different ways, perhaps pro and con, the authors say an ____ has been defined.
questions.explain: An issue lies between authors who answer a question one way and those who answer it in an opposing way.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, when is an issue truly joined?
options: When two authors use exactly the same words in their books
When more than two answers are given to the same question
When one author explicitly attacks another by name
When two authors who understand a question the same way answer it in contrary or contradictory ways
questions.explain: Often answers differ because the authors conceive the question differently, so the syntopical reader must frame issues to ensure they are joined as well as may be.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A number of issues revolving around a closely connected set of questions may be termed the ____ about that aspect of the subject.
questions.explain: The syntopical reader must sort out such controversies and arrange them in an orderly fashion, even if no author managed to.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match the stage of a syntopical project with the analytical-reading questions the authors say it lets the reader answer about the discussion.
pairs: First four steps of syntopical reading
What does it say? and How does it say it?
Questions similar to Is it true? and What of it?
First two groups of analytical rules
The single-book counterpart of the first four steps
questions.explain: The authors say the first four steps correspond to the first two groups of analytical rules; the fifth addresses questions like Is it true? and What of it?

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: For a perennial problem, where do Adler and Van Doren say the truth is to be found, if at all?
options: In the conflict of opposing answers, many of which may have persuasive support
In whichever single set of answers the syntopical reader prefers
In the answers of the oldest and most respected author
In the answers that most of the authors agree upon
questions.explain: They say it would be presumptuous to expect the truth in any one set of answers; it lies, if anywhere, in the conflict of opposing answers.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: For a perennial problem, the authors say the truth consists rather in the ordered ____ itself than in any set of propositions about it.
questions.explain: The ordered discussion, not a set of assertions, is where the solution insofar as available lies.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say the syntopical reader must do before claiming to have analyzed the discussion of a problem?
options: Ask the questions in a certain order and be able to defend that order
Show how the questions are answered differently and try to say why
Point to the texts that support the classification of answers
Declare which answer to each question is correct
Read every book on the subject analytically from cover to cover
questions.explain: Ordering, explaining differences and pointing to texts are required. Declaring the correct answers would break the objectivity the next section demands.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What further benefit can a thorough analysis of the discussion of a problem provide, according to the authors?
options: It can settle the problem for good so no further work is needed
It can clear away deadwood and prepare the way for an original thinker's breakthrough
It can replace the need to read the original books
It can prove which of the authors was the greatest thinker
questions.explain: The analysis may make the dimensions of the problem visible, which is the groundwork for further productive work by others.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put in order what the authors say has been accomplished by the time a syntopical reader reaches the fifth step.
items: Found the relevant passages in the works
Created a neutral terminology for the authors
Framed and ordered questions most authors answer
Defined and arranged the issues from differing answers
questions.explain: The authors summarise the first four steps in this order before asking what remains to be done.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Why do the authors say the syntopical reader's task on a perennial problem is not merely to answer the framed questions himself?
questions.a: On problems about which good men have disagreed for centuries, it would be presumptuous to expect the truth in one set of answers. The truth, insofar as it can be found, lies in the conflict of opposing answers and in the ordered discussion itself. So the reader must order the questions, show how and why answers differ, and cite supporting texts.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A manager reads five reports on a hiring problem, each using different words: talent, staff, human capital. Following step 2 of syntopical reading, what should she do?
options: Adopt the terms of the most authoritative report throughout
Summarise each report strictly in its own vocabulary
Set up her own neutral terms and interpret each report in them
Discard the reports that use unfamiliar words
questions.explain: The authors say we will quickly be lost if we accept any one author's terminology; the reader must establish the terms and bring the authors to them.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Sort these activities into those that belong to analytical reading of a single book and those that belong to syntopical reading.

items.t: Accepting the author's key terms and discovering how he uses them
Finding the author's key sentences and propositions
Treating the author as master and oneself as disciple
Constructing a neutral terminology for many authors
Framing questions all or most authors can be read as answering
Defining issues between authors who answer differently

questions.explain: The authors contrast the two: analytical reading serves understanding of one book on its author's terms, syntopical reading serves the reader's problem across many authors.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put in order how the syntopical reader moves from questions to the analysis, as the authors describe steps 3 to 5.
items: Frame neutral questions
Record authors' differing answers as issues
Group connected issues into controversies
Arrange the controversies in an orderly, perspicuous way
questions.explain: Questions yield issues where answers differ, connected issues form a controversy, and sorting the controversies brings the reader to the final step.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What do Adler and Van Doren say the disagreement of human beings on a question establishes?
options: A counter-presumption that none of the conflicting opinions may be wholly true
A presumption that the majority opinion is true
Proof that the question can never be answered
A presumption that the oldest opinion is true
questions.explain: Agreement establishes some presumption of truth; disagreement establishes the counter-presumption that none of the conflicting opinions may be wholly true.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which of these possibilities about conflicting opinions do the authors explicitly allow?
options: One may be wholly true and the rest false
Each may express some portion of the whole truth
All the conflicting opinions may be false
The majority opinion must be the true one
Conflicting opinions can never contain any truth
questions.explain: The authors allow all three, and add that some opinion not yet expressed may be nearer the truth; they do not say the majority must be right.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A syntopical report that asserted the truth or falsity of views on the issues would be dogmatic, not ____.
questions.explain: By taking sides it would become one more voice in the discussion and lose its detached, objective character.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren sum up the special quality a syntopical analysis tries to achieve in the two words dialectical ____.
questions.explain: Dialectical objectivity means being resolutely objective and detached throughout.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say it is easier for the syntopical reader to look at all sides than to take no sides.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: taking no sides is easier, while looking at all sides is where the reader will undoubtedly fail, since all sides cannot be enumerated.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren name as subtle ways partiality can intrude into a syntopical analysis?
options: The manner in which arguments are summarized
Shades of emphasis and neglect
The order in which answers to key questions are presented
Quoting authors in their own words
Using a neutral terminology
questions.explain: Summary, emphasis, tone and order can all slant the account. Quoting authors and using neutral terms are the remedies, not the dangers.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What obvious device do the authors recommend to guard against partiality in a syntopical report?
options: Avoid summarising any author's argument at all
Refer constantly to the actual texts and quote authors in their own words alongside summaries
Present only the views the reader finds most convincing
Use each author's own terminology in all summaries
questions.explain: Summaries stay in neutral language, but the author's own words, quoted in context, must accompany them so readers can judge the interpretation.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: How do the authors reconcile their advice to quote authors in their own words with their earlier insistence on a neutral terminology?
questions.a: The need for a neutral terminology remains, so summaries of an author's argument are presented in the reader's language, not the author's. But the author's own words, quoted carefully and in context, must accompany the summary. That way the reader of the report can judge for himself whether the interpretation is correct.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Why do the authors say a syntopical analysis would cease to be syntopical if it tried to prove the truth of a view on the issues?
questions.a: Such a report would be dogmatic rather than dialectical. By asserting or proving a view, it would become simply one more voice in the discussion and lose its detached and objective character. The distinctive contribution of syntopical analysis is to look at all sides and take no sides.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Sort these practices into those that support dialectical objectivity and those that threaten it, according to the authors.

items.t: Quoting an author's words beside a summary of his view
Rereading the relevant passages over and over
Balancing question against question
