A slanted tone in posing a question
A coloured passing remark
Over-emphasising one side's arguments

questions.explain: The authors list tone, passing remarks and emphasis among the subtle intrusions of partiality, and recommend quoting and balancing as safeguards.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A student writes a fair report on a school uniform debate but always presents her own preferred answer last and at greatest length. What would the authors say?
options: The report is objective because she never states which side is right
The report is fine because order never affects a reader's judgment
She should state her view openly instead of quoting anyone
Partiality can intrude through emphasis and the order of answers even without explicit judgments
questions.explain: The authors warn that avoiding explicit judgments does not guarantee objectivity; emphasis and order of presentation can slant it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: The bibliography for the authors' study of the idea of progress finally ran to more than ____ items.
questions.explain: It was built through inspectional readings of several times that many books, articles and other pieces.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: True or false: According to How to Read a Book, many items finally judged relevant to the idea of progress were found more or less by accident or through educated guesses.
questions.explain: Many recent books have progress in their titles, but others do not, and most older relevant books do not even use the term.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Which of these are reasons Adler and Van Doren give for the difficulty of including novels, plays and poems in a syntopical project?
options: The essence of a story is its plot, not its positions on issues
Characters seldom take clear positions on an issue
We cannot be sure a character's speech represents the author's view
Fiction is always less truthful than exposition
Novels never mention ideas such as progress
questions.explain: The authors give these three reasons. They do not say fiction is less truthful, and they cite Settembrini's speech on progress as an example.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Why do the authors mention Settembrini in Thomas Mann's Magic Mountain?
options: Even when a character speaks about progress, we cannot be sure it is the author's view and not irony
He is the clearest statement of the idea of progress in any book
He shows that novels always argue against progress
He proves that fictional characters never discuss ideas
questions.explain: A character may hold forth on progress, but the author may be ironic, so placing a fictional work on an issue needs dubious interpretation.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Authors who used the word progress for forward movement in history that is not an improvement were referred to as asserting non-meliorative ____.
questions.explain: Because betterment is of the essence of the majority's conception, the word progress could not be applied to the minority's view.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Explain why the authors could not use the word progress for the minority faction that used it for non-improving historical change.
questions.a: Most authors use progress to mean historical change for the better, and betterment is of the essence of the concept. The same word could not cover both views without confusion, so the majority usage prevailed in the neutral terminology. The minority were described as asserting non-meliorative advance, even though they had used the word progress themselves.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: What did the authors find to be the primary question in the study of the idea of progress?
options: Is progress necessary or contingent?
Does progress occur in history?
Will progress continue indefinitely?
Is there progress in the fine arts?
questions.explain: The first question is whether progress occurs; the other three are issues joined only among authors who already assert that it does.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Which of these are the basic answers the authors found to the question whether progress occurs in history?
options: Yes
No
We cannot know
Only in the distant future
Only in ancient times
questions.explain: There are three basic answers, each with several variations.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Match each controversy or set of issues in the study of progress with its description.
pairs: Answers to whether progress occurs; every author takes sides
Nature or properties of progress, joined only by progress authors
The respects or areas in which progress occurs
questions.explain: The general controversy involves all authors; the special and subordinate issues arise only among authors who assert progress occurs.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Which of these are among the three issues of the special controversy about progress?
options: Whether progress is necessary or contingent
Whether progress will continue indefinitely or plateau out
Whether there is progress in human nature or only in institutions
Whether progress occurs in history at all
Whether progress occurs in the fine arts
questions.explain: Whether progress occurs belongs to the general controversy, and the fine arts belong to the subordinate issues.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Put the six areas of progress in the order the authors list them among the subordinate issues.
items: Knowledge
Technology
Economics
Politics
Morals
Fine arts
questions.explain: The authors list progress in knowledge, technological, economic, political, moral, and progress in the fine arts.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors report that many authors genuinely assert that progress occurs in the fine arts.
questions.explain: In their opinion no author genuinely asserts aesthetic progress, although a number of writers deny it; that is why this point raises special problems.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Sort these questions into the general controversy about progress and the special controversy about progress.

items.t: Is the general course of historical change toward improvement?
Can we know whether progress occurs?
Does progress occur in history?
Is progress necessary or contingent?
Will progress go on indefinitely?
Is there progress in human nature itself?

questions.explain: The general controversy concerns whether progress occurs; the special controversy concerns properties of progress among those who assert it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Which steps of syntopical reading do the authors say their analysis of the structure of the progress discussion exemplifies?
options: The first and second steps: finding passages and bringing authors to terms
Only the third step: getting the questions clear
The preparatory steps of building and inspecting a bibliography
The fourth and fifth steps: defining the issues and analyzing the discussion
questions.explain: The structure of general, special and subordinate issues shows defining the issues and analyzing the discussion.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Put in order the stages of the progress study as the authors recount them.
items: Amass a bibliography through inspectional readings
Develop a neutral terminology, e.g. non-meliorative advance
Ask the primary question whether progress occurs
Define the general, special and subordinate issues
questions.explain: The example follows the steps: bibliography, terms, questions, then issues and analysis.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren state the paradox of syntopical reading in the section on the Syntopicon?
options: Unless you know what books to read you cannot read syntopically, but unless you can read syntopically you do not know what to read
Unless you read syntopically you cannot read analytically, and the reverse
The more books you read on a subject, the less you understand it
A neutral terminology is needed, yet no terminology is neutral
questions.explain: They admit they had not really solved this paradox, and restate it before introducing the Syntopicon.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: What is the fundamental problem of syntopical reading, as the authors state it?
questions.a: If you do not know where to start, you cannot read syntopically. Even with a rough idea of where to begin, the time required to find the relevant books and passages may exceed the time needed for all the other steps combined.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: True or false: According to How to Read a Book, asking an expert who has done special research on your subject is a simple and reliable solution to the problem of where to start.
questions.explain: Such an expert's advice may be almost as much a hindrance as a help, since he would find it hard to point out passages without telling you how to read them.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: The Syntopicon is a topical ____ to the set of books titled Great Books of the Western World.
questions.explain: Under each of its topics it lists references to pages in the set where that subject is discussed.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: What do the authors say a reference book for syntopical reading must do that a knowledgeable advisor often cannot?
options: Tell you how each passage should be interpreted
Tell you where to find relevant passages without prejudging their meaning or significance
Summarise every relevant book in a few pages
Rank the authors by the truth of their views
questions.explain: What is needed is a guide to where passages are, without saying how they should be read; the Syntopicon is an example.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say the Syntopicon's major defect is that it indexes just one set of books.
questions.explain: It gives only a rough indication of passages in books outside the set, though it always gives a place to start.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Match each way the Syntopicon helps a beginner with what it does, according to Adler and Van Doren.
pairs: Lets one read in the great books before reading through them
Arouses interest in related subjects and the context of passages
Teaches interpretation through topics and contrasting passages
questions.explain: The authors say the Syntopicon helps the beginner in these three ways.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Put in order the three ways the Syntopicon helps the beginner, as the authors present them.
items: Initiatively
Suggestively
Instructively
questions.explain: The authors name and discuss the three ways in this order.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Why do the authors think reading programs that move from easier to harder great books seldom achieve their aim?
options: They choose the wrong books for beginners
They skip the easier works too quickly
They require the reading of whole books or large parts of them
They are designed only for mature scholars
questions.explain: The Syntopicon offers a radically different solution: reading relatively short passages from many authors on subjects of interest.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Put in order the three instructive effects of reading with the Syntopicon as the authors list them.
items: The topic gives direction in interpreting a passage
Passages from different authors on one topic sharpen each other
The same passage cited under several topics shows its amplitude of meaning
questions.explain: The authors give these three instructive ways in this order.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Explain the first instructive effect of reading a passage under a Syntopicon topic.
questions.a: The topic gives the reader direction in interpreting the passage, but it does not tell him what the passage means, since a passage may bear on a topic in several ways. The reader must discover precisely what relevance the passage has to the topic. Learning to do this is a major skill in the art of reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Which of these are ways the authors say collecting passages from different works on one topic sharpens interpretation?
options: Passages from the same book read in sequence each become clearer
Contrasting passages from different books are accentuated when read against one another
One author's passages amplify or comment on another's
The topic heading states what each passage means
Reading the passages replaces reading any whole book
questions.explain: The authors list these three effects; they explicitly say the topic does not tell the reader what the passage means.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A passage cited under two or more topics has an ____ of meaning that the reader perceives as he interprets it differently for each topic.
questions.explain: Such multiple interpretation is a basic exercise in reading and makes the mind alert to the many strains of meaning in a rich passage.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: What distinction do the authors draw between syntopical reading with a small s and Syntopical reading with a capital S?
options: Capital S is the wider term and small s is reading with the Syntopicon
Small s applies only to fiction and capital S to exposition
The two are simply different spellings of the same thing
Capital S means reading the great books with the Syntopicon; small s is the much wider term
questions.explain: Syntopical reading in the narrower sense can be part of any syntopical project, and it may always be wise to start there.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A reader curious about justice looks up the topic in a topical index of classic books and reads a dozen short passages by different authors. Which benefit of the Syntopicon do the authors call initiative?
options: It lets her start reading in the great books on a subject she cares about before reading through them
It tells her which author's view of justice is correct
It obliges her to read each great book whole first
It supplies a finished summary of the debate on justice
questions.explain: Working initiatively, the Syntopicon helps us read in the great books before we have read through them.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each objection to syntopical reading with the authors' reply.
pairs: Like denying translation; the difficult is not the impossible
Each author is a separate little universe
Aristotle could talk with us; books can talk through the reader
Style is the man; how matters more than what
Rational content exists beyond tone, as in the Corridor B example
questions.explain: The authors answer the three charges one at a time with these replies.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Against the objection about terminology, the authors repeat that the difficult is not the ____.
questions.explain: Translating between terminologies, like translating the Koran, may be difficult, but that does not make it impossible.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Why do the authors mention a new translation of the Koran?
options: It shows that holy books cannot be read syntopically
Its translator said translation was impossible and then explained how he had done it
It proves that no translation is ever faithful
It was one of the books in their study of progress
questions.explain: They took him to mean translation is particularly difficult for a holy book, which they accept, but difficult is not impossible.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren use an imagined visit from Aristotle to answer the objection that authors are separate universes?
questions.a: They imagine Aristotle in their office with an interpreter knowing both modern English and classical Greek, and are confident that within ten minutes they could be discussing shared philosophical problems. Recurring difficulties about conceptions could be recognised and resolved. If that is possible, one book can talk to another through an interpreter, namely the syntopical reader.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: In How to Read a Book, the authors say the syntopical reader acts as the interpreter through whom one book can talk to another.
questions.explain: They say books can talk through the medium of an interpreter, namely you, the syntopical reader, who should know both books as well as possible.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What point do the authors make with the example of following Corridor B to the exit?
options: Tone of voice always matters more than the words used
People usually lie when giving directions
Beyond tone of voice, communication has rational content that is right or wrong whatever the tone
Body language tells us more than words
questions.explain: Whatever tone the speaker uses, he is right or wrong, and you find out by following Corridor B; you understood what he said, not just how.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which of these are objections to syntopical reading that the authors set out and reject?
options: Imposing any terminology on an author is wrong
Authors widely separated in time cannot be read as talking to one another
The way authors discuss subjects matters more than the subjects
Syntopical reading takes too long to be practical
Syntopical reading is only for professional philosophers
questions.explain: These three are the charges the authors answer one at a time; the others are not among the objections they list.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put in order the three objections to syntopical reading as the authors answer them.
items: Terminology must be treated as sacrosanct
Authors are separate, unique universes
Manner or style matters more than subject
questions.explain: The authors take the charges one at a time: first terminology, second the separateness of authors, finally manner or style.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Summarise the three beliefs on which Adler and Van Doren rest their claim that syntopical reading is possible.
questions.a: They believe translation is possible because it is done all the time, and that books can talk to one another because human beings do. They also believe there is an objective, rational content of communication when people try to be rational, since we can and do learn from each other. Hence syntopical reading is possible.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The first of the two main stages of syntopical reading in the authors' summary is called ____ the Field.
questions.explain: Stage I, Surveying the Field, is preparatory; Stage II is syntopical reading proper.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: In the summary of syntopical reading, the authors note that the two preparatory steps are not strictly chronologically distinct, with the second modifying the first.
questions.explain: Inspecting the books changes the tentative bibliography, so the two steps affect each other.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: In the summary of syntopical reading, how should questions and issues be ordered in analyzing the discussion?
options: More general issues should precede less general ones, with relations among issues clearly shown
Issues should follow the chronological order of the authors
The most controversial issues should come first
Issues should be listed alphabetically to avoid bias
questions.explain: The aim is to throw maximum light on the subject, so general issues come before less general ones.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the summary in How to Read a Book, an issue always exists explicitly between authors and need only be reported.
questions.explain: The summary says an issue sometimes has to be constructed by interpreting authors' views on matters that may not have been their primary concern.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: In the summary of syntopical reading, what note is added about dialectical detachment, and what device is recommended to secure it?
questions.a: Dialectical detachment or objectivity should ideally be maintained throughout the whole process. One way to ensure it is always to accompany an interpretation of an author's views on an issue with an actual quotation from his text.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each step of syntopical reading proper, as summarised by the authors, with what it produces.
pairs: A neutral terminology the authors can be read as using
Neutral propositions via questions the authors answer
Major and minor issues from opposing answers
An ordered analysis that throws maximum light on the subject
questions.explain: The summary lists these products for steps 2 to 5; step 1 finds the most relevant passages.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the summary, how is a neutral terminology defined in step 2 of syntopical reading proper?
options: One that every author actually uses in his own text
One that all or most authors can be interpreted as employing, whether they use the words or not
One taken from the most widely read author
One that avoids every word any author has used
questions.explain: The terminology must fit all or the great majority of authors by interpretation, not by their actual vocabulary.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Why does the chapter on syntopical reading come after the chapters on analytical reading and on reading different kinds of books?
options: Syntopical reading is a minor technique added as an appendix
Syntopical reading replaces the earlier levels entirely
Syntopical reading is the fourth and highest level, and the levels are cumulative
Syntopical reading is easier than analytical reading
questions.explain: The chapter title calls it the fourth level, and the authors stress that a higher level includes all those below it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The title of Chapter 20 presents syntopical reading as the ____ level of reading.
questions.explain: The title, The Fourth Level of Reading, places it above elementary, inspectional and analytical reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put the four levels of reading in the order the book treats them, ending with the subject of Chapter 20.
items: Elementary reading
Inspectional reading
Analytical reading
Syntopical reading
questions.explain: Chapters 3 and 4 treat the first two levels, the analytical chapters follow, and Chapter 20 treats syntopical reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Why does the Chapter 20 section on inspection come before the section on the five steps?
options: Inspection is the last step of syntopical reading
Inspection is unrelated and discussed only for review
The five steps were invented after the inspection section was written
The first stage of syntopical reading, surveying the field, depends on inspecting all the books first
questions.explain: The section shows how inspection clarifies the subject and cuts the bibliography before syntopical reading proper begins.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 20, the example of the idea of progress is placed after the five steps and the need for objectivity so that it can illustrate them in practice.
questions.explain: The progress example walks through bibliography, neutral terms, questions and issues, showing the steps already explained.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: How does the Chapter 20 section on bringing authors to terms link back to earlier parts of How to Read a Book?
options: It adapts the first rule of interpretive reading, coming to terms with an author, from the analytical chapters
It repeats the rules for reading lyric poetry
It adapts the advice on using a dictionary to look up words
It reverses the advice on pigeonholing a book
questions.explain: The authors explicitly contrast the new step with the first rule of interpretive reading, coming to terms with the author.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put these chapters of How to Read a Book in order.
items: How to Read Social Science
The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.explain: Chapter 19 on social science precedes Chapter 20, and Chapter 21 closes the book.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Why is it fitting that the chapter on syntopical reading directly follows the chapter on reading social science, and comes before the closing chapter on the growth of the mind?
questions.a: The chapters on kinds of books, ending with social science, apply analytical reading to single books in different fields; syntopical reading then goes beyond any one book to many books on one problem. As the fourth and highest level it completes the account of the levels of reading. The final chapter can then reflect on what good books and reading do for the growth of the mind.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: How does the Chapter 20 example of the idea of progress connect the chapter's argument to the authors' own work?
questions.a: The authors chose progress because they had done extensive research on it, published as The Idea of Progress under the Institute for Philosophical Research. Their study shows each step in practice, from the 450-item bibliography to neutral terms like non-meliorative advance and the structure of issues. It shows that the method described is one they have actually carried out.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 20 with its role in the chapter.
pairs: Shows how earlier levels prepare for syntopical reading
Sets out the method of syntopical reading proper
The Syntopicon and How to Use It
Offers an aid to the paradox of where to start
Answers those who say the method is impossible
questions.explain: Each section has a distinct role in building and defending the account of syntopical reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Why do the authors say that limiting an inquiry to human love still leaves the problem of identifying the same subject unsolved?
questions.a: Even within human love, writers conceive it as acquisitive desire, as pure benevolence, or as an intellectual rather than emotional act. And even if a common meaning is found, love seems to differ between courting and married couples, parents and children, friends and lovers. Each such question adds to the difficulty of saying what one is reading about.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say the syntopical reader will undoubtedly fail in trying to look at all sides?
questions.a: Absolute objectivity is not humanly possible. The reader may manage to take no sides, presenting views impartially, but all possible sides of an issue cannot be exhaustively enumerated. Nevertheless he must try.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Why might the advice of a knowledgeable person be almost as much a hindrance as a help in starting a syntopical project?
questions.a: If the person has done special research on the subject, he will find it hard to tell you the relevant passages without telling you how to read them, which may get in your way. If he has not done such research, he may know little more than you, though it may seem otherwise to both of you. What is needed is a reference that locates passages without prejudging their meaning.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put in order the sequence of reading the authors recommend once a bibliography on a subject is assembled.
items: Inspect all the books on the list
Cut the list to the relevant books
Read the relevant books syntopically, using analytical skills
questions.explain: You should not read any book analytically before inspecting all of them; then you proceed to read the relevant ones syntopically.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put in order the ways the authors narrow the love example as they show the difficulty of finding the same subject.
items: Love attributed to almost everything in the universe
Love limited to human beings
A common meaning sought among conceptions of human love
Questions about how love differs across relationships
questions.explain: Each narrowing still leaves a great range of reference, leading to the paradox that the subject must in a sense follow the reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put in order the reasoning the authors give for why a syntopical report must not assert the truth of any view.
items: Disagreement suggests no conflicting opinion may be wholly true
So the aim is not final answers to the questions
Asserting a view would make the report dogmatic
It would become one more voice and lose its objectivity
questions.explain: The authors move from the counter-presumption raised by disagreement to the conclusion that the report must stay dialectical.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Put the three basic answers to whether progress occurs in history in the order the authors list them.
items: Yes
No
We cannot know
questions.explain: The authors list the answers as (1) Yes, (2) No, and (3) We cannot know, each with several variants.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which of these sources does the authors' summary name for creating a tentative bibliography?
options: Library catalogues
Advisors
Bibliographies in books
The table of contents of a single book
Book reviews in newspapers
questions.explain: Step 1 of Stage I names library catalogues, advisors and bibliographies in books.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each author or novel with the role it plays in the opening of the chapter on syntopical reading.
pairs: Shares only a great war as background with War and Peace
Wrote the Waterloo account Tolstoy learned from
Author of a novel set in the Napoleonic Wars
questions.explain: The authors use these novels to show that books about a war are not necessarily about war as a subject.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each attitude toward a discussion with how the authors describe it.
pairs: Establishes a counter-presumption that none may be wholly true
Asserting one view in the report
questions.explain: The authors contrast the presumption from agreement with the counter-presumption from disagreement, and call a report that takes sides dogmatic.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Match each term with its meaning in the chapter on syntopical reading.
pairs: Topical index to Great Books of the Western World
Reading the great books with the Syntopicon
The wider term for reading many books on one subject
questions.explain: The authors adopted the Syntopicon's name for this level of reading, and distinguish the narrower capital S sense from the wider one.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Sort these into what the authors say inspection does and does not do in preparing for syntopical reading.

items.t: Shows whether a book says something important about the subject
Cuts the bibliography to a manageable size
Acquaints the reader with all the intricacies of the subject
Reveals precisely what a book says about the subject

questions.explain: Inspection tells you whether a book matters and trims the list; what the book says precisely usually waits for another reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Sort these into the three special-controversy issues about progress and the six areas of the subordinate issues.

items.t: Necessary or contingent
Indefinite or plateauing
In human nature or only institutions
Moral progress
Economic progress
Progress in the fine arts

questions.explain: The special controversy concerns the nature of progress; the subordinate issues concern the areas in which it occurs.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Sort these into the suggestive and the instructive ways the Syntopicon helps a beginner.

items.t: Arouses interest in related subjects
Leads the reader to explore the context of a passage
The topic gives direction in interpreting a passage
Passages on one topic sharpen each other
One passage under several topics reveals its range of meaning

questions.explain: Suggestively it spreads interest; instructively it trains interpretation in three distinct ways.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Sort these into objections to syntopical reading and the authors' grounds for believing it possible.

items.t: Books should never be read out of context
Words are not controllable like mathematical symbols
The style is the man
Translation is done all the time
Human beings talk to one another
We can and do learn from each other

questions.explain: The objectors call imposed terms and cross-author reading distortions; the authors reply that translation, conversation and learning show the method is possible.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Sort these steps into Stage I, Surveying the Field, and Stage II, syntopical reading proper.

items.t: Create a tentative bibliography
Inspect all books to see which are germane
Find the most relevant passages
Bring the authors to terms
Define the issues
Analyze the discussion

questions.explain: The summary divides the work into a preparatory survey and five steps of syntopical reading proper.

questions.q: True or false: In the final chapter, the authors say that because How to Read a Book is a practical book, a reader who accepts its aim and its means is obliged to act on them.
questions.explain: They recall that the reader of a practical book who accepts its ends and agrees its means are effective must act as proposed, so the reader must now make the effort to read as never before.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say that the reader's task is not finished when their own task of writing the book is complete?
questions.a: Their book is a practical book, and the reader of a practical book has a special obligation. If you accept its aim, reading as well as possible, and agree that its means, the rules of inspectional, analytical and syntopical reading, are appropriate, then you must act on them. The work, and the benefits, now fall mainly on you.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: In the final chapter of How to Read a Book, the authors say 'means' can refer to the rules of reading or to the ____ you read.
questions.explain: Besides the method, the means of improvement are the materials it is applied to, namely the books you read. A method with no materials is as useless as materials with no method.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, why will you not improve as a reader by reading only books that are well within your capacity?
options: Such books usually contain too many factual errors
Only books that seem beyond you make your mind stretch
Easy books cannot be read with the analytical rules
Easy books are always works of fiction and amusement
questions.explain: You must tackle books that are over your head, because only they make you stretch: “And unless you stretch, you will not learn.” The problem with easy books is lack of demand, not errors.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that reading a book purely for information improves your reading skill, because your mind ends up holding more facts.
questions.explain: They say reading for information stretches the mind no more than reading for amusement. The change is merely quantitative; the mind is essentially in the same condition as before.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: In 'Reading and the Growth of the Mind', why do the authors say Homer is in many ways harder to read than Newton?
options: Homer wrote in an older language that is hard to translate
Homer's poems are much longer than Newton's treatises
Homer deals with subjects that are harder to write well about
Homer's arguments are deliberately concealed from the reader
questions.explain: Great scientific authors help the reader come to terms and find propositions and arguments, aids absent from poetry; and Homer treats subjects harder to write well about. Length and language are not the reasons given.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren say about the books that keep challenging a reader in the final chapter?
options: They are not only scientific or philosophical books
Great scientific books are in many ways easier to read than non-scientific ones
Poetical works may be the most demanding books you can read
They are mostly found in unfamiliar technical fields
A bad book is hard in the same rewarding way
questions.explain: The authors reject the mistake of thinking only science and philosophy qualify, noting science gives the reader helps that poetry lacks. A bad book is hard too, but it gives no reward for the struggle.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether Adler and Van Doren apply it to a good book or a bad book, in the final chapter.

items.t: Rewards you for trying to read it
Can make you wiser about the world and yourself
Slips through your fingers whenever you think you have it pinned down
There is really nothing in it to pin down
Improves your reading skill when you tackle it successfully
Gives no reward for the struggle

questions.explain: Both are hard to read, but a good book repays the effort with skill and wisdom, while a bad book defies analysis and is not worth the effort.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: What two rewards do Adler and Van Doren say a good book gives, and which do they call more important?
questions.a: First, successfully tackling a good, difficult book improves your reading skill. Second, and in the long run much more important, it teaches you about the world and yourself, so you become wiser and not just more knowledgeable. Wiser means more deeply aware of the great and enduring truths of human life.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say a great book makes you not just more knowledgeable but ____, more deeply aware of the enduring truths of human life.
questions.explain: Books that only inform can make you more knowledgeable; the best books make you wiser, which the authors treat as the more important reward.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren say the greatest books can help with problems such as the relation between parents and children, even though such problems have no final solution?
questions.a: Some human problems have no solution and no one can have the last word on them, in everyday matters as well as in science and philosophy. These are matters you cannot think about too much or too well. The greatest books help you think better about them because their authors thought better than other people about them.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.q: In 'The Pyramid of Books', how do Adler and Van Doren say the vast majority of books, more than 99 per cent, should be read?
options: Analytically once, then shelved
Syntopically, alongside related books
Analytically and then reread often
Only for amusement or information, and skimming will do
questions.explain: These books do not make enough demands to improve your reading, so you need not read them analytically: “Skimming will do.” Reading analytically once fits the second class, not this one.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.q: Match each class in Adler and Van Doren's pyramid of books to the way it should be read.
pairs: Read analytically once, then consulted to check points
Fewer than a hundred great books
Returned to over and over throughout life
questions.explain: Each level of the pyramid makes greater demands and deserves a different kind of reading, from skimming up to lifelong rereading.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.q: True or false: Adler and Van Doren say that when you return to a good book of the second class, you find more in it than you remembered.
questions.explain: Returning to a second-class book is disappointing because there seems to be less there; you have grown. It is the highest class of books that seems to grow with you.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.q: Adler and Van Doren say that when you return to a good but exhaustible book you find less than you remembered, because the book has not changed but ____ have.
questions.explain: Your mind is fuller and your understanding greater in the meantime: “The book has not changed, but you have.”
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.q: How do Adler and Van Doren explain the impression that a great book seems to grow as the reader grows?
questions.a: A book cannot actually change once published. The great book was so far above you to begin with that it has remained above you, because it is accessible at different levels. Your earlier understanding remains true, but on return you see whole sets of new things, and it can keep lifting you until you die.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.q: Which of these signs do Adler and Van Doren give that a book may belong to the small class of inexhaustible books?
options: After a careful analytical reading you suspect there is more there than you got
You find you cannot forget the book and keep thinking about it
On returning, you see new things you did not see before
You can say exactly what you missed the first time
On returning, it seems to contain less than you remembered
questions.explain: The reader has a sneaking suspicion of more, keeps thinking about the book, and on return sees new things. If you knew exactly what you missed you would go back at once, and finding less is the mark of the second class.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.q: Why do Adler and Van Doren refuse to say that any particular book must be great for every reader, using Newton and Shakespeare as an example?
options: Readers differ in tastes, so different books can be great for each
Great books lose their value once lists of them are published
Newton and Shakespeare are equally hard for every reader
Only experts can judge which books are truly great
questions.explain: People differ in tastes as well as mental power; someone like Darwin might find Newton great and not Shakespeare. So each reader should seek the few books that can have that value for them.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, why should a reader seek out the handful of books that remain above them?
questions.a: These are the books that will teach the most, both about reading and about life. They are the ones you will want to return to over and over, and they keep challenging you however skilled you become. They are the books that will help you to grow.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: According to Adler and Van Doren, what is the main lesson of the desert island test of choosing ten books?
options: It reveals which books are most popular with readers
It shows which practical articles matter most in isolation
It shows what you learn about yourself when cut off from outside sources
It proves that ten books are enough for any person's lifetime
questions.explain: Identifying books to reread is of minor importance compared with what you learn about yourself imagining life without the usual sources of amusement, information and understanding.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Adler and Van Doren warn that the mind, like a muscle, can ____ if it is not used.
questions.explain: The mind can keep growing, unlike the body, but it carries a peril: atrophy is the penalty for not taking mental exercise.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether Adler and Van Doren apply it to the body or to the mind, in the final chapter.

items.t: Is usually as good as it will ever be by about age thirty
Does not keep growing in strength and skill indefinitely
Can keep growing until the brain loses vigor in senescence
Its unlimited growth may set humans apart from other animals
Is kept alive in busy people by the demands of their work

questions.explain: The authors contrast the body's limited development with the mind's capacity for growth, which needs exercise from within rather than external props.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Order the stages in Adler and Van Doren's account of how outside stimuli such as television fail the mind.
items: They give an impression that the mind is active
We grow used to them and need more of them
Eventually they have little or no effect
Lacking inner resources, we cease to grow and begin to die
questions.explain: Like drugs, external props lose their power over time; without resources within ourselves we stop growing intellectually, morally and spiritually.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Which of these do Adler and Van Doren call artificial props for the mind in the final chapter?
options: Television and radio
The demands of a busy job
Sources of amusement and information around us
Reading actively
Rereading a great book
questions.explain: Work demands keep busy people going artificially, and television, radio and similar sources act like drugs. Active reading builds the inner resources the props lack.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: A manager who rarely reads retires, finds daytime television fills the hours, and soon feels mentally dull. Which idea from Adler and Van Doren's final chapter best explains this?
options: Reading for information stretches the mind as much as reading
Bad books slip through the fingers of an analytical reader
Every reader needs a list of ten desert island books
External props fade, and without inner resources the mind atrophies
questions.explain: Work demands propped the manager up from outside; when they stopped, television could not substitute, since such stimuli lose effect and only inner mental activity keeps the mind growing.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.q: Why does 'Reading and the Growth of the Mind' come after the chapter on syntopical reading in How to Read a Book?
options: It introduces a fifth, higher level of reading
It closes the book by turning from the rules to the books and the purpose of reading
It applies syntopical reading to a list of history books
It returns to elementary reading for younger readers
questions.explain: With all four levels covered, the authors say their task is complete and turn to the remaining means, the books themselves, and the end, keeping the mind alive and growing.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind

questions.q: Order the sections of the final chapter of How to Read a Book as they appear.
items: A summary of the four levels and of active reading
What Good Books Can Do for Us
The Pyramid of Books
The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.explain: The chapter moves from summing up the method, to the books it should be used on, to the few great books, and finally to why reading matters for the mind's growth.
questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
